item.title: Thousands of African birds are missing from sound libraries. A massive grassroots effort hopes to change that
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 4.63
Thousands of African bird species remain missing from the sound libraries that train AI-powered research and conservation tools. Now, the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and BirdLife South Africa are leading an ambitious continent-wide grassroots effort to fill in the gaps. Alexandra Owens reports.

item.title: Are hikes, homestays and conservation-first tourism an alternative to Cancún’s heady nightlife and sprawling hotels?
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 4.62
In the 1960s, the Mexican government backed mass-market tourism with its development of Cancún, but a 2026 directive by President Scheinbaum now puts the focus on regenerative tourism. What does that mean for the region? The Yucatán Peninsula is a dichotomy. You only need to look out of the airplane window as you start your descent into Cancún to see the contrasts. One moment, you’re looking at a 12-mile-long (20-kilometer) spit of sand lined with huge hotel resorts. The next, as the plane drops further, an impenetrable carpet of dark-green jungle rolls out as far as the eye can see. Cancún’s Hotel Zone sprung up in the 1970s and since then, has cultivated its reputation for all-inclusive resorts, high-energy nightlife and out-of-the-box holiday experiences. Overdevelopment has placed a strain on natural resources; the demand for fresh water is draining the region’s ancient cenote (sinkhole) network, while sudden demand for workers is creating overcrowded, unplanned inland neighborhoods. But you don’t have to go far to find pockets of low-impact, community tourism. And this year, for the first time ever, the Mexican government has recognized the importance of the latter. In March 2026, Mexico’s National Fund for Tourism Promotion (Fonatur) and the government signed an agreement to encourage its tourism industry—which represents nearly 10 percent of the country’s GDP—to serve as a tool for social justice, allowing local communities to become active participants in a region’s economic growth. While the Mexican government’s focus was on resorts like Cancún several decades ago, President Claudia Sheinbaum’s current vision is different. They want to support destinations where local communities are the protagonists, ensuring the conservation of natural resources under the stewardship of people who have lived there for generations. The government has named three community tourism projects—Pueblos Mancomunados in Oaxaca, and Maya Ka’an and Camino del Mayab in the Yucatán Peninsula—to receive support during 2026. For the latter, the investment will fund better water and wastewater management, trail maintenance, project equipment, public space maintenance and signage. With the Maya Ka’an and Camino del Mayab within 180 miles of Cancún, it appears to show a change of focus. “Maya communities are not treated as attractions or objects of observation. Instead, they’re recognized as active participants, storytellers and custodians of their own culture and territory.” - Fernando Sarvide, local guide This summer, I hiked the Camino del Mayab in Yucatán with local guides José Luis Bé and Fernando Sarvide. The Camino is a 68-mile (110-kilometer) trail through the jungle just south of Mérida, in the northwest of the Yucatán Peninsula, which connects 14 Mayan communities. The terrain on this route, which opened in 2020, is flat and undemanding, but the high temperatures add challenge to the distances, which average around 14 miles (23 kilometers) per day. My hike began with a short opening ceremony in which our guide Fernando reminded the group that we were guests in the jungle, walking through a place that had existed long before us. The three-mile (five-kilometer) walk from X‘Matkuil to Molas, two of the communities on the Camino, runs along the disused railway that once transported henequen (sisal) from haciendas to the coast for export. In Molas, we learnt more about the Mayan way of life, the history of the haciendas, and the surrounding jungle from community members, before finding refuge in the home of Doña Norma for lunch; we enjoyed traditional pibil chicken and refried beans alongside jugfuls of ice-cold horchata (white rice with milk or water, sweetened with cinnamon and sugar). I soon learnt that mornings start early in these communities, with most activity is done and dusted by lunch. Afternoons are set aside for cooling off with a dip in a cenote or taking a siesta in a hammock in the shade. Camino del Mayab was founded by EcoGuerreros, an initiative that promotes community development, environmental conservation and sustainable tourism. One of the project’s greatest achievements is creating opportunities for local people to earn a living within their communities, instead of having to relocate to Yucatán cities such as Mérida or Cancún for work. Doña Norma is a case in point. She had no way of earning money in her community before but now, she loves cooking lunch for trekkers, welcoming them in her home as part of the Camino del Mayab ‘package’. “It opens the door to new experiences for everyone,” she told me. “Visitors learn about our culture, and we learn from them as we share stories, traditions and perspectives. These meaningful connections go far beyond a shared meal.” Chatting to José Luis, who grew up in the Tzacalá community, he said he believed the Camino has had a positive impact. “It’s helped diversify the local economy while strengthening our cultural identity. It’s encouraged us to value and preserve the traditions, knowledge and heritage that make our community unique.” Thanks to the Camino del Mayab and EcoGuerreros, the community now has a library in a previously disused building. As well as distributing books and keeping local stories alive, it’s also a place where young people can get help applying for university, and other life and work opportunities. For Fernando, a guide from Mérida and former teacher of Mexican history, the hike has changed the relationship between visitors and local people. “Maya communities are not treated as attractions or objects of observation,” he told me. “Instead, they’re recognized as active participants, storytellers and custodians of their own culture and territory.” During the afternoons, we bathed in cenotes, the sinkholes scattered about the Yucatán Peninsula. Now a welcome respite from the merciless heat for hikers and locals, they were once believed to be doorways to the Mayan underworld and are still seen as sacred spaces by many. The hike had been an enriching experience. I had gone hoping to learn more about Mayan culture and met many passionate locals keen to share their way of life with me; particularly memorable was learning to play pok da pok, an ancient Mayan ball sport still played in seven Latin American countries, and sees players hitting the ball with only hips, knees and elbows with the aim of getting it through a hoop suspended from the ceiling. “Those of us who live here have fallen back in love with it, thanks to our visitors. Seeing someone’s eyes light up in wonder… that’s the most powerful thing I’ve experienced.” - Manuel Enrique Galindo Triay, guide and biologist It was the more recent history of the haciendas and henequen dictatorships that struck home the most. Haciendas in Yucatán operated as dictatorships until the 1980s, taking land from Indigenous communities and small farmers. José Luis told me part of the Camino’s mission is to change the mindset in the communities: “You work hard, you accept your lot and you have no power.” I’d met old men who’d worked in the hacienda regime as young boys, while the grand buildings, many of which now lie in ruins, are an ever-present reminder of the injustices of the past and of how life once was in those communities. I was heartened to know that 80 percent of what I’d paid to hike the Camino del Mayab would go directly to local people. Mariana Ramos, commercial coordinator for Camino del Mayab, was optimistic about the impact of government support: “It will help improve infrastructure and signage,” she told me, “and fund safe places where visitors can obtain information, eat, shower and stay overnight, supporting the expansion of our self-guided hiking experiences.” The other initiative in the Yucatán Peninsula to receive support from the government is Maya Ka’an, a large sustainable tourism project that encompasses the Sian Ka’an Biosphere Reserve 16 miles (25 kilometers) south of Tulum, created in 2012 to protect the area’s tropical jungle, wetlands, mangroves, freshwater canals and coastal marine environments while prioritizing community leadership in tourism. Like Camino del Mayab, Maya Ka’an focuses on nature-based and cultural experiences and it’s hoped that government support will help improve infrastructure as well as visibility. Román Caamal Coh, general manager of Community Tours Sian Ka’an (CTSK), led by a 100 percent Maya cooperative and one of the projects within Maya Ka’an, explained why he thinks it was chosen by the government. “It’s a low-impact model, managed by communities and community-based enterprises, and it’s one of the most mature and representative examples in Mexico of conservation led by the communities that live there.” Maya Ka’an’s jungle walks, kayaking, birdwatching, cooking and handicraft workshops are a far cry from the pools, beach bars and snorkeling boats that line the Mexican Caribbean coast. And its accommodation offering—intentionally limited to eco-lodges, rustic cabins or guesthouses—contrasts with the large chain hotels that lie behind gated perimeters along Highway 307 from Cancún to Tulum. I met the team behind Community Tours Sian Ka’an to see how the initiative has been transforming the lives of locals. For its treasurer Lucía Pacheco May, her work has enabled her to pay for her children’s education. “I’m happy, because I never had the chance to study,” she told me. “Where I’m from, there’s only a primary school.” Boat captain Ricardo Caamal Aban, who takes visitors on the project’s Ancient Canal tour through Mayan lagoons and mangrove channels, told me: “I’m proudly Maya… I’m passionate about being in contact with nature and sharing what I know with the people who visit us.” It’s a similar story for guide and biologist Manuel Enrique Galindo Triay: “Those of us who live here have fallen back in love with it, thanks to our visitors,” he said. “Seeing someone’s eyes light up in wonder… that’s the most powerful thing I’ve experienced.” For the Camino del Mayab and Maya Ka’an, recognition by the national government as a worthy alternative to the mass tourism and private investment of Tulum and Cancún has been a significant gamechanger. As CTSK’s Román told me, “”The Maya Ka’an tourism model translates into dignified employment, less migration to the cities, and a community that values its own culture and natural resources.” ** The writer traveled with her family and self-funded this trip including their time with Community Tours Sian Ka’an. Her own spot on the Camino del Mayab was hosted by environmental conservation organization, EcoGuerreros. **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. item.title: How did an ancient Māori stargazing tradition become Aotearoa/New Zealand’s mid-winter public holiday?
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 4.56
Matariki in Aotearoa/New Zealand is believed to be one of the first Indigenous celebrations in the world to be recognized as a national public holiday. Lee Mylne travels to Ōtepoti/Dunedin to attend Matariki Day celebrations, marking the traditional Māori New Year.

item.title: Scotland’s ‘Instagram Highway’ is a lesson in road trip overtourism. But this new route in northwest England is doing things differently
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 2.91
While Scotland’s NC500 road trip has become a victim of its own success, an English version now aims to learn from its mistakes. But, asks Sarah Baxter, can you build a successful route that locals don’t come to resent? And if so, could the Cumbrian coast become a blueprint for regenerative route-making elsewhere?

item.title: On a yoga mat, this Irish writer rediscovers the language of her motherland
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 2.84
The Irish language—Gaeilge—is experiencing a cultural revival in Ireland. Éalú Aran is one of a wave of retreats and courses that teach the language in an informal setting outside the classroom, keeping it alive for generations to come. “Up onto the toes. Na méara coise, as they’re called. The ‘fingers of your feet’.” Weaving between Irish and English phrasing, Áine Seoighe is directing a yoga and breathwork session. We’re on Inis Oírr, the smallest of the Aran Islands off Ireland’s western coast. This is a Gaeltacht region, where Irish, or Gaeilge, is the dominant language. We’re a few hours into an Éalú Aran day retreat, a bilingual wellness program run by native islander Seoighe since 2023. Through activities such as meditation, nature walks, basket-making and sea swimming, participants are gently immersed in the language. It’s one of many Irish-language-focused events cropping up all over the country, propelled by a resurgence of interest in the vernacular. Now a mandatory subject in the Irish education system, Gaeilge is Ireland’s first official language, followed by English. It seems more people are embracing this aspect of Irish identity that was historically marginalized under British colonial rule. However, despite enjoying it in school, I rarely had cause to use it in my hometown, Dublin, afterwards. But when I recently returned to Ireland after living overseas, I realized attitudes to the language had shifted. Peers are doing re-immersion courses, Irish-speaking cafés have opened, and I’ve started to hear more families speaking ‘as Gaeilge’, a colloquial turn of phrase that means ‘in Irish’. A short ferry ride from Doolin village brings us to the island, with the Cliffs of Moher looming in our rearview as we sail west. On the approach, Inis Oírr’s waymarks emerge: The rusting MV Plassy shipwreck, striped Fardurris Point Lighthouse, O’Brien’s Castle. By the pier, horse-drawn carriages and bicycle rental shops await visitors—the few cars on the island belong to its population of roughly 340 residents. Meeting us by the harbor, Seoighe launches into a welcome ‘as Gaeilge’ before guiding us on a walk around the island’s wind-whipped perimeter. Limestone forms Inis Oírr’s foundations, ground down into white-sand beaches along the shore. Generations of islanders spread seaweed across the land to render it tillable. Miles of dry stone walls crisscross the island’s 2.3-square-mile (5.9 square kilometer) expanse. “The language is such an important part of the island, of the community, of our past and present. Doing anything here on the island has to incorporate the language.” - Áine Seoighe, Éalú Aran retreats An ancient Celtic language, Irish was gradually excluded from legal proceedings, classrooms and state affairs when Ireland was under British rule. Clandestine educators (known as ‘hedge schools’) and rural communities quietly kept the language alive, but it was threatened with extinction by the Great Famine of the 1840s, when Irish-speaking rural areas were plagued by high death rates and mass emigration. When the Irish Free State was founded in the 1920s—giving independence to 26 of Ireland’s 32 counties—its status was restored. English nevertheless remains more widely spoken, but 40 percent of the Republic of Ireland’s population reported that they could speak Irish in the latest census, recorded in 2022. Gaeltacht regions are pivotal to the language’s survival. Seoighe, now 36, was raised speaking Irish at home on Inis Oírr. “When I was growing up, island life was still quite slow,” she tells me. “Irish was very much the only language really spoken in the community.” Though still fluently spoken on Inis Oírr, its use on the island has waned somewhat in recent decades for a number of reasons, including societal changes, social media and TV, Seoighe admits. Bringing Gaeilge into Éalú Aran retreats, which vary in length from a day to a week, was instinctual. “The language is such an important part of the island, of the community, of our past and present,” she says. “Doing anything here on the island has to incorporate the language.” Fionnuala Ní Uallacháin, multimedia officer for Scéal.ie, which catalogues Irish-language events around the country, confirms there has been a surge in their number and variety, from “ciorcal comhrá” (conversation circles) and park runs to stained glass workshops and hillwalking meet-ups. Language courses are “increasing in popularity exponentially,” she says. High-profile Irish artists such as Kneecap, the Belfast group that lyricize in Irish, are partially to credit for the resurgence, and widely seen as a “cool band doing new things with Irish,” Ní Uallacháin tells me. A fresh wave of Irish-language podcasts, such as How to Gael and Beo Ar Éigean, and content creators (among them, Cúán de Búrca and Mollie Guidera) is also driving renewed interest. This grassroots revival is something Declan O’Connor, who teaches surfing through Irish and English at Tonn Nua Surf School in County Mayo on Ireland’s west coast, has observed. “There’s definitely been a resurgence. I’ve noticed it with the surf school, but also I’ve noticed it outside at festivals and in random meetings with people.” This year, he started hosting bilingual surf and yoga retreats on the Mullet Peninsula in the northwest of the county, in collaboration with Irish-language surf group Surfála. “The informal setting, it just loosens [people] up and gives them the opportunity to give it a try,” he says. On the yoga mat, the vocabulary I studied in classrooms of my childhood resurfaces. I’m surprised by how much I remember. A recent study by Irish language course provider Gaelchultúr found nearly 70 per cent of adults want to improve their grasp of the language while almost half of those aged under 25 reported using Irish when socializing. Its research also showed that close to half of people under 44 would send their child to a Gaelscoil, where subjects are taught through Irish—a 20 percent increase on a similar 2015 study. Older generations feel a “wistfulness” for the language, Fionnuala observes. “You see a lot of people going back to [learn] Irish when they retire,” she says. Éalú Aran retreats are open to Irish-language novices, as well as experienced speakers. Attendees have visited from wider Europe, North America and Australia. My British partner finds he can follow along without any basis in the language. Participants are “surprised at how much communication isn’t vocal,” says Seoighe. During one of our hikes, Seoighe forages sea beet, an ancient plant often called ‘wild spinach’, for us to taste and points out currachs stacked on the sand, the traditional Irish boats that once were the only way to access the island. Alternating between Irish and English as we go, she translates Gaelic turns of phrase without interrupting the conversation’s flow. Eventually, we reach a ‘garraí’, a walled plot overlooking a freshwater lake, Loch Mór. Inside is a yurt, the setting for our yoga class. “I’ll go in and out of Gaeilge, but you’ll follow that, I’m sure,” Seoighe tells us, as we begin. The tent is open to the elements. Currachs move across the lake, while a sleepy calf is feeding in the adjoining garraí. “Learning a language keeps the mind active, curious and engaged,” she says. “So for me, wellness and language-learning are a very natural combination: We are looking after the body, the mind and our connection to our culture and the world around us.” For Seoighe, movement facilitates learning. “When we move, we are focused mainly on the movement, not the words. We hear the language repeatedly and naturally, and over time the sounds and words begin to become familiar.” This is certainly my experience. On the yoga mat, the vocabulary I studied in classrooms of my childhood resurfaces. I’m surprised by how much I remember. “Dún na súile … weʻll close the eyes here,” Seoighe says, encouraging us to think of the “gaineamh agus an fheamainn, the sand and seaweed that made the land” as we stretch out on the “talamh” (ground). Lunchtime arrives. A picnic of cheddar cheese, homemade bread and potato salad has been prepared by the island’s Teach an Tae café. It’s been spitting rain all morning, but suddenly the sky brightens and the water glitters; we enjoy lunch on the rocks overlooking the lake. Later, on the island’s main beach, Seoighe fires up the sauna, and we join locals and holidaymakers in the icy water. By the shore, the words snámh (swim) and fuar (cold) come back to me. My time on Inis Oírr has proven I haven’t fully lost my Irish, but I’ll have to put in some work to find it again. It’s a beautiful language to rediscover and we owe so much to its custodians, like Seoighe, who are safeguarding it for future generations. “Keeping the language living is about much more than preserving words,” she says. “It is about preserving a different way of seeing and understanding the world.” ** The writer was a guest of Éalú Aran. Retreats are priced from EUR€95 ($110/AUD$155) per person. Transport and accommodation were arranged by the writer. **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. item.title: Traditional gumbo, kettle-boiled bagels, Chelsea buns: What do ‘endangered dishes’ tell us about the world today?
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 2.06
Globalization, overtourism, climate crisis, and social change can all contribute to the loss of beloved cultural practices—including what we eat. But what does this mean for cultural and food heritage? And how can travelers help preserve the flavors that make our experiences so much richer?

item.title: You Hit the SOS Button. What Happens Next?
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 5.95
Spot Device SOS button (Photo: Adam Roy) Pushing the SOS button feels like a big responsibility. We shoot a signal through the atmosphere, from wherever we’re sprawled out on the ground in the middle of nowhere. That signal triggers a technological and human machine that will cause dispatchers, emergency departments, and rescue operators to assume their own risks as they work to spring us from the consequences of ours. Ultimately, pressing it means handing over over one of the core responsibilities we sign up for in the backcountry: The responsibility for our own safety. There’s a weight that comes with the decision to summon boots on the ground to save us. So, what actually happens when we do? In short: details vary by provider. Texas-based Garmin takes a communication-forward approach that leverages the strong messaging capabilities of its devices. British PLB maker Ocean Signal, occupying a tighter niche, links directly to a SAR-specific satellite network. Regardless of the process, one thing’s for sure: it gets set in motion a lot. Garmin estimates it has received over 250,000 SOS alerts since 2007, from virtually every country on earth. More than 20,000 of them have required responses from Garmin, for an average of more than 1,000 per year. Calls continue to increase. In 2025, the company reported 3,000-plus yearly incidents. Trail and mountain calls, it said, had “notably” increased. Unsurprisingly, Garmin keeps its emergency response center staffed 24/7. The bigger picture follows a similar trend. Cospas-Sarsat, the SAR-dedicated satellite system used by Ocean Signal, services a network of 45 of the planet’s largest economies. In the 1990s, it was recording a few hundred “SAR events” per year. By 2024, that number climbed to well over 1,000. Beacons themselves have become standard field gear. Cospas-Sarsat estimated over 3,354,000 devices capable of communicating with its 406 MHz network were deployed in the field in 2024. In 2017, that number was well under 2 million. In 2024 alone, the parent company of Garmin competitor SPOT reported a gigantic 35% year-over-year increase in device sales. In one sense, activating the SOS beacon on a backcountry satcom device is straightforward. The signal hits a satellite, a dispatcher or dispatch team receives it, and a rescue crew moves out. But in any rescue, details matter. Depending on who you choose, variables throughout the industry hinge on communication style, intermediaries, and networks used. Network: Iridium Signal Path: User > Iridium > Garmin Response Center > Local Rescue Network Messaging: High – two-way text; automatic location updates; emergency contact communication; voice on compatible inReach Plus devices Photo Messaging: Yes (depending on device) The de facto standard of backcountry satcom services, Garmin’s SOS process stands out for its range of user options and continuity of communication during a rescue event. When an SOS is triggered, the device sends the user’s GPS coordinates via the expansive Iridium satellite network to Garmin Response, its 24/7 emergency coordination center. Garmin acknowledges the alert and opens two-way communication to assess the emergency. Simultaneously, Garmin coordinators work to find and contact a local rescue agency. The user’s location automatically updates every minute for the first 10 minutes of an SOS event, then once every ten minutes after that. Coordinators reach out to the user’s emergency contacts if available, and relay information between rescuers and the user. If possible, Garmin will connect rescuers directly with the user through the device. Garmin Response continues monitoring the user’s location and providing updates until the incident is resolved. Network: Globalstar Communication Path: User > Globalstar > FocusPoint International > Local Rescue Network Messaging: High on SPOT X – two-way text with rescue coordinators and personal contacts. Older/basic SPOT devices are one-way Photo Messaging: No Aside from a smaller satellite network and a third-party response center (still 24/7), SPOT’s SOS response system mirrors Garmin’s on its newer devices. When an SOS is triggered, SPOT sends the user’s GPS coordinates to FocusPoint International’s 24/7 rescue monitoring center. FocusPoint confirms the location and contacts a local SAR agency. Coordinators may also contact the user and their designated emergency contacts to gather additional information and monitor the incident through completion. These steps take place according to the user’s pre-set instructions. The Gen4 and the company’s earlier devices are limited to one-way communication, while SPOT X provides two-way messaging with rescue coordinators. SPOT X also sends locations every 2.5 minutes until the alert is acknowledged, then every 5 minutes. Documentation for Gen4 shows it updates at least every five minutes. Network: Cospas-Sarsat (406MHz), plus 121.5MHz homing Communication Path: User > Cospas-Sarsat > Mission Control/Coordination Center > Local Rescue Network Messaging: Very low – distress/location transmission only. RLS acknowledges that the distress alert was received, but messaging is not available Photo Messaging: No Like other PLBs, Ocean Signal’s rescueME beacons bypass a commercial response center entirely. Instead, SOS signals travel directly through the Cospas-Sarsat international search-and-rescue system, no subscription required. (Cospas-Sarsat was founded in 1979 by France, Canada, the United States and, believe it or not, the Soviet Union. It has since grown to include over 30 member nations). When a PLB3 is activated, it transmits its unique device identity and GNSS location at 406 MHz to Cospas-Sarsat satellites. The alert travels through a ground station to one of the network’s Mission Control Centers, which routes it to a Rescue Coordination Center. The RCC uses the beacon’s registration information to verify the emergency – user-provided facts like how they typically use the beacon, an emergency contact that knows about this specific trip, and so on. After verifying, the RCC dispatches local SAR resources. Communication is extremely limited: there’s no text or voice messaging. Return Link Service (RLS) can acknowledge the distress alert was received and routed, but does not confirm that rescuers have been dispatched. Where Ocean Signal stands out is locating the user. In addition to the global 406 MHz alert, PLB3 continuously transmits a 121.5 MHz radio homing signal that rescuers can follow once nearby. At sea, it also broadcasts an AIS distress position to AIS-equipped vessels within VHF range, allowing nearby vessels to see and navigate directly to the beacon.[source: 1]

item.title: Three Hikers Used AI to Plan Their Mount Shasta Climb—and Ended Up Needing Rescue
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.88
Mt. Shasta (Photo: Mimi Ditchie Photography via Getty) In what rescuers called a “mentally challenging” operation, a team of three young climbers safely descended Mt. Shasta over the weekend after spending an unplanned night on the peak with no warm sleep systems or shelter. The group had hunkered down off trail in a potentially dangerous location after running out of food and water—and rescuers say their reliance on an AI chatbot to plan some aspects of their trip contributed to their ordeal. From going too light on food and water to camping in a prohibited location, virtually on top of a mountain headspring, rangers said the three college students came ill-prepared to meet the challenges of the mountain. “These were smart guys,” said Nick Meyers, program manager for the Forest Service’s Mt. Shasta climbing rangers and avalanche center. “But they just missed the mark. It led to spending all day, all night, and all day again walking up and down off the mountain.” The three men, college students in their early 20s, arrived at the Clear Creek Trailhead to climb 14,179-foot Mt. Shasta on Saturday, August 29. They ascended that night to a well-known base camp area at 8,600 feet, arriving around 8 p.m. The next morning, they launched their summit bid with an alpine start at 3 a.m. They advanced very slowly. Ten hours later, they had managed to ascend another 2,600 feet, covering only about one mile. The summit of Mt. Shasta was still another 3,000 feet up and well over a mile ahead. While their slow pace didn’t signal any specific problem, it was becoming a downstream hazard, because their AI-assisted food and water planning had only fueled them for an 8-hour round trip. “We don’t know why they were as slow as they were,” Meyers said, noting that the group did have a conversation at this point about whether to turn around. By 3 p.m., they had reached a distinctive waypoint at 12,800 feet called Mushroom Rock. According to rangers, the group again debated going up or down, consulting two other parties. One said up, one said down. At 7 p.m., they finally summited Mt. Shasta, 16 hours after they had departed base camp. The climbers turned around quickly, reaching Mushroom Rock again by 8, but ran into another problem right away: the phone they had been using to navigate via AllTrails was dead, and the portable charger they’d brought along refused to charge it back up. The men dialed 911, asking for directions. But they mis-navigated nonetheless, wandering significantly off route to the south. After several more hours, they had proceeded in the dark over a neighboring ridgeline into Mud Creek Canyon, an area with dangerously loose rock where there is no established route up or down the mountain. The group had already called rescuers again to report hypothermia and a knee injury when one of them slipped after dark with no headlamp on. “One thing was leading to another on these calls, and we knew they needed help,” Meyers said. Teams reached the group the next morning, Aug. 31, after an exposed bivy near 11,000 feet. A helicopter rescue—often the standard on the steep, uneven and rocky terrain above treeline on Shasta—was unfeasible due to the location. “They were exhausted, but we had to hike them out,” Meyers said. He added that their condition was less than desperate: They had avoided serious hypothermia, and the injured party member was ambulatory. After some food, water, and a pep talk, all three walked down under their own power. Passing their campsite, rangers found the group’s tent pitched damagingly close to the headspring of Clear Creek, among scattered food wrappers and cookware. They reached Clear Creek Trailhead at 6:30 p.m, concluding the planned 8-hour trip after 39.5 hours. Meyers attributed the incident to lapses of information and mentorship. The group said they knew about the robust Mt. Shasta information website, shastaavalanche.org, but didn’t use it to prepare. They also had suitable gear—a solid tent, headlamps, and snow travel equipment, as well as summit passes—but lacked other equipment that would have supported their plan, like a reliable charging system for their phone or a backup method of navigation.. “Our objective is always to give people information,” Meyers said. “We don’t try to influence what people do, but instead give them the knowledge and resources they need to make good decisions in the mountains. “We know people are going to use AI to prepare themselves, and it’s happening more and more – especially with educated young people. But there’s no excuse for ignoring the information when it’s freely available. We just try to encourage everyone to talk to a real person first. We’re here to help.”

item.title: Forget the Camino: Europe’s Newest 191-Mile Thru-Hike Features Wilderness Wine Bars and Zero Crowds
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.16
Logar Valley (Photo: Mediaspeed, foto: Jan Godec) The trail passes through the 3,000-foot-high Logar Valley cinematic as a Peter Jackson sequence: Gnarled apple trees and wildflowers line long, narrow fields of bright green grass, and forests of knobby conifers sweep toward a horizon of snow-capped peaks. Historic stone and plaster homes with low-slung shake roofs huddle near the woodline. The path follows the upper Savinja River, which flows clear and aquamarine over a bed of off-white rock. It passes into silvery linden and elm forests as the valley narrows. A tiny, log cabin-style pub offering wild-fermented wines, žganje (berry liquors), and Carniolan sausage plates overlooks the entry to the cirque. Stairs climb toward a high, bowled ridge. The sound of crashing water echoes off stone. Another bend and Rinka Waterfall erupts from a notch in the sheer cliffside, plunging 300 feet into a bright blue pool. Trekkers can admire the action from the deck of a cantilevered, hike-in bar and café that clings to an escarpment about halfway up the falls, or walk another half-mile to take in the view from an alpine meadow where villagers once summered sheep. A Scandinavian-style mountaintop lodge operated by the Alpine Association of Slovenia offers cheap and comparatively luxe overnight accommodations for thru-hikers. The walk and stay are part of the nation’s newly designated Kamnik-Savinja Alps Water Trail (KSAWT). The 191-mile route connects numerous preexisting paths in a loop that showcases the aquatic resources of Slovenia’s second largest mountain range. The trek is divided into 11 stages that link more than a dozen historic villages and towns, and features three lakes, four rivers, numerous waterfalls, and more than 200 springs and streams. “The international backpacking community has started to call Slovenia Europe’s hidden gem,” says hiking enthusiast and Trail Angel Central (TAC) founder, Scott Vanderlip. The retired software engineer and serial entrepreneur operates a seasonal hiker camp on the Pacific Crest Trail. He’s traveled the world to connect with trekking communities for the TAC and logged miles on many of Europe’s most notable long routes—including the new water trail. “To me, Slovenia is a treasure trove for long-distance backpackers,” says Vanderlip. Particularly those who prefer their alpine views with a hardy side of cultural history and traditional foods, yet want to avoid big crowds. Europe’s most popular long trail, the Camino de Santiago, attracts more than 530,000 thru-hikers a year. The Alpine Association of Slovenia, meanwhile, says just 10,350 people have completed the nation’s cross-country Mountain Trail since it was founded in 1953. What’s more, Slovenia—which borders Northern Italy to the west and Austria to the north—is about the size of Massachusetts and home to some 6,200 miles of hiking trails. That gives its 1.7 million annual trekker tourists plenty of room to space out. The notoriously tough Mountain Trail features more than 23 miles of cumulative elevation gain and 14 peaks above 7,000 feet. The KSAWT, however, is a more laid back adventure. Stages average 10.6 miles a day, inviting hikers to soak in the views and indulge in picturesque swimming holes. The route climbs to high points like the overlook above Rinka Waterfall, but forgoes tough-to-reach peaks like 8,392-foot Grintovec in favor of more accessible alpine valleys, meadows, and the banks of the pristine waterways that flow through them. Mountain huts and lodges pepper the route with affordable places to sleep. Electric shuttle vans patrol nearby roads and make it easy to slackpack to and from amenity-packed stopovers like the Medieval fortress town of Kamnik. Points of aquatic interest like Lake Črnava—which is backed by a 16th century castle and bowl of 7,000-foot peaks—are showstoppers. But the trail was actually inspired by less visible resources. The loop was the outgrowth of a 2022 project to map and raise awareness around the region’s abundant springs. Local stakeholders and conservation groups joined forces with the Slovenian Tourist Board and European Union Common Agricultural Policy Network to map and analyze the most productive natural founts. The group identified fifty-four pristine watering holes, including carbonated iron and mineral springs. Infrastructure like hardened treads, stone headwalls, spring boxes, and outflow pipes were added to both invite and protect sites from hiker visits. Annual drinking water festivals were organized to showcase the aquatic wealth and how it influences local products like wine, beer and spirits. “Then we thought, why not connect these amazing resources in a network that provides a very different kind of experience than your usual mountaineering trail,” says Slovenian Tourist Board spokesperson, Maša Puklavec Polutnik. The KSAWT linked trails to the 54 springs and some of the most scenic portions of the waterways they feed into in 2023. Signage provides insight into their geology and historic importance. “These mountains have acted like a natural water tower that supplies clean, potable water to settlements and villages for millennia,” says Polutnik. Hikers are encouraged to challenge their palates and try to distinguish the subtle differences between springs. They can then compare their own observations to scientific breakdowns with exact mineral compositions and taste-notes for each. “It’s a really cool side quest to do as you’re passing through these astoundingly beautiful and historic areas—and unlike anything that I’m aware of in the U.S.,” says Vanderlip. He encourages trekkers to up the culinary ante by immersing themselves in local foodways. “Every town and village you pass through has its own version of popular regional dishes and drinks,” says Vanderlip. “And they all take deep pride in those differences and traditions.” Wines, for instance, feature unique and often much older grape varietals compared to those typically found in western Europe and the U.S. That and ancient techniques like whole-cluster fermentation (where the stems are left on) or the use of native yeasts brings wildly different flavors than your typical chardonnay or merlot. Pair them with traditional cured meats like zgornjesavinjski želodec—a mix of fresh pork leg and shoulder meat, cubed bacon, sea salt, pepper, and garlic water that’s pressed flat during curing—and iconic cheeses like Trnič, which shepherds on the high-elevation Velika Planina plateau craft from cottage cheese, cream, and salt. “There’s just so much to love,” says Vanderlip. “On one hand, the hiking is world-class and filled with scenery that would more than justify a visit without any of the other perks.” But when you factor in refreshing spring water, historic villages, delicious eats, and nifty cultural traditions? That elevates the KSAWT to a bucket list walk.

item.title: Hiking Norway's heavily monitored Russian border
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 6.98
Hiking Norway's heavily monitored Russian border A series of scenic paths trace the Norwegian-Russian border. But as you trek through the tundra and forests, you may notice watchtowers and cameras hanging in trees. I'm standing at a hillside clearing in the tundra along the Russian-Norwegian border, watching the Pasvik River ripple and writhe below. Maybe it's the rustle of birch leaves overhead or the buzzing sound of mosquitoes circling all around me, but I have an unshakeable feeling that I'm being watched. Then again, those hairs on the back of my neck could be triggered by the nearby military watchtower, and the fact that this public hiking trail is under constant surveillance. Located in the far reaches of north-eastern Norway on a jagged fjord close to where Finland, Russia and Norway meet, the small town of Kirkenes is best known among travellers as the final turnaround port for a number of small Arctic cruise lines. But increasingly, local operators are leaning into another opportunity: leading cruisers on wind-whipped treks along Nato's northernmost land border to the unfenced-but-heavily-monitored 198km-long line separating Norway and Russia. Here, surrounded by taiga forest, travellers can explore a network of public trails where cameras hang in the trees, watchtowers dot the horizon and military patrols ensure visitors are abiding by the periodic pillars (yellow for Norway, red for Russia) marking the international boundary between the two nations. Drawn by the prospect of exploring the Arctic's most closely watched frontiers, I've set out on a three-hour trek through a birch forest strewn with boggy puddles. The trail runs parallel to the Pasvik River for roughly 1km before it reaches the "border corridor": an 8m-wide (26ft) strip of cleared forest that's a veritable no-man's land where travellers can't go. From there, the trek culminates in a scramble up Russehøgda, a hillside overlooking the Storskog border crossing that is the only legal land border between the countries. But as we enter the forest, my guide, Henrik Hoffmann, switches off his mobile to avoid connecting to Russian data networks. He instinctively taps a satellite phone in his pocket, and I'm reminded that this is no ordinary walk in the woods. The lure of Russia's land border Hoffmann has been leading these border-trek trips since 2025 but relocated to Kirkenes in 2021, just before Russia's invasion of Ukraine a year later. Since then, he says that both Russia and Norway have increased security along their respective borders here. Now, seemingly minor offences, like throwing stones towards Russia, risk heavy fines and wandering beyond the marked international boundaries has resulted in detainments. Still, he says that after travelling along Norway's coastline, many passengers who arrive in Kirkenes on Hurtigruten and Havila cruises are eager to escape the confines of ships and shuttle buses and get an up-close look at where these two nations meet. "Many older travellers are particularly interested because they remember the Cold War and have followed relations between Europe and Russia over many decades," Hoffmann explains. "The hike allows them to experience the landscape for themselves while learning about the history and present-day realities of living beside Russia." More like this: While Kirkenes Tours is the newest operator to offer border excursions, it's not the first. Havila Voyages has been leading visitors to this area since 2000, while Hurtigruten told the BBC that its Norwegian Border tour – which also leads travellers through a WW2 atomic bomb shelter – recently became the most popular of its eight Kirkenes excursions. "Interest in the border has definitely increased over the past few years," says Hoffmann. Despite an initial reduction in tourism following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he explained that understanding the border is now a driving motivator for those visiting Kirkenes. Plan your trip: Kirkenes Tours , Havila Voyages and Hurtigruten all offer year-round walking excursions along the Norwegian-Russian border. In addition to Kirkenes Tours' standard May-November hike, it also offers treks that take in the Boris Gleb Church and ones set under the midnight Sun (May-July). Travellers can hike independently on the public trails, but given the strict border rules, it's recommended to book through a regulated company. Littering, photographing military personnel and touching or climbing markers are prohibited by law. Hikers must carry passports, as Norwegian military patrols regularly request formal identification. According to Anja Tellervo Hansen, destination manager at Visit Kirkenes, these border treks allow visitors to "learn more about what everyday life in our region looks like, and how the closeness to the border has shaped the Kirkenes region over the years". Evidence of this shared history is everywhere in Kirkenes. The town is the only place in Norway where street signs are marked in both Norwegian and Russian. Near the centre, the towering Russia War Monument commemorates the day in 1944 when the Red Army liberated Kirkenes from Nazi occupation. And the nearby Borderland Museum highlights how Norwegians, Finns and Russians have intermixed here for generations. Trekking the trail Soon after landing at Kirkenes Airport, I was whisked into a van that cut through the city, past the port where cruisers had already docked for the day and dropped off at an unassuming layby flanked by dense walls of birch and conifer trees. "Ready?" said Hoffman, who was waiting in the layby with a rucksack, beckoning for me to follow along a stony track. An hour later, I'm stepping up a rocky outcrop as Hoffmann nimbly picks the way ahead. As beads of sweat form on my forehead, I pause, taking in the eerie expanse of birch trees dipping down towards the Pasvik River. Soon, the outcrop slopes onto a flattened summit. Standing on Russehøgda, surrounded by desolate tundra and a horizon of hazy peaks, I momentarily forget that I'm at one of Europe's most scrutinised borders and am consumed by the sheer beauty of the terrain. Then I glance to the right, notice a yellow and red set of markers only a few metres away, and am sharply reminded where I am. Hoffman and I throw down a blanket on top of a smooth rock and sit for a drink. "There's Storskog," he says, gesturing towards two lakefront checkpoints below. From a few kilometres away, I can just make out the occasional truck driving along the E105 to cross into Russia. He says that recreational crossings have reduced, but a handful of vehicles still make the journey on a daily basis. He also explains that while more visitors are trekking these border trails, fewer residents are; Hoffmann has seen more military patrols than local hikers. "You don't see many Norwegians here," he says, "Perhaps it's a classic case of not exploring your own doorstep." As we turn away from Storskog and descend Russehøgda, I find myself silenced by the gravity of the experience. I've spent a lifetime crossing borders and collecting stamps, but I could have sat for hours just looking at Storskog. From painted markers to the distant outline of Boris Gleb Church, centuries of politics and negotiations have shaped this terrain. It's easy to understand why more and more cruise passengers are disembarking to witness it firsthand. --

item.title: Vienna's great surprise: The Globe Museum
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.57
The museum charting how humans understand the world Beautiful, surreal and eerily empty, Vienna's Globe Museum the only public museum on Earth dedicated to globes, and it – quite literally – tells the story of our world. It's a chilly afternoon in Vienna, and the line for the Austrian National Library has already spilled out the door, curling like a ribbon around the grand Josefsplatz square. I'm not in the mood to wait – I've already struck out at several crowded nearby attractions where timed-entry tickets were sold out. Rather than join the queue, I walk down the street and stumble onto a smaller, somewhat hidden site: The Globe Museum. Tucked inside Vienna's 17th-Century Palais Mollard, it's the only public museum on Earth dedicated entirely to globes, and one of Vienna's greatest surprises. Different worlds I soon realise that I've wandered into another world – or more accurately, many of them. Just steps from some of the city's most celebrated, crowded attractions, Vienna's Globe Museum displays more than 220 rare and antique spheres, most created before 1850, ranging from towering Coronelli globes to tiny, foldable pocket orbs. Beautiful and surreal, the museum's extensive collection goes beyond geography to reveal how humanity has mapped and imagined the Earth and heavens above. It's a chronicle of human curiosity, and – quite literally – the story of our world. "Globes show the change in our imagination of our planet," says Nikolaus Schobesberger, the director of museum. "And this is the only place in the world where you can see so many of them at the same time." Visitors start by travelling through the Golden Cabinet, a lavish room with centuries-old frescoes depicting scenes from Greek mythology. It's the backdrop for a stunning array of globe-related instruments, like telluriums, which illustrate the Earth's orbit around the Sun, and armillary spheres, which use a framework of rings to visualise the movements of celestial bodies. As I reach the museum's four main galleries, I realise the whole place is pin-drop quiet. I shuffle slowly from one glass case to another, holding my breath to not disturb the stillness, even though I'm alone with centuries-old objects. I find myself marvelling at two spherical worlds suspended in time. One is terrestrial, with oceans awash in vivid blues and squiggly brown coastlines. The other is celestial, where mythological creatures and constellations spill across a tea stain-coloured backdrop. Barely bigger than beach balls, these two time capsules were made by the same craftsman 10 years apart in the mid-1500s and preserve a world as it was still coming into focus. In one, Europe, the Mediterranean and Africa's coasts are filled with place names, while North America fades into the uncharted Arctic. Asia is distorted, a hypothetical southern continent stands in for Australia and Antarctica and the Pacific is populated by sea monsters instead of islands. In the other, Renaissance astrological observations exist alongside Pegasus taking flight and Perseus brandishing Medusa's severed head. "They're some of the oldest globes we have in our collection," says Schobesberger. Moving from one globe to the next, I notice how these relics extend beyond geography and depict what people once believed. Many fill the space of unexplored oceans with dragons, while some confidently depict my home state of California as an island. Some pieces also preserve colonial-era prejudices with elaborately painted scenes depicting Indigenous people as cannibals. On one, African coastlines are dotted with Spanish and Portuguese flags, showing "ownership". "They're a part of this colonial thinking. And so, they're beautiful art, but you also have to think about the time they were created," Schobesberger says, explaining that every globe is as much a record of what people knew as what they didn't. That's why he believes the museum resonates with all types of people, not just historians or cartography enthusiasts. One of Schobesberger's favourite objects is a lunar globe from 1961. The front portion of the Moon is meticulously mapped. The back, however, is a stark white strip, intentionally left blank because the far side of the Moon had not yet been seen. An updated lunar globe made two years later, also on display, contains the missing portion. I can't help but circle back to a showstopper in the front hall, a replica of the Behaim Globe – completed by Martin Behaim in 1492, the year Christopher Columbus sailed west – which shows a world without the Americas. There's simply an expanse of ocean between Europe and Asia. "A globe is such a great thing because it's a small-scale model of our planet, so you can tell stories about the world on it," he says. "Climate, geology, topography, trade routes, everything." From curios to cultural cornerstones Walking through the museum, visitors can see the globe's own journey unfold. The earliest examples were luxury objects reserved for aristocrats and wealthy merchants. Over time, globes lost their exclusivity, shrunk in size and became more affordable and popular. They entered schools, appeared in living rooms and even became playthings for children. Today, they are so commonplace that my son even won his desktop globe in a classroom raffle. I entered the museum expecting to view globes as historic artefacts, but I'm surprised by how alive they still feel. Even with Google Earth at my fingertips, these tactile objects invite curiosity and imagination in a way that a screen doesn't. "It's not just that the globe is a scientific instrument. It's also an object which lets you dream of foreign countries," says Schobesberger. Globes in pop culture Beginning 24 September 2026, the museum's newest exhibition, Globes in Everyday Life, Art and Culture, will explore how globes evolved from a status symbol to a familiar fixture. It also showcases the globe's enduring place in pop culture, from architecture to art and film, like Charlie Chaplin's famous dance with an inflatable globe in The Great Dictator. "The main idea was to show that globes are almost everywhere as a part of everyday life," Schobesberger says. Schobesberger's own fascination began as a young child, when he became captivated by the ships, sea monsters and mythical creatures that filled the blank spaces of historical maps and globes. He began to draw his own world maps when he was just six years old. "You can think about what's possible on the other side of the world, even when you're sitting here in Europe," he says. "Nothing else can capture the imagination quite like it." More like this: That sentiment resonates with author JF Penn, who stumbled onto the Globe Museum while researching her novel Spear of Destiny, based on a relic housed in Vienna's Imperial Treasury. Like me, she ended up lingering far longer than planned. "I particularly loved the oversized antique globes with the patina of age and use," she says. "I considered how many fingertips have turned them over generations and wondered if they thought of travelling to these far-off places that I do." Even after visitors leave Palais Mollard, the search continues. Across Vienna, some 50 globes are perched on rooftops and facades, hidden in plain sight. The museum even charts them on a virtual map in its new exhibit, encouraging people to look upward as they wander the city. When I finally step back outside, the sky is dark and the streets are even more crowded. Earlier in the day, I had been seeking a quieter corner of Vienna. Instead, I was given a whole new way of seeing the world – a place that's constantly being redrawn and reimagined. --

item.title: When Russia colonised California
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.89
'The forgotten empire': When Russia colonised California For nearly 30 years, part of Sonoma was ruled by Tsarist Russia, and it played a pivotal – if little-known – role in shaping the US. It's a pretty, two-hour drive north from San Francisco to Крѣпость Россъ. After slicing through the Golden Gate fog, I wound past sunburnt vineyards to Sonoma's remote coast and rolled down the windows. To my left, California plummeted into the Pacific and seals barked from boulders cropping out of the foamy surf. To my right, cliffs rose sharply and titanic redwoods shot up from the road's switchbacks. Suddenly, a lonely twin-domed chapel topped with Orthodox crosses appeared against the blue ocean. I got out and followed a footpath past a Cyrillic sign towards a wooden, frontier-like stronghold built 150ft (46m) atop a bluff hanging over the sea. Every year, millions of travellers set out on the Pacific Coast Highway to twist and turn their way along, one of the US's most stunning roads, as it hugs the entire California coastline. But chances are, few of these road-trippers realise that hidden here on a secluded headland 90 miles (145km) north of San Francisco lies a relic from the days when part of California was ruled by Tsarist Russia. I didn't, and judging by Fort Ross's eerie emptiness, it seems I'm not alone. "Even most Californians don't know Russia once had a colony in California," Kent Lightfoot, an anthropologist at the University of California, Berkeley, later told me. "They all know about the Spanish and the Mexicans, but almost no one knows anything about the Russians being here. It's kind of like the forgotten empire." While some Americans may recall that the US's largest state, Alaska, was part of Russia for nearly 70 years, the Russian Empire's only permanent overseas colony, known as Russian America, also extended into California from 1812-1842. In fact, Russians settled in California decades before newly independent Americans did. Innovative and surprisingly cosmopolitan, Fort Ross (short for Rossiya, meaning "Russia") was intended to be a breadbasket for Russia's struggling Alaskan settlements, but it also became the source of hotly debated plans for Russian expansion across North America. The beginning of Russian America As European powers expanded west in the 1500s and 1600s, Russia expanded east. By the 1640s, Russian fur traders and mercenaries had swept their way across Siberia to reach the Pacific coast. This rush led to permanent Russian settlements along Alaska's islands and coasts. In 1799, Tsar Paul I formalised the empire's Alaska claims by chartering the Russian-American Company. Modelled after the British East India Company, the for-profit venture didn't just control the fur trade; it now controlled all of Alaska as a corporate colony. But there was a problem: while the company was growing rich on sea otter pelts, the colonists were growing hungry because they couldn't farm in much of Alaska's frozen landscape. So, the Russian settlers sailed south in search of warmer climates and Spanish trading partners. California dreaming In April 1806, with his colony stalked by starvation and his crew decimated by scurvy, Russian-American Company director Nikolai Rezanov steered the prow of his ship, the Juno, into San Francisco Bay. As the brig limped towards Spain's northernmost California settlement, a Spanish soldier grabbed a megaphone and demanded the strange vessel identify itself. "Russia," a voice called back. It was a response the Spanish had been expecting for nearly 40 years. Though Spain claimed all of California starting in 1542, it didn't actually occupy it until 1769, after getting word that Russian fur traders were rapidly moving east across the Alaskan islands. To prevent Russian and British advancement, Spain created a chain of presidios (military outposts) along the coast, starting with San Diego. "The expansion of all of Alta [Upper] California, in many ways, was stimulated by the Russians," Lightfoot said. "The Spanish were nervous about the Russians coming south. So, the founding of San Diego, Santa Barbara, Monterey and San Francisco were a response to the Russians in Alaska." During Rezanov's six-week stay in San Francisco, the 42-year-old statesman secured enough food from the Spanish to save the starving Alaskan colonists by getting engaged to the 15-year-old daughter of San Francisco's Spanish commandant. As he sailed back through the Golden Gate, Rezanov realised that the entire northern coast of California was undefended and far sunnier than Siberia or Alaska, so he hatched a plan to extend Russian America into California. In 1812, after years of stealthily surveying the coast, 25 Russians and 80 Native Alaskan hunters settled on a shelf-like plateau overlooking the Pacific on what is now Sonoma County's rugged coast. Here, close enough to the area's abundant sea otter population but far enough from the Spanish Empire's sparsely guarded northern frontier, they lived in a Siberian-designed settlement hewn from California redwoods under the tsar's double-eagle flag. Exploring Russian California Today, Russia's far-flung California colony remains a solitary, surreal place. Set 12 miles (19km) from the nearest town or mobile phone service, the weathered wooden remnants of a once-bustling settlement open onto a 180-degree view of the sea. In two days at the 3,400-acre Fort Ross State Historic Park, I counted 14 other visitors, and except for the occasional chime from the St Nicholas chapel, the only noise breaking the stillness was the waves crashing below the bluff. "There's a magical feel to Fort Ross," said Robin Joy Wellman, who worked as an interpreter with California State Parks for nearly 30 years. "It's something of a mystery, but once people discover it, they say it's one of the most beautiful places they've ever visited." The site's dramatic setting straddles the San Andreas fault, and the same earthquake that flattened San Francisco in 1906 also levelled much of the original wooden outpost. But detailed displays of the partially reconstructed fortress paint a vivid picture of frontier life in Russia's wild, wild East. The heart of the colony was the fort-like stockade, where a handful of high-ranking Russian soldiers, officers and company officials lived in barracks enclosed by a 12ft (3.6m) palisade. I followed Kimsey up the steps of two blockhouses armed with enough cannons to command the coast. He explained that while the Russians chose this natural overlook to defend against Spanish attacks, the two empires never actually clashed, and even depended on each other for survival. "The Russians and the Spanish were at the very far edges of their overstretched empires. They both needed things the other side could provide, so they traded illicitly," Kimsey said. In the warehouse, drying sea otter pelts worth $100 each (a year's salary for a Pennsylvania farmer at the time) destined for China, Europe and Spanish California would have hung from the rafters. Under the bulbous dome of one of the oldest Orthodox churches in the Western hemisphere, the little settlement gradually grew into a cosmopolitan colony, complete with banyas, bakeries and some 60 buildings. "It was a bustling, pluralistic mercantile village, with lots of languages and people from different homelands living together," Lightfoot said. "The stockade was just the tip of the iceberg. The real action was outside." Beyond the fort As Kimsey and I walked out of the palisade, he explained that as the colony expanded to include nearly 400 people by the 1830s, it became one of the most diverse places in California – and virtually everyone there worked for the Russian-American Company. Here, where the sloboda (village) once stood at the edge of the cape, paid Aleutian and Kodiak hunters lived with Native California women, mixed-race Russian and European Creoles married local Kashaya Pomo and Coast Miwok workers and people were buried next to each other at the Old Russian Cemetery up the hillside. Compared to other European colonies, it was also largely tolerant. "The Russians didn't come here to 'civilise' like the Spanish," said Kimsey, who serves as the tribal liaison for the area's Native communities. We then followed a steep path down to a crescent-shaped beach where coopers, carpenters and blacksmiths brought in by the Russian-American Company from as far afield as Finland and Hawaii once worked side by side. "This is where the first ocean-going ships in California were built," he said. It's also where the first bricks, glass and windmills in California were made. As workers crafted longboats, forged iron, cast brass and made metal, Fort Ross became the centre of manufacturing in California. The Russians traded these highly coveted goods with their Spanish and (later) Mexican neighbours in exchange for further provisions for their Alaskan settlements – and in doing so, they unwittingly helped their rivals settle California. More like this: This shallow-water cove was also where cargo boats and kayak-bound hunters would set off for the colony's main deep-water port 20 miles (35km) south in Rumyantsev (present-day Bodega Bay) and its sealing station off the coast of San Francisco on the Farallon Islands. As Fort Ross' footprint grew, so did the calls from within the Russian-American Company to heed Rezanov's recommendation of annexing North America's west coast for Russia. In 1821, Tsar Alexander I issued an imperial decree claiming Russian control over modern-day Oregon through Alaska. The US's soon-to-be sixth president, John Quincy Adams, swiftly objected and his warning to Russia that the Americas "are no longer subjects for any new European colonial establishments" established one of the most fundamental principles of US foreign policy: the Monroe Doctrine, which opposes foreign interference in the Western hemisphere. From the beach, Kimsey and I climbed a steep hill past the stockade to the orchard the Russians started with a single peach tree in 1814 and pushed open the gate. Of the hundreds of citrus trees and crops the Russians planted, only a single branch of a 200-year-old Capulin cherry survives. Yet, the Russians actually left a far greater agricultural legacy here than most people realise. "It was the Russians who planted the first grapes in [what is now] Sonoma County in 1817," said Megan Jones, Sonoma's official wine librarian. As Jones explained, while Sonoma is now considered "the birthplace of the modern American wine movement", Russian traders introduced the now-rare Mission grape to Sonoma and produced small batches of light red wine. For all its innovations, however, Fort Ross never succeeded in its two main goals: turning a profit and feeding hungry Alaskans. By the early 1820s, the Russian-American Company's Native Alaskan hunters had speared so many sea otters they wiped out the local population, and a combination of heavy coastal fog and rampant rodents yielded just 13 tonnes of wheat annually between 1826 and 1833. When the British-run Hudson's Bay Company agreed to supply Russian Alaska with provisions from its Pacific Northwest settlements starting in 1839, it was the beginning of the end for Tsarist California. Two years later, a Swiss emigrant named John Sutter purchased Fort Ross' buildings and assets from the Russians for $30,000. He cannibalised parts of the structures to create his new settlement in Sacramento. Seven years after the Russians sailed back to Alaska, a chance discovery on Sutter's property ignited the California Gold Rush. Russia's California legacy Today, reminders of California's Tsarist past are still scattered across the Golden State as you drive north from San Francisco. One of the city's most famous neighbourhoods, Russian Hill, gets its name from the graves of Russian-American Company sailors discovered there during the Gold Rush (look for a plaque near 1120 Vallejo Street). A historical marker at Bodega Bay shows where Russians set sail for their Alaskan capital, Novo-Arkhangelsk (present-day Sitka). And more than a million people visit the Russian River Valley each year to splash, hike and taste some of the US's best wines. "The Russians called this river Slavyanka, and it's one of the main arteries they used to exploit the area," said Suki Waters, a Kashaya Pomo descendant and the owner of WaterTreks, which leads eco-tours along the Russian River. As we kayaked past harbour seals and migrating pelicans, she recounted stories from her great-great-grandmother, who was alive when the Russians sailed in. "Fort Ross was a seasonal fishing village called Metini for thousands of years," she said. "When the Russians first came, the Elders called them the 'Undersea People', because from high on the bluff, it looked like they rose out from under the ocean." Later that afternoon, I walked back through Fort Ross' Cyrillic signs, stockade and sloboda towards a lone bench at the edge of that bluff. Peering across the Pacific, I wondered how many days it would take to reach Russia. But as a distant chime from the chapel echoed in the air, I was reminded of something Wellman told me. "The fact that a little part of Russia was right here in California is amazing. Why would we ever want to forget that?" --

item.title: Five unwritten rules for visiting Spain
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.83
'Paella is just for lunch' and other unwritten rules for visiting Spain Spain is famous for its laid-back lifestyle, but beneath the long lunches and late nights are social codes that shape everyday life. Our expert explains how to read them. While Spain is beloved for its beautiful beaches, romantic architecture and delicious food culture, one of its strongest draws is its famously relaxed pace. No hay prisa ("no rush") and tranquilo ("relax") are oft-uttered phrases here; meals are drawn out and nightlife lasts until morning. Even non-Spanish speakers know the meaning of siesta. Get to know your expert Jill Petzinger is a British journalist and professional travel advisor who specialises in Spain and Southern Europe. Based in Valencia since 2021, she has travelled extensively throughout Spain to explore the many regional cuisines and cultural traditions. But "relaxed" doesn't mean there's no order. Beneath Spain's easy-going surface are silent social codes that shape everything from how people queue to how they structure their days. Instinctive rather than explicitly stated, Spain's unwritten social rules are often based on respect for regional identity, a belief that life is best lived sociably in public and a historical need to work with, not against, the searing Sun. Locals might not say them out loud, but that doesn't make them any less important to learn. From relinquishing your personal space to skipping paella at dinner, here are five unwritten rules that will help you understand Spain from the inside. 1. Trust the invisible queue Try to order at a covered market, pharmacy, bakery, bar or local shop in Spain and you'll typically find people standing around randomly, no clear line in sight. It may seem confusing to the outsider, but there's a deeply ingrained system at play, rooted in a cultural preference for interaction, informality and social trust. "Queues" in Spain do indeed exist, but they are typically spread-out crowds rather than prim lines because of space constraints in small premises or market aisles; standing where it's most convenient solves the issue. But how do you know when it's your turn? What to do: When you arrive, approach the closest person and ask "¿Quién es el último?" (Who's last?) or simply "¿El último?" They will point to whomever is. Once you know who's last, you're free to walk along the displays and peruse what to buy without losing your place. But stay alert: you will get asked "¿El último?", too. 2. Don't assume the meal is over when it's over You've just had the last bites of Spanish tortilla and the last drops of Rioja. But before you ask for the bill, look around. The tables next to you, strewn with empty glasses and crumpled napkins, may look like they've finished too, but they're just entering another phase: the ritual known as la sobremesa. Literally translated as "over the table", la sobremesa is the hour (or hours) after the meal when everyone settles in for a long conversation. It may involve another round of coffee or drinks, but there's no pressure: la sobremesa is all about enjoying each other's company. The tradition is thought to stretch back to the agricultural past, when families sat around the table after lunch as it was still too hot return to the fields immediately. Most Spaniards may no longer till the fields, but the sobremesa continues its role in maintaining relationships. The joy of enjoying each meal for as long as possible has never gone out of style. What to do: Simply relax, put away your phone and keep chatting away. Waiters are used to letting people enjoy their conversations, so just raise a hand to ask for the bill when you're (really) ready to leave. And feel free to linger even longer. 3. Follow the Sun Spain's famously late rhythm can bewilder visitors, with dinners that last until midnight and shops that close for hours after lunch. But there's a logic behind the seemingly languorous rhythm. In Spain, people work with, not against, the Sun. Historically, Spanish farmers started the day early to get their work done before the Sun grew too hot, saving lunch until they were through. Then, in the 1940s, General Franco moved the clocks forward to align with Nazi Germany. Though the country now found itself in the Central European time zone, many stuck to the traditional solar schedule: lunch at 13:00 became lunch at 14:00 as the sun reached its zenith an hour later than before, and dinner happened later, too, as the light now lasted longer. More like this: In Spain, the workday is also slightly longer than the EU average: 36.3 hours per week versus 35.9 hours. Perhaps that's why Spain's famous "siesta" is increasingly less the norm, since 80% of its population now lives in cities. Unable to head home at lunchtime and have a nap, workers now often return to the office or use the post-lunch time to tackle chores. What to do: Shape your day around avoiding the worst of the afternoon Sun between 13:00 and 18:00 – a light breakfast. Check shop hours to avoid slogging through the heat to a shuttered destination, and keep in mind that only tourist restaurants open at 19:00. If you can hold off until 20:30 or 21:00 you'll be able to eat at better establishments. Consider a strategic siesta to help you stave off the hunger, or prepare for a long night. 4. Make room for the crowd Spain is a tactile nation, where touching an arm for emphasis, greeting with hugs and (lots of) kisses, bumping shoulders in a bar and standing close to strangers in a line are all everyday aspects of social behaviour – though they can surprise visitors from places with stricter norms around personal proximity. Furthermore, whether you find yourself in the city or the village, Spanish social life has traditionally been lived in public places like plazas, bars and streets. These shared spaces can get quite closely packed, meaning you end up very close to your neighbours by default. What to do: Don't automatically read physical closeness as rudeness. Stake out your own (little) space but accept that you'll still catch accidental bumps and jostles in busy areas. If you need to squeeze past someone, a simple "perdón" (sorry) suffices, and almost always elicits "no pasa nada" (no problem) from the other person. 5. Don't order paella for dinner or sangria at a bar Thanks to Spain's thriving tourist industry, you'll find the same supposed Spanish staples – sangria, paella and tapas – wherever you go. But Spain is a huge country, with 17 autonomous communities on the mainland, and an equal number of regional cuisines. Traditionally, people ate what was produced locally, and that love for and loyalty towards regional identity when it comes to food is still strong today. Embrace the opportunity to enjoy the beloved dishes of the city you're visiting. Paella is revered as a native dish of Valencia and Catalonia, but wherever you try it, do it like the Spanish and order it just at lunchtime, as it is considered a heavy meal to digest. Tapas bars will serve regional specialties depending on the city, but the sheer creative variety of pintxos is best enjoyed in their Basque homeland. If you're in Madrid in the colder months, don't miss the famous meaty chickpea cocido stew; enjoy gazpacho in Andalusia and most of Spain in the summer. Year-round, consider swerving the sangria. Locals do drink it, but it's not regarded a bar drink: it's more commonly consumed as a punch at parties. What to do: If a restaurant has a photo menu, it will likely be a tourist trap. To explore regional dishes, try a three-course menú del dia in local restaurants during weekdays. These menus are dying out in Spain partly because of shorter lunch breaks and the rise of new, trendier eateries, so look out for places full of locals with daily chalkboard menus, generally indicating fresh, seasonal food. To drink at the bar like a local, order the nationally adored tinto de verano, a mix of red wine and lemonade that contains no hard liquor, or tiny caña draft beers, which stay colder longer. --

item.title: The smoky plant goo that Finns can't stop eating
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.52
Pine tar: The surprising, smoky goo that Finns can't stop eating Once used to waterproof boats and treat infections, this smoky plant byproduct is now used to flavour everything from schnapps to bread. But how does it taste? I've been in the sub-Arctic city of Oulu, Finland for only a few hours when I'm caught under a torrent of late summer rain. I take refuge in a cafe and order a coffee and sugar-dusted pannukakku (a thick pancake). The waiter asks me, "What flavour? We have almond, tar, blueberry..." I'm certain I've misunderstood: "Did you say tar?" He nods nonchalantly. Welcome to Oulu, the northern Finnish city where terva (pine tar, usually translated in English simply as "tar") is on the menu. Produced by heating pine wood without oxygen, this thick, dark substance flavours everything from lager to ice cream, lending a distinct, rich smokiness. "It's an intense flavour, so a little goes a long way," says Matti Moller of the Arctic Food Lab, an initiative showcasing northern Finland's culinary culture. "But it's brilliant to experiment with in everything from fish to desserts." To Finns, pine tar's aroma has long been associated with wooden boats, summer cottages and sauna scents. So what's the recent culinary appeal? I've decided to find out. From sealant to meal Yet just two centuries ago, Oulu had a very different reputation. Encircled by dense pine forests and the winding channels of the Oulujoki delta, it was famed as the tar capital of the world. "Oulu has been a major trading hub since the 15th Century thanks to its position on the Oulu River," says local guide Sirpa Törmä. "By the 1860s, it had become the world's largest tar-exporting port." Essential for waterproofing wooden sailing ships, tar was produced by smouldering wood in tar pits across villages along the river, then transported in narrow boats to Oulu's harbour for global export. Thanks to its antibacterial properties, tar had also long been used as a natural wound treatment all over Finland. "As the well-known saying goes: 'If sauna, spirits and tar do not help, the disease is fatal,'" explains Ritva Kylli, a food historian at the University of Oulu. But how did it make its way to the Finnish palate? Tar-as-flavour made its debut on pharmacy shelves.
