Archives at the National Library of Finland reveal that tar-flavoured medicinal lozenges date back to the early 1900s, and Oulu's local papers advertised tervakaramellit ('tar sweets') as early as 1902. "These were medicinal lozenges sold in apothecary shops for coughs and respiratory diseases," says Kylli. Even if not every Finn enjoys the taste of tar, virtually everyone has tried the iconic black terva pastille. The nation's most famous brand is Terva Leijona (Tar Lion), sold to this day. Launched in 1933, the pastilles were created by Oulu pharmacist YW Jalander after watching locals inhale smoky tar fumes for their health. Facing low profits, he invented a tar essence (tervaessanssi) and infused it into liquorice pastilles, which he sold through his confectionary company, Merijal. Terva Leijona eventually changed hands, but it is still made using his recipe. As popular as they were, tar didn't make the leap from pastille to gourmet treat until the end of the 20th Century, says Kylli, as living standards rose and interest in regional heritage cuisine grew across the country: "[It] seems to be connected to a growing interest in the cultural memory of Oulu's tar economy, a trend spreading beyond northern historical trade routes to all of Finland," she says. "It was reimagined into a distinctive heritage flavour." 'It can be addictive' Matti tells me he buys tar chocolate and syrup a few times a year. "The taste is unique – sweet, smoky, medicinal and completely unmistakable," he says as we walk across the picturesque island of Pikisaari, connected to Oulu's city centre by a short bridge. "Why do we love it? Perhaps we're tasting our roots, the Finnish forest and our heritage." The Oulu region, as the historic heart of the pine tar culture, has also become the symbolic centre of pine tar cuisine, with a high concentration of restaurants, cafes and bakeries that produce terva foods. At Pekka Heikkinen, a family bakery in Kajaani founded in 1913, owner Kaisa Marin bakes traditional bread and pastries. "Tar boats used to sail right past our bakery to Oulu," she explains. "When pine tar food innovations emerged in the '90s, it was natural to start baking tar-flavoured bread." For Marin, the connection is deeply personal: "My grandmother washed my hair with tar shampoo in the sauna, and our cabin's boat was sealed with tar. To me, the scent is cosy, nostalgic and rooted in home. I love it!" She always keeps thinly sliced tar bread in the freezer, ready to fry in butter when guests arrive. Though not for everyone, she warns it can be addictive. "My uncle, a master confectioner, created a rich tar chocolate that we bake every Christmas. We've even made cakes with pine tar and spruce needles." Rina Hirviniemi, owner of the cosy Kahvila Kiikku, also bakes tar bread at least once a week, usually pairing it with gravlax. "In summer, I serve vanilla ice cream with tar syrup, and in winter, we grill with tar outside," she says. "I like keeping tar products on hand, though I don't put them on the menu – I have an eye for people I can recommend it to." So what does it taste like? Convinced, I decide to – literally – bite. According to Marin, ice cream is the best starting point for tar newcomers, so I head to Market Square's ice cream van. Cone in hand, I sit by Toripolliisi, the brawny bronze police statue keeping watch over the square, and take my first hesitant taste. A smoky-sweet aroma rushes from nose to palate – the unexpected whiff of bacon. Yet, it's surprisingly sweet. Intrigued, I can't stop eating. Bite by bite, it completely wins me over. Just as Marin predicted, I find myself becoming addicted. I head next to ChocoSomnia, an Oulu chocolate maker. "We make tar pralines, chocolate bars and tar coffee. We get curious first-timers, but also loyal regulars," says co-owner Mika Lähteenmäki. Sampling a square of dark chocolate infused with pine tar and cranberry, I'm struck by the balance of smoky depth, rich cocoa bitterness and soft berry sweetness; the very taste of a pine forest in midsummer. I can't stop there. My local friend leads me to a supermarket for Terva Leijona pastilles. Like impatient children, we tear open the box and pop the tiny black sweets. Instead of subtle sweetness, an intense, smoky rush clears my airways. My friend introduces me to two of his mates, and I discover that local usage varies widely: some drizzle tar syrup on bacon, others serve tar schnapps before nights out. For others still, tar candies reign supreme. While most Finns buy ready-made tar products, today's skilled chefs craft them from scratch. This is what brought me to Lasaretti, a restaurant tucked into the riverfront oasis of Oulu's Hupisaaret Park. Today, head chef Laurance Robinson is serving smoked whitefish pasta with tar pearls, pickled fennel and red onion. "I can't build a tar pit, so I buy flavouring from Kujala's farm to make my syrup for sweet and savoury dishes," he says. "Balancing its strong, pungent taste took time." Resembling caviar, the tar pearls burst in my mouth against the whitefish, sharp fennel, and sweet archipelago bread. It is pure umami with subtle smokiness. More like this: Originally from the Isle of Man, Robinson cooked across Europe before settling in Finland. "I'll never forget my first taste of tar in 2011 – a sauna soda from my future father-in-law. It tasted like an ashtray at first, but the smokiness mellowed. Later, when I had the freedom to experiment, I said, 'I want to be the tar chef.'" His tar pavlova recently won best dessert at an Oulu culinary contest. "I wonder how far I can push it." Watching passersby drift through the sunny park, I marvel at how tar shifted from a maritime necessity to the flavour of local identity. "You know what," says my friend. "I've had a horrible headache since morning, but after eating this dish, it's completely gone." I can't promise it cures headaches, but in every sense, tar remains a uniquely Finnish ingredient that still works its quiet magic. --

item.title: Why Swedes think standing out is embarrassing
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.29
'You're not to think you're anything special': Why Swedes hate standing out Swedes prize equality, dislike boasting and are famously reluctant to stand out – yet they're also fiercely individualistic and know how to celebrate. The century-old idea of Jantelagen helps explain these contradictions, and offers visitors a fascinating key to decoding Swedish culture. As an utlandssvensk – a Swede who grew up abroad – I've always been fascinated by the unwritten rules that shape Swedish social life. I once got to chatting with a fellow Swede at a party. It was 4 July, and we discussed why our country didn't celebrate its national day as fervently as Americans. No fireworks, no parades – how come? "Well, it would be fairly embarrassing wouldn't it?" she said. "All that self-celebration. It's a bit over-the-top," she added, lowering her voice, as if there was an American hovering inches away from our table. As she explained, setting off fireworks for your nation (and therefore yourself) smacks of back-patting and ostentatiousness – two things that are anathema to much of Scandinavia. When I complimented my companion on how well she'd outlined the issue, she looked askance and waved my praise away like a bad smell. "No, please. That's just my little opinion, of course." A modest code of conduct To understand this aversion to basking in even the smallest of spotlights, many Swedes point to Jantelagen, or the Law of Jante: an unwritten social code embedded across Scandinavia that prizes humility, equality and not placing yourself above others. The term comes from Danish-Norwegian author Aksel Sandemose's satirical 1933 novel A Fugitive Crosses His Tracks, set in the fictional town of Jante. Sandemose used Jante to skewer the conformism of small-town Scandinavian life, laying out 10 "laws" designed to put anyone who considered themselves exceptional firmly back in their place. Rules such as "you're not to think you're anything special" and "you're not to think you're smarter than [anyone else]" leave the reader with a deliberately bruised ego – and that's the point. Nearly a century on, Sandemose's laws remain memorable and highly quotable, helping Jantelagen endure as cultural shorthand. How to connect with Swedes Be proactive: Small talk with strangers isn't the norm, so don't mistake reserve for unfriendliness. "Swedes tend to be very loyal and trustworthy once a friendship is established," says Gossner. "I often advise newcomers to take the initiative. Don't wait for Swedes to come to you, as they appreciate when others make the first move." Suggest fika: The Swedish ritual of cake and coffee offers a low-pressure way to socialise. Meet over coffee and a modest but delicious kanelbulle (cinnamon bun) rather than trying to force conversation in the street. Be punctual: Swedes place a high value on being on time, particularly when you're invited to someone's home. Stefan Dahlberg, a professor of political science at Mid Sweden University, has written a paper on Jantelagen's modern legacy. He sees the rules less as firm laws governing Swedish behaviour. Instead, he explains, "they are better understood as a cultural shorthand for a set of familiar norms […] that you can recognise in everyday Swedish interaction. Status differences tend to be played down, social relations are relatively informal and conspicuous self-promotion can be viewed negatively." Visitors to Sweden will likely see this in action when chatting to locals. Compliment a Swede on their English, for example, and they may quickly play it down – switching to Swedish and muttering, "Äsch, det är ju inte flytande…" (Shucks, it's not like it's fluent…). Sandemose would be proud. The qualities can also be seen in everyday Swedish rituals, from Fredagsmys – unpretentious "cosy Fridays" with friends or family – to Lördagsgodis ("Saturday-candy") that's practiced by parents as the one day that kids can unleash their sweet tooth after a week of modest abstention. That doesn't mean that Jantelagen functions as a literal rulebook – or identically across Scandinavia. Dahlberg's study of Jantelagen in Norway, a geographical and cultural neighbour, found the average respondent tended to disagree with the Jante statements. After all, Dahlberg explains, Sandemose invented the list as a scathing takedown of conformity. "So there are really two things mixed together in the concept: an egalitarian idea that nobody is inherently better than anyone else, and a more negative pressure not to distinguish yourself too much." Jante's mirror image Jantelagen has another, less obvious side. In a culture where seeking the limelight is usually frowned upon, Swedish reserve can disappear at parties when a tradition of snappsvisor (increasingly risqué songs belted out while drinking heroic amounts of aquavit) and performative speeches create safe social spaces to open up. So, while Jantelagen is often used as a reasoning for Swedish reserve and diffidence, it can also reveal the inverse. More like this: As Dahlberg notes, "'Don't think you are better than anyone else' can be read in the opposite direction: don't assume that somebody is better than you simply because they are richer, more successful or have a more prestigious title." With so much bubbling under the surface, Sweden can feel deceptively complex. Luckily, there are classes designed to help mystified foreigners. Yvonne Gossner runs Learn Swedish Culture AB – and business is booming. "I realised there was a big demand for practical insights into Swedish culture, especially for foreigners trying to navigate life here," she says. "Many felt lost or misunderstood in everyday settings, or even when trying to make Swedish friends." Case in point: a South American client once arrived at a Swedish woman's party an hour late, carrying a big dish of food as a surprise. The hostess "was not pleased" as the guests had already eaten, and the immodestly large, late-coming dish was left untouched in a bedroom. Swedes, Gossner says, place a high value on punctuality and politeness; if you're invited to a Swede's house, she suggests sending a post-party message of thanks. "There is even a Swedish joke: 'Don't forget to send a thank-you note for the thank-you note'," she adds. An unasked-for dish can risk looking like a statement that "my food is better than yours", while failing to acknowledge someone's politeness can jar the sense of social balance. Cracking the Swedish ice Lola Akinmade Åkerström, a Nigerian-American author, travel writer and photographer who moved to Sweden more than 15 years ago, was initially "a bit floored by the unspoken ethos" of Jantelagen, as well as the contradictory layers of national character. "Sweden is the most open society, run by the most private people," she says. If you want to deeply discomfit a Swede, she advises, just make eye contact on a quiet train, and hit them with "Hi! How you doing?" Yet they're not being cold, just respectful of the idea that no one should impose themselves on a stranger's space. That preference for understatement extends beyond social interactions. Travel through the countryside and you can see it reflected in the nation's beloved summer houses. "I think Swedes hold the world record in the number of summer houses per capita – around half the population has access to one," says Orvar Löfgren, professor emeritus of ethnology at Lund University. Yet these are rarely flashy second homes; instead, they reflect rustic, rural values, even among wealthy owners. (Don't think your cabin is better than other cabins, Sandemose might say.) While in Sweden, visitors might also notice small Swedish flags on birthday cakes, supermarket products and during student celebrations. "Swedes who love to see themselves as non-nationalistic are actually good at waving the flag," says Löfgren. And despite their quiet reputation, "Swedes are great at celebrating," he adds. Christmas, Easter, Midsummer, birthdays, and student exams are celebrated "with more intensity than in most European countries". You could say these occasions showcase Swedes at their best – not that they'd put it so boastfully, of course. --

item.title: The Nazi shipwrecks emerging from the Danube
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.27
The Nazi shipwrecks emerging from the Danube As the Danube shrinks under extreme heat, the river is revealing a startling remnant of Europe's wartime past. This month, record-low water levels on the Danube have exposed at least 20 German warships near Prahovo in eastern Serbia. Rusted hulls and broken masts are emerging from the river – the remains of a Nazi Black Sea fleet deliberately scuttled during World War Two. Wrecks have surfaced during previous droughts, but this summer's extreme heat and drought have brought dozens of vessels back into view. Some are believed to contain weapons and explosives, turning this stretch of one of Europe's great cruising rivers into an eerie, visible battlefield. For travellers cruising along the Danube this summer, the falling water is revealing a landscape – and history – normally hidden beneath the river. Eighty-two years beneath the Danube The story of how they got there begins more than eight decades ago. By 1944, German forces were retreating on the Eastern Front as the Soviets advanced through the region, leaving a fleet of around 200 Nazi Black Sea vessels stranded in what was an area rapidly falling under Soviet control. The Danube offered an escape route, but the Iron Gates – a narrow and historically treacherous stretch of the river – created a bottleneck. In September 1944, German Rear Admiral Paul-Willy Zieb ordered more than 200 vessels scuttled as the Red Army closed in. The ships were deliberately sunk to prevent their capture and obstruct the Soviet advance. Most have remained submerged beneath the river ever since, partly because many still contain unexploded ordnance and pose a hazard to navigation. Serbia has launched an estimated €30m removal programme to remove some of the vessels, but progress has been slow because clearing the riverbed safely is complex. For travellers, it's a striking sight along Europe's second-longest river, which stretches roughly 2,850km (1,770 miles) across 10 countries and centuries full of falling empires and shifting allegiances. Kenneth Reece, a travel planner who recently cruised the lower Danube aboard the Avalon Passion, says reminders of the region's turbulent history surrounded them throughout their trip. "We visited medieval fortresses, heard stories about life under communism and dictatorship, learned about the wars that have shaped this region and travelled through places where some of that history is still within living memory," Reece said. "Hearing about the WWII-era German shipwrecks beneath the Danube added another layer… The history wasn't only in museums or monuments. Some of it was quite literally beneath us." How to see what the Danube has revealed Nazi shipwrecks – Prahovo, Serbia: At least 20 wrecks have been visible from the riverbank at Prahovo, near the Serbian-Romanian border, this summer. Some are still believed to contain weapons or explosives, so they should be viewed from the bank rather than approached. Visibility will change as river levels rise and fall. Woolly mammoth remains – Ruse, Bulgaria: Bones exposed near the village of Ryahovo in July have been recovered by specialists from the Regional History Museum in Ruse. After conservation and study, they're expected to go on display at the museum, about 30km from where they were found. What else the river is revealing The Nazi ships aren't the only remnants emerging as the Danube falls. This August, receding water has also exposed a German army Wehrmacht motorcycle in Budapest and a 1,543lb British bomb near Virt, Slovakia, which was later safely detonated. At Gigen in Bulgaria, falling water has revealed the remains of the ancient Constantine Bridge, while near Ryahovo, archaeologists unearthed woolly mammoth tusks and bones dating back thousands of years. "For archaeologists, these moments are extremely valuable," Pavel Popov of the Regional Historical Museum in Pleven told Reuters. "It gives us a rare opportunity to observe, document and study it in its real environment." Droughts and fluctuating water levels are not new to the Danube. Europe is the fastest-warming continent, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service, warming at more than twice the global average. Rising temperatures are intensifying heat extremes and altering rainfall patterns, contributing to repeated low-water events that disrupt navigation along the river. "The Danube was revealing warnings from our past while, at the same time, perhaps giving us a warning about our future," Reece said. What low water means for travellers The consequences are already being felt by visitors to the region. This summer's low waters have forced Danube cruise operators to cancel sailings, change itineraries, transfer passengers between ships and use coaches to bypass unnavigable sections of the river. More like this: Yet the changing river can also transform what travellers encounter along the way. "We never realised that we would sail directly over the sunken German warships," said Suzanna Fulton, who recently cruised on the Viking Honir. "It was humbling and quite honestly, a cool experience." Reece said seeing evidence of the Danube's wartime history made the beauty and peacefulness of the river feel more poignant. "Today, you can sit on the deck of a river cruise ship with a glass of wine and watch these beautiful countries pass by, but this same landscape has witnessed war, fascism, oppression and tremendous human suffering," he said. "I think that's what stayed with me most. The Danube wasn't simply taking us through Europe. In many ways, it was taking us through Europe's history." --

item.title: Inside the places that shaped Dolly Parton
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.21
'Everything about her was East Tennessee': The places that shaped Dolly Parton From her Appalachian childhood to Nashville and Dollywood, a journey through the Tennessee she loved – and transformed in return. On a sunny day on 24 June 2026, hundreds of travellers, locals and Dolly Parton fans from across the US gathered in the small rural community of Cornersville, less than an hour's drive south of Nashville, for the unveiling of her Tennessean Travel Stop. It was the country star's last public appearance before her death just two months later. Wearing her signature fringe and rhinestones and a grin as bright as that Tennessee morning, Parton cut the ribbon and welcomed travellers to the new roadside stop, complete with a Southern meat-and-three restaurant, live music and – of course – a Dolly-themed gift shop. It was a fitting final chapter for an artist whose life and career were inseparable from Tennessee. From crooning about the Smoky Mountains to investing in rural East Tennessee where she grew up, Parton spent decades sharing her home state with the world – and transforming it in return. Explore Parton's Tennessee mountain home In 1964, US President Lyndon B Johnson launched the War on Poverty, a federal effort to reduce poverty and expand economic opportunity across the United States. Southern Appalachia, one of the nation's poorest regions, was thrust into the national spotlight. Media portrayals often depicted its residents as backward and destitute, reinforcing the caricature of the "hillbilly", a stereotype that had persisted since the 19th Century. But when Dolly Rebecca Parton came into the spotlight, this daughter of Appalachia who grew up in a two-room cabin with 11 brothers and sisters offered the world a different view of her home: one of joy, dignity and talent. Follow Dolly Parton's story across Tennessee Sevierville: See the bronze statue of Parton outside the Sevier County Courthouse and The Pines, where she performed for a paying audience for the first time at just 10 years old. RCA Studio B, Nashville: Visit the legendary recording studio on Music Row where Dolly Parton and other iconic artists like Elvis Presley recorded some of their greatest hits. The Country Music Hall of Fame, Nashville: A must-visit Nashville institution that chronicles the history of country music through artefacts, exhibits and the stories of the artists who trailblazed the genre. Dollywood, Pigeon Forge: Set in the Smoky Mountains that Parton loved so dearly, Dollywood takes guests on a journey through the singer's roots, from an exact replica of her childhood two-room cabin to the Dolly Parton Experience, which displays childhood memorabilia. "Dolly Parton told a new story about Appalachia that was rooted in her very particular experience," said Dr Jessie Wilkerson, a history professor and Appalachian scholar at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. "Yes, her family was poor, but they weren't desperate or hopeless, and they took care of one another. There was a lot of love and beauty in the place where she grew up, and so we get a different story about Appalachia through her." In the title track of her 1973 album, My Tennessee Mountain Home, Parton describes her Appalachian home as "peaceful as a baby's sigh". The landscape around her childhood home on the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains, along with Appalachia's storytelling traditions and bluegrass heritage, inspired much of Parton's music. In Great Smoky Mountains National Park, a blue-grey mist that gives the Smokies its name settles over the peaks and valleys and waterfalls tumble through the forest. The 522,000-acre expanse is threaded with hiking trails and scenic overlooks, with autumn bringing a canvas of brilliant jewel tones and spring a kaleidoscope of wildflowers to the lower slopes. The landscape was a reoccurring muse, from the mountain blooms that inspired her 1987 ballad Wildflowers to the fog-covered peaks evoked in Blue Smoke, the title track of her 2014 album, and the pastoral idyll captured in My Tennessee Mountain Home. In nearby Sevierville, the main town serving rural Locust Ridge, where Parton grew up, the region's pride in its local legend is evident. A bronze statue on the courthouse lawn depicts her as a young girl playing guitar. Down the street is the Wings of Wander mural, inspired by her hit song Love Is Like a Butterfly, and the Red's Cafe mural, another larger-than-life depiction of Parton as a child, this time getting a cheeseburger from her favourite childhood restaurant. "People in East Tennessee really, really adore her, and it's something that's been important for the region to have someone who's really proud of coming from there, and who's a positive representation of Appalachia, when historically the representations of the region are the opposite," Wilkerson said. Retracing Parton's path in Nashville On the day Parton graduated from high school in 1964, she boarded a Greyhound bus headed west for the neon lights of Nashville. In a letter home shortly after arriving, feeling homesick and uncertain, she wrote, "Nashville isn't what I thought it was gonna be, but I think I'll like it once I get used to it." "When she came to Nashville, she came with a very distinct East Tennessee identity and made that very clear in both her music and her accent," said Robert K Oermann, co-author of her memoir Dolly Parton: Songteller, My Life in Lyrics and a longtime collaborator. "Everything about her was East Tennessee and mountain, and I think that was the message she brought to Nashville." Nashville looks very different today from when Parton first stepped off that bus 62 years ago, but visitors can still trace Parton's path from her early days fresh out of Sevier County to her rise as a country music icon who never lost the Appalachian sound of home even as she became one of Nashville's biggest stars. On Music Row, the city's historic record-industry district, visitors can step inside RCA Studio B where a blue X marks "The Sweet Spot" where Parton recorded hits including Jolene and I Will Always Love You – both of which she wrote on the same day. Nearby, the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum is featuring Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker, an exhibition spanning her career and featuring memorabilia like her Gibson five-string banjo and handwritten music drafts. A few blocks away, the historic Ryman Auditorium is where a 13-year-old Parton made her Grand Ole Opry debut in 1959 and earned three encores. Murals of Parton dot the city in her honour, museum exhibits display her stage costumes and in the wake of her passing, fans have left flowers on her star on the Music City Walk of Fame. Visiting Parton's Appalachia Nashville, however, was never the end of Parton's journey. The further her career carried her from the mountains to Nashville and eventually Hollywood, the more firmly she seemed to plant her roots at the centre of her story. In 1982, she told Barbara Walters in an interview about her dream of opening a "mountain Disneyland" in her Appalachian home region. More like this: Today, that "mountain Disneyland" is Dollywood, a major tourist destination in Sevier County that invites visitors into the version of Appalachia Parton spent her career sharing with the world. Beyond the thrill rides and water park are shows featuring Parton's music, some performed by members of her own family. But to Parton, Dollywood was also a way to give back to the mountains and the community that nurtured her. --

item.title: French 75
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.57
This crisp, citrusy French 75 cocktail combines gin, fresh lemon juice, and Champagne for a bubbly, festive drink that’s remarkably easy to make. It’s equally at home at a New Year’s Eve party, holiday brunch, or summer gathering. Shaking the gin and lemon juice with simple syrup and ice properly dilutes the cocktail and adds a delicate sweetness. Be sure to pop your Champagne into the fridge for at least 4 hours before assembling to keep everything cold. And don’t skip the lemon twist: It perfumes this elegant cocktail as you sip. French 75 FAQ Isn’t a French 75 made with cognac? It can be. Gin is common in modern versions, including this recipe, but cognac does have historical precedent. Making the drink with gin gives the French 75 a crisper, more botanical flavor; using cognac makes one that tastes richer and more warming. Feel free to substitute cognac here for the gin in equal measure. Can I use prosecco instead of Champagne? Yes. Cava, prosecco, or another dry sparkling wine can stand in for Champagne. Look for a bottle labeled “brut” to keep the finished French 75 from becoming overly sweet. Read more about buying Champagne: What if my French 75 is too sweet? If you prefer a drier cocktail, reduce the simple syrup to ½ or ¼ oz. You can always add more to taste. Why is it called a French 75? The cocktail takes its name from the French 75-millimeter field gun used during World War I—a reference to the drink’s considerable kick. Its precise origins are debated, but, according to Chris Hannah, head bartender at Arnaud’s French 75 Bar in New Orleans, allied French and American military celebrated with cognac and Champagne, toasting the French 75 cannon for keeping them safe. Today, you’ll more often see the drink made with dry gin. Can I make French 75s ahead? Not entirely. It’s best to keep the Champagne chilled and sealed until you’re ready to serve, but you can mix the gin, lemon juice, and simple syrup up to 6 hours ahead. For 8 servings: Stir 1½ cups gin, ¾ cups fresh lemon juice, ¾ cups simple syrup, and ½ cup water (the water replaces the dilution caused by shaking) in a pitcher to combine. Chill until ready to use. To serve, pour 3½ oz. of your chilled gin mixture into a flute glass and top with 2 oz. Champagne as directed. Recipe information - Total Time 5 minutes - Yield Makes 1 Preparation - Step 1Combine 1½ oz. gin, ¾ oz. fresh lemon juice, and ¾ oz. simple syrup in a cocktail shaker. Fill shaker with ice, cover, and shake vigorously until outside of shaker is very cold, about 20 seconds. Step 2Strain cocktail through a Hawthorne strainer or a slotted spoon into a large flute. Top with 2 oz. Champagne and garnish with long spiral lemon twist. Editor’s note: This French 75 recipe was first published in our May 2016 issue; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our favorite gin drinks →

item.title: Pumpkin Chili
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.65
This pumpkin chili gets an entire can of pumpkin purée—but you’d hardly know it. Rather than making the chili taste like pumpkin, the purée gives it velvety richness, body, and an autumnal hue. (Be sure to buy pure pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling.) Best of all, it comes together on the stovetop in just 35 minutes, making it an easy weeknight dinner that’s equally at home on game day or Halloween. One unusual step makes this quick chili work: Instead of browning the ground beef separately, you’ll cook it directly in the spiced pumpkin mixture. This keeps the meat tender during the short cook time while a vigorous stir breaks it down into chunky, satisfying bits. Worcestershire sauce brings in plenty of savory depth. Top each bowl with sour cream, sliced jalapeño, and crunchy toasted pepitas. Pumpkin chili FAQ Can I use a different ground meat? Yes. Ground turkey and chicken both work well, but ground pork makes an especially rich, savory chili. Swap an equal amount of any of these for the beef and otherwise follow the recipe as written. Can I substitute butternut squash purée for pumpkin purée? Yes. Canned butternut squash or even sweet potato works well here—just make sure it’s 100% purée, not pie mix or otherwise sweetened. How should I store leftover pumpkin chili? Let leftover chili cool, then refrigerate it in an airtight container for up to 5 days or freeze it for up to 3 months. Reheat it gently on the stovetop or in the microwave, adding a splash of broth or water as needed to loosen it. Recipe information - Total Time 35 minutes - Yield 4 servings Ingredients 2 1 1 4 1 2 1½ 1 2 3 1 1 4 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Add 1 onion, coarsely chopped, and 1 medium jalapeño, coarsely chopped; cook, stirring often, until slightly softened, 3–4 minutes. Step 2Add 4 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add one 15-oz. can pumpkin purée, 2 tsp. smoked paprika, and 1½ tsp. ground cumin and cook, stirring often, until some of the liquid in purée has evaporated, 3–4 minutes. Step 3Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 2 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, breaking up beef with a wooden spoon and stirring often, until meat is cooked through and incorporated into purée to create a thick paste, about 5 minutes. Step 4Add one 15-oz. can black beans, rinsed, one 15 oz. can pinto beans, rinsed, and 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Reduce heat so mixture is at a simmer and cook, stirring occasionally, until thickened to the consistency of chili, 15–18 minutes. Stir in remaining 1 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce. Step 5To serve, ladle chili into bowls and top each with a dollop of sour cream; scatter unsalted, roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas) and thinly sliced jalapeños over.

item.title: Classic Chicken Noodle Soup
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.56
There are plenty of shortcuts you could take with homemade chicken noodle soup, but this recipe isn’t interested in them. A whole chicken simmers with onion, carrots, celery, garlic, dill, and peppercorns to make its own deeply savory, golden broth. It takes a little time, but the result is about as classic and comforting as chicken noodle soup gets. The key to juicy chicken is treating the breasts and legs differently. Once the breast reaches 155°, you’ll pull the bird from the pot and remove the breast meat to keep it moist. The legs, wings, and carcass go back in, allowing the dark meat to become fall-apart tender while the bones and cartilage-rich wings impart richer body and flavor. A fresh round of carrots and celery goes into the strained broth along with the pasta, so the vegetables cook until tender without turning to mush. Ditalini is ideal here because the tiny rounds cook quickly right in the broth; other small shapes work too (more on that below). A generous handful of fresh dill added at the end keeps things bright, but parsley or chives make good substitutes. Chicken Noodle Soup FAQ What are the best noodles for chicken noodle soup? Ditalini is ideal because it cooks quickly enough to go directly into the chicken broth. Orzo, ABC pasta, or small macaroni work too. If using longer-cooking pasta, such as egg noodles, spaghetti, or fusilli, cook it separately. The extra starch and cooking time required by larger noodles can cause the broth to become too reduced. Can I use chicken breasts instead of a whole chicken? For this particular recipe, stick with a whole chicken. The breast provides tender shredded meat, while the legs, wings, bones, and cartilage give the homemade broth richness, flavor, and body. Removing the breast meat early prevents it from drying out while the rest of the chicken continues to simmer. Can I make chicken noodle soup ahead of time? Yes. The strained broth and shredded chicken can be made up to 3 days ahead; refrigerate them separately. The carrots and celery can also be cut up to 3 days ahead and refrigerated. To finish the soup, bring the broth to a boil over medium-high heat, then proceed with the recipe, adding the pasta, chicken, and fresh vegetables as directed. Can you freeze chicken noodle soup? Yes. Freeze the broth and shredded chicken, separately or combined, for up to 3 months. Add the pasta, fresh carrots and celery, and dill when reheating and finishing the soup. You can also freeze leftover chicken noodle soup in portions for up to 3 months, though the pasta will soften somewhat after thawing and reheating. Watch Molly make chicken noodle soup: - Fork Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour 40 minutes - Yield 6 servings Ingredients 1 1 2 4 4 2 ½ 1 6 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Season one 3½–4-lb. whole chicken all over with 1 Tbsp. plus 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 2¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and place in a large pot. (For even better-tasting meat, season chicken up to 24 hours ahead and refrigerate until ready to cook.) Step 2Cut 2 medium onions into quarters. (No need to remove the onion skins; leaving them on helps the broth develop its golden color.) Trim and coarsely chop 2 medium carrots, peeled, and 2 celery stalks. Cut 2 heads of garlic in half crosswise. (These will eventually be strained out, so there’s no reason to be precious with your cuts here.) Step 3Place chopped vegetables, 2 sprigs dill, and 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns in pot with chicken. Pour in 14 cups cold water (or just enough to barely cover chicken) and bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Cook, reducing heat as needed to maintain a simmer, adding water as needed to keep the chicken submerged, and skimming off any foam from surface with a large spoon, until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of breast registers 155°, 20–25 minutes. Step 4Using tongs, carefully lift chicken out of pot and transfer to a cutting board. Let sit until cool enough to handle. Step 5Arrange chicken breast side up. Grab a wing and pull it outward so you can see where it attaches to the body. Using a sharp boning or chef’s knife, cut through the joint to separate wing from breast (if you hit bone, you’re in the wrong spot; pull the wing out farther to help you get to the place where the joint meets the socket). Repeat with wing on other side. Step 6Cut through skin connecting 1 leg to carcass. Pull leg back until ball joint pops out of its socket; cut through joint to separate leg. Repeat with leg on other side. Cut along left side of breastbone (which runs right down the center of the breast). Angling your knife, cut breast meat away from carcass on left side. Repeat process on right side. Step 7Pull off and discard any skin from legs and breasts (removing this skin prevents excess fat from rendering into the broth; no need to discard skin on the wings). Return legs, wings, and what remains of the carcass to pot. (You should now have only the chicken breasts remaining on your cutting board.) Return soup to a simmer and cook, occasionally skimming fat from surface with spoon, until reduced by 1–2", very flavorful, and leg meat is very tender and pulls apart easily, about 40 minutes. Step 8Meanwhile, shred cooled chicken breasts with 2 forks into bite-size pieces. Step 9Cut remaining 2 medium carrots, peeled, on a diagonal into ½" pieces. Thinly slice remaining 2 celery stalks, then finely chop enough dill to yield ¼ cup. Step 10Using tongs, transfer 2 chicken legs to cutting board and let cool slightly before shredding. Set a large fine-mesh sieve over another large pot. Strain broth into second pot; discard bones, carcass, wings, and vegetables. Do Ahead: Broth and shredded chicken can be made 3 days ahead; refrigerate separately. Carrots and celery can be cut 3 days ahead; refrigerate. Broth and chicken can also be frozen, separately or combined, for up to 3 months. Step 11Bring broth to a boil over medium-high heat. Add 6 oz. ditalini and stir once. Cook 5 minutes. (If using a larger or longer-cooking pasta, cook it separately according to package directions rather than in the broth.) Add carrots, celery, and all of the shredded chicken meat to pot and cook until pasta is cooked through and carrots and celery are tender but not mushy, about 5 minutes. Step 12Remove pot from heat and stir in dill so it stays bright and fresh; season very generously with salt and freshly ground black pepper. Ladle chicken soup into bowls and season with more pepper. Editor’s note: This chicken noodle soup recipe was first published in January 2020; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our favorite noodle soup recipes →

item.title: Saucy Pork Chops With Coconut Crisp
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.02
If the only pork chops you’ve encountered are dry and leathery, give this recipe a try. Thick-cut pork chops are more forgiving of extended cook times and the generous pour of sauce makes up for any mistakes, should they occur. The buttery pan sauce takes a page from Chris Morocco’s Steak for One, gaining its silky texture from a bottle of oyster sauce. Anything with the word “premium” on the bottle is preferred for flavor, and avoid any oyster-flavored sauces—they are too salty. The coconut crisp is the star of the show. For the best visual effect, you want big shards of coconut flakes rather than shredded here. Doubled up and stored in an airtight container, the crisp will be good for up to five days. Use it over seared tofu or chicken breasts, or buttered white rice with a drizzle of soy sauce. Find more great pork chop recipes here: Green Chile Puttanesca Pork Chop; Rosemary and Dried Cherry Pork Chops; and Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops. Recipe information - Total Time 45 minutes - Yield 2 servings Ingredients Coconut Crisp 1 1 3 ½ 1 1 ½ Pork Chops and assembly 2 2 1 2 2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Coconut CrispStep 1Cook 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, one 2" piece ginger, peeled, cut into matchsticks, and 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large cast-iron or other heavy skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until scallions and ginger are barely golden and wilted, 6–8 minutes. Add ½ cup unsweetened coconut flakes and cook, stirring often, until coconut is golden, about 5 minutes. Transfer to a medium bowl; reserve skillet. Stir 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1 tsp. garlic powder, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt into coconut crisp. Do Ahead: Coconut crisp can be made 5 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature. - Pork Chops and assemblyStep 2Sprinkle two 1"-thick bone-in well-marbled pork rib chops all over with 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and a generous amount of freshly ground pepper. Heat 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil in reserved skillet over medium-high. Cook pork chops, undisturbed, until browned underneath, about 5 minutes. Turn and continue cooking, turning every 2 minutes or so, until pork chops are deeply browned on both sides, 10–12 minutes (an instant-read thermometer inserted near the bone should register 145°). Transfer pork chops to a cutting board and let rest while you make the sauce. Step 3Reduce heat to medium and cook 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan, swirling occasionally, until it foams then browns, about 1 minute. Pour in ½ cup water and bring to a simmer, scraping up any browned bits. Stir in 2 Tbsp. premium oyster sauce and cook sauce until it thickens enough to lightly coat a spoon, about 2 minutes. Step 4Thinly slice pork chops and transfer to a platter; spoon sauce over. Top with coconut crisp and thinly sliced jalapeño.

item.title: Pear Tarta De Santiago
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.42
I’m fascinated by the North African influence on Spanish cuisine. Take this traditional flourless almond cake, or Tarta de Santiago, which was a by-product of increased almond cultivation and culinary traditions during Spain’s Moorish era. The dense cake is perfectly suited for a relaxed breakfast, morning coffee break, or afternoon tea. This seasonal version includes chopped pears, though apples (or no fruit) work just as well. After the cake has cooled, I like to rest it in the fridge; then bring it back to room temperature for a soft and fluffy texture. The oldest recorded recipe for Tarta de Santiago dates back to the 1830s, via Luis Bartolomé de Leybar; written references to a similar almond cake, “Torta Real,” imply it has existed for centuries longer. A popular option at bakeries and cafés throughout Spain, particularly in the Galicia region, during the Feast of St. James, it was—and still is—served to travelers of the Camino de Santiago as a traditional reward when they reach Santiago de Compostela. More bakes for almond lovers here: Extremadura Almond Pie; Anytime Almond Cake; and Almond Croissant Galette. Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour - Yield 6–8 servings Ingredients 5 1¼ 1 1 2 2½ 1–2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Lightly coat a 9"-diameter cake pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Using an electric mixer on medium-high speed, beat 5 large eggs and 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar in a large bowl until aerated and very pale yellow, about 5 minutes. Reduce mixer speed to medium-low and beat in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, 1 Tbsp. finely grated orange zest, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Add 2½ cups (250 g) almond flour or meal and beat just to combine. Using a rubber spatula, fold in 1–2 Bartlett pears, cored, cut into ¼" pieces (about 2 cups). Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Step 2Bake tarta until golden brown and it springs back when gently pressed, 35–40 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack; let tarta cool in pan 10 minutes. Run an offset spatula or small knife around sides of pan to loosen cake. Turn out onto rack, carefully turn right side up, and let cool completely. Step 3Just before serving, transfer tarta to a large plate and dust with powdered sugar. Do Ahead: Tarta can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature (or chill if you prefer a softer texture).

item.title: What My Job Is Like as a Culinary Producer
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.41
It takes a village to publish a magazine—and website and app and Youtube channel and more. Phew! Today we’re introducing you to Bon Appétit’s senior culinary producer Mallary Santucci, who gets our recipes ready for their closeups. Bon Appétit: Hey, Mallary! How would you describe your job to someone you’re sitting next to on a plane? Mallary Santucci: I always say “I make food for TV” because that’s the simplest explanation. But really, I handle all culinary logistics behind the scenes to make food appear on camera for our YouTube and social channels (like Instagram and TikTok). It’s a lot of project management: anything from buying groceries, to writing recipe prep lists, to sketching out a production schedule for culinary stylists and producers. I basically get food hair-and-makeup-ready for camera! What’s a typical day like for you at Bon Appétit? Or does a typical day even exist? No! And that’s the best part of my job. Some days I am shopping at the farmers market or a specialty grocery store. Other days I am making a spreadsheet about recipe ingredients or writing what we call a run of show. Sometimes I’m in front of the camera (though you’ll only see my hands!). It’s managed chaos at all times and I love that. My favorite days are when I am searching for specific ingredients. It’s like a city-wide scavenger hunt. What’s on your shoot schedule for this week and/or next? This week I prepped and then shot an episode of Taste Panel for Epicurious while overseeing another team on a new show in the Test Kitchen with our food director Chris Morocco. Next week we are filming Bake Club, which we do every month. Then I’m shopping and prepping for French Fundamentals with chef Alexia Duchêne. It’s always a balance of shooting one thing and simultaneously preparing for the next shoot coming down the pipeline. What are your favorite types of assignments to work on? I love the shoots that are culinary-heavy. I have a knack for logistics and organization, which helps with my role, but my background is in restaurants, and cooking is the fun part of my work. It sounds cheesy, but I want to help people learn to cook. I want the average person at home to feel confident making dinner for their friends and family—and have fun doing it. How about an assignment that was particularly challenging or taught you something new? We did a shoot with chef Dominique Crenn that was definitely challenging! And so fun and interesting. She does a lot of molecular gastronomy, which is not my area of expertise. I was able to play with new ingredients and techniques, and it challenged me to learn a style of cooking I otherwise had not worked with. Though they may not know it, our readers have seen your adept hands many times! What’s a video where your hands star that you’re particularly proud of? This is so funny! My hands appear on camera all the time and my friends and family will send me a video and ask, “Is this you?” Usually, yes! In this salsa taste test, it was even the manicure from my wedding. How does someone break into this part of the food industry? Any advice? Honestly, there's no one right way to break into this (or any) industry. A lot of people go to culinary school and get into food media or the restaurant industry that way. But I never went to culinary school; I went to college for art and education. As soon as I graduated I knew I wanted to work in food. It took a few years to make it happen—I moved to New York, worked in an unrelated field, left New York, taught abroad, traveled. When I came back to the US, I got a job working in front of house in restaurants. I was too intimidated to apply for a job cooking with no experience. But I showed such interest in the food and details, a chef told me I would “need to start somewhere” and encouraged me to start working in the kitchen. That’s how I got my first professional cooking job. I just jumped in and worked hard. I had some basic skills from growing up in a family that cooked a ton, but learned all of my professional skills live fire while on the line. What recipes have you recently saved on Bon Appétit? Watermelon Som Tam: I could slurp it up all day during this hot sweaty summer! Miso Curry Beef and Green Beans: A flavorful, quick dinner after a long work day. Tiny Tomato Galettes: Adorable and absolutely delicious. Have eaten for breakfast! What’s the Bon Appétit recipe you make most often? Our cooking director Emma Laperruque’s Sheet-Pan Halloumi With Avocado and Citrus. I am truly obsessed. I often sub croutons for the pita and think of it as a spicy citrus panzanella. I love anything acidic, spicy, creamy and crunchy. This one checks all those boxes. Also, new in the rotation, our senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewyck’s Grilled Steak With Spicy Peanut Dressing from the summer issue. I love to grill, and the peanuts and herbs are so texturally satisfying and fresh! You often test for our cookbook roundups. What’s a cookbook you’ve loved from this past year? And what about a timeless, all-time favorite on your shelf? I have a secret: I rarely ever cook a full recipe from a cookbook. (I swear I stick to the rules when reviewing for roundups!) But in my day to day, I tend to read cookbooks more for inspiration and the gorgeous stories and visuals. Some recent favorites are Boustany by Sami Tamimi, My Cambodia by Nite Yun, and Setting a Place For Us by Hawa Hassan. Some standbys I’ve loved are Six Seasons by Joshua McFadden, The Food Lab by Kenji López-Alt, and Made in India by Meera Sodha. I also collect older cookbooks because the outdated food styling cracks me up. My wife urges me to not pick up the free cookbooks being given away on the sidewalk, but I can’t resist. The pictures are funny! What kitchen tool or gadget or appliance are you obsessed with right now? I am a less-is-more type of cook. I stick to the most basic and necessary tools, and find it hard to be convinced otherwise. For me, the essentials are: a chef’s knife, wooden spoon, whisk, rubber spatula, Microplane, fish spatula, cast-iron skillet, Dutch oven, and cutting board. Gadgets take up space and have to be realllllly worth it for the space in a kitchen. I don’t think people need as much as they think they do (don’t tell the commerce editors!). Make Mallary’s go-tos To support our team’s journalism and access our full collection of Test Kitchen–vetted recipes (there are thousands!), please consider subscribing.

item.title: Craft Retreats Are all the Rage—These Are the Ones Worth Booking
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.65
In a studio in Kenya, hands smooth a mound of clay on a spinning pottery wheel. In a women's cooperative in Morocco's High Atlas Mountains, members weave wedding blankets, and at a workshop in Bagru in India, artisans pound block prints onto fabric. It's all captured in the new documentary Handmade Future, directed by Kirsten Dickerson, the cofounder of Artist & Nomad, a social-impact business focused on craft. “Things made by hand connect souls and so are worth preserving,” she says. “Craft doesn't just provide income; it provides community and cultural identity.” Artist & Nomad's 2027 retreats to Kenya, Morocco, and Oaxaca will take travelers into the homes and studios of artisans from the film, a trend that nods to rising interest in artisan-based itineraries. Yi Crafts founder Yiran Duan, hailing from the Bai ethnic group in China, is broadening the textile-focused retreats she leads in her hometown of Dali to explore vanishing handicrafts throughout Yunnan, such as wood carving in the mountain town of Shaxi and bark papermaking practiced by Naxi priests in the village of Baisha. Oaxaca-based travel company Thread Caravan has new itineraries exploring Portugal's esparto-grass-weaving tradition, Iceland's wool heritage, and the preservation of Mexico's heirloom cottons. Majestic Disorder Travels recently introduced an Egypt itinerary combining the Pyramids with visits to weaving and pottery studios; a 2027 Brazil trip will focus on the food, music, and textiles of the coastal cities of Guarujá and Santos. Japanese hospitality brand Maana runs a collection of renovated machiya town houses in Kyoto that showcase traditional crafts such as fuki-urushi, a 9,000-year-old lacquering technique, and double as bases for the brand's pottery and design retreats; a fourth property and its first new build, Maana Annex—designed in collaboration with award-winning studios Norm Architects and KAD—is set to debut this December. Molly Berry, the founder of the Luna Zorro textile brand, recently renovated a two-room guesthouse in the heart of Antigua, Guatemala, with textiles handwoven by artisan partners and locally made ceramics, lighting, and woodwork. The space hosts artists in residence as well as travelers attending classes at her nearby studio. Next year Berry will expand her trips to Morocco, Mexico, and Spain. “People want a deeper connection to the creative landscape of a country and culture,” she says. “Craft is that connection.” This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: The Best Ways to See Cappadocia’s Hot Air Balloons—And What Mistakes Not to Make
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.47
Each morning at the crack of dawn, in one of the great Instagram moments of our time, 165 enormous balloons begin to swell in Cappadocia's half-light, their burners briefly illuminating the valley floor. One rises, then another, then seemingly all of them—great striped bulbs of crimson, lemon yellow, and turquoise drifting between the fairy chimneys as the first sunlight catches the dusty pink folds of the landscape. It is an extraordinary sight, and while taking to the skies in a wicker basket is the headline experience, you needn’t actually fly to get the best of it. In some ways, the view is better from terra firma, where the balloons themselves become part of the scenery, skimming ridge lines, disappearing behind rock formations, and occasionally floating so close that you can hear the roar of the burners. There is, however, a little more to seeing Cappadocia’s balloons than booking a cave hotel and setting an alarm. Flights are weather-dependent, launch sites change according to the wind, and the difference between standing in precisely the right spot and watching hundreds of balloons disappear over the opposite ridge or missing them completely can be a matter of minutes. Here's how to do it properly. Jump to… Where to see the hot air balloons in Cappadocia Göreme is the center of the action. Most of the photographs that have made Cappadocia famous are taken in and around the valleys surrounding this small town, where the combination of deeply carved terrain, fairy chimneys, and hundreds of cave dwellings gives the balloons something suitably theatrical to float over. For the classic panorama, head for one of the elevated viewpoints around Göreme or towards Love Valley, where you can watch balloons rise from the valley floor and gradually scatter across the sky. The precise spectacle changes daily because balloons travel with the wind rather than following a fixed route. Love Valley is particularly photogenic when the wind cooperates, its improbable stone pinnacles providing scale beneath the balloons, while Rose and Red valleys offer a wilder backdrop of corrugated pink rock and the higher ground around Uçhisar gives a far broader perspective. The easiest option requires considerably less commitment. Many of Göreme’s cave hotels have terraces facing the valleys, which means you can watch the morning migration with coffee in hand and return to your bed immediately afterwards. Just check the orientation before booking, since where the balloons actually drift will always depend on that morning’s wind. What time do the hot air balloons fly in Cappadocia? Flights are organized around sunrise, when the atmosphere is generally at its coolest and most stable. The first balloons begin lifting off before the sun itself appears, with another wave following shortly afterwards if conditions allow. The exact clock time therefore changes dramatically through the year—summer can mean being in position before 5 a.m., while winter affords a rather more civilized start. If you're watching rather than flying, arrive while it is still dark. Inflation is part of the show, as across the valley floor, enormous envelopes lie crumpled in fields before fans slowly give them shape—then the burners start, sending pulses of orange through the fabric. By the time the horizon begins to turn pink, the first baskets are already leaving the ground. How to book a hot air balloon flight in Cappadocia Book directly with a licensed balloon operator through your hotel or via a local tour agency. Balloon flights are one of the region’s biggest draws, and so the most reputable operators can fill up weeks ahead, particularly from spring to autumn. Prices fluctuate considerably according to demand, season and the type of flight, and usually include an early-morning hotel pick-up, transfer to the launch site, the flight itself, and a post-landing celebration. When comparing options, look beyond the cheapest price. Check the basket capacity, expected flight duration, cancellation and refund policy, and whether the operator will rebook you if weather intervenes. Cappadocia’s baskets can be large, so paying more for a smaller group can mean rather more room to move—and fewer elbows competing for the same sunrise photograph. The best viewpoints for watching the hot air balloons in Cappadocia There is no single best viewpoint because the horizontal direction of Cappadocia's balloons is dictated largely by the wind, so the most dramatic location changes from morning to morning. However, the panoramic viewpoints above Göreme are the safest all-round bet, offering enough altitude and a sufficiently wide field of vision that you should see plenty even when the balloons drift elsewhere. Love Valley is better if you want the archetypal Cappadocia composition of balloons punctuating a forest of fairy chimneys, while the ridges around Rose Valley give the landscape more room to breathe. Meanwhile, from Uçhisar's higher terraces and viewpoints, Cappadocia unfurls below in great geological folds, with Göreme and its surrounding valleys in the distance. The balloons may be smaller in the frame, but on the right morning you can see dozens spread across the horizon. How to book a hot air balloon photography tour in Cappadocia The photographs of Cappadocia that appear effortless generally involve a surprisingly energetic morning. Dedicated tours see a driver and professional photographer collect you before dawn and move between locations according to the wind, launch sites, and light. Tours range from straightforward sunrise photography trips for people carrying their own cameras to elaborate private shoots involving photographers, flowing dresses, carpets, and vintage cars, the latter becoming almost a Cappadocian sub-genre of their own. When booking, ask exactly what is included, how many locations you are likely to visit, whether transport is private or shared, and—crucially—what happens if flights are canceled. Some photographers can substitute a sunrise shoot elsewhere in Cappadocia or reschedule for another morning. Do Cappadocia’s hot air balloons fly every day? The hot air balloons are scheduled to operate year-round, but they certainly don't fly every day. Wind, visibility, rain, snow, and other atmospheric conditions can keep the entire fleet on the ground, and the decision ultimately rests on whether conditions are safe for flying. If seeing the balloons is non-negotiable, give yourself several mornings in Cappadocia rather than arriving for a single night. Book any balloon flight for the first morning of your stay, and if weather grounds it, that leaves some possibility of being moved to a subsequent day. How long are Cappadocia's balloons in the air? Most standard passenger flights spend roughly an hour in the air. For viewers on the ground, however, the spectacle lasts longer. Inflation begins before sunrise, balloons launch in waves, and different wind speeds mean some remain visible long after others have disappeared behind a ridge. Allow at least 90 minutes if you want to watch the whole performance. What is the best time of year to see hot air balloons in Cappadocia? There is no official balloon season, since flights can operate throughout the year whenever conditions permit. But your odds—and the Cappadocia you see beneath them—change considerably with the calendar. From late April into June, the valleys are greener, and the mornings are milder. September and October bring settled conditions, softer autumnal light, and none of midsummer’s fiercest daytime heat. Summer generally offers reliable flying conditions, but also the year’s earliest alarms and largest crowds. In winter, weather cancellations become more frequent and standing on a ridge before sunrise requires considerably more clothing, but fresh snow changes Cappadocia completely, as white settles into every crease of the valleys and caps the fairy chimneys. Whichever month you choose, stay for more than one dawn. Cappadocia’s great trick is that the photograph you have seen a thousand times is never quite the photograph you get—the wind changes, the balloons scatter differently, the light lands somewhere new. And shortly after sunrise, almost as quickly as they appeared, they are gone. This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller Middle East.

item.title: Airfares Are at Record Highs. Here's How to Find Affordable Flights
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.04
To the chagrin of budget travelers everywhere, airfares have continued to climb to new highs throughout 2026. In July 2026, for example, average airfares were nearly 26% more expensive than in July 2025, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics—a significant hit to travelers’ wallets. And unfortunately, due to a complex web of geopolitical and economic factors, prices aren’t expected to drop anytime soon. Historically, fall is the time of year when airfares cool off, but this year, shoulder season deals are harder than ever to find. In fact, airfares for fall are trending about 2% higher compared to summer prices, according to Expedia. Average airfares this autumn for domestic flights range from about $150 to $400 roundtrip, according to data emailed from Going. On international routes, flights to Europe are as high as $800 roundtrip, and airfares to the Caribbean are reaching up to $500. However, while it might sound hopeless to try to scour booking sites for a good deal, rest assured there are tried-and-true strategies that travelers can use for finding reasonably priced fares through the end of the year. “Flexibility is key—both with dates and destination—to find affordable flights this fall,” says Jennifer Yellin, managing editor of Points Path, which shows travelers flight search results priced in points and miles. Here are our top tips for unlocking affordable airfares through the end of the year. Target an airline and airport known for deals Your choice of carrier, airport of origin, and destination can all play a major part in the final cost of your airfare. Aim to fly into or out of an airport that has a strong track record of offering affordable flights. Going analyzed its 2026 flight deal data to find the US airports that have offered the most affordable departing flights so far in 2026. It found the best airports for cheap domestic flights were Denver (DEN), with 150 departing flight deals that cost an average of $219; New Orleans (MSY), which had 166 deals that were about $228; and Orlando (MCO), which offered 146 deals at an average of $211. Other top airports for domestic deals were Fort-Lauderdale (FLL), Los Angeles (LAX), Charleston (CHS), Raleigh-Durham (RDU), Tampa (TPA), Portland (PDX), and Las Vegas (LAS). The best US airports for international flight deals were Boston (BOS), with 415 deals at about $451 roundtrip; New York (JFK), which has seen 404 international deals so far this year at an average of $445; and Newark (EWR), which has had 333 international deals for about $450 each. Other top airports for international deals included Chicago (ORD), Los Angeles (LAX), Raleigh-Durham (RDU), Orlando (MCO), Miami (MIA), Washington Dulles (IAD), and Austin (AUS). Departing from one of these airports can add up to significant savings. If it’s feasible, consider driving or taking a train to one of these to score discounted airfare for your next big trip. Some airlines offer a greater number of deals, too. Going found that American Airlines offers the most domestic deals (646 so far in 2026), and United offers the most international deals (1,850 and counting this year). Looking to these carriers first could help uncover the most affordable fare quickly. Carefully time your trip The timing of your vacation can make all the difference in finding affordable airfare. Shoulder season is traditionally an off-peak stretch with added savings for travelers, but with off-season deals shrinking, fliers need to get even more specific with timing. Specifically, consider pushing back your fall getaway as late on the calendar as possible, and just before hitting the start of the winter holidays. “Summer demand has spilled into fall,” according to Expedia’s fall travel outlook report. Pushing trips later into October or the first week of November could be a sweet spot for fare savings. In most years, the week of Thanksgiving is usually a guaranteed window for international flight deals from the US because domestic travel soars at this time. But 2026 has put a bit of wrench in that convention, too. International flights around Thanksgiving this year are averaging $1,096 roundtrip, according to Going. It’s still the more affordable window compared to December, when the average international fare swells up to $1,695. Travelers on the hunt for an international deal should plan to fly on the Thanksgiving holiday itself to save up to 25% and plan to book their flights by early October, per Going’s guidance. Using search tools that allow you to look over a stretch of several days to find the cheapest fare, like Google Flights, also helps. “You might find shifting your dates by a date or two in either direction can save you a significant amount of money,” Yellin says. As a general rule of thumb, Saturdays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays tend to be the most affordable days of the week to fly, according to data from Expedia and Going. Leverage your points and miles Put those hard-earned frequent flier miles and credit card points to work for you to unlock airfares. It’s possible to compare the best airfare deal across credit cards and loyalty programs if you use the right search tool. Points Path, for one, plugs into Google Flights to help travelers compare prices. The tool will “tell you if using cash or points is a better deal, without having to search multiple airline websites individually,” Yellin says. Target your flight search to departure airports that regularly offer the greatest number of points and miles deals. In the US those include: New York (JFK), Boston (BOS), Los Angeles (LAX), Chicago (ORD), Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW), Going says. Where to find specific deals this shoulder season Going’s intel shows that a handful of destinations have a better chance of offering flight deals this fall. For international trips “Portugal, Spain, Italy, Greece, the ABC islands, and Scandinavia are seeing nice shoulder season fare dips,” according to Anna LaBrie, Going’s senior PR manager. “Japan and Southeast Asia are worth watching too, along with Mexico, outside of Día de Muertos.” On the domestic side, “Hawaii, Florida, Phoenix, the Pacific Northwest, Atlanta, the Carolinas, and San Diego are showing softer prices this fall," LaBrie says, noting that travelers should avoid ski towns like Jackson Hole and Aspen, where airfares are beginning to spike. Recent fall fare deals from Going include Boston to Madrid for $517 roundtrip—a 49% discount—and Los Angeles to Tokyo for $613 roundtrip, which is 48% cheaper than average. That’s encouraging evidence that there are good flight deals to uncover this fall, if you know the right tactics for finding them.

item.title: Where Was 'The Shards' Filmed? Where ‘80s LA Nostalgia Still Exists Today
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.03
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Shards filmed? The Shards, FX’s new adaptation of American Psycho author Bret Easton Ellis’s 2023 autofiction thriller, opens with protagonist and narrator Bret (Igby Rigney) driving to the Bruin Theater in the Westwood neighborhood of Los Angeles. He buys a ticket at the booth out front and sits down to watch The Shining in 70-mm. His present-day voice-over floats in, remarking on how strange it was to see a movie in 1980, without distractions like smartphones and social media. While waiting, he glances at the ornate Art Deco ceiling, taking note of every gorgeous detail. In reality, the Bruin is now shuttered; there was never a ticket booth out front, and the ceiling featured in the show is from the Fox Theater across the street. But thanks to production designer and native Angeleno Cat Smith, Bret’s day at the cinema feels as true as memory. Memory is central to The Shards, as a fictionalized Ellis recounts how he and his elite prep school pals were targeted by a serial killer nicknamed “The Trawler” during their senior year. While Smith was thankfully never the subject of a manhunt, she did go to an LA prep school in the ‘80s, and it’s her ultra-specific memories of the time that flesh out such an authentic and believable backdrop for the show. I spoke with Smith about The Shards, the city so integral to its story, and how she went about recreating such a distinct version of it—here are some excerpts from our conversation. The Shards is so intrinsically LA that it feels like a character. When you began this process with Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis, what was the main thing they asked of you in curating the vibe of the city? I’m a local, so I know the city really well. And I also went to a private school in Los Angeles, kind of in the period just about when Bret wrote his book. So I had a really intrinsic memory of that, and we just try to get as close to the actual as we can. Ryan’s influence from the beginning was American Gigolo, and what’s great about that movie is that it was filmed in 1981. He takes walks through areas of Los Angeles that are completely authentic to the time because it wasn’t a period piece, and it’s amazing what he sees. The entire Westwood Village was there. Ryan thought of a very muted palette, grays and whites, and this is ‘81, so it’s not the height of ‘80s design, just the edge. You’re turning into the ‘80s from the late ‘70s, where you would have those browns and reds, while the ‘80s were those pastels and stronger colors that came later. So it was kind of a combination of those two distinct eras. Are there any places in the city that have stayed in that same design style as in American Gigolo? We did shoot in the Westwood Village, and the Bruin and Westwoods theaters are the same because they were built in the ‘30s. Although the theater [Bret] went into was closed temporarily, and it didn’t have a concessions booth outside, so we had to build that. But when you come outside, we were able to copy the street from Westwood at the time. When you pass by the theater and you look behind, all of those are façades we put up, but that street was mainly still the architecture of that time. There’s this beautiful shot of the ceiling of the Bruin Theater in the pilot. Why are design details like that so important in your storytelling? Right! Because that’s what you’ll find in LA, those theaters kept those details. That’s something that either we, as a city, thought was worthwhile, or they renovated it. In this particular case, it’s actually the Fox Theater interior. We cheated it. They really loved the way the Bruin looked on the outside, but the inside of the Fox was in better shape. There’s certain things that people find important, that they keep. And one of those things that they don’t keep is shopping malls. Were you guys shooting in the [Sherman Oaks] Galleria? No. The Galleria, even though it still exists under that name, is not what you would see then. They shot Fast Times at Ridgemont High there, and that’s what it would’ve looked like at that very time. I had to find something that looked like the Galleria in 1980, and there’s not a lot in Los Angeles that would give you that. I mean, the most memorable thing was this amazing skylight that covers the whole ceiling and glass elevators and escalators that go up three stories. So we went to the South Coast Plaza, and they do have all of that, but the problem is, of course, they’ve renovated it probably more than once. Now it would be a shopping experience that’s recognizable to you today: it’s all glass, the signage is either very subtle or completely crazy. And the stuff they have is so specific to today, like they have this weird virtual reality room. None of it is appropriate for the ‘80s, so we had to go there and figure out exactly what our shots were, and then redo the facades of like ten spaces. We did the movie theater, Orange Julius, Licorice Pizza, Swensen’s Ice Cream—although you never saw that one—and we did Vince’s Pets. All those existed in the Galleria. We did a Casual Corner, Judy’s, this horrible place called One Potato, Two Potato. It was so much fun. We weren’t given a huge budget, but I wanted it to recall that very strong memory I had of shopping in the Galleria and going to movies in that theater. How do you think your experiences as an LA native helped create such an authentic depiction of that time period without feeling forced? Well, I was a little bit disdainful going into this, thinking “I’m gonna show them what it was really like.” And then I realized everybody who worked on this, who had lived through it, has a different memory of what it actually was, which I think leads to more interesting design, because then you end up with layers. This person remembers this, and that person remembers that, and when you put them together, that’s what it really was. But also AI has completely corrupted people’s view of what the ‘80s was, so I had to be really careful that I wasn’t getting mesmerized by these fake images of what the ‘80s was versus an actual advertisement for a bedroom set or a picture from Architectural Digest from that year. You always see something unexpected there that you don’t see in the AI images, like weird artwork or way too many plants. You’ve got to throw it into a blender because it gets so caught up in what people’s personal tastes were, which weren’t always great. They may see something in an Architectural Digest and their version of it in their own house is not quite as tasteful as you’d want it to be. I love that. We did a lot of location scouting of houses where they kept the ‘80s design, which is crazy if you think about it. There was this street in the Valley that looked almost untouched from the ‘80s, even the signage wasn’t that bad. What do you think The Shards says about LA as a city now? It’s very insular. I always worry that when people come to LA, they’ll be very lonely. It’s hard to meet people, you have to get around by car. There’s people who already have a community who don’t allow new people to be a part of that community. But the interesting thing about LA is that there’s so many layers here, I’m never bored looking around. I’ll look around and see the craziest detail. It’s such an ambiguous place that the detail stands out, because you’re not looking in a sea of that. You’re looking at a sea of blankness when this beautiful thing appears that tells you something about life situations. And we’re living in a time that’s very similar to the 80s. I always told my son: “You shouldn’t love the 80s, it was a dark, depressing time.” There were a lot of drugs, a lot of gun violence, everybody was out for themselves. The rich were kings. Sound familiar? And then I left him this world that was identical.

item.title: Decoding Ho Chi Minh City's Vibrant Fashion Scene
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.79
A mosaic of skyscrapers, colonial mansions, and aging shophouses, Qun 1—or District 1—forms the heart of Ho Chi Minh City, still referred to by its former name, Saigon. Once the cultural and administrative hub of French Indochina, the area has evolved into Saigon's luxury corridor, where international boutiques, art galleries, Michelin-starred restaurants, and some of the city's most expensive retail real estate now cluster within a few dense, walkable blocks. In the last decade District 1 has also become the clearest stage for Vietnam's fashion transformation. For years the country was known globally as a manufacturing powerhouse, producing garments for brands like Nike and Calvin Klein, but few outside the region could name a Vietnamese designer. That has changed. A new generation of labels—drawing from Saigon street culture, contemporary art, and heritage textiles—has repositioned Vietnam from production base to cultural exporter. That shift is increasingly visible with domestic brands like Latui Atelier and Lsoul appearing on such celebrities as Katy Perry and Blackpink's Jennie, while Ho Chi Minh City itself has emerged as a shopping destination for international travelers.
