Fueling this renaissance is the country's youthful optimism: Vietnam is one of the world's fastest-growing economies, and more than half its population is under 35. A new era of creatives and consumers is forging a fashion identity that is distinctly Vietnamese yet globally minded. Along streets like Đng Khi and Lê Li, locals and clued-in tourists hunt homegrown labels in stores once dominated by Western brands. From youth-driven collectives to refined tailoring studios, here's a curated guide to shopping in District 1. The multibrand retailers The new luxury anchor of the scene, Rue Miche is often compared to Dover Street Market for its gallery-like staging of local talent. The original boutique on Phùng Kh c Khoan street was joined in late 2025 by Rue Miche L'Édition, a roughly 50,000-square-foot flagship in the basement of the sprawling Union Square mixed-use complex. Since opening, the store has amassed nearly 90 Vietnamese labels across both locations; standouts include Americana-inspired Aah Midnight Club and Latui Atelier, known for shredded denim and provocative cuts. Built on a philosophy its founders sum up as “beautiful fashion and beautiful people,” the fast-growing, sustainability-minded concept store Compound Garment now houses 22 local brands within two adjacent shophouses on Nguyn Công Tr. Showcasing labels that share a visual language of oversized silhouettes, gender-fluid styling, and streetwear-inflected design, it's the most reliable read on what young Saigonese are wearing. The OG of multiconcept retailers in Vietnam since 2017, the New Playground boasts 70-plus Vietnamese labels, including Hades and Dirty Coins, across two District 1 locations (plus one in Hanoi). The original 26 Lý T Trng mainstay, with 40-plus stores, feels like a street market crossed with a concept mall kitted out in industrial mesh, neon, and Gen Z energy. The indie standouts At Gia Studios, fourth-generation tailor Lâm Gia Khang, a Project Runway Vietnam alum, translates regional craftsmanship into globally fluent looks. Traditional materials like Lãnh Mỹ A, a black dyed silk, appear in sharply modern cuts: double-breasted blazers, flowy trousers, and draped skirts. Now stocked at Lane Crawford and Ssense—and recently worn by Zoe Saldaña and Emma Stone—it's among Vietnam's most internationally recognized labels. Gia means “home” or “family”; fittingly, the designer's mother oversees production. On the more experimental end, Parsons-trained designer Tom Trandt's Môi Điên (literally, “crazy lips”; figuratively, “outspoken”) has built a cult following around pleating, sculptural minimalism, and gender-fluid silhouettes that feel both futuristic and traditional. Since launching a decade ago, the label has mined Vietnamese folk imagery, street culture, and dead stock textiles for its collections. Rather than treating the men's traditional áo dài as ceremonial dress, photographer-artist Thiên Minh's Mêman reframes it for everyday life. The label works primarily in Japanese linen and neutral palettes, producing collections that reinterpret Vietnamese heritage through a practical minimalist lens. New-school rebels Keep Fashion Weird is the motto of Duc Studio, whose voluminous, deconstructed pieces evoke a sense of daring. Think full-print riffs on Vietnam's national dress, the áo dài, and handcrafted denim and layered silhouettes. Designer Nguyn Minh Đc started the label in 2019 and entered ready-to-wear in 2021. A puffy bag of his was later spotted on Bella Hadid; more recent pieces have been worn by astronaut and activist Amanda Nguyen and the Vietnamese rapper Hieuthuhai. Nguyn Trng Lâm's Lsoul focuses on hyperfeminine glam: corsetry, lace, and shapes that seem engineered for svelte pop stars. To wit, the members of the pop group Blackpink and singer Madison Beer have all worn the brand, which also recently debuted a runway collection at Shanghai Fashion Week. The label Victim of the Prime launched at a small District 1 boutique in 2022; two years later it opened a larger flagship store right around the corner. The gender-neutral aesthetic is clean, youthful, and slightly cerebral—the brand's slogan is We're All Victims of Something Bigger Than Us. This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: The Distinctly Brazilian Flavor of São Paolo's Japanese Cuisine
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.31
At Aizomê, a stylish Japanese restaurant shrouded by a thick wall of trees just off São Paulo’s main thoroughfare, Avenida Paulista, the food is both recognizable to devotees of Japanese cuisine and distinctly Brazilian. You might find pirarucu, an enormous Amazonian riverfish, in saikyo yaki, a traditional Japanese sweet-miso preparation more commonly used on black cod. Ponzu incorporates tucupi, a tart yellow sauce made from fermented wild manioc, a root native to the Amazon. “I’m third generation,” says owner Telma Shiraishi, who was born and raised in São Paulo and whose grandparents hail from the Wakayama and Iwate prefectures of Japan. “It doesn’t make sense for me to make a cuisine that is 100% Japanese, bringing 100% of ingredients from Japan.” Over the past 20 years of leading Aizomê, Shiraishi has been on a journey to determine how these two cultures come together in one place. What began as an effort toward a fiercely traditional Japanese eatery has evolved into a cuisine that better reflects her own experience, which she calls Nipo-Brazilian, blending Japanese and Brazilian techniques, influences, and ingredients. Of Brazil’s 214 million people, an estimated 2 million people are of Japanese descent, making it the largest community outside of Japan. The vast majority live in São Paulo. It’s a history that reaches back to 1907, when the two countries signed an agreement permitting Japanese migration to meet labor needs on coffee plantations in the southern Brazilian states of São Paulo and Paraná. Eventually those immigrants founded agricultural settlements or moved into major cities. The São Paolo neighborhood of Liberdade, often referred to as the city’s Japantown, has been the nucleus of the Japanese Brazilian community since then. When the first Japanese restaurants emerged, they largely catered to members of their own community. For decades, Japanese cuisine faced stereotyping and suspicion—Brazilians were highly wary of raw fish—but later American imports like huge sushi boats, or rolls that included cream cheese, widened the appeal. For Shiraishi, these restaurants “helped break down prejudices” and accustomed palates to the likes of soy sauce and raw fish. Now even that era feels like the past: South America’s largest city has grown to contain a kaleidoscope of options when it comes to Japanese restaurants. There is high-end omakase and kaiseki, a raft of izakayas, specialist ramen, udon, tempura, and tonkatsu joints. The scene has hugely diversified, including both truer interpretations of original dishes and a marriage of Brazilian flavors that builds on, rather than flattens, Japanese roots. There are currently 3,000 Japanese restaurants across São Paulo, and they aren’t confined to Liberdade either; they stretch throughout the city, allowing the former enclave to take on a pan-Asian personality. Shiraishi’s Nipo-Brazilian approach isn’t new, but speaks to the way that Japanese immigrants, since they first arrived in the early 20th century, needed to adapt to local ingredients: Papaya root instead of burdock; water hyacinth stalks replacing lotus roots. Shiraishi recalls her grandmother making sushi with chard leaves, which are far more plentiful in Brazil, instead of seaweed. Unlike the Philadelphia rolls and all-you-can-eat buffets, which Shiraishi felt “didn’t have any connection…to what I grew up eating,” the items now on her menu are reminiscent of the food she was raised on. This spirit lives on in Aizomé’s multicourse tasting menu, and Shiraishi continues to scour the country for ingredients that highlight the history and evolution of Japanese food in Brazil. Guests might eat chayote marinated in cachaça, a Brazilian spirit, and soy sauce. Mapará, another Amazonian fish, often replaces eel. Her dashi uses dried Brazilian fish rather than katsuobushi, and when possible, local wild mushrooms over shiitake. “The only ingredient [which] we don’t have something similar in Brazil is kombu,” says Shiraishi, referring to the umami-rich sea kelp used in much of Japanese cuisine. A rising interest in Japanese food beyond sushi has fueled another distinctly Brazilian boom: izakayas. While these casual pubs have existed in the city for decades, it's only in the past 10 years that they have become some of the city’s most popular hangouts. Izakaya Matsu, an excellent bar in Pinheiros, is perennially packed. In Liberdade, Izakaya Issa and Kintaro have thrived since the 1990s. Wagner Higuchi runs the latter, a tiny bustling bar that his parents founded in 1993. On a warm, breezy evening, the kind where paulistanos like to spill out onto the streets with ice-cold beers, patrons at Kintaro squeeze side-by-side, drinking Japanese beers and shochu with Yakult, while tucking into an array of dishes served in small aluminium containers. The food, says Higuchi, is a mix of traditional—think braised burdock root and carrot, a side dish that dates back to the Edo period—and those from the “colony,” which is how Japanese Brazilians refer to the agricultural settlements of the early 20th century, when the Japanese first settled and adapted to local ingredients, such as a vinegary marinated tilapia. Higuchi took over from his parents in 2018 and now runs the bar; his aunt and nephew man the kitchen. “We focus on homemade Japanese food,” says Higuchi. “We evoke the fond memories of our Japanese descendants, the famous ‘batchan’ [grandma] food. It’s important to maintain these traditions because the flavor of this food is unique.” Higuchi adds that a Japanese person visiting from Japan might find some of the dishes unusual, “but for a descendant who remembers the food from home and batchan’s cooking, it can bring back wonderful memories.” On the northern edge of Avenida Paulista, the elegant, minimalist Kanoê represents another recent shift: toward classic Japanese fine dining. In 2024, the Michelin Guide returned to São Paulo, and a number of Japanese spots, including Kan Suke, Kazuo, Kuro, and Kanoê, were awarded a star. Many are run by Brazilian-born chefs of Japanese heritage who spent time in Japan in an effort to master the art of sushi. Kanoê is an exclusive omakase, packed each night despite its hefty price tag—the tasting menu costs $268. Inside, though, chefs expertly slice the finest fish—from Brazil, Japan, and beyond—and serenely cook over induction stovetops. Most revered is the rice, whose provenance is a closely guarded secret and whose result is deeply vinegary and warm enough to melt the most delicate tuna imaginable. On a buzzy Saturday night, sitting across the counter from several supremely confident and concentrated chefs, the pairing of rice, Spanish bluefin tuna, and Niigata salt is arguably the greatest mouthful of sushi in the city—the kind that makes strangers turn and smile to tables beside them. São Paulo–born owner Tadashi Shiraishi (no relation to Telma) spent years cooking in Japan, Europe, and the US, honing his craft to become one of Brazil’s great sushi chefs. Though deeply rooted in Japanese tradition, he likes to break rules. Tuna is served first because most guests are too full to enjoy the fatty fish at the end of an omakase. It’s a masterstroke, highlighting the fish’s richness before more delicate scallops and hamachi. These types of high-end Japanese restaurants have emerged, in part, thanks to an increasingly wealthy and well-traveled Brazilian populace, says Tadashi, allowing São Paulo’s sushi scene to compete with the world’s gastronomic capitals, like New York. “São Paulo is one of my favorite places to eat Japanese food," he adds. Though Tadashi uses some Brazilian-grown ingredients, his restaurant has never been explicitly focused on creating Japanese Brazilian cuisine. Rather, he explains, it has always been about studying and preserving aspects of traditional Japanese cooking to share with a Brazilian audience. “The restaurant aims to operate within principles closely linked to Japanese tradition, respecting technique, seasonality, hospitality, and the creation of flavor within this framework.” Food among diasporas, perhaps inevitably, can veer further from its origins as people adapt to new countries and cultures intertwine. As with Indian food in the UK or Mexican cuisine in the US, Japanese food in São Paulo is today defined by a multitude of interpretations. There are, Tadashi says, “formats more adapted to Brazilian tastes [and] those closer to traditions and techniques originally developed in Japan, but with a more personal touch.” Indeed, Japanese cuisine in Brazil has never been more popular or varied, from the experimental to the fiercely traditional. There are temakerias in gas stations, beach kiosks selling sushi, and, still, all-you-can-eat sushi rodízios in every town. “The new generation, they don’t want to eat McDonald’s, they want sushi,” says Telma, referring to the ongoing—and yet, in this case, usurped—Brazilian adoration for international chains. This year Telma will open a new spot in Saúde, a neighborhood in the city’s south that is now home to one of the largest Japanese Brazilian communities. “As a community of descendants, we have to tell our story.” Thanks to the continued efforts of São Paulo’s vast array of Japanese Brazilian chefs, the options are better—and the story told louder—than ever before.

item.title: In Uzbekistan, a Prized Religious Artifact Sits at the Heart of a New Museum
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.12
At Tashkent's new Islamic Civilization Center in Uzbekistan, the star attraction is built around a single object. The Uthman Quran, a seventh-century manuscript written in Kufic lettering on gazelle parchment, sits beneath a 213-foot dome in a space designed for maximum impact. Lapis-lazuli-inlaid steps lead toward the holy text. Portuguese pink marble wraps the walls. Eight handwoven silk carpets, each inscribed with Quranic verses, hang like royal tapestries. Guards are posted throughout to protect one of the oldest surviving Qurans in the world, and a full sound-and-light show—incorporating over 1 million Swarovski crystals—fills the hall from floor to ceiling. The effect of the Quran Hall, which anchors one of the most ambitious cultural projects in Central Asia, is almost psychedelic, like a Pink Floyd concert reimagined as an act of religious devotion. Opened in March on the grounds of the Hazrati Imam ensemble, a 25-acre architectural site that includes a historic mosque and madrassa, the center is a research library, a digital learning hub, and the world's largest museum of Islamic civilization. Beyond the Quran Hall, its exhibitions trace Uzbekistan's history from pre-Islamic cultures and Silk Road exchanges to the Timurid period and the country's modern era. Interactive displays, rare manuscripts, and newly repatriated artifacts show how this part of the world became an intellectual crossroads; objects in the collection range from a 10th-century Samanid silver tray and copper inkwell to Baburid armor, a silk covering once used at the Prophet's tomb in Medina, and Bactrian-period gold pieces related to the Amu Darya Treasure. The center arrives as Uzbekistan's design profile is rising, fueled by growing interest in ikat, suzani, and ceramics, plus a new wave of arts investment that includes the Bukhara Biennial, the forthcoming Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent, and Tadao Ando's planned National Museum of Uzbekistan in Tashkent. But for all that momentum, the Quran Hall may be the clearest expression of the country's cultural ambition: a lavishly staged encounter with a sacred text bound up in centuries of faith, scholarship, craft, and Uzbek identity. This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: 15 Oregon Coast Airbnbs for Pacific Sunsets, Storm Chasing, and Eclectic Beach Towns
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.49
There are few places in the United States as breathtaking as the Oregon Coast, where towering spruce trees make way for vast blue horizons at what feels like the edge of the Earth. An exquisite marriage of colors, the Beaver State’s famous shoreline stretches from the Columbia River in the north to the California border in the south, lending itself to a misty, nature-filled getaway. Whether you’re interested in exploring the tide pools and gazing at the hordes of seabirds that congregate around Cannon Beach’s Haystack Rock, or staring down Thor’s Well (otherwise known as the “Drainpipe of the Pacific”) over in Yachats, these 15 Oregon Coast Airbnbs offer cozy respites for all kinds of outdoor excursions. Some are vacation spots in and of themselves, with amenities like cedar hot tubs and barrel saunas; others’ main focus is the dreamy ocean views. From A-frame cabins and tiny floating homes to glass-walled lookouts and lighthouse-shaped properties, these are the best Airbnbs for an unforgettable Pacific Northwest escape. Our top picks: - Best for solo travelers: Tiny home on Tillamook Bay - Best for views: Nehalem home five minutes from the beach - Best for families: Cabin with views of Twin Rocks - Best for beach access: Arch Cape home with a sauna and hot tub FAQ: Which Oregon Coast vacation rentals offer the best views? For truly cinematic views, Manzanita’s hillside homes provide a sweeping overlook of seven-mile Neahkahnie Beach. For quieter vistas, Oceanside and Yachats deliver raw, less-developed coastal scenery with panoramic reach. How do I get to the Oregon Coast? Most travelers begin in Portland, Oregon, which is served by Portland International Airport. From there, a rental car is essential—there’s no comprehensive train or bus network along the coast. The northern coast (Cannon Beach, Manzanita, Seaside) is about a 1 hour and 30 minute drive west via Highway 26. The central coast (Lincoln City, Depoe Bay, Newport) is reached via Highway 18 or 20 in around two to three hours. Highway 101, the coastal route, winds southward all the way to California—ideal for a slow, scenic drive with stops along the way. Be prepared for occasional fog, winding roads, and in remote stretches, limited cell service. When is the best time to visit the Oregon Coast? The Oregon Coast has no high season in the traditional sense—each season offers a distinct atmosphere. Its summer season (July to September) brings the most sun and mild warmth, perfect for beach walks, kayaking, and long coastal hikes—but also the most visitors. Fall (October to early November) is quieter, with crisp mornings, fiery foliage inland, and excellent conditions for storm-free trail adventures. Winter (late November through February) invites travelers seeking solitude and drama—this is storm-watching season, when towering waves crash under moody skies, best enjoyed from a fireside perch. Spring (March to May) is fresh and green, with fewer crowds, migrating gray whales, and tide pools alive with seasonal marine life. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Kyler Alvord.

item.title: How We Pulled It Off: A Monastery Wedding With Drag Queens in Sintra, Portugal
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.38
As a couple, Taylor Rains and Carter Joyce have a shared sense of romance, particularly as it relates to travel. “Exploring the world has just helped to deepen our relationship,” says Carter. Since meeting online in 2016, they’ve spent their holiday seasons in Belgium hopping around Christmas markets. It was during their 2022 trip that they became engaged. “We got our mulled wine and got on the Ferris wheel in the main market in Brussels, and Carter proposed,” says Taylor. “It took two full rotations of the Ferris wheel for me to pick my jaw up off the ground.” It makes sense, then, that they’d want to have their wedding in a storied venue or a gorgeous destination—or both. Their early research found the Charleston-based duo looking into opulent venues, such as the Biltmore Estate in North Carolina, chateaux in France, and villas in Italy. They realized that plotting a destination wedding would allow them to curate a gorgeous experience for their loved ones. “One of our favorite things to do is share recommendations—these are the restaurants, this is the little cafe, this is the person to ask for—and we saw this as an opportunity to do that on a grander scale,” says Taylor. “We could curate all these vignettes and experiences that you, as our guests, could then enjoy and experience.” Once they viewed their wedding that way, going international was an easy decision. Ahead, the grooms explain how and why they pulled off their unique 100-guest Portugal destination wedding—which featured a fado performer, drag queens, flamenco dancers, and a ceremony set within the crumbling stone walls of a 16th-century garden—in the magical town of Sintra. Find a planner who feels like a friend When they began their planning process, Carter and Taylor weren’t sure about which country they wanted to marry in—yet they knew who they wanted to oversee the wedding. In Taylor’s research of wedding planners who specialized in European destination celebrations, he found the London-based firm Matthew Oliver Weddings, and adored their Instagram feed. “One of our criteria when we were examining portfolios was that every event and every wedding had a unique identity and felt like an extension of the couple,” says Carter. Living in Charleston, the couple are accustomed to seeing cookie-cutter weddings with an established echoing the city, and they wanted theirs to be more reflective of who they are. Matthew Oliver’s events fit that bill. “That alone made them top contenders,” he says. In their first conversation with staff planner Georgia Haldenby, about a year and a half out from their wedding, they knew she was the one. “We all clicked, and she understood us very well,” says Taylor. “We didn’t want it to be a strictly transactional relationship, like ‘Here’s the final invoice, it’s been lovely seeing you.’ We wanted it to feel a friendship.” A small snag came when the couple had to pause planning due to one of their parent’s health issues. When they came back to Georgia, they were heartbroken to learn she’d booked up the rest of the year. They reluctantly started chatting with her recommendations for another planner—and then they got a happy text “She said, ‘I don't know what voodoo you worked, but one of my couples has canceled and you guys are back on,’” Carter laughs. Check every single possible box Georgia’s first order of business was a big one: helping the grooms determine which destination they should choose in the first place. In the months they’d paused their planning, the pricing on venues in France and Italy for their desired time frame had shot up. “Prices had doubled or tripled since we’d started looking at chateaux and villas,” says Carter. “So Georgia sat us down and we had an honest conversation about budget, as well as where we’d been in the world and what places we really liked.” She then encouraged them to imagine, in a dream world, what qualities their perfect destination wedding could include. Their list was: a place they’d visited together, with historical significance, that was architecturally stimulating and beautiful, with a modern (and wheelchair-accessible) resort for guests within walking distance, and an international airport 30 minutes away that offered nonstop flights from New York, Atlanta, and DC. Better than any AI generator, their planner immediately suggested Sintra, a town in Portugal 20 miles from Lisbon known for its whimsical castles—but which also had a sprawling Ritz-Carlton property, the Penha Longa Resort, that included all contemporary conveniences as well as multiple event spaces on site. “We both lit up,” Taylor remembers. “We loved Sintra. The castles are beautiful. The Portuguese people are so nice. The food is great. It’s super accommodating. We were surprised it had not entered our minds prior, to be honest.” Choose venues for their flow During the planning process, Carter and Taylor made two trips to Portugal: one for a gut-check visit to the venues, on which they’d already put down deposits, and one for menu tastings and other final vendor conversations. They did book the Penha Longa Resort, the place that had made their planner think of Sintra in the first place, and held all of their events within the property. While the convenience and historical significance of the venues were paramount, the spaces offered additional benefits. “They were beautiful—that much is a given,” says Taylor. “But the layout of the spaces could not have worked better for the vision we had of ushering people throughout the afternoon and evening, keeping them surprised and entertained.” Their welcome dinner was held at the charming pink mansion, Casa Dos Penedos, while the wedding day was held around a monastery. The ceremony itself—which was officiated by a friend—was set within the crumbling, 16th-century, stone-walled Nuncio Gardens, built near the monastery and featuring ivy-covered stone walls, archways, and a shallow reservoir at the center. A cocktail hour following in the monastery courtyard and dinner in the Sala Dos Arcos, a dramatic space with a ceiling comprised entirely of archways. Dancing occurred in the Salão Nobre, a soaring salon with wall-to-wall carvings and a stunning carved-wood fireplace. Keep the aesthetic simple While their wedding venues were stunning in their ornate details, from the peacocks painted on the ceiling of the Casa Dos Penedos to the blue and white tiles along the courtyard, the couple wanted to go slightly cleaner and more masculine with the wedding decor they’d be bringing in. “The brief was Ralph Lauren, late ‘90s, equestrian,” says Carter. “We didn’t want to compete with the setting and the property itself,” says Taylor. “We wanted that to be more of a flourish in the last five to 10% of the design, and really let the spaces breathe.” For their welcome dinner, they brought the formality down a bit with light linens, bamboo chairs, potted herb plants on the tables, and no assigned seats. Their ceremony was spare, with only a few urns filled with dusty pink and peach roses, while dinner featured loads of thin white candles set in bronzed candelabra at staggered heights. Their florist was Atelier Decorelle, while tableware and furniture came from Rental Co. Purge your people-pleasing tendencies As Carter and Taylor put it, giving people recommendations is their love language, so they were eager to help their guests plot their trips to Portugal—whether they were coming for just the wedding weekend or expanding their vacations to visit major cities like Lisbon, Porto, and beyond. They created a wedding website that included the pertinent wedding info, like hotels and schedules, but also offered their favorite spots in all the aforementioned cities. The couple was interested in helping their guests even more—”I would have rented a bus and driven [guests] from the airport to Sintra if anybody had asked me,” cracks Taylor—but Georgia gently stopped them. “She recognized our innate people-pleasing and how it could really hurt us in the long run,” says Carter. So while they did help their immediate families book their flights and accommodations, they simply listed their planner’s own contact information so she could field all questions about transportation, timing, and other logistics. “She served as a travel agent as much as a wedding planner,” says Carter. Start the weekend with a bang. To properly welcome their loved ones to Portugal, the couple threw a Portuguese barbecue dinner on Friday night. “It was an indoor-outdoor experience, with a bar overlooking the cityscape, the mountains, and the sea,” Taylor says. “We had our guests dropped off and they walked through the forest up to the venue. When they entered, we had flamenco dancers and live musicians playing.” Flamenco dancers from Rueda Flamenca lined the garden path while guests walked in, as a nod to Taylor’s mother who is Spanish. During dinner, a musician named Manel Ferreira performed fado, the Portuguese folk music, playing guitar and serenading guests. Front load the cultural elements The fado performer wasn’t the only hit of Portuguese culture the guests received upon arrival. In their hotel rooms, guests found welcome bags offering a hand-drawn map of the area, as well as the beloved pastry pastel de nata (egg tarts) and a fan printed with the designs of azulejos, the instantly recognizable blue-and-white ceramic tiles the country is known for. Food was another major way of integrating the local culture into their wedding. Aside from the Portuguese barbecue foods at their welcome dinner, their wedding meal featured several traditional flavors, such as cod fritters and sausage, while the mains were more continental. “We tried to balance it and make the appetizers very Portuguese, and the principal plates were a fish and a meat—turbot, a very flaky white fish, and a version of beef Wellington—still with Portuguese flavors, but identifiable for all the guests,” says Carter. Consider some cultural complications The elephant in the room of their wedding planning, says Carter, was that they were a same-sex couple trying to marry in a majority-Catholic country. “Even though we know that [most of] Europe is exceptionally accommodating and supportive, there’s always that tinge of concern, like ‘How’s this going to work?’” he says. Happily, they found that their vendors went beyond accepting; they actually were “amplifying,” as he put it, noting that they actually felt more comfortable being “loud” in their affection in Portugal than they did at home in the southern United States. Don’t be too precious in the pretty spaces The couple were thrilled to work within the lavish rooms in their chosen venues, but worried aloud about the possibility of damaging the details. But the events team at the Penha Longa Resort were particularly befuddled, for example, when they fretted about high-heeled shoes damaging or scuffing the gorgeous mosaic tile on the floor of one courtyard. “‘No, the tile’s meant to be walked on. You’re meant to experience it that way,” Taylor remembers as the response. Similarly, they were concerned about the Salão Nobre, which they used for the dancing portion of the evening. What if someone spilled a drink on the wood floors, or bumped against the plaster molding? The event manager responded that “This place has been around for 600 years with people having parties and carrying on, and it will be around far longer,” Taylor recalls. “It’s meant to be lived in and enjoyed and experienced.” Find a glamorous way to stay awake The dancing portion of the evening was powered by a DJ from Your Jukebox. But the couple knew that weddings in Portugal (and much of Europe) typically last until sunrise; their own rental of the space gave them free rein until 6 a.m. “We talked to Georgia about how to keep the momentum up, other than just pumping people with espresso martinis, which we also did,” says Taylor. “But how do we usher in a new element for the last three hours without shifting locations again?” The solution was drag queens. The newlyweds surprised their guests with midnight performances from three drag performers, via Pride Talent: one who was shockingly tall (at 7’8”), one who was playing the saxophone, and one who could breathe fire (though wasn’t permitted to do so within the historic venue, which understandably did have some limits). Starchy late-night snacks came out, too, including Belgian waffles and Spanish croquettes. “The arrival of the drag performers will live forever in my mind as the most fun reaction shot of the night,” says Taylor. “Their bringing in all the guests as part of their show, to walk the catwalk or dance, really propelled the party forward for another three hours.” The glamorous event finally wound down around 3:00 a.m.

item.title: Asanas at Sea? The Best Places for Yoga Around the World Are Also the Most Unconventional
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.12
The best places for yoga are at once picturesque and contemplative, whether it be pranayama in Ladakh’s austere landscape, dhanurasana in the thick of Thailand’s jungles, or shavasana beside an Alpine lake in New Zealand. These experiences offer as much external peace as they do internal, and even long after the session and trip have ended, it's those stirring, outdoor moments that endure. They feel like they’ve stopped time and are worth going out of the way for—planned or spontaneous. And what's better than practicing your asanas in a phenomenal natural setting? With these 10 best places for yoga, grab your go-to mat and embrace your inner yogini. Lux* South Ari Atoll, Maldives The middle of the Indian Ocean is possibly the most unique spot one can find to do yoga. Practice asanas while sailing on a traditional wooden dhow at this Maldivian resort. Lux* South Ari Atoll organizes this cruise at golden hour with an instructor guiding you on Tibetan Sound Bowl therapy, breathwork, and yoga. Sip on a refreshing drink, inhale a mood-enhancing oil blend, and float on the waves as you meditate and feel your mind reset. The Kyagar, Nubra Valley, India This boutique hotel is located on the ancient Silk Route in Ladakh’s stunning but stark landscape. Sitting on the sandy banks of the Siachen River and surrounded by the icy Karakoram peaks, it has a very special location that owner Rinchen Kalon believes furthers your yoga practice. To that end, she hosts a retreat at the property every season, and when the weather permits, outdoor classes are held on a river trail surrounded by wildflowers and sea buckthorn bushes. The Kyagar's regular yoga classes are free of charge for guests and last 30 to 90 minutes. Haritha Villas and Spa, Sri Lanka This luxury villa property in Hikkaduwa has an open-air jungle yoga pavilion nestled amidst lush tropical greenery, overlooking the serene canopy of the surrounding forest. Haritha offers hour-long, private lessons in Hatha Yoga, which are apt for beginners. Guests love the serene jungle setting with sweet birdsong in the background and a gentle wind rustling through the trees. Many cite the yoga lesson as one of the most memorable parts of their stay here. Anantara Al Jabal Al Akhdar Resort, Oman This rocky mountain resort is one of the highest hotels in the world and has a spectacular deck which can be booked for a yoga session (based on weather and availability). Diana’s Point is a platform where Diana, Princess of Wales, once stood back in 1986 and has a breathtaking canyon view of the fabled Green Mountain. Anantara offers hatha, sarvanga, meditation, and monthly full-moon yoga classes, but this spot is not for the fainthearted, as it juts out into a valley with a steep drop-off. March to May is rose season in this region, and the entire valley below erupts into unbelievably fragrant Damask roses. The Kumaon, India The exquisitely-designed Kumaon is located in a remote part of the Himalayas, and its most magical setting for yoga is the rooftop terrace located at the highest point of the property. Views extend to the valley of the Kosi River on one side and the Binsar Forest on the other, all under the watchful gaze of the upper Himalayas, including the divine Nanda Devi peak. With reclaimed Himalayan slate as the cooling floor of the terrace, a wispy breeze scented with pine and carrying birdsong, Kumaon's yoga space feels magical. It offers traditional hatha yoga along with basic pranayama, and guests describe them as rejuvenating and peaceful. Qasr Al Sarab, Desert Resort by Anantara, Abu Dhabi Doing yoga surrounded by vast sand dunes is certainly an unusual proposition. The wellness and meditation center at Qasr Al Sarab by Anantara is nestled on the edge of the resort, a sanctuary that opens to an uninterrupted panorama of the golden Liwa Desert. Guests can practice in the midst of raw nature as the sun rises or sets; in the early morning, the desert sky turns pink and gold, while at twilight, it twinkles with stars. Yoga instruction is available year-round, and the resort also collaborates with yoga gurus specializing in yin yoga, immersive sound healing, and yoga nidra from October to April. Those looking for silence and stillness to escape a chaotic lifestyle will truly appreciate this setting. Keemala Resort and Spa, Thailand This luxury jungle resort in Phuket has a special focus on wellness with a tropical spa, healthy cuisine, and eco-friendly operations. Keemala has two outdoor yoga spaces, one intimate wedding venue nestled within the forest, and the other on a rooftop, offering scenic views. The forest yoga takes place amid lush foliage under a 300-year-old Takian tree; guests are encouraged to practice barefoot so that they can ground themselves directly to the earth for a soulful experience. The resort also has a meditation cave with a waterfall designed to help guests heighten their focus and fully immerse in the present moment. Group classes are complimentary, and private instruction is available at an additional charge. Aro Hā Wellness Retreat, New Zealand A world-famous retreat in the Southern Alps, Aro Hā is located on serene Lake Wakatipu, just 40 minutes from Queenstown. Its yoga classes take place in the Aro Hā Room, which is well known for its striking views of the alpine lake. It offers a range of hatha styles that cater to a wide range of skill level, and all classes are complimentary. Yoga is a key element of their larger program, which also includes subalpine hikes, daily massages and spa time, and a variety of wellness workshops. Jumeirah Olhahali Island, Maldives You may have done yoga on a beach, but have you ever done yoga on a private sandbank? Jumeirah Olhahali Island takes guests on a five-minute speedboat ride to reach a private sandbank at sunrise or sunset. Its Oceanic Balance Retreat is an all-encompassing yoga experience tailored to its surroundings, whether energizing at dawn or grounding at sunset. Pleasant ocean breezes, uninterrupted horizons, and the sense of pure seclusion create space for profound clarity and calm. Acro Suites, Greece Located on the cliffs of Crete, Acro Suites describes itself as a restorative retreat. Its asana wellness studios are sleekly designed with bamboo and local stone, overlooking the Aegean Sea and dramatic cliffs of Mononaftis Bay. The studios offer a variety of yoga styles, including hatha, vinyasa, yin, and yoga nidra, all guided by certified instructors. In addition to complimentary daily practices, guests can also partake in intimate couples sessions, healing circles, and sound healing journeys, each designed to deepen connection. A version of this article originally appeared on Condé Nast Traveller India.

item.title: The Last-Chance Tourism of Iceland's Glacier Raves
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.76
Weaving through the crowd, I pause next to Kali Van Horn, a 30-year-old architect from Brooklyn with glitter dripping from her eyes like crystallized tears. We share the moment as strangers, pressing our backs against the frozen wall as two DJs spin house and techno tracks in the heart of Langjökull—Iceland’s second-largest glacier. “It’s healing,” Van Horn says, as rainbow lights illuminate the ice cave’s blue hues. Surrounding us are people wearing winter coats accessorized with light-up scarves, sparkly snowflake-shaped sunglasses, and hoods lined with lavender fur. This is part of Iceland Eclipse, a festival on the Snæfellsnes Peninsula, offering late-night raves, cacao ceremonies, and lectures on whale communication to 3,333 total attendees. With an energy akin to Burning Man, the vibe is distinctly hippie; guests are gnawing to get into heady discussions. Most are here to extend their experience of the total solar eclipse two days prior, for which they’ve traveled great distances and invested even more grandly. This experience, an 11-hour, $600-price-tagged excursion called “Into the Glacier”, is perhaps the most exclusive event on the lineup. More than ever, rare natural wonders and phenomena are gaining top billing for luxury travel experiences—and this one, both in ambition and vibe, is a standout, drawing just 100 attendees to commune with this 395 square-mile mass of ice. As we drive from the festival grounds toward Langjökull, the stark landscape is punctuated by the occasional sprig of purple flowers. Spikes jut from the massive tires of our car—a vehicle bearing a Jägermeister sticker and the license plate JAGER (the owner just really likes Jager, he says)—which crunches over gravel as the Red Hot Chili Peppers blasts through the speakers, and ravers in the back seat discuss ketamine and the rise of AI. The cars climb higher on the glacier until they begin to get stuck. Then, when they inevitably do, drivers jump out and release air from the tires, redistributing weight so they can continue. The rocks around us fade into sheets of textured ice as we drive onto the glacier, streams of clear water rushing through jagged indentations. This glacier is thousands of years old, our driver explains, formed from layer after layer of snow compressing into ice. As we exit the vehicle, I notice a metal-wrapped entrance in the ice—a portal beckoning us to another dimension. We enter the passage, its walls carved entirely from the glacier. I’m still dangling my crampon—a spiked traction device for walking on slippery ice—in one hand when an Into the Glacier staff member swoops in, gliding it over my hiking shoe in a single fluid motion. “Cinderella treatment,” he says with a grin. I follow a faint beat as I meander through a 1,640-foot labyrinth—the largest manmade ice tunnel in the world—before stepping into a wider, taller space within the ice. It’s designed like a chapel, with wooden benches and faux flowers forming a heart on the wall. Near the exit stands a bearded Into the Glacier tour guide whose name is Hjalamroli Hjalmrsson, I learn, and who tells me his age is “young and old at the same time.” We’re lucky to be partying in the Icelandic Highlands, he impresses upon me: 1,300 meters above sea level, surrounded by “500 billion tons of snow, water, and ice.” The sound dances around us. “It's very echoey. You feel the bass is bouncing off the icy walls,” Hjalmrsson says. “The sound kind of drowns, but that's interesting. It's something that you can compare to a big warehouse.” Just two days ago, when I met with Iceland Eclipse’s co-producer Fridrik Olafsson, 41, he told me that he chose not to haul up large amounts of audio or lighting equipment for the event—“the setting itself does the trick,” he said, spreading his hands on the table. His wife was stenciling a drawing of a moon embracing the sun on his thumbnail. On his other hand, a crescent moon with a face howled. Olfasson took a phone call four minutes into our interview, speaking in terse Icelandic, before telling me that three days of storms had ravaged the festival, damaging three main-stage tents, and ruining 50 glamping tents. He described roaring gusts of nearly 70 miles per hour, desperately tying down tents with heavy machinery, and crew members working for 24 hours to make repairs. “Us Icelanders would call it a windy day, but our foreign counterparts were absolutely shocked,” Olfasson said. Olfasson received permission from local authorities and the mayor for Iceland Eclipse excursions. He had previously collaborated with Into the Glacier—which offers daily tours inside Langjökull—while organizing a music event for Secret Solstice, an Icelandic festival he founded that ran from 2014 to 2019 and offered $1 million ticket packages for groups of six guests, including private jet rides and a personal chef. This post-eclipse event is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to upscale glacial experiences. Inside Langjökull, I follow the steady pulse of music to a mass of 100 people swaying in a hypnotic trance. Hólmar Thor Filipsson, 52, an Icelandic DJ known as Hólmar (Acid Tourist), is playing back-to-back with Margeir Steinar Ingólfsson, 51, an Icelandic DJ known as Margeir. “Everyone there was experiencing something for the first time ever,” Thor Filipsson tells me, later, back at the camp. “It was like the eclipse in a way, but more concentrated, and it felt a little bit sci-fi.” Ingólfsson operates on the same wavelength. “I even came with a special gift for the glacier from my friend, who is a glacier specialist,” Ingólfsson, 51, says. His friend has collected water from glaciers around the world, and Ingólfsson placed a few drops near the DJ booth. When I ask about the night's song selection, Ingólfsson says they took their cue from the glacier itself. Was the glacier in the mood for house and techno, I ask? “Yes,” Ingólfsson replies. “That was the vibe that the glacier wanted at this time.” As the rave beats on, cans of pink vodka cocktails appear in our gloved hands. The beverage packaging suggests that “Flamingo” is an adequate description for a flavor—apparently, that means something like the nostalgic taste of liquified pink Starbursts. Iceland Eclipse staff members are on task with collecting trash in plastic bags, the goal being to leave the glacier just as it was found. Hours later, our two-drink-maximums met, we exit the glacier and totter down to the Into the Glacier Klaki Base Camp, about 10 minutes from the ice cave’s entrance. I meet Lyndsay Klebba, a 36-year-old writer from Chicago, who is wearing a fluffy yellow hat and a pashmina decorated with spotted mushrooms. She decided to visit Iceland after a 23andMe test revealed her Viking heritage: “To be surrounded by ancient ice and listening to New Age music—it's just a clash of titans,” she says. She spent most of the party tucked behind the DJ booth, her heart against the ice to feel the bass. She also wandered into an icy alcove and stuck out her tongue to catch droplets trickled from the ceiling. “The freshest water I ever tasted.” Klebba is the exact audience that Iceland Eclipse is after—those moved by the specialness of the glacier as a setting. “Ice holds a lot of history,” says Mitch Morales, CEO of IMXP and founder of Iceland Eclipse. “The ice in the glacier is thousands of years old–I think about what was happening in the world when this ice was frozen, all the memory, and thinking about this as being a temple in the same way." Morales, 41, is planning IMXP’s “Eclipse Trilogy” of annual totality events. Just this month, he was scouting for the ideal 2027 Luxor site; he is considering Australia or New Zealand for 2028. His ambitions extend even further, though, he says: He eventually wants to host an eclipse viewing on the moon. “In Egypt, there are stone temples that are dedicated to the things that came before them. In a way, I think that a glacier party is similar to that,” Morales says. Gazing out the window as the car crept down the glacier, Klebba observes small signs showing how far Langjökull’s ice once extended. The glacier has lost an estimated 29 percent of its mass between 1890 and 2019, according to a 2020 study published in Frontiers in Earth Science. “Where we were right now would have been glacier probably 40 years ago,” Klebba says. “The fact that we had to drive up several miles just to get to it makes you think about what's going on today.” Some travelers seek out landscapes threatened by global warming, a phenomenon known as “last-chance tourism.” Langjökull has already outlived nearby Okjökull, which became Iceland’s first glacier lost to climate change in 2014. Its name was shortened to Ok, dropping jökull—Icelandic for glacier. “Knowing that this was the last chance to party inside a glacier because of climate change was a big factor in me deciding to attend,” says Hayley Sharkey, 27, as our car jostles away from the ice. Sharkey is a Miami public relations coordinator who has adorned her blue snow jacket with faux-fur cuffs. “Future generations will not be able to understand how it felt to be inside a glacier. The feeling of natural ice surrounding you will be seen as a myth.”

item.title: NYC’s Newest Glamping Stay Is Dressed Like the Wild West
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.74
If you woke up inside the new Urban Cowboy Tent at Collective Retreats and had to guess where you were, New York City would probably not be your first answer. The red Pendleton fabric, saddle blanket rugs, antique lanterns, old canteens, and chandelier made of antlers overhead make it feel like somewhere wooded and considerably farther away—maybe a cabin upstate, or a particularly well-designed camp out West. Then you unzip the canvas and see the Statue of Liberty across the water, the World Trade Center in the other direction, and ferries moving through the harbor: It's a pretty wonderful way to realize you are still in New York. The singular seasonal tent is the newest accommodation at Collective Retreats Governors Island, thanks to Dovetail + Co—the ownership group behind both the retreat and Urban Cowboy Lodge. Reservations opened August 17 for stays through November 2026. The 325-square-foot tent is expected to return for the 2027 season, adding Urban Cowboy's very specific take on Western Americana to Collective’s existing collection of simple yet spruced up canvas tents and suites. Out of the 29 accommodations at the retreat, you’ll want to book this bad boy for a truly fun, transformative, and one-of-a-kind experience—completely made over by Urban Cowboy’s signature Western-styled design. Just last week, I checked into the tent myself after leaving the office and taking the ferry from Lower Manhattan. The scenic ride takes about eight minutes, and a golf cart picked me and my partner up when we arrived at the island. I’ve stayed at Collective Retreats before, and I’ve also stayed at Urban Cowboy in the Catskills, so I was especially curious to see how the two would translate together. Collective has the setting, with canvas tents, open grass, harbor breezes, and the feeling of being away (without going very far), while Urban Cowboy has the design language: Western lore, cool vintage furnishings, a little bit of cowboy camp, and a whole lot of personality. The new tent brings the two together in a way that feels majorly different than its neighbors, not only at the retreat, but in all of New York City. Inside the Urban Cowboy tent The new Urban Cowboy tent is a retreat for two, with one comfy king-size bed and an en suite bathroom. Out front, the private deck’s red Adirondack chairs with patterned pillows face the water, making it a great place to start the morning with coffee in hand. Above the entrance, a pair of horns hangs over a small plaque reading “Camp Cowboy.” Inside, a Pendleton Harding–patterned fabric wraps around the walls and ceilings and continues onto the custom upholstered headboard. El Paso saddle blanket rugs cover most of the floor, while 1920s canteens, old books, a deconstructed vintage camera, and a little bear statue fill the room. I have an affinity for anything remotely Western, and happily consider myself a cowgirl at heart, so I was immediately into the design. What kept the tent from feeling like a collection of cowboy props was the tasteful curation of vintage pieces. This is very much what Urban Cowboy’s aesthetic is all about: Lyon Porter, Urban Cowboy’s cofounder and creative director, designed the tent through Cowboy Creative, while Kevin Jacob Design worked on custom elements including hand-painted stencil work, signage, and the mounted antlers. The poetically placed vintage finds were sourced from popular seasonal outdoor markets: Beacon Flea Market and Elephant’s Trunk. One of the most picture-perfect pieces in the tent is the antique, patinated French cast-iron soaking tub, positioned toward the harbor so that Lady Liberty is directly in view. A vintage-inspired speaker hangs above it, and a nearby chair serves as a base for handcrafted bath products from Species by the Thousands, as well as a little rubber duckie with a cowboy hat on (the perfect touch). While there aren’t windows, open the outer canvas flap, keep the screen zipped, and let the light pour in. Given this tent is one of the closest ones to the water, the harbor appears almost as part of the room. The proper bathroom is tucked in a separate but adjoining tent towards the back. The space is bigger than I thought it might be—home to a standing shower, big mirror, and toilet. The western lore continues here with (yes, more) antlers; the coziest, tribal-pattered robes; and one of my favorite pieces: a framed desert landscape that hangs across the shower and looks like a scene right out of New Mexico. Food and drink at Collective Retreats We started the evening with a drink at Sunset Terrace, also home to sweeping city views, before heading to Three Peaks Lodge for dinner. The restaurant overlooks the harbor, where orange Staten Island ferries pass by. Order the crudo, a cheeseboard to share, the heirloom melon and prosciutto salad, and chicken entrée, along with a bottle of wine to bring back to your tent. (The in-tent Yeti cooler comes in handy here.) Along with its oversized Jenga and cornhole, the retreat’s Great Lawn has firepits where guests can roast sweet s’mores in the evening. Because of the rain, we missed the usual setup, but the team thoughtfully plated them for us as dessert. In the morning, head to Three Peaks for a casual breakfast buffet with hard-boiled eggs, bagels, pastries, coffee, and more. → For more options of where to eat and drink on Governors Island, check out our full guide to the island. What to know before you book If you visit on a warm day, not to worry—the tent’s air conditioning works well, and was especially welcome after walking around in August humidity. But do note, this is still a tent, so sound travels. A boat parked out front played music for a while during the night (earplugs are provided, I simply failed to use mine). I do wish we had received a quick walkthrough when we arrived: The lights were unplugged and took some figuring out, and one outlet sits awkwardly near the middle of the room, so watch your step and perhaps ask for some guidance right away. The logistics are easy enough, though, and employees regularly pass through the property in golf carts, so it was simple to get help when we needed it. The next morning, with an early ferry to catch, we called for a golf cart and made it to the landing with time to spare. You can book the Urban Cowboy Tent online through the Collective Retreats website. Bookings for the tent are open now for weeknight and weekend stays until the end of November 2026. The team has already promised its return next year, too—with the tent available for bookings all season, from May through November 2027. More stays on Governors Island: If you missed the booking window for this particular tent, you can get a glimpse of the experience at the two properties that birthed the collaboration. At Collective Retreats, there are 29 container suites and glamping tents available from May to November. If you're looking for a classic-cool Catskills getaway, Urban Cowboy Lodge, in the woodsy town of Big Indian, is never a bad idea.

item.title: 20 Fall Getaways From NYC for Apple-Picking, Wine-Tasting, and Leaf-Peeping
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.57
All the leaves are brown, and the sky is turning gray…well, not quite yet, but you can't stop us from dreamin'. Though instead of California, our seasonal hopes and wishes turn to the hues of fall foliage season just within reach. And if you live in and around the Big Apple, there's no better way to take your sweet time soaking in the vistas without carving into precious OOO hours than checking into one of the best weekend fall getaways around NYC. The most idyllic towns on the East Coast, charming enough to make any Transcendentalist swoon, are but a hop (in your car) and a skip (on a train) away—think the Hudson Valley, the Catskills, the Berkshires, the Adirondacks, and even some tucked-away corners of Pennsylvania and New England. And there are plenty of adorable hotels in these areas ready to welcome you with a warm flannel blanket and a generous mug of hot chocolate to kick off a cozy stay. The properties you see below are some of our editors' favorites because they go above and beyond being a place to rest your head. They're the secluded cabins snuggled into the woods with modern suites and crackling fireplaces. They're the lovingly restored inns that embody the souls of their small towns, and the multihyphenates that also function as cider mills, apple orchards, and pumpkin patches. Most of all, they're the best excuse to take that romantic getaway or family road trip you've been putting off. Without further ado, find our 20 favorite properties for weekend fall getaways around NYC—we promise taking an extra day or two off won't hurt. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Skaneateles, NY With a can’t-miss farm-to-table restaurant, an impeccable wellness area, live music, and a welcoming upstate atmosphere, Skaneateles Fields Resort & Spa is a mini-retreat that will satisfy all your off-the-grid cravings as an urbanite or Skaneateles resident. With 89 total rooms, options range from deluxe kings to double queens, as well as a family-style room with multiple semi-private sleeping areas for those traveling in a group. This is the kind of resort where I would have made core memories as a kid, with pools, trails, nine-hole putting, a pond (essential for childhood shenanigans), and nightly s’mores by the firepit. There’s also a game room with two racing games, a duck claw machine, and an old-school Pac-Man that was born out of the vision of the owner’s own young daughter. The caring staff has truly built something special here, and walking through the lobby every morning feels akin to being the suave, popular quarterback walking down a high school hallway, getting fist-bumps from everyone who passes. —Bridget Knowles Fall festivities: Welcome to the Finger Lakes, New York’s biggest wine region, where a Riesling is the glass to order, but there's much to discover beyond the area's famous bottles. Find all the fall foliage your heart desires and then some as you hike the 1.7-mile loop around Bahar Preserve and Carpenter Falls, where you'll get a chance to spot the trail's 90-foot waterfall misting the changing leaves. Bring home one of the season's best souvenirs by apple-picking at Beak & Skiff Apple Orchards to round off your trip. How to get there: Take the Amtrak Empire Service from Penn Station to Syracuse, and from there rent a car or take the regional bus to Skaneateles. If you're driving from the city, the route will take just over four hours. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Stockton, NJ For a woodsy escape to the Delaware River Valley, the Stockton Inn puts you in close reach of New Hope, Lambertville, and Frenchtown—each worth exploring for picturesque main streets, surprisingly good restaurants, and robust vintage shopping scenes. Brimming with history (once a place of retreat for F. Scott Fitzgerald and Jackie Kennedy Onassis), the 300-year-old inn was reinvigorated in 2024. While the interior design feels delightfully contemporary, every now and again you’ll get a glimpse of the past—for example, in the museum-worthy hand-signed registry of former guests splayed open in the guest lounge. The hotel houses nine rooms, split between the original inn and neighboring carriage houses, and each features king-sized beds, white marble bathrooms, and Sangra de Fruta bath products. Fresh pastries are walked in daily from nearby Stockton Market and made available in the guest lounge, while the Stockton Inn Restaurant, helmed by chef Bob Truitt, is a seasonal eatery that’s a destination in its own right. Perhaps one of the best ways to explore the area is with the hotel’s complimentary bikes, which you can take along the D&R Canal Towpath for a scenic ride along the Delaware River. —Jessica Sulima Fall festivities: The placid region of Bucks County has a certain celebrity allure, with stars like Leonardo DiCaprio and Justin Bieber spotted popping into town. But there’s far more to this bucolic stretch of land than its A-listers. Get to know its architectural spirit on a guided tour of Japanese woodworker George Nakashima’s home in New Hope, which is ensconced by the gorgeous golden treeline. And don’t leave the area without grabbing a PSL at Lambertville Trading Company (which also pioneered the coffee ice cube) just across the New Jersey border and hitting up the Golden Nugget, an expansive flea market where your next favorite comfy sweater is just waiting for you to pick it out. How to get there: Ride the Amtrak Keystone Service from Penn Station to Trenton, New Jersey. From there, book a local taxi service to Stockton. If you're driving, the route will take just shy of 90 minutes. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Big Indian, NY Big Indian isn’t Woodstock. It’s not even Phoenicia. It’s small and tucked away. That’s one of the best things about the location: the sense that you’re further away from things than you really are, and that makes it the perfect place to settle in and hunker down. But if being sedentary isn’t your thing, the McKenley Hollow Trailhead starts at the property line, and there are several other great hikes (the Hunter Mountain Trailhead, for instance) and attractions (West Kill Brewery) within driving distance. This cozy getaway is designed for vintage lovers and hygge seekers—and is almost guaranteed to make it onto your Instagram feed. Tucked deeper into nature than its older sibling in Windham, Eastwind Oliverea Valley derives its special sauce from its harmony with its surroundings, complementing rather than taking away from the landscape. Its wood-fire-warmed lounge, sauna, and proximity to ski slopes make for ideal companions as the mercury drops. A small but excellent seasonal food menu and cocktail list round out its offerings. —Arati Menon Fall festivities: Eastwind Oliverea Valley is a property made for fall. Case in point: its firepits for s'mores roasting, saunas for warming up from the crisp fall chill, and on-site Dandelion Restaurant & Bar, where hearty root veggies, crisp apples, and sumptuous squashes are the high notes on the menu. Should that not be enough to satisfy your wanderlust, stretch your legs on the McKenley Hollow Trail, which starts just steps from the hotel. How to get there: The easiest way to reach Big Indian is by renting a car and making the 2.5-hour drive, but it is possible to make the trek from Port Authority on the Trailways ADT P704 bus that will drop you off right in town. The drive should take just under 3.5 hours. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Manchester, VT The Weston is the latest endeavor of the Sharp family, whose impressive hospitality lineage includes The Carlyle and Gramercy Park Hotel in New York City and the Beverly Wilshire in Los Angeles. Formerly the Inn at Weston, the two-building property with nine uniquely designed rooms underwent a sweeping two-and-a-half-year renovation that left no detail unattended. Visiting the exquisitely restored property feels like being hosted in your well-traveled aunt’s country home. Turns out, there's a good reason for the hotel’s worldly, yet distinctly personal, atmosphere: Much of The Weston’s decor is sourced from the Sharps’ personal art and antique collection. The small-but-mighty spa offers massages and facial treatments featuring the Natura Bisse skincare line. Overall, The Weston shines during winter, but remains a lovely getaway in nature regardless of the season, with plenty of year-round activities available both on- and off-site. —Hannah Towey Fall festivities: Ditch the Central Park horse carriages and opt for a tractor ride through the corn maze at Equinox Valley Nursery. Make sure you go jack-o'-lantern shopping through the giant pumpkin patch before you leave. Afterwards, take a deep breath and let the alpine cure of the mountain air work its magic. While you could also break into a sweat hiking up nearby Prospect Rock or Equinox Mountain, save your energy and leaf-peep in style by riding the sky gondola up Stratton Mountain. Manchester itself is just as worth perusing as its scenic landscapes, with the Hallmark-movie-worthy Northshire Bookstore and the art lover's haven that is the Southern Vermont Arts Center. How to get there: The best way to get to Manchester from NYC is by renting a car and taking the four-hour drive. While there's not much in the way of public transit that makes this New England more accessible, this is a road trip that is well worth the gas money. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Hudson, NY This is all of the upstate charm of Hudson in a nutshell, far and away from the hokey and kitsch. Hudson is oft-cited as the “downtown of upstate,” and if we're expanding on the analogy, then consider this inn the subtly cool address in town in-the-know regulars keep in their back pockets. With one of the best restaurants in Hudson just downstairs, plus the fact that it's within walking distance of the Amtrak station and offers easy access to the city's innumerable and impossibly cute shops, the inn truly moves to the heartbeat of the city. No two rooms across the inn's three buildings—The Merchant House, Wm. Farmer, and the Annex Suites—are the same. Whether you're traveling on a weekend getaway for two, a retreat for a large crew, something in between or beyond, the inn's combined portfolio of 15 rooms and suites has your needs covered. —Kat Chen Fall festivities: Step into “upstate’s downtown,” where Hudson Valley’s eponymous crown jewel is always keeping things fresh. Restock your home decor to better fit the fall with antiques on and around Warren Street. Or, take a short drive up to the High Falls Conservation Area, where there's a moderately challenging 1.5-mile loop. If you like your art with a little side of the outdoors, find Art Omi in nearby Ghent, a 15-minute drive from Hudson, which boasts an impressive 120-acre sculpture park made for frolicking. How to get there: Ride the Amtrak Empire Service up to Hudson for an easy hop up that lasts shy of two hours, or take the equivalent amount of time driving. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Kingston, NY It's clear from the outset that Kinsley is a beautiful hotel, fit for guests who expect more than unblemished greige carpeting from their stays. You can expect sophisticated, if slightly bubbly, spaces; think solid-wood midcentury credenzas, ivory-and-maroon checkered hallway carpeting, deep red oriental rugs, white-as-the-driven-snow Frette linens, a bar that just looks like it makes a delicious cocktail (and boy, does it), and a top-tier selection of art, dispersed all around the space. In short, good looks are a cornerstone of the project. The 42-room hotel, restaurant, and cocktail bar are all part of a collection of four architecturally distinct buildings, tastefully restored from the 17th through 19th centuries. That said, don't miss the on-site dining at the Kinsley, where the seasonal New American cuisine with Southern and French influences comes courtesy of Spencer Coplan, or the bar, where you’ll find unfussy, albeit complex cocktails in an intimate, well-lit space. Kingston, in many ways, feels like Brooklyn—if Brooklyn wanted a hit of fresh air. You’ll find the same kooky, slightly off-beat vintage shops and artfully spare apothecaries lined with overpriced tinctures, along with the same bushy beards and blunt bangs plastered on the folks that frequent them. —Betsy Blumenthal Fall festivities: The on-site restaurant offers autumn dishes like squash doughnuts, pumpkin mole tacos, and chicken pot pie; you can also enjoy craft cocktails made with apple cider and local spirits in the chic, historic setting. Off-property, visit Kingston’s farmers market, where you can pick up seasonal produce and handmade fall goods; take a quick drive to Olana State Historic Site, the home of late artist Frederic Edwin Church, for a hike and sweeping views of the Hudson Valley's fall foliage. Hudson River Maritime Museum will give you a peek into the region’s history, then enjoy a scenic riverfront walk for even more fall colors. How to get there: Around a two-hour drive or a two-hour Metro-North train ride to Kingston from Grand Central. The town is walkable, so the train is a convenient option for this urban-meets-rural getaway in the heart of the Hudson Valley. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Washington, CT The Mayflower Inn and Spa is in Litchfield County, Connecticut—a stunning area of New England that still feels like somewhat of a secret, though urbanites have been moving here for some time in search of a place close to New York City and Boston with both outdoor space and city comforts. The resort itself attracts a similar crowd of New Yorkers and New Englanders looking for a weekend getaway where there’s something for everyone—including fantastic food, outdoor activities, and an unforgettable spa. The stately hotel looks grand and impressive from the exterior, with its manicured gardens and white lounge chairs. But inside is a property updated for what we’re looking for when we travel now: fun. The common spaces are places to linger, from the yellow parlor room to the quiet library. The aesthetic doesn’t sound like it would work on paper—mustard yellow walls, striped couches, tasseled chairs, a gallery wall of floral prints, and antique furniture. But thanks to designer Celerie Kemble's careful vision, it gets pulled together into a relaxing space where there's always a new detail to catch your eye. —Stephanie Wu Fall festivities: You can spend hours cozying up and indulging in s’mores by the fire, but the hotel also hosts seasonal cooking classes focusing on fall harvest ingredients. You can also enjoy a luxury spa day with autumn-inspired treatments, like pumpkin facials and apple cider massages. Nearby, explore Steep Rock Preserve, a stunning area for hiking with vibrant fall foliage, waterfalls, and scenic views. Take a short drive around Litchfield County for the best farm-to-table restaurants, cider tastings, and local weekend festivals, and visit the White Memorial Conservation Center for a hike through forested areas with fall colors in full bloom. How to get there: The property is about a two-hour drive from NYC, or you can take the Metro-North to New Haven, Connecticut (about two hours), then drive 30 minutes. Driving offers the greatest flexibility for exploring the retreat’s semi-rural surroundings. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Tannersville, NY In Greene County’s town of Tannersville, you’ll find the 18-room restored oasis that is Hotel Lilien, formerly the Washington Irving Inn. The Victorian gem dates back to the 1890s and was recently (and impeccably) restored with modern touches, most noticeable in the guest bathrooms, which now include brass fixtures and marble floors. Luxury lies in the velvety feel of the property, where natural light pours in from the stained-glass windows and bounces off dark wood paneling. Since opening, the cocktail bar and dining spaces have become a hub for a trendy local crowd, who have the option to join guests enjoying the wood-burning stove. The hotel is just five minutes away from the region’s buzzy Hunter Mountain, too. —Jessica Chapel Fall festivities: Other than leaf-peeping from your hotel window, you can relax near the fire in the common lounge area with a craft cocktail, around the pool table or jukebox, or while enjoying a s’mores dessert skillet. Off-property, visit Tannersville’s local shops and farm stands—be sure to pick up some pumpkins, apples, and cider. Nearby is also the small, artsy town of Hunter, where you can take part in pumpkin-carving contests or browse through fall farmers markets. Park at Kaaterskill Falls for waterfalls surrounded by vibrant autumn foliage—take the Escarpment Trail for extra-special panoramic views. How to get there: Hotel Lilien is just over a two-hour drive from NYC or a two-hour Metro-North ride to Hudson, followed by a 30-minute drive. It’s best to drive directly from NYC if you can, as it’s easier to access the Catskills region and navigate hot spots surrounding the semi-remote hotel. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Chatham, MA The Chatham Bars Inn, considered a benchmark of luxury on the Cape, manages to reinvent itself over and over again to keep up with the times. If you’re looking for a full-service resort with all the bells and whistles and then some, this is it, including one of the better spas on the Cape; an expansive pool deck with food and beverage service; a private quarter-mile beachfront; tennis courts with lessons available; and a 24-hour gym. Check out its popular farm-to-table dinner series, held a few miles away at the resort’s very own eight-acre farm. —Todd Plummer Fall festivities: The hotel's farm-to-table menu highlights fall ingredients like squash, apples, and root vegetables. You can take in the breathtaking view of Cape Cod's fall coastline from the on-site spa, which offers seasonal treatments like pumpkin facials. Off-site, explore Chatham’s pumpkin patch tours or visit local farms like Cape Cod Organic Farm for seasonal produce and apple picking. For a day of adventuring, take a scenic drive along Cape Cod National Seashore, where the fall colors meet the coastline in harmony, and pay a visit to Monomoy National Wildlife Refuge for bird-watching, strolling, and discovering the area's wildlife. How to get there: This iconic Cape Cod inn is around a 4-hour drive from NYC, or you can take Amtrak to Boston (about 3.5 hours), followed by a bus or a 1.5-hour drive to Chatham. The direct drive is the most convenient and scenic option for exploring the Cape. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Bedford, PA 11 US presidents have stayed at this 2,200-acre old-fashioned resort in the Allegheny Mountains; it takes you back in time in style. For more than 200 years, the property’s eight springs have served as a gathering place and still feature in the treatments at the 30,000-square-foot spa. With the utmost respect for its heritage, the resort has restored some guest rooms; most include balconies with rocking chairs overlooking the creek or mountains. The 1796 Room is the signature steak and chophouse; at Frontier Tavern, linger over artisanal brews or toast marshmallows over a firepit. The Crystal Room is one of the oldest restaurants in America and serves breakfast, lunch, brunch, and dinner, all created by a fantastic chef. —Stefanie Waldek Fall festivities: Indulge in the resort’s Autumn Harvest Afternoon Tea, with seasonal teas, pumpkin bread, and cinnamon scones. For those interested (and even for those not), the resort’s on-site golf course offers breathtaking views of the surrounding fall landscape. Nearby, visit the Bedford County Fall Foliage Festival, one of the top autumn festivals in the region, which features craft vendors, local produce, and live music. Or, explore the Allegany National Forest for hiking, biking, and scenic drives. How to get there: Omni Bedford Springs Resort is nearly a 5-hour drive from NYC, or you can take Amtrak from Penn Station to Harrisburg (3.5 hours), and then it's a 1-hour drive from there. That said, driving directly from NYC is the most straightforward option for this remote destination. - CNT Triple CrownGold List 2024Readers' Choice Awards 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025Read Full ReviewLocation: Nantucket, MA Nantucket's hotel scene has grown up quite a bit over the past few years, with exciting new boutique offerings (Faraway, Life House) making waves and drawing younger, more trend-setting travelers to the island than ever before. But the most tried-and-true hotel here is one of the oldest: the harborside White Elephant, a historic inn-and-cottages resort that masters classic New England chic whilst keeping up with the times. Case in point, the resort is a 54-key hotel with 11 on-site cottages, including an artist-in-residence program and airy interiors paying homage to the island's basket-weaving and seafaring heritage. Cerulean textiles, brass elephant-head door knockers, wood-and-leather armchairs, and marble accents complement the ocean and white caps just beyond your window (or spacious seating area and balcony, if you spring for a suite). The serene great lawn and Brant Point Grill make up perhaps the most spacious stretch of waterfront dining on the island—perfect for a hearty lobster-leaning breakfast, or a perfectly balanced cocktail and raw-bar spread if you're just visiting to take in the bobbing sail boats and passing ferries. And it's all mere steps (or a complimentary bike pedal, all of about three minutes) from all the cobblestones, climbing roses, and crowds in town—something that, on this historic and well-loved island, you really can't beat. —Shannon McMahon Fall festivities: Sip a warm cider cocktail on the inn’s terrace while enjoying the cool autumn breeze and views of the harbor. Outside, the charm of Nantucket in fall, with its mild weather and peaceful atmosphere, provides an idyllic escape. Take a fall ferry ride through Nantucket Sound to witness the coastline’s autumn transformation; Explore Nantucket’s Cranberry Bog, where you can watch as the berries are harvested; and walk or bike along the island’s Sconset Bluff Walk for sweeping views of changing leaves. How to get there: From NYC, it’s around a four-hour drive to Hyannis, followed by a one-hour ferry to Nantucket; alternatively, you can take Amtrak to Hyannis (about five hours) and then the ferry. Of course, driving gives you more flexibility—but the island itself is walkable and easy to navigate without a car. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Aurora, NY The Inns of Aurora is a five-inn lakeside property of meticulously restored buildings from the 1800s and early 1900s. Guest rooms are decorated with furniture and art from founder Pleasant Rowland’s personal collection, and each inn has a distinct feel. Initially constructed in 1833, The Aurora was the first of the inns to be restored in 2003, and was the property of Edwin Barber Morgan, co-founder of the New York Times and American Express. Four more properties were restored to their former glory over the years, the last of which was the 1909 home of Morgan’s grandson, Robert Zabriskie. Renovations were finished in 2019. —Alexandra Sanidad Fall festivities: A quintessential Finger Lakes experience, this property offers seasonal wellness packages, including autumn-inspired spa treatments using apple cider and pumpkin for skin rejuvenation. Off-property, enjoy apple picking at The Apple Farm in nearby Ithaca, one of the best spots in the region for fresh apples, cider, and fall produce. Head to Cornell University's Botanical Gardens for vibrant fall walks and to experience nature in full autumn glory. Or, spend an afternoon at Long Point State Park, where you can hike (or lightly stroll) through trails with views of Cayuga Lake’s fall foliage.
