How to get there: This property is a four-hour drive from NYC, or you can take Amtrak from Penn Station to Syracuse (about three hours), followed by a one-hour drive to Aurora. Driving offers a more direct and scenic route through the Finger Lakes. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Eldred, NY Rustic and upscale design meet here to create a dreamy forest getaway. There are plenty of great stays in the Catskills, but as Goldilocks might say after a breath of relief, this one feels just right. Off a winding road bordered by tall, full trees, the property structures wrap around the parking lot where guests first enter. The lobby boasts a simple yet classy design adorned with heaps of glass, wood, and stone. Floor-to-ceiling windows can be found throughout the majority of the resort's 11 on-site structures, and the openness allows for the sweeping forest backdrop to take center stage. From stand-alone cabins to the sweetest suites, the rooms are spacious and nature-forward, with delicate oak and a light palette on the painted walls. As the resort is located on the gigantic, lush, and historic Eldred Preserve, there’s serenity to be found amidst the trails and three ponds on the grounds. The vastness of the 600-acre preserve, though, remains unassuming—until a meander through the property’s trail network, where guests will approach the serene 65-acre Sunset Lake and perhaps soak in the outdoor ambiance of a dinner at The Homestead. Set adjacent to a pond, restaurant diners enjoy a clear view of the stars with their farm-to-table meals. From day to night, the property feels like a welcoming, warm, decadent paradise in the middle of the woods. —J.C. Fall festivities: Staying on-site means dreamy fall amenities, like rustic country dining, floor-to-ceiling windows, and in-room fireplaces, all surrounded by a colorful mountain backdrop. Don’t skip out on local farm stands and apple orchards in Bethel for a taste of fresh seasonal produce, or a visit to Bethel Woods Center for the Arts for an autumn festival. How to get there: Expect slightly longer than a 2.5-hour drive from NYC or a 2-hour Metro-North ride to Port Jervis, followed by a 30-minute taxi or Uber ride (you can also call the hotel’s concierge for their ride suggestions). Driving is most convenient, as the hotel is tucked in a more remote area. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Beacon, NY The Roundhouse brings a touch of modern flair to the idyllic town of Beacon. With a chic, industrial aesthetic and stunning waterfall views, it finds a balance between the edgy and the bucolic in a very Hudson Valley way. With a popular on-site restaurant and an even more popular wedding venue, the Roundhouse has become an institution in East Beacon, where it sits surrounded by cute coffee shops and swanky boutiques. The nearby contemporary art museum Dia: Beacon and the many fantastic hikes within walking distance of the hotel make it a great home base to explore the lower Hudson Valley. After a long day, guests in one of the penthouse suites can enjoy a bath in a freestanding tub surrounded by large, curved windows showing off the incredible natural surroundings. —Oscar Moss Dorr Fall festivities: Enjoy seasonal cocktails crafted with local apple cider and pumpkins from nearby farms, or cozy up by the riverside fireplace with a glass of mulled wine. Nearby, find fall hiking trails at Mount Beacon (with some of the best leaf-peeping views in the Hudson Valley), or visit wineries like Millbrook Vineyards (in our opinion, one of the best wineries near NYC) for fall tastings. Every Sunday, head to Beacon Farmer’s Market to pick up some seasonal produce, pumpkins, and fresh apple cider. And don’t miss out on Dia:Beacon, an expansive tree-lined art museum housed in a former factory, offering year-round exhibitions with a tranquil atmosphere in the fall. How to get there: Nearly 1.5 hours by car from NYC, or just over a 1.5-hour train ride on Metro-North from Grand Central to Beacon. The Roundhouse is a short walk from the train station. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Bridgehampton, NY Topping Rose House is the Hamptons’ ultimate refined hideaway and feels like a cultivated sanctuary—where splendid white wooden beams meet open-air vistas, spa rituals follow sunset poolside prosecco, and spacious, colorful rooms cradle you. Tucked in the quiet, ritzy town of Bridgehampton, this historic and iconic stay balances grandeur with warmth, and feels like a quiet and classy celebration of old and new. Rooted in a 1842 Greek Revival mansion, the property now offers 22 historic rooms (16 spacious guest rooms and 6 one-bedroom suites). Inside, each of these spaces feels intimate yet expansive, elevated by on-site Jean‑Georges dining, holistic wellness at Naturopathica, and polished personalized service (from wellness programming to private transportation). Topping Rose is home to lawns trimmed to perfection and alcoves of blooming hydrangeas tracing pathways from the main house to a heated pool, where aqua sparkles under beige umbrellas and Adirondack chairs clutch rosé-chilled glasses. —J.C. How to get there: By car, Bridgehampton is around 2.5 hours from NYC, and you’ll have a far better chance of evading the dreadful Hamptons traffic once the summer fades and fall comes around. You can also take the Long Island Rail Road (LIRR) from Penn Station to Bridgehampton, which takes around 2 hours; however, driving offers more flexibility once you’ve arrived. Fall festivities: On the property, surrounded by colored leaves, guests can indulge in autumn-inspired dishes when dining on dishes made using local seasonal produce. Nearby, explore local farms like The Apple Farm for apple picking and pumpkin patches. - Read Full ReviewLocation: North Adams, MA Inspired by the American roadside motor lodge of yore, Tourists is built for contemporary design lovers, with lots of light wood on the banks of the Hoosic River. Many of the large windows in the guest rooms look straight into nature, helping blur the line between the outdoors and indoors. Opened in 2018, Tourists still feels like the cool new kid on the block, with the clientele to match. Ideally situated for those exploring Williamstown and North Adams, it’s approximately three miles from the Clark Art Institute, Mass MoCA, and Bright Ideas Brewing. If you’re visiting this corner of the Berkshires, there’s nowhere more stylish to stay. —Devra Ferst Fall festivities: Guests can enjoy s’mores by the firepit in the evenings, a perfect way to unwind after a day of exploring. Just a short drive from Tourists, Mass MoCA is one of the largest contemporary art museums in the US, featuring rotating exhibits and installations, including seasonal and fall-themed exhibits. How to get there: Tourists is a little over a 3.5-hour drive up the Taconic Expressway. If you need to make a pit stop, the charmingly old-school Millbrook Diner is almost exactly at the halfway point. - Read Full ReviewLocation: New Paltz, NY Experience living history at Mohonk Mountain House, where you will be immersed in the wholesome pastimes and stunning natural beauty of an American icon. Mohonk offers a seemingly limitless array of activities to try while visiting; choose your own adventure or simply embrace doing nothing at all. The spa is a must-visit for time in the tranquil setting that frames the nearby Shawangunk Mountains alone. Whether enjoying the Belgian waffles with caramelized bananas at the divine breakfast buffet or grabbing cookies and tea as an afternoon snack, service is warm and personal. The rooms achieve a cozy elegance by leaning into what makes Mohonk so special: incredible views, simple luxuries like wood-burning fireplaces and claw-foot bathtubs, and an eye for aesthetic details inspired by the Arts and Crafts movement. An ideal place for a solo trip or a family gathering, Mohonk offers a respite from our overstimulated, overscreened culture. Visit and get back to the most important things in life: nature, connection, beauty, and the best breakfast buffet this side of the Atlantic. —Katie Mathews Fall festivities: The on-site spa offers autumn-inspired treatments like pumpkin facials and apple cider massages. Join other guests for the hotel’s bonfire nights: a cozy, fall tradition where guests gather around a firepit in the evenings to enjoy hot cider, warm blankets, and marshmallow roasting. Off-property, head to Minnewaska State Park—located about 10 minutes from Mohonk, the park is famous for its fall hiking, with panoramic views of the Shawangunk Ridge. And with over 85 miles of trails, Mohonk offers one of the best fall foliage experiences in the region. (Hike up to the Sky Top Tower for panoramic views of the colorful landscape.) Dressel Farms in New Paltz offers apple picking and cider tasting throughout the fall; visit nearby wineries such as Whitecliff Vineyards for tastings, located just 20 minutes from the resort. How to get there: It’s around a two-hour drive from NYC to Mohonk Mountain House. You can also take a bus via the Adirondack Trailways from Port Authority to New Paltz, or take an Amtrak or Metro-North train from Grand Central to Poughkeepsie. Book the Mohonk Mountain House Shuttle service in advance—they will organize a seamless transfer from either of these stations. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Newport, RI In the Agassiz mansion, no two rooms are alike. And while this is a historic property, everything is beautifully maintained, and far from dusty. We stayed in the duplex Turret Suite, which occupies, as the name suggests, the property’s iconic highest point. The king-sized bed was cozy, the antique millwork felt reminiscent of another time, and–the pièce de résistance–a spiral staircase leads into the highest section of the mansion’s turret, where a freestanding soaking tub sits surrounded by windows, offering panoramic views of Newport. It is, by any measure, sublime. Fine dining aside, Castle Hill also gets it right with its more casual outposts, too. The Terrace Bar offers elevated takes on grilled New England fare, with an infallible burger, and a housemade peach barbecue sauce I’m still dreaming about days later. A full gourmet breakfast is included for (and exclusive to) overnight guests. Castle Hill is also a great spot for drinks—there are few more quintessentially Newport experiences than posting up in one of the Adirondack chairs on The Lawn, ordering a Dark and Stormy, and waving to the sailboats that go cruising on by. —T.P. Fall festivities: The hotel provides warm fireplaces in the lounge and dining areas, making it the perfect place for a cozy evening. You can also find one of the best spots to view fall foliage in Newport nearby: the Cliff Walk is a scenic 3.5-mile walk along the coast, offering ocean views and picture-perfect colorful leaves. Find apple picking and wine tastings at Sakonnet Vineyards, a short drive away from the property, as well as a handful of local fall festivals, like the Newport Harvest Festival (typically in early October) or the Newport Food and Wine festival. How to get there: It’s about a four-hour drive from NYC to Castle Hill Inn. You can also take the Amtrak to Kingston Station, then meander through a 40-minute drive to Newport with coastal views (the Inn offers free transport from the rail station). - Read Full ReviewLocation: Lake Placid, NY Built in 1883 as a private home, this Adirondack Mountain resort is on the shores of Mirror Lake, one block from Main Street and close to the Olympic Center. Mirror Lake Inn wrote the book on customer service—staff welcome you back with open arms and treat you like family. Rooms have mahogany walls, vaulted ceilings, polished walnut floors, and private balconies with beautiful water vistas. Although there are plenty of things to do on-site throughout the year, the inn’s proximity to the center of town and nearby Whiteface Mountain makes it easy to try many outdoor activities. An absolute must is a massage in the spa. The lakefront Cottage Café serves pub-style dishes. —Charu Suri Fall festivities: Other than views of Mirror Lake’s dreamy fall foliage, guests can enjoy autumn-inspired dishes with locally sourced ingredients, as well as s’mores by the lakeside fireplaces. Off-site, head up Whiteface Mountain on the aptly named Cloudsplitter gondola and take in views from atop a mountain where Olympians have trained. Or you can head downtown and see the Olympic Museum, with exhibits spanning the history of the Games (in case you missed it, Lake Placid is the only US town to host the Winter Olympics twice). How to get there: Around a 5-hour drive from Manhattan up I-87, or a 6-hour trip from Penn Station on the Amtrak Adirondack line to Westport Station, which is about a 40-minute cab or Uber ride from the inn. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Finger Lakes, NY Upstate New York’s Finger Lakes region, a nine-county sweep of state parks and small towns, forests and farmland, has pulled vacationing families and nature lovers to its 11 slender, digit-like lakes for more than a century. But it's really only over the past decade that the area has come into its own as one of the country’s top wine regions, pulling a new crew of savvy visitors who come as much for the local vintages as for the Walden-esque natural setting. The newly reimagined Lake House resort on the north end of Lake Canandaigua, one of the loveliest (and toniest) corners of upstate, sits at the intersection of old guard and new. The expansive compound of recently built white gabled structures on the site of a former roadside motel retains some of the old local flavor but is casually upscale enough for well-heeled weekenders from Toronto and New York City. Rooms have a New England resort feel—plenty of white painted wood and four-poster beds—and the food is excellent: Sand Bar turns out the perfect lobster roll alongside potent classic cocktails, while the more upscale Rose Tavern taps into the area’s local bounty. But, truth be told, you’re there for the lake: To watch it go from blue to pink-gold from the Adirondack chair on your balcony, to head out for the afternoon in a canoe with a picnic lunch, and to listen to it settle for the night from a shorefront firepit as you toast marshmallows or sip a local off-dry Riesling—or, better yet, do both.—Jesse Ashlock Fall festivities: Guests can photograph the foliage around the lakes and indulge in seasonal dishes featuring locally grown squash, apples, and pumpkins. (Menus change with the harvest.) Drive down to Naples (stop and grab a picture at the County Road 12 scenic overlook), or hit a U-pick farm and gather apples. If you want more of an adrenaline rush, take the chairlifts to the top of Bristol Mountain during the fall months for the Fall Sky Ride weekends. How to get there: A leisurely five-hour drive from New York City on I-80 toward Rochester gives you ample time to marvel at the foliage along the way. There is also Amtrak service from the city to Rochester, which is 45 minutes away from Canandaigua Lake. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: 7 Famous Homes From Movies and TV Shows You Can Actually Rent, Including Harry Potter’s Childhood Home and the 'Bachelor' Mansion
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.44
If you’ve ever dreamed of waking up in Bella Swan’s moody Forks home, where a vampire might pop in to say hello at any moment, or planning a Girls-style weekend trip out to Long Island’s North Fork, there’s a world of movie-famous rentals out there for turning your fictional fantasies into a reality. The seven properties on this list span famous homes from film and television, from Harry Potter’s childhood home in Godric’s Hollow to the Bachelor mansion in Agoura Hills. Whether you’re looking to relive your favorite series or cosplay as a main character, these rentals have a certain star quality—after all, it took many professional location scouts to find them. From whimsical lofts in Tokyo fit for solo travelers to Cornwall, England, mansions that double as wedding venues, there’s a recognizable rental below for every kind of travel scenario. Just be sure to book ahead; these famous sets fill up fast. Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bed, shared bathroom Why we love it: Courtyard view, wood-burning fireplace, backyard Featured in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part One, the Vere House serves as Harry’s childhood home in Godric’s Hollow. But its history can be traced back to the 15th century, when the De Vere family built it as a hunting lodge; the front door, with its medieval wooden carvings, is one of the most photographed sites in Lavenham, a village in Suffolk. The house features four en suite bedrooms (another is available to rent here), with access to the shared sitting room, where guests can gather and enjoy a roaring fire (and some crumpets, marshmallows, and sweet chestnuts in the winter months), or the courtyard when the weather’s nice. You’ll also have the option to order a full English breakfast, enjoyed in the communal dining room surrounded by centuries-old objects and artwork. Location: Lavenham, England Things to do nearby: The Crooked House, Six Bells Preston, Great Cornard Country Park Number of guests: 8 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 baths Why we love it: Proximity to riverfront, film memorabilia, patio While it’s booked out for months, Bella Swan’s home from Twilight is out there—not in Forks, but St. Helens, Oregon. And it never left 2008: The home is remarkably similar to the way it appears in the film, down to Bella’s purple floral bedspread (while not available for use, it is on display). Though the movie makes it seem like close quarters between Bella and Charlie, the house actually contains five bedrooms for you and your seven closest Twihards to spread out across. One reviewer wrote, “Watching the Twilight movies while staying in the house is every teenage girl's dream, and I can't believe it happened to me!” Location: St. Helens, Oregon Things to do nearby: St. Helens Historic Riverfront District, Historic Columbia Theatre, Crooked Creek Brewery Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bed, 1 bath Why we love it: Quirky architecture, indoor fireplace, in-unit washer/dryer Season five, episode three of Girls, simply titled “Japan,” is a world unto itself, and Shoshanna’s cartoon-like home away from home is no different. A jungle gym of sorts, the loft is decked out in primary colors, with bulbous fixtures and a wraparound layout. The bathroom, for instance, is housed in its own circular pod, while the kitchen sits in a central pit. This is a personal unit within a shared residential building, so guests might run into each other along common walkways and staircases. Quirky design lovers, this one’s for you. Location: Tokyo, Japan Things to do nearby: Nogawa Park, Ghibli Museum, Fuchu Art Museum Number of guests: 13 Bed and bath: 6 bedrooms, 4 baths Why we love it: Beach access, pet-friendly, private pool Of the North Fork, Marnie from Girls says, “It’s for people who think the Hamptons are tacky and don’t want to be on a beach that’s near a J.Crew.” Once a Coast Guard lifesaving station built in 1893, the East Marion home that fueled one of the most iconic episodes in the show’s history is available to rent. But that’s not the property’s only claim to fame; the home also appeared in The Undoing, when Grace (played by Nicole Kidman) flees to the beach after her husband (Hugh Grant) goes missing. Right on the Long Island Sound with its own private slice of sand, this spacious home has enough room for up to 13 guests (hopefully your bachelorette weekend is more synchronized dance, less fighting). Location: East Marion, New York Things to do nearby: Orient State Park, Kontokosta Winery, town of Greenport Number of guests: 13 Bed and bath: 7 bedrooms, 8 baths Why we love it: Private pool, hot tub, mountain view Bachelor fans will revel in a stay at Villa de la Vina, the 10,000-square-foot Mediterranean-style mansion nestled within the Santa Monica Mountains of Malibu. You and 12 other guests can spread out across seven bedrooms and get a real-life glimpse of your favorite moments from the show. Whether you compete for love is up to you (may we suggest a bachelorette weekend instead?), but the romantic archways, infinity pool, and Agoura Hills views are sure to make you feel like you’re on a reality TV show. Bonus: Chef-prepared meals, airport transfers, and a chauffeur service are all available upon request. Location: Agoura Hills, California Things to do nearby: Liberty Lane Farms, Ladyface Trailhead, Malibu Wine Hikes Number of guests: 4–6 Bed and bath: 2–4 beds, 1–2 baths Why we love it: Film memorabilia, guided tours, gift shop While the house from A Christmas Story is available for daily tours in Cleveland, real fans of the beloved holiday classic will want to stay overnight in suites styled after the film, including the main house (lovingly restored) or the neighboring Bumpus House. All rooms are decked out in 1940s “hillbilly chic” interiors, and the loft, located in the main house, is where two lucky guests can sleep in Ralphie and Randy’s beds. Be sure to plan ahead, as these coveted rentals get booked up quickly around the holidays, and don’t leave without buying a pair of pink bunny pajamas in the gift shop. Location: Cleveland, Ohio Things to do nearby: Rowley Inn gastropub, Hooper Farm, Lincoln Park Number of guests: 21 Bed and bath: 12 bedrooms, 8 baths Why we love it: Seaview rooms, proximity to beach, grand piano, game room Ideal for an English seaside wedding, the Porthpean House is as romantic as it gets, not least because it was featured in the cult-favorite 2013 film About Time. Overlooking Porthpean Beach, the salt-sprayed home was originally built in 1793 and has belonged to the Petherick family for five generations before becoming a dreamy vacation rental. Sleeping up to 21 guests, it houses several historic rooms, including a drawing room, gaming room, dining room, multiple kitchens, and an office, as well as acres of fresh lawn to frolic around. Location: Cornwall, England Things to do nearby: Porthpean Beach, Porthpean Golf Club, RAF Quadrant Tower

item.title: The Most Beautiful National Parks in Canada, From the Tourist Favorites to the Hidden Gems
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.29
From the peaks of the Canadian Rockies to the deep woods of northern Ontario to the prairies where bison still roam, Canada’s national parks span some seriously beautiful and ecologically important terrain. Since I moved to the Great White North more than 20 years ago, I’ve wanted to visit all of the country’s protected areas—and I’m now about halfway through the country's 37 national parks and 11 national park reserves. Some of Canada's most stunning parks are well-known, like Banff National Park, where turquoise lakes, natural hot springs, and miles of mountain hiking trails draw more than four million visitors each year. Others, like Auyuittuq National Park in Nunavut’s Arctic wilderness, or Mingan Archipelago National Park Reserve in northeastern Quebec, are harder to reach and less trodden—but just as gobsmacking. Below, I’ve spotlighted 11 of the most beautiful national parks in Canada, from coast to coast, to inspire your own travel wish list. See what speaks to you, and I'll see you on the trails!

item.title: Planning a Fall Foliage Trip? Book These Amtrak Routes
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.17
A fall foliage train ride is the quintessential autumn getaway. US rail routes glide through some of the nation’s best scenery, including dense forests, glittering lakeshores, and rippling foothills. Even better: unlike a road trip through these colorful landscapes, a rail journey allows travelers to be completely absorbed in the bright red, orange, and yellow hues flicking past the windows. Amtrak trains stop in foliage-rich destinations across the US and Canada. And while the journey itself is certainly a highlight of the trip, travelers will also find seasonal attractions upon arrival at many of the routes’ stops, like apple picking, hikes through vibrant woodlands, and cozy stays at historical inns. Consider this your guide to booking a fall foliage train ride, from the best time to book for peak colors to the top Amtrak trains for reveling in all autumn has to offer. Simply buy your ticket, sit back, and enjoy Mother Nature’s awe-inspiring spectacle. This story has been updated with new information since its original publish date. What is the best time to plan a fall foliage train trip? Don’t forget that when planning a fall foliage trip, timing is key. You’ll want to visit your destination of choice when the changing leaves are decked out in their peak colors. There are several reliable online tools for predicting when the leaves will be the most vibrant. If you’re not sure where you want to visit, start with the Smoky Mountains fall foliage map, which shows predictions for the progression of the entire country’s leaves based on date. Another good choice is the Farmer’s Almanac, which lists the dates each state is predicted to reach peak foliage. Once you have your dates squared, these are the best Amtrak routes and destinations for an unforgettable fall foliage trip. Vermont Train line: Vermonter On its way from Washington DC to St. Albans, Vermont, Amtrak’s Vermonter train ambles through lush northeastern forests and charming small towns. (The entire 13-hour journey crosses nine states, from the Mid-Atlantic to New England.) Once in Vermont, you’ll have your pick of picturesque villages with plenty of fiery trees to view. The train's first stop in Vermont is a solid choice for a fall weekend getaway: the historic town of Battleboro. This pretty hamlet sits right on the Connecticut river in the foothills of the Green Mountains, so expect undulating blankets of colorful foliage in every direction. The train station is right in town, so most activities and amenities are accessible by foot. Stop by a local café or browse the shops lining Main Street. Rent a kayak from one of the local outfitters and gaze over the water toward hills filled with vibrant leaves. Or, head to nearby Fort Dummer State Park (about a 45-minute walk along South Main Street) for easy hiking trails and lookout points over crimson-tinged maple, oak, and birch trees. Peak time for foliage: Early to mid-October Michigan Train line: Pere Marquette Amtrak’s Michigan Services are a series of rail lines running all throughout the Wolverine State. For an autumn sojourn, plan to hop aboard the Pere Marquette, a daily route that runs from Chicago to Grand Rapids. The train winds up Michigan’s west coast, offering brief but sweeping views of Lake Michigan and bisecting lush, Midwestern farmland dotted with trees resplendent in their autumn wardrobes. Once in Grand Rapids, the city’s 200+ local parks offer up-close views of nature’s shifting kaleidoscope. Among the highlights are Blanford Nature Center, which offers extensive walking trails through an old-growth forest of blazing red sugar maples. Don’t miss the Calvin Ecosystem Preserve and Native Gardens, with its network of scenic trails through more than 100 acres of forests and wetlands. The 1,500-acre Millennium Park is just five minutes from downtown Grand Rapids, yet is home to an 18-mile network of treelined trails that wind along lakes and rivers. After you’ve had your fill of forest-bathing, be sure to explore the local brewery scene for seasonal craft beers—after all, Grand Rapids is known as “Beer City, USA.” Fall-themed activities are available throughout the city as well. Don’t miss apple picking from century-old orchards at Robinette’s Apple Haus and Winery. Extend the historical charm to your accommodations with one of the area’s charming bed and breakfasts, like The Leonard at Logan House, which was built in 1914. Peak time for foliage: October 6 to 15 Wisconsin Train line: Empire Builder As Amtrak’s Empire Builder stretches from Chicago, across all of the Upper Midwest, and into Washington state, it offers plenty of foliage-centric destinations to choose from. Just under a four-hour ride from Chicago is a perfect locale for soaking in autumn’s glory: Wisconsin Dells. Head to Dells of the Wisconsin River State Natural Area for views of trees in their seasonal finery among numerous pines and set against Cambrian sandstone cliffs, canyons, and unique rock formations. Back in the center of town, a leisurely stroll along the scenic River Walk offers a chance to behold the bursts of color while weaving your way along the water. Unwind from all that hiking at one of the area’s local breweries. Then check into Sundara Inn & Spa, one of the first destination spas in the Midwest with treatments like Reiki and CBD massages. Peak time for foliage: Mid-October California Train line: California Zephyr Travelers looking for an extended fall train journey would do well to board Amtrak’s California Zephyr. The line stretches all the way from Chicago to Emeryville, California, in the Bay Area. But the scenery becomes especially dramatic once the train reaches Colorado and traverses the unique landscapes of the West. After passing through Denver, expect to ascend the Rockies, glide over Utah’s salt flats, past red rock canyons, and along the Sierra Nevadas. Hop off the train in Truckee, California, the gateway to the Lake Tahoe region, which transforms into a wonderland of colorful foliage come October. Here, visitors are treated to displays of yellows and reds as quaking aspens, willows, and cottonwoods morph into rich golds, ambers, and chartreuses, and oaks and dogwoods that add splashes of maroon and crimson, all contrasting with the mighty pines and deep blue lake. There’s no shortage of outdoor activities to soak in the autumnal atmosphere, either. Everything from mountain biking and kayaking, hiking and horseback riding will immerse travelers among the vivid trees. For a full outdoor experience, try camping at one of the numerous state-run sites along the lake’s perimeter, or opt for a bit of pampering at a resort and spa like the Hyatt Regency Lake Tahoe. Peak time for foliage: October 15 to 31 Maine Train line: Downeaster Amtrak’s Downeaster line weaves north from Boston through Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Maine, where it ends in the city of Brunswick. Expect smatterings of New England leaves to be on display throughout the journey. Hop off the train in Portland, about a two-hour ride from Boston. While there’s plenty to do in the city itself, we recommend taking a quick 15-minute ferry ride across Casco Bay to Peaks Island. The quaint island can be navigated by visitors without a car. Grab a bike or a golf cart at one of the rental shops in town or simply use your own two feet: the area is quite walkable. There’s one hotel on the island, The Inn on Peaks Island, and plenty of waterfront dining, making it a great choice for a quick overnight or weekend stay. Take a bike ride around the two-mile island loop to absorb the incredible views. The island has a mix of deciduous and evergreen trees, so you’ll get to see bursts of oranges and rubies as well as rich, dark greens, all set against a sparkling waterfront. Peak time for foliage: Early to mid-October Virginia Train line: Cardinal Whisking passengers through the Blue Ridge and Allegheny Mountains, the Amtrak Cardinal train offers a visual feast of fall colors. The U-shaped route curves down from New York City, swooping through 11 states and the District of Columbia before terminating in Chicago. Charlottesville, Virginia, is a stop along the way that’s perfectly situated for reveling in autumnal scenery. Seated smack dab in the middle of the Blue Ridge Mountains, the city is a fall wonderland come October. There are plenty of places in town to spot vibrant leaves, including the bosky campus of the University of Virginia and the historic Downtown Mall, which is pedestrian-only. But for the true leaf-peeping extravaganza, you’ll want to rent a car and head to Shenandoah National Park, about an hour’s drive away. Hike the easy 1.6-mile Stony Man loop to an awe-inspiring lookout point with a vista of the rolling hills of deciduous trees all around. Peak time for foliage: Mid- to late October Montana Train line: Empire Builder Spanning eight states across the Northwestern US, the Empire Builder line operates from Chicago to Seattle and cuts through prime landscapes for foliage viewing. Leaf enthusiasts will want to hop off at Whitefish, Montana—a Rocky Mountain town that’s known for its access to Glacier National Park. Though the colors are spectacular, don’t expect to see rich reds or oranges. Here, it’s bright yellow tones that rule the day. Across the rolling hillsides and along the area’s scenic rivers, you’ll find brilliant honey-hued aspen trees and gold-tinged larches, a unique type of pine tree with needles that change from green to flaxen and fall away when the weather turns crisp. For the ultimate scenery, rent a car for a day and drive a quick 40-minute jaunt to Glacier National Park. There, you’ll see the resplendent larch trees framed by the park’s snow-capped peaks above and its sparkling lakes below. Drive the famous Going-to-the-Sun Road, which is less crowded in the fall months, to get a look at the most iconic views. Note that portions of the 50-mile road begin to close down in the third week of October, so be sure to check the official road status page for the latest information. Peak time for foliage: Mid-October Massachusetts Train line: Lake Shore Limited In the fall months, the Berkshires are a true leaf-peeping paradise. The rolling mountain landscape becomes an undulating patchwork quilt of searing scarlets, terracottas, vermillions, and more. Amtrak’s Lakeshore Limited route puts fall travelers right in the colorful action, with its stop in Pittsfield, Massachusetts. During the four-hour trip from Boston, the route passes through open countryside and picturesque towns until it enters Western Massachusetts after Springfield. Then, the train follows the Westfield river and trundles through dense forests bedecked in autumnal grandeur. Pittsfield station is located in the heart of the downtown district, so travelers can step off the platform and straight into charming shop-lined streets and walkable accommodations like the Hotel on North. Farther afield, there are cozy inns like The Old Inn on the Green in New Marlborough and 33 Main in nearby Lenox. Explore the region’s surrounding farms, like Bartlett’s Orchard for u-pick apples and extensive farmer’s markets at Berkshire Grown. For a deep-dive into the region’s vast foliage, try a longer hike along Yokun Ridge, which offers eight-miles of trails that connect Pittsfield and Lenox, with three lookout points over the tie-dyed treetops. Peak time for foliage: October 5 to 21 Connecticut Train line: Northeast Regional One of Amtrak's most popular routes, the Northeast Regional train also doubles as a fall foliage express come October. Spanning from Virginia all the way to Boston, almost every stop is a chance to spot tie-dyed treetops. Hopping off in Connecticut—we recommend the charming town of Mystic— is a great bet to experience the wondrous effects of Mother Nature’s paint brush. Located right in Mystic is the Denison Pequotsepos Nature Center, which offers numerous hiking trails winding through forests of stately oaks, red maples, and American beech trees aflame with color. Heading a bit farther north (40 minutes by car) to the Pachaug State Forest will afford even more chances to soak in a bevy of autumnal hues. On its many miles of trails, you’ll meander through a cathedral of trees in metamorphosis. For a truly awe-inspiring view over the treetops, hike to the Mount Misery Overlook. Contrary to its name, this vista is sure to delight the foliage-minded among us. At 441 feet high, the lookout is the highest point of elevation in the area, meaning a bird’s eye view of the forest’s colorful canopy. At the end of the day, treat yourself to a seaside tipple at Mystic’s waterfront bar Red 36 or dinner at The Shipwright’s Daughter, which offers seasonal fare from local purveyors. Peak time for foliage: Mid- to late October Minnesota Train line: Borealis One of Amtrak’s newest lines is also among its best fall journeys. Launched in 2024, the Borealis train runs between Chicago and St. Paul-Minneapolis through historic small towns, Mississippi River bluff landscapes, and verdant farmlands of the Upper Midwest. Trees are plentiful along the route, with oaks, maples, birches, and more awash in a palette of oranges, yellows, and reds. Foliage-seekers can alight in the town of Winona, Minnesota, located on an island in the Mississippi—where visitors hike, kayak, or fish amid craggy river bluffs carpeted with ever-changing treetops. Key sites include the 3,000-acre Great River Bluffs State Park, whose hiking trails offer broad vistas over the colorful canopies and across the Mississippi and Black rivers; Sugar Loaf Bluff, a distinctive rock formation with hikes and advanced rock climbing; and Lake Park, with easy, paved trails encircling Lake Winona. Enjoy the foliage from the serenity of the river with a guided boat tour. Be sure to stay at a hotel with scenic views, too, like the boutique Hotel 44 Degrees North, located in the heart of downtown with rooms that overlook the river bluffs and forests. Peak time for foliage: October 5 to 20 Montreal Train line: Adirondack Restarting operations just in time for fall trips across the Canadian border is Amtrak’s full Adirondack line, which stretches from New York City to Montreal. The route was shuttered for six weeks over the summer in order to complete track modifications. It reopened to the public in early September. That’s good news for autumnal fanatics, as this foliage-rich route—lined with maples, oaks, birches, and more—becomes postcard-perfect each October. Expect multicolored arboreal panoramas to fill the giant picture windows as you weave through the Hudson River Valley, past Lake Champlain, and along the hills of the Adirondacks. Notable stops along the way include Hudson and Saratoga Springs in New York, but we recommend riding the entire 10-hour route to Montreal to absorb the full force of the fall ambience. Once in Montreal, there are plenty of options to continue the leaf-appreciation tour. Mount Royal, the famous mountain peak overlooking the city, will be a riot of color. Less than an hour outside the metro area are dazzling nature reserves chock full of morphing trees, like the Morgan Arboretum and Parc-Nature du Cap-Saint-Jacques. Peak time for foliage: Early to mid-October

item.title: What Rockaway Film Festival Can Teach Us About Going to the Movies
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.09
Despite its endless appetite for novelty, New York City really is a creature of recursion. Memories never remain too far behind, or rather, too far ahead, before they’re back again wearing a familiar form. One of the city’s finest resurrections in recent memory is moviegoing in the Rockaways. Like the millionaire colonies born of Gilded Age excesses or the Coney Island-rival Rockaways’ Playland that formerly occupied this area of coastal Queens, it’s a stretch of the imagination to conjure up the heyday of movie theaters by the beach. Their near-absence on the peninsula today obscures the foreign era they once thrived in, a few golden decades that spanned from the 1920s to ‘50s earmarked by 25-cent tickets to double features, smoking-friendly cinemas, and faux tuxedoed attendants. A combination of factors ranging from demographic shifts following the Second World War to devastating building fires to general neighborhood decline led to the gradual shuttering of Rockaways’ theaters. The last gasp came when Jerry Lewis Cinema closed its doors in 1996, and the Rockaways went without a commercial indoor theater for the next 25 years. The dry spell was finally broken in 2021 by the nonprofit Rockaway Film Festival organization, when it led the effort of building Arverne Cinema, now the only one of its kind. Ever since the festival itself started nine years ago—popping up screens in venues from Fort Tilden to Jacob Riis Park—hope for the return of moviegoing as a neighborhood pastime has abounded, as one might expect following any reported sighting post-extinction. I arrive at this year’s Rockaway Film Festival (RFF9) in local uniform, with swim trunks donned beneath my work slacks and flip-flops afoot in case of any impromptu beach-going. With the day’s storms recently broken, the muggy summer air made way for a preview of the better days of fall to set the stage for an evening at the open-air movies. The outdoor cinema is wrapped by a rough-hewn Brutalist perimeter—half-lined with concrete cubes, the other half enclosed with planks salvaged from the boardwalk destroyed during Hurricane Sandy. Filled with gravel and sand, it’s like we’re on the bottom of a riverbed with the constant stream of smooth-bellied airplanes taking off above us from the nearby JFK airport. The space certainly feels scrappier than the black-and-white photos of its predecessors. For one, the former Arverne Theater—once a venue for Yiddish acts from the Rockaways’ vibrant Jewish community—broadcasted itself with an outsized vertical marquee until its dismantling in 1952. And the Arverne Pier Theater wore its neoclassical inspirations on its sleeve, complete with Corinthian columns and a half-round pediment. The main centerpiece of the cinema that stands today is its screen, and behind it, there’s not much in the way of scenery. Peeping over the horizon, tower cranes hover forever paused in their progress at the defunct concrete facility, leaning over with their trussed necks, a family of mechanical sauropods. The warmth of the space only truly activates once it’s brimming with people: within my earshot, some trade stories on their convoluted commutes to get here; others debate the ethics of documentary-making; but most exchange reports on what they’ve seen recently and the homework they’ve done on what’s about to screen. Though, those conversations might only apply to the crowd for the world premiere of Eternity One, a documentary from Baltimore-based filmmaker Marnie Ellen Hertzler regarding the precarity of Tangier Island, a remote island community in the Chesapeake Bay eroding from the climate crisis. While the film is the first screening of the festival, it’s not necessarily indicative of the programming (or the crowds) to come. The exciting truth is that none of the films quite are, with the RFF9 lineup reading as an eclectic yet affordable menu. Tickets are capped at $10, and a handful of movies are even being shown for free to ensure that everyone who wants a seat can get one. To name but a few of the movies showing, there’s the 1979 Muppets Movie (the one with “Rainbow Connection”), a generational crowd-pleaser sure to work its magic once again with young families in attendance; a collection of animated shorts themed around “Romantasy” for the old school Adult Swim crowd; and a Dabke dance workshop led by El Funoun, a traditional Palestinian dance company braiding celebration with resistance. As the latter item suggests, there’s much more to the festival than just what’s on screen. Most movies are paired with local live acts to fill the air as the crowd mills in or to keep the party going long after the projector shuts off. You might walk into one screening to the processional music of Brooklyn slacker prog and exit the next to a Roots reggae DJ set. Kyp Malone, in all his braid-bearded glory, plays before Eternity One, at times playfully directing us, “now pretend I’m a movie, and pay the fuck attention,” and later offering light conversation starters between straight-from-the-bottle sips of Casamigos like, “did you think fascism was going to feel different?” One particularly inspired pairing comes from the combination of Ridgewood-based documentarian John Wilson’s first feature, The History of Concrete, with a set from Bellerose rapper Heems (of Das Racist fame for any lovers of combination Pizza Hut-Taco Bells). Wilson’s whispering, Kermit-ish cadence juxtaposed with Heems’s audacious bars shorthands the borough’s rejection of one-size-fits-all characterization as one of the most diverse urban centers in the world. Tying a bow on the Queens-ness of it all is the al-fresco setting itself. This might be the one pocket of the city that does sleep. Call it the influence of the local surf culture, or the protected peace of the nearby nature reserves, but the Rockaways are just the kind of place made for prying sticks out of asses. Take it from friendly neighborhood rockstar Patti Smith, who put it simply on her Substack: “Being at Rockaway Beach makes me happy.” It’s long ceased to be a neighborhood that puts on airs, an attitude that liberates us all tonight. Under the darkening sky, I’m oddly comforted by the couple next to me taking advantage of the shifting tenebrism for some drive-in-style PDA. Tucked inside the cul-de-sac of a residential street off of Beach 67, Arverne Cinema is right at home amongst the two-story houses hosting their own celebrations, with one particularly passionate birthday party across the street beating out the volume of Hertzler’s Q&A. While the festival bounced around for its first few years, finding a permanent home in the community had always been the goal. “There’s not much that’s like the joy of sharing a movie that you love very much in a space that was built by friends and neighbors with a full audience,” said RFF co-founder and organizer Courtney Muller, reflecting on the festival’s sixth year at Arverne Cinema. At the risk of sounding like another trite moral about the importance of social gathering post-pandemic, the Rockaway Film Festival is as much about movie-going as it is about movie-watching. Thankfully, the act is not nearly as endangered as it was once reported to be, with chains like AMC boasting booming attendance numbers. But factors such as surging ticket prices and shorter gaps between theatrical runs and streaming releases contribute to the perception that going out to the movies is a luxury, and shrink crowds accordingly. That image is only bolstered by the glamorous superlatives we’ve come to expect from premiere film festivals around the world—the record-smashing standing ovations at Cannes, a bigger and better revamp of Sundance, the making or breaking of Oscar contenders at the Toronto International Film Festival. Between the flimsy baskets of superb beach shack grub and seating reminiscent of a school play, the Rockaway Film Festival is doing the remedial work of bringing movies back to the people by reminding its attendees that a movie theater is not supposed to be a sarcophagus. My favorites in New York, and the ones I’d champion are worth traveling for, are all framed by their own signs of life, from the faint roar of the subways that rumbles through the Angelika to the shoulder-to-shoulder sardine can theaters of Film Forum (though one should never go so far as to condone cellphone use for QR code ordering at an Alamo Drafthouse). That a film festival grows in the Rockaways after more than two decades without a single theater is a feat in its own right, and its longevity for the past nine years speaks to the simple human desire shared by cinephiles and curious locals alike that watching a good movie in a crowd of peers, perhaps even with your toes in the sand, should come at no exorbitant cost. “When this festival began as a four-day experiment in 2018, it was not just about showing movies—it was about saying clearly to this community that it deserves cinema,” shared Rafael Espinal, Commissioner of the Mayor’s Office of Media and Entertainment, to kick off the start of this year’s events, “Rockaway reminds us that cinema belongs everywhere in New York City, not just in the places where people expect them, but right here, by the beach with this community.” In an interview with Hell Gate, Muller described the undercurrent of this year’s programming as the “stories of things coming apart” and what grows in the spaces left after collapse. It might as well be the unofficial motto for the Rockaways, where surfers dropped everything to shovel out sunken homes after Hurricane Sandy, grassroots mutual aid networks opened their doors to displaced New Yorkers after 9/11, and neighbors came together to convert a vacant lot into a movie theater. RFF9 is an exemplary case study that the local flavor of the Rockaways is best appreciated up close. I can’t write about what it was like to taste the salt air seasoned with New York atmosphere and make the flavor materialize on your tongue. A high-budget documentary exclusive to the streaming platform that produced it can’t either. You might have to wait another year for the next festival, take the A train as far down as you’ve ever taken it, come early, and claim one of the beach chairs while you can to feel it for yourself, but the point is that you must. How to Visit Rockaway Film Festival This year's festival runs from September 2-6, and while tickets to the remaining screenings have all sold out online, some have limited capacity for tickets sold at the door, and for others, you can sign up to be on a waitlist at the ticket stand before showtime. For the most up-to-date information on this year's screenings, visit the programming page of the festival here. As far as getting yourself to Arverne Cinema, you have a few options. You could take the Far Rockaway-bound A train to Beach 67 and walk eight minutes to the theater, ride the Q22 bus to the Rockaway Beach Blvd / Beach 73 St stop or the Beach Channel Dr / Beach 71 St stop (and connect to the bus from the LIRR Far Rockaway station), or ride the NYC Ferry, which by and large offers the most scenic views. The festival's website also hosts an extensive Rockaway guide with recommendations ranging from where to get your morning coffee to the best cannabis dispensary in town. Take full advantage of these expert recs by basing yourself directly in the Rockaways. For a weekend stay, the beachy sanctuary of the Rockaway Hotel is the way to go.

item.title: Where the Chefs Eat: Mario Carbone travels the world for these five restaurants – and one is so good he arrives 90 minutes early
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.99
Where the Chefs Eat asks your favourite chefs for their top restaurants in cities across the world. For this edition, we sit down with Mario Carbone. The last time I walked into what is now Carbone London, on Grosvenor Square, it was the American Embassy – an imposing building that looms large over one of Central London’s leafiest and prettiest squares. Fast forward nearly 30 years and I’m back, but this time it’s to chat with Mario Carbone, the New York chef behind the 2025 opening. The experience, I’m glad to say, is far less intimidating than when I was here to apply for a student visa in the ’90s. That isn’t to say Carbone isn’t formidable, though. His Carbone in New York opened in 2013 to rave reviews and he’s since opened locations across the States and in Hong Kong, Doha and Riyadh, too. Described by The New York Times as “a fancy red-sauce joint”, he and his team have carved out an impressive corner in the highly competitive Italian American food market, and he is clearly not planning on stopping anytime soon. We meet in the corner of the enormous London location. Carbone himself is immaculate in chef whites, not a hint of jet lag around his bright eyes. He spends half the year travelling, and he clearly has a militant work ethic. Based between New York and Miami, he was keen to open a British location from the get-go. “When New York was established,” he tells me, “we kind of assumed London would be the next smartest place to open, and we felt it had to be in Mayfair. Eventually this became available, and we thought the fact that it was in the old American embassy building made for a great story. It had the 1960s, JFK vibes and it just worked.” The result is a stunning space that is light and breezy upstairs with an outdoor terrace and a theatrical downstairs area with a fabulous bar and Manhattan flair. The Italian food market in America is serious business with generations dominating in cities across the States. Carbone admits that the first opening was, initially, “a little nerve-racking because there are so many well-established places that are 75 or 100 years old, serving amazing American Italian food. And they look and feel a lot like Carbone, but this is the food we grew up knowing and loving, and there can always be another great pizzeria, more bagels or another great Italian restaurant. Now that we’re established, hopefully, we are the torchbearer of the next generation.” There was, he tells me, “Initial surprise that young owners were doing such an old nostalgic thing so well and I think I caught the industry by surprise. The trend, 13 years ago, was fine dining and a very minimalist tasting menu. That’s what was in vogue then, and that was sort of what was expected of us, but we did the opposite of that, which caught everyone off guard. My partner Rich [Torrisi] and I took our training, having worked with some amazing chefs, and applied it to this food. We took it to another level.” I’m curious about Carbone's upbringing with food. He was born to a mother whose family hailed from Northern Italy, a father whose ancestors came from Sicily. “I grew up with food, and this is the only job I’ve ever had,” he says. “I started cooking in local restaurants when I was about 15 years old. I wasn’t very good at anything else, to be frank with you." Later training came under the guidance of greats such as Daniel Boulud (“that was definitely the most difficult kitchen I’ve ever worked in, but I made some of the greatest friendships while I was there”). Travel is a huge part of Carbone’s life, even if it is under the guise of work, and he loves, by his own admission, “just being in restaurants. I’d rather an incredible environment than amazing food, if I had to choose. It’s all about atmosphere because I can cook at home if I want to. I’m very sensitive to music and light and the energy in the room. I can tell by the energy of a restaurant if it’s well run and organised. I can always tell if a place is in a groove and, if they are really good at what they do, then it puts you at ease.” Apart from a second London opening next year, he is also working on new locations in Mexico City and in São Paulo “and I’m hoping to try and sign Tokyo but the brand, for sure, is going to continue to grow.” With that, Mario Carbone gives us five restaurants around the world he visits time and again as favourites. Katz's Delicatessen, New York Katz's is one of my favourite places in the world. I think one of the few places that really lives up to a huge reputation. The food is delicious, and the execution is incredible. Although I always think about ordering something different, I really do, I get pastrami every time. They make so many great things, but it’s their signature thing, and it’s done unbelievably well. Katz's has been operating since 1888, so it’s a real New York institution. Joe's Stone Crab, Miami I eat here probably once a week, either at the restaurant or by getting takeout. And I love it. They are just great at what they do, and they also put you at ease, even though they’re incredibly busy. It’s such a well-oiled machine, and you know they’ve got it. I rarely get the crab, even though that’s what they’re famous for. I eat my way through the menu, so I will get their famous chopped salad, and they have a great coconut shrimp appetiser. I also get the blackened grouper or the fried chicken and, if it’s Sunday and I’m craving Chinese, they do a Chinese chicken dish. It’s orange chicken, and it’s not that it’s really good, but there isn’t a lot of Chinese in Miami, and it really scratches the itch. Carbone in Miami is right behind Joe’s, so I’m there multiple times a month. If I’m dining in, I like to eat at the bar; it’s such a great, busy, bustling bar. I like to watch them fill the orders because it’s chaos, but it’s so slick. Mezzatorre Hotel, Ischia There is the most incredible hotel in Ischia, in the Bay of Naples, called Mezzatorre. They have this casual lunch restaurant by the pool, overlooking the sea, that is simple and perfect, and maybe my favourite place in the world. It’s unbelievable. There’s one particular table that I always sit at, in the same chair, and I get there about an hour and a half before they open for lunch. I like being in restaurants, so I’m happy just watching them set up, catching up on emails and working. I will sit there all the way through lunch, for up to six hours, and I smoke a cigar at the end; it’s just the best. They have exactly what you’d hope to eat in that environment, so lots of delicious salads, (they do a great chickpea salad) and this giant rigatoni with lobster. They always have great specials, too. It’s just an unbelievable place. Ho Lee Fook, Hong Kong I absolutely love Hong Kong. It’s a great food city, but I wouldn’t recommend going any time when it’s warm because it gets so hot. It’s so condensed and busy with traffic in the city, so it’s unbearable when it’s hot. When I’m there, and I’ve checked in at Carbone, I like to go out, and Ho Lee Fook is incredible. It’s really well balanced, has super high execution and it’s familiar. I know them, so they take good care of us, and it’s one of those places I crave when I get into town. Everything from the music and the lighting to the food is great. It’s all the things I try for at Carbone. I let them choose what to eat for me, and they know I’m pretty much down for anything, so I don’t generally order off the menu when I go, but I’d recommend it to everyone. APL by Adam Perry Lang, Los Angeles In Los Angeles, there is a genius of a human being called Adam Perry Lang who does a pop-up barbecue restaurant. He only does it on the weekend, and it’s called APL. It’s outside of a bar called Gin Rummy in Marina del Rey. He’s there Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays; he takes the back patio over. They have these enormous smokers and he’s the most talented barbecue human being on the planet – there is no doubt about it. He is incredible. I know him because he’s a very good chef; he’s classically trained (he worked for Daniel Boulud), and he’s been through a lot of the same doors I have. He’s brilliant, and it took me a while to get there the first time because I’m not in California often. When I first went a few years back, it was just a life-changing experience. He’s great at traditional barbecue stuff like ribs and brisket, but he also has some untraditional things on the menu, so he can be smoking tuna or he’ll do whole Peking duck. He’s a master, and it’s fun because it’s literally in the backyard of a dive bar; it’s amazing. Carbone London, 30 Grosvenor Square, W1; carbonelondon.com

item.title: The UK’s oldest recorded town has more than 2,000 years of history – and where it is may surprise you
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.03
When I found out where the UK’s oldest town was, I wasn't expecting it to be a place I've passed through quite so frequently, or one still thriving today. I’ve been lucky enough to travel the breadth of Britain over my 31 years, from tiny hamlets in the Scottish Highlands to artsy towns in Cornwall. I’ve spent half my life calling London home and the other half in East Anglia; holidayed in Wales, visiting beaches accessible only by wooden swing; slept in cabins in the Cotswolds; road-tripped through Northern Ireland; and spent years studying in Newcastle. All of which is to say, if you’d asked me to guess where it was, I’d have imagined a barely-there archaeological site somewhere in rural Northumberland, rather than a thriving modern city in Essex, close to the Suffolk border and just 60 miles northeast of London. I’m talking, of course, about Colchester. Today, the city is popular for its fast commuter trains into the capital, relatively affordable housing, open green spaces and, of course, its rich history. But in around AD 43, it was known as Camulodunum: the first major Roman city and the initial capital of Roman Britain, before it was destroyed during Boudica’s rebellion in AD 61. The story of the Roman settlement didn’t end there, however, and Colchester was rebuilt in the years that followed. During the Anglo-Saxon era, the city was largely neglected before later falling under Viking control. In AD 917, Edward the Elder drove the Vikings out, and Colchester began to regain its former stature. Following the Norman Conquest, Colchester Castle was built in 1066 over the ruins of an earlier Roman temple. Dating to the 1070s, it became the first and largest of the Normans’ great keeps, cementing Colchester’s importance as one of England’s key centres. But the city’s history stretches back even further than the Roman conquest. Colchester began as an Iron Age settlement, ruled by Cunobelin, known as the ‘King of the Britons’. Evidence of this early history can still be found in the city today, including a collection of Iron Age and Roman artefacts at Colchester & Ipswich Museums. There’s something slightly confusing about calling Colchester the oldest town in the UK, given that it is also one of the country’s newest cities. It gained city status in November 2022 as part of the late Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours, one of eight towns to receive the upgrade. It joined Doncaster, Milton Keynes, Dunfermline, Bangor, Wrexham, Douglas and Stanley. Of course, when compared with some of the world’s oldest cities, Colchester is relatively young in the grand scheme of human history. Jericho, on the West Bank near the Jordan River, is thought to have been inhabited as early as 9000 BCE, and is often described as the world’s oldest known walled city. Across Britain, several places lay claim to the title of oldest town, from Thetford in Norfolk and Ipswich in Suffolk to Amesbury, near Stonehenge, where evidence of settlement dates back as far as 8820 BC. Colchester’s claim rests on a specific point of difference: it is officially recognised as the UK's oldest town on record, based on a reference to the settlement by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder.

item.title: Bound for Bath? These are the hotels our editors love most for a romantic city stay
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.52
Bath has long been a popular choice for city-breakers, and some of the best hotels in Bath are also some of our editors' favourite places to book for a last-minute staycation. Like us, many are attracted by the city's combination of healing waters and Regency history. After all, where else can you start the day in Ancient Rome and end it with a Jane Austen-themed afternoon tea? Perhaps unsurprisingly, it’s got a thriving hotel scene, with a mix of accommodation to suit every taste. There are heritage properties, like the Gainsborough Bath Spa and Royal Crescent, where five-star luxury is a given; the hipster boutiques, like No 15 Great Pulteney, and gallery-come-hotel 8 Holland Street, which cater to discerning eyes; and the country piles located just outside the city centre, where you can cosplay as an extra from Bridgerton as you roam the grounds. Without further ado, here’s our guide to the best hotels in Bath. item.title: 14 best hotel resorts in Mallorca to book for 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.40
Mallorca does resorts with more subtlety than most islands its size. The infrastructure is there, of course: beach clubs, sprawling spas, kids’ clubs, adults-only sanctuaries, golf courses curling through the hills. But the best resort stays here do not feel air-dropped in. They tend to grow out of the landscape or the island’s own visual language, whether that means a honey-stone hill village above the northeast coast, a 14th-century finca estate folded into vineyards, or a cliff-hugging hideaway where the Tramuntana mountains drop theatrically into the sea. Even the bigger, shinier properties still feel distinctly Mallorcan rather than generically Mediterranean. The island also makes resort-hopping by mood unusually easy. In the north and northeast, around Formentor, Alcúdia and Playa de Muro, the draw is beach life, family ease and a kind of clean, athletic outdoorsiness shaped by cycling routes, sailing and long pale bays. The southeast, around Porto Petro, softens into quieter coves and low-key fishing villages. Inland and toward the west, the tempo shifts again. Here, resorts become more introspective: monastery estates, adults-only retreats among pine trees, well-being hideaways where the point is not to be entertained but restored. What ties the best of them together is that they know their lane. They do not try to be everything at once. They know whether they are for families, aesthetes, golfers, spa obsessives or people who want to spend a week in linen moving between sea, shade and lunch. Here are the resorts that do it best. item.title: 9 best hotels in Albania for an affordable escape in 2026: from luxurious Riviera stays to buzzy boutique favourites in Sarande
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.24
Ask any visitor to Albania, and they'll tell you the same thing – it's the warmth of the people that makes this country so memorable, and some of the best hotels in Albania present a stellar example. Yes, it has crystal clear rivers, snow-dusted peaks, a glittering Ionian shoreline, and ancient UNESCO heritage sites galore, but it’s the Albanians and their innate kindness and hospitality that make a visit here truly special. For decades, Albania was cut off completely from the outside world due to a brutal communist regime. Under dictator Enver Hoxha’s iron grip, the country was in a state of self-imposed isolation. Religion was outlawed, private property seized, and travel beyond its borders was unthinkable. Even today, echoes of its past linger in the thousands of stark concrete bunkers that pepper the landscape. Recently, however, the small Balkan nation has been making its way onto the world stage. And thanks to a series of new flight routes, it is now firmly on the tourist map. Visitor numbers are increasing year on year, and, with EU membership pending, and development occurring at every corner, this is a place to discover now. Larger brands and resorts are moving in fast, and there’s a distinct sense that Albania is repositioning itself as an upmarket destination, much like neighbouring Montenegro and Croatia. However, for the time being, there are still plenty of lovely hotels in Albania – from traditional guesthouses to boutique boltholes and heritage properties – these stays bridge the old and new, which could be the country's best USP. item.title: Everyone tells you to do New York at full speed. But what if you physically can’t?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.42
Before I landed in New York, I’d already convinced myself I’d be doing the city wrong. New York is a trip that seems to demand your top speed. 30,000-step itineraries, early starts after late nights, neighbourhoods stacked one after another, and the pressure to jigsaw every viral experience into each waking hour. I’d watched others arrive with enormous lists and somehow leave having seen it all. I wanted that accomplished feeling too. But I live with lupus. My mobility isn’t what it once was. I love travelling deeply, but my energy and comfort levels don’t often match my enthusiasm to see the world. I wondered if New York might expose that more than anywhere else. I planned excitedly for months. But underneath that excitement was a nagging worry that I’d come home feeling as though I hadn’t really done New York at all. Social media only amplified it: crossing the Brooklyn Bridge, coffee in Soho, a rooftop or gallery, somehow all before lunchtime. Why couldn’t I be on the go for hours without thinking about it? The journey The first thing I had to accept was that New York is physically exhausting. And that began long before I arrived at JFK. For years, I approached long-haul flights by booking a ticket and simply getting on in discomfort. This time, I advocated for myself. Flying with Virgin Atlantic, I discovered how much support was available when I asked for it, from extra space to assistance from staff who genuinely wanted to help. I realised how often I’d tried to adapt myself to travel rather than asking how travel could adapt to me. The pace Then came the walking. Distances add up quickly in New York and the subway, while useful, isn’t straightforward when you need step-free access. Not every station is accessible, so I used the StepFree NYC app to plan routes, sometimes travelling further to avoid stairs. But no amount of planning could remove fatigue altogether. The solution was something I’d previously considered a waste of holiday time: rest. I scheduled naps and left gaps between plans. Instead of filling every moment with another attraction, I started taking breaks without feeling guilty about them. Greenwich Village quickly became my favourite neighbourhood. I could walk a few blocks, mooch in boutiques like Greenwich Letterpress and Artisanal Cornucopia, rest my legs in Washington Square Park and get a glimpse of everyday New York. There were no landmarks to queue up for. That was the beauty of it. For once, doing nothing still felt like doing New York. I wasn’t just seeing the city. It felt like I was in it. Where to rest NoMad was exactly the kind of New York neighbourhood I wanted to wake up in, and Hotel Park Ave put me right in the middle of it. Designed by Jacu Strauss, the hotel is playful and seriously stylish, but crucially, its accessible rooms haven’t been treated as an afterthought. Mine was spacious and thoughtfully laid out, with a roll-in shower and grab bars. Choosing accessibility didn’t mean compromising on the fun either. I could head upstairs for drinks overlooking the city at rooftop bar Golden Child without adding another journey to my evening. Suddenly, staying in wasn’t really staying in. Choosing where to spend my energy One of my braver decisions was setting an alarm before sunrise for Sky High Yoga at Edge. After deliberately protecting my rest, getting up that early felt counterintuitive. High above Manhattan, with the city waking beneath me, I moved through the class and watched the skyline change. It reminded me that movement didn’t have to mean pushing myself. For once, I was up and moving before the city was, but I wasn’t racing it. The same approach changed how I ate. At Sushi Kai, I gave an entire evening over to omakase. Course after course was prepared in front of me, turning dinner into something to watch, taste and linger over rather than another stop between plans. Once, I might have worried about what else I could squeeze into the evening. This time, dinner was the plan. Permission to do less By the end of the trip, I’d stopped worrying about whether I was doing New York ‘right’. I didn’t experience less of New York. I just experienced it differently. The irony was that slowing down allowed me to absorb more. I’d learned that accessible travel isn’t about lowering expectations. It’s about working out what I need to enjoy a place without exhausting myself in the process. Travelling smarter meant being selective about where I spent my energy, building in rest and letting go of the pressure to see everything. I hadn’t failed at doing New York. I’d simply stopped trying to do it like everyone else. How to do it - Fly: Virgin Atlantic – accessible flights available between London Heathrow and New York JFK. - Stay: Hotel Park Ave, NoMad – accessible rooms available, including mobility-accessible layouts and bathrooms. - Do: Sky High Yoga at Edge – early morning yoga overlooking Manhattan. - Eat: Sushi Kai – an intimate omakase experience in New York. - Getting around: StepFree NYC – an accessible journey planning app for finding step-free routes around the city.

item.title: 11 best restaurants in Porto to visit for a gastronomic weekend
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.30
In Porto, more than anywhere else in Portugal, the wine is as integral an ingredient to a dinner as the food. Just the way it should be, in fact. Here, it seems, knowledge of wine is imbibed with a mother’s milk; children in the countryside grow up understanding the seasons, harvests and the bounty that nature provides. Chefs proliferate, as do winemakers, resulting in a city that offers rich pickings for the visiting gourmand. I live at the other end of the country, where freshly caught grilled fish with a drizzle of local olive oil and my feet in the sand is all I want when there, but in Porto my culinary demands are higher. The Portuguese are, after all, a nation that lives to eat, as opposed to eating to live. Restaurants – from simple tascas to fine dining – are frequently full, often noisy and always tangibly happy places; platforms for celebrations and family get-togethers, the food central to the experience. The cooler weather in Porto increases my appetite, which heightens my curiosity, and I become intent on trying the latest trends, the newest restaurants, and, of course, checking that my recommendation among the top chefs is still on point. item.title: Tate Britain is bringing the 90s back to life with the biggest art and fashion exhibition of its kind
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.27
In the latest of an exciting series of autumn/winter exhibitions coming up in the capital, Tate Britain is set to stage the first exhibition exploring the art, photography and fashion of the 1990s from 8 October 2026. The 90s: Art and Fashion is a deep dive into a decade synonymous with optimism and an audacious spirit, exploring the decade’s surge of creative energy through the world of almost 70 artists. Former British Vogue editor-in-chief Edward Enninful OBE is the lead curator, lending his decades of industry experience and knowledge to the season’s hottest showcase. As the economic uncertainty of the 1980s faded somewhat, the turn of the decade welcomed a resourceful new generation of young talent in Britain. The crowd’s taste for imperfection and ‘realness’ opens the exhibition space with photography by the likes of Corinne Day, Nigel Shafran and Juergen Teller, the talent behind the lens for magazines such as i-D, Dazed and Confused. Further on, Roshini Kempadoo and Eileen Perrier examine the influence of print media and how it expanded mainstream notions of beauty during what’s now seen as one of the most iconic fashion eras of recent times. Film and photography present the youthful attitude of the ’90s, with exhibits including Mark Leckey’s 1999 film Fiorucci Made Me Hardcore to images documenting young people at iconic club nights across the UK, including the Haçienda in Manchester and Bagley’s in London. In a similar vein, Dave Swindells, Peter J. Walsh and Tony Davis document the birth of acid house and its influence on the decade's culture. Other key highlights of the exhibition include an exploration of the ‘Cool Britannia’ movement, Chris Ofili’s Turner Prize-winning 1998 painting No Woman, No Cry – a poignant tribute to Doreen and Stephen Lawrence – and work from artists such as Hamad Butt that responded to the ongoing impact of the AIDS crisis. The exhibition ends with artists and designers who, at the close of the 20th century, reckoned with Britain’s past and addressed questions of its future, from Yinka Shonibare to Maud Sulter, via icons including Vivienne Westwood. The 90s: Art and Fashion runs at Tate Britain from 8 October 2026 – 14 February 2027.
