item.title: 14 best loungewear brands: upgrade your airport uniform with these luxury pieces actually worth the hype
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.18
Comfy, layered, security-friendly and stylish: the best loungewear brands are having a moment. Gone are the days when cosy equated to frumpy. Slouchy joggers, sharp sweatshirts, leggings and hoodies are now de rigueur in the business class lounge and economy cabin alike. Traveller writers and editors have learned that a smart yet comfortable loungewear set is the go-to for surviving red-eye flights, prioritising cashmere co-ords and silky soft, thermoregulating bamboo to create a chic, elevated set you won't feel sheepish to wear out of the house. Below, we’ve curated the definitive guide to the best loungewear brands to know in 2026, so your next flight will be the most comfortable yet – and you won't have to compromise on style. Varley It’s the fabrics that Varley uses that makes its separates so supremely comfortable, and despite initially investing in a few of its sportswear separates for a wellness escape in Ibiza, it’s become one of my most revisited brands at home, too. Now, I wear its oversized sweatshirts on travel days, when working from home and on route to the gym. The simplistic silhouettes are easy to style (read: you don’t need to do much to make them look good) and if you’re partial to a print, the leggings are a fun way to amplify your off-duty wardrobe. Sarah Bannerman Uniqlo Uniqlo remains the ultimate destination for affordable lounge essentials, with its signature mix of minimal Japanese design paired with pleasingly high quality fabrics. The result is stylish everyday wear that’s comfortable as anything. Tactile textures elevate downtime dressing in the brand's loungewear offerings – think soft washable knit ribbed trousers and ultra-cosy fleece pieces that are still smart enough to wear out of the house. These low-maintenance separates work equally well for a quiet morning at home, afternoons running weekend errands and to keep you comfy on your yearly far-flung long haul flight. Tala Founded by former fitness influencer Grace Beverley, British brand Tala balances style, functionality and a dose of cool, alongside a strong commitment to sustainability. Pieces are made with organic cotton and recycled blends. The brand excels at crafting relaxed cuts twinned with modern touches – your classic tracksuits gets an instant upgrade thanks to rich shades like deep Americano. Whether you are working from home, heading to a Pilates class, or travelling, these heavy-weight, peachy-soft sets make off-duty dressing feel intentional rather than slapped together. Asceno Everyone at Traveller rejoiced when pyjama-inspired fashion entered the scene. We’ve always wanted to wear our cosiest nightwear on a flight (especially those we’d like to try and sleep on), and now it’s not only socially acceptable, but actively stylish. Asceno is unbeatable on this front – Its signature Aurelia trousers and London shirt are made from 95 per cent lambswool and five per cent UK-sourced cashmere, for a look that’s as easygoing as it is effortlessly chic. Pangaia We previously tested a jacket from Pangaia that used flowers as down – the brand is an industry leader in innovative sustainable practices. Its loungewear is no exception, banishing manmade materials in favour of a 50/50 split of organic and recycled heavyweight cotton, which is both casual enough for the sofa and cool enough to wear into town. You can even get a set for the whole family, as Pangaia makes their colour-popping separates for women, men and children. Cos Known for its minimalist aesthetic and understated cuts, Cos stands out as one of the cooler high street fashion brands offering clothes at a pleasing price point. It has a strong year-round loungewear offering, including a lovely selection of cashmere pieces that wouldn’t look out of place in the office, let alone in an aeroplane cabin. H&M H&M are masters of the high street, consistently offering soft, effortless pieces that punch above their price point. This season’s collection runs the gamut from lightweight, breezy fabrics for warm afternoons to plush brushed cotton ready for when the nights start to draw in. There are plenty of styles that work well for mixing and matching, too. Lilysilk Not content with creating ultra-luxurious sheets for your bedroom, Lilysilk turned its attention to creating a silk clothing range too. The brand’s loungewear collection is crafted from a premium silk-blend knit, turning your comfy clothes into elegant, breathable mainstays that, with good care, should keep you cosy for years to come. Pieces are designed to move naturally and fluidly with the body – if you’re after casual separates that feel as luxurious as eveningwear, the below make good options. Alo Yoga If you love the slouchy style of the Adanola tracksuits but you want something less sporty, more elegant, Alo Yoga is the best loungewear brand for you. There’s a reason the style set is regularly spotted kitted out in this US activewear brand. They’re known for creating quality, fashion-forward pieces that take the likes of Gigi Hadid, Taylor Swift, Kendall Jenner and Hailey Bieber seamlessly from pilates class to brunch. Although some of these sets are loose-fitting, with comfort and freedom of movement at the forefront of the designs, others are more body-sculpting, if you prefer a form-hugging look. Adanola Sportswear brands are the easy win when it comes to loungewear and Adanola treads the line between style and functionality especially well. Instead of choosing the boldly labelled sweatshirts and socks that have become the brand’s signature, choose more subtle pieces like the leg-lengthening wrap-over yoga pants in black, or the light-grey knitted two-piece. The latter combines to make for a polished yet easy look that’s as soft as sleepwear but worthy of a Business class plane seat. Sarah Bannerman Adidas Originals Adidas Originals has made a fashion comeback of late. Despite launching almost 30 years ago, it was the 2024 collaboration with Wales Bonner that secured its spot as fashion brand first, sportswear choice second. Simply stroll the streets of London and you’d be hard-pushed not to spot a pair of suede Sambas or a track jacket worn ironically (consciously or not) in a nod to the 90s. We’ll call that one the Oasis effect. I’ll admit it took me a minute to jump onboard with the return of the three-stripe trackpant, but styled with a chunky knit and a leather jacket, the burgundy pair has quickly become my airport-to-city go-to. Sarah Bannerman Lululemon Lululemon’s leggings remain the gold standard for flights – multiple Traveller editors rave about their buttery-soft finish, elevated design, gentle compression and squat proof waistbands that looks as at home in the yoga studio as in a business class airport lounge. Its loungewear brings all the same technical precision, flattering fits and quality materials in a cosier, snugglier form. Sporty & Rich Canadian founder Emily Oberg used to work in magazines, so she’s always had an eye for style. She founded Athleisure-luxe label Sporty & Rich in 2015, more as a creative outlet than a genuine business idea, but the brand’s vintage-leaning all-American sensibilities soon garnered a following, and now it’s a beloved staple for discerning types, made with a triple-threat of nostalgic cuts, vibrant colours and quality, sustainable materials. Vuori Californian fashion is synonymous with laid-back chic and Vuori brings that relaxed West Coast feel to its extensive range of active pieces and loungewear with its thoughtful, minimalist designs crafted with sustainability in mind. The brand requires all suppliers to sign and uphold a code of conduct covering labour, working conditions and environmental practices, while prioritising ethically grown cotton. I have multiple Vuori pieces – from leggings to joggers to t-shirts, and not one has bobbled, lost its shape or faded after two-plus years of washes – and I’ve worn them on flights everywhere from Saint-Tropez to India to Finland.

item.title: The Dinner Party Has Left the Building
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 4.22
A few months ago, a small group gathered for a picnic during a retreat in upstate New York. In lieu of sitting on a grassy knoll with a checkered blanket, the diners huddled on a flat rock by a waterfall while the retreat’s co-organizer, Charles Michel, began priming its surface with vinegar before painting it with brushtrokes of vegetable purees and embellishing it with flowers and foraged elements to create an abstract composition. As an artist, chef, and self-described “food futurist,” Michel has been creating these food paintings for 15 years. But this painting in particular, he tells Eater, broke new ground for his practice with its fully nature-immersed setting — no tables, chairs, or even plates. “It also became the excuse to provoke interesting social dynamics,” Michel says; he references the relational aesthetic philosophy of French curator Nicolas Bourriaud that anchors his work, and which calls for the art world to create pieces that explore “human relations and their social context” in a more public way. In this instance, the picnic’s context encouraged childlike playfulness (scooping up vegetable puree with sourdough bread) and reverie (“Nobody rushed toward the food. There was a collective pause, [and] a moment of presence and gratitude before we began eating”). One bite from the puree-filled brushstrokes might be umami-rich, floral and delicate, or bright and acidic; much of the food was also reworked from the group’s retreat-sourced leftovers, such as the fibrous trimmings of grilled white asparagus they ate the day prior, now transformed into a delicate velouté for their collective palette. Michel’s work is a prime example of earthwork dining, an increasingly popular trend of curating experiential, artistic culinary moments designed around dining in (and with) nature. The traces of earthwork dining are everywhere, from multicourse dinners with dirt-made “placemats”’ to the collaborative dinner series The Ever-Changing Table, a series unfolding this month as part of the culinary program for Art Biesenthal where “leaves replace porcelain, vegetables become sculptural centrepieces, and the surrounding landscape becomes part of the table itself.” Earthwork dinners also have their sea legs, as evidenced by Banquet on the Sea, an aquatic dinner that took place a few months ago in the waters of Marseille, presented by Résidence Vue Mer and designed by the culinary artist Alix Lacloche. Every aspect of the event was either locally sourced or upcycled, as Lacloche explains in this interview with Ready to Host; the table was built from the panels of an old fishmonger’s cold room, and the menu was designed to pay homage to simple, seasonal offerings with a bouillabaisse-inspired, locally foraged seaweed soup, which was served with bread that the organizers baked in recycled leather flip-flops (a fun nod to Daniel Spoerri). Not only did the event go viral, but outlets and Instagram accounts made a point of underlining that it was not AI. In many ways, the blueprint for these earthwork dinners was laid decades ago. Consider Bread & Puppet Theater, the revolutionary 1960s puppet-activist group that has been feeding its audience house-made sourdough rye and pumpernickel loaves in the fields of Vermont since its early days, and continues to do so in the state’s rolling hills. The company’s underlying philosophy is that theater, like bread, should be consumed outside of a commerce-driven mentality, and dignified as a human-nourishing necessity. The farm-to-table movement of the 1970s reinvigorated the food world’s passion for placing local, seasonal ingredients front and center, undoubtedly laying the groundwork for larger-scale land art dinners such as Outstanding in the Field: a traveling, outdoor dinner series by land artist Jim Denevan that started in 1999 and continues to this day. Together, Denevan’s crew serves hundreds of diners at a single, sprawling communal table — on beaches, in fields, and in orchards — around the world, with the evening’s menu featuring seasonal dishes prepared by a local chef. This week, the culinary caravan went to Menorca for an eclipse dinner. Denevan’s tables, for all of their bucolic achievement, do rely on a more clearly demarcated indoor-outdoor contrast, a retention of certain dining decorum. At every dinner, one can expect rows of chairs and an impossibly long, tablecloth-covered table (complete with the comforts of cutlery and tableware) that becomes a visual foil to its surroundings. Works like Lacloche’s Banquet on the Sea and Michel’s rockface food-painting picnic, however, were stripped of some of those dining conventions. That meant “almost none of the rituals resembled the way we normally eat,” Michel tells Eater. “There were no individual plates, [and] no courses; No clear distinction between audience and participant. And yet everyone arrived hungry and left nourished.” Last fall, a similar experience unfolded at a dinner titled Farm Is Table at Treiber Farms in Peconic, New York, where the table and seating was literally carved into the dirt by organizers — there were plates, but no tablecloth in sight, and the weed-strewn earth was instead elevated to the elbows of the diners, who were served local oysters off repurposed irrigation pipes from the farm. Artist Allan Wexler was one of Farm Is Table’s co-organizers, and tells Eater that the event was one of 10 dinners building up to the March 2027 release of his new book in collaboration with Michael Yarinsky of Office of Tangible Space, which reinterprets The Futurist Cookbook. The content of the nearly century-old conceptual Italian cookbook is rich with relational aesthetic dining fodder; its concept of Aerofood, for example, asks diners to serve themselves food with one hand while the other strokes sandpaper or velvet. Farm Is Table leaned into that notion of a sensory-heavy, social-norm-disrupting dinner by carving 30-foot-long troughs for its 30 guests (tickets were $125) to dine on a multicourse, locally sourced dinner. Wexler drilled holes into the ground, and put candles along the entire length. “As the sun went down and the moon came up,” he says, “it was a gorgeous evening. It just became magical.” “It was very seafood-forward, and we really just worked with what was available locally,” Peter Treiber Jr., who co-runs Treiber Farms with his father, tells Eater. “There was delicata squash and mustard greens; we cooked tilefish, and Davy Jones Shellfish Co. delivered the oysters. It all created a bigger picture of what North Fork is about through the land and the sea.” As far as who attended the event, Treiber Jr. says it was a mix of friends, artists, and folks from New York City, with their common trait being an interest in a nature-driven, communal experience at the cross section of the arts and agriculture. “That cross section is something I’ve been exploring for years both as an artist and a farmer,” he says with a laugh, “it really is fertile ground.” That fertile ground, however, is not always sown with purely artistic intentions. In recent years, earthwork meals have also attracted adept marketing minds who know that the well-oiled mechanics of social media are best suited for thumb-stopping images, even if they’re no longer art for art’s sake and are increasingly promotional commerce and brand activations. A few years ago, a dinner in this remote Menorcan stone quarry for the fast-fashion brands like Mango went viral; this past winter, L’Oréal carved a table and seating into the snowy mountains of Savoie, France, for an influencer brand trip. These events, while visually captivating, feel less attuned to the low-waste ethos of most earthwork artists and more tapped into the type of virality-baiting digital content (or worse, AI slop) that envisions them as moments of exclusivity and luxury. Marketing has a history of mining the fringes of subcultures and art movements, but the ways in which these earthworks coax us into getting our hands and feet dirty feels especially precious in 2026. “It’s a pretty simple concept,” Treiber Jr. says about Farm Is Table, “but it’s pretty effective about getting people grounded. Being at root level.” Michel echoes this sentiment, explaining how such dining experiences can help us confront overconsumption, loneliness, and a growing disconnection from the land and people that nourish us. “That’s the message,” he says, “food is the Trojan Horse.”

item.title: Why Anthony Bourdain’s Editor Wanted ‘Tony’ to Be Darker
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 4.18
There are two types of biopics: those that unconventionally show, and those that exhaustively tell. Thank goodness that Tony, the highly anticipated A24 biopic about the late Anthony Bourdain, takes the former route. “When we are writing a biopic,” screenwriter Todd Bartels told me, “[co-writer Lou Howe and I] are allergic to cradle-to-grave narratives. We like to pick a window on someone’s life that serves as a microcosm for their longer journey.” In this instance, that window is the summer of 1975, when a young Tony first cuts his chops in a Provincetown, Massachusetts, kitchen. “[It’s] more a movie about the relatable arc of knowing who you want to be but not quite knowing how to get there and raging against that,” writes Eater’s Bettina Makalintal in her review of the film, and “it happens to be a movie about someone we all loved.” Then again, successfully pitching a Bourdain biopic to his estate was always going to be a big swing. I spoke with Todd Bartels and Lou Howe about what made that swing possible (for one: bringing on Kimberly Witherspoon, Bourdain’s literary agent and friend, as an executive producer); which cast member demonstrated the best culinary chops; and who they could imagine playing an older, more seasoned Anthony Bourdain. Eater: How did you strike the balance between making a movie for the passionate Anthony Bourdain fans, and viewers who may know very little about him? Lou Howe: I was anxious about that [laughs], especially at the very beginning. But [we] just [tried] to make a good movie, and hope that the entertainment factor and emotional engagement hits the target well enough. We started this whole process as fans, so in that way we felt relatively comfortable servicing fellow fans. You want to write a good story that people can plug into no matter who the character is. Of course, there are some Kitchen Confidential Easter eggs. Such as? How did you manage to tap into the emotional, and not just factual, truths of Bourdain’s story? Todd Bartels: As [Lou] mentions, when we work on a biopic we’re very allergic to cradle-to-grave narratives. We prefer to focus on a window in someone’s life. The biography written by Laurie Woolever, who was Bourdain’s longtime assistant and collaborator, was essential at helping us answer questions like, How did this person “in need of a good ass kicking” — as Bourdain famously wrote about himself as a young man — become this enlightened figure for so many people? He wrote that he treated the world like his ashtray, that he was narcissistic and insufferable. How do you go from little shit to guru? How did you gain the trust of Bourdain’s estate? LH: That was a multistep process. We knew we had to go to the estate first, and our executive producer, Emily Rose — who is also a big Bourdain fan — chased down Kimberly Witherspoon, Bourdain’s literary agent and someone who helped build his career as a writer. Witherspoon and Ottavia Busia-Bourdain are the executors of the estate, and [Rose] was finally, after much chasing, able to get us a meeting with them. What was the elevator pitch? LH: That it would be a love letter: a Provincetown summer coming-of-age story that ends in a clambake. [Witherspoon and Busia-Bourdain] were kind of like, “Well, that’s different from what we’ve been getting pitched,” which was a lot of stuff focusing on his later years, and trying to understand his death. We rejected that consciously. They liked that idea, but basically said, “Prove it,” so we then went back to them when we had a script, and A24 involved, and [co-writer and director] Matt Johnson and Dominic Sessa; those two kind of came on board as a team. [Witherspoon] also came on board as an executive producer and was very creatively involved throughout everything. Was anyone else considered to play Bourdain? LH: It was always Dom. Who do you think could play an older version of Bourdain? TB: That’s such a fun thing to think about, and no one has asked us that yet. I have two thoughts, amongst many, but a friend once suggested Bobby Cannavale. I can see it. LH: And [Cannavale] would really have the voice down. Kim Witherspoon knew Bourdain so well. How did her input impact the film? TB: She’s really one of the keepers of his legacy, and would help us to gut-check these moments where we’d be like, “Okay, does this feel like your friend?” We were always surprised at how she wanted us to get even darker. She’d say, “No, don’t make him so nice. [At this stage] he was a punk.” We were showing the devil and angel on his shoulder, as represented respectively by the characters Sal, who was played by Leo Woodall, and Ciro, the chef played by Antonio Banderas. She insisted that we really not sanitize that [journey]. LH: She didn’t want him to look like the innocent little victim of bad influences. The whole idea of having Eric Ripert make a cameo was also her idea. What was Eric Ripert like on set? That must have been emotional. TB: Well, Ripert is a Buddhist, always wearing his mala beads, and was extremely humble and just curious about the acting process. At no point was he swaggering around like the grand chef from Le Bernardin that he is [laughs]. LH: It was such an honor. With him and [Witherspoon] being involved, it really just felt like we had the people who loved him honoring him the right way. Can you tell me more about the on-set food logistics? TB: Christine Tobin was our food culinary consultant, and was there every day making all the food in a little shack behind the kitchen. I think Dom [Sessa] ate like, eight lobster rolls at a time [laughs]. Leo Woodall also became unbelievable at shucking an oyster. He made it look effortless, which is also such an important aspect of his character. LH: Antonio [Banderas] is also a restaurateur. Leo [Woodall] and Dom [Sessa] trained beforehand in kitchens, but [Banderas] didn’t need any help. In fact, during a lot of scenes, he’s actually off to the side making paella. Wait, Antonio Banderas was literally just always making paella on set? LH: Yeah! Incredible, right? He just loves to do it — which, again, was also so perfect for his role as the chef as well. Were there any other scenes or moments you would have loved to show in the movie? LH: I have one that comes to mind that was never shot. Bourdain’s favorite hot dog stand is this spot called Hiram’s in Fort Lee, New Jersey, and in earlier drafts of the script we see him head to this place — a real childhood favorite, and a true greasy spoon haunt — to see the amount of joy that it gives him. It’s a first insight into his relationship with food. TB: Provincetown’s history as this Portuguese fishing town, too, is also [front and center]. There’s a kind of melancholic, longing singing known as fado in Portuguese culture. If you pay attention, you can hear it in the background during the striper run scene and when Tony and Ciro are sitting by a bonfire. At one point, we were going to have an actual fado singer’s character who was perhaps the unrequited love of Antonio [Banderas’s] character. But we wanted his character’s backstory to be more mysterious. How did you familiarize yourself with that old-school Provincetown energy? TB: We hung out for the better part of two days at Bourdain’s favorite dive bar, the Old Colony Tap, which is still there on the main drag of Commercial Street, and covered in all of its maritime flotsam and jetsam, Red Sox [memorabilia] glory. I’d say it’s the best bar in America.

item.title: Tea Is So Hot Right Now
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 2.81
In Los Angeles, Tea at Shiloh describes itself as a “late night teahouse.” Here, visitors can reserve slots from 7 to 11 p.m. to sip unlimited amounts of tea — at this hour, all herbal, with blends made by each day’s staff — and sprawl out in nooks of plush cushions, in a warmly lit loft with tall ceilings and exposed brick, while jazz musicians play in a corner. “I was looking for soft spaces in the evening,” says founder Shiloh Enoki, who opened the eponymous teahouse in 2022. Tea Is So Hot Right Now The success of bubble tea and matcha has opened the door for more tea businesses to gain traction Enoki previously worked in the music industry, and her experience with nightlife was often loud and centered on the more performative aspects of dating (“being perceived by guys,” she says). For her new venture, “All I wanted to do was drink tea, listen to jazz, be cozy, and still have the opportunity to meet strangers.” Tea felt like a conduit to an alternative space. While coffee shops tend to encourage a practice of grab and go, or of work or hustle culture, “that’s not the energy of tea,” according to Enoki. “Tea is like, I’m gonna sit here for hours and I’m gonna have a deep conversation with the person sitting across from me, and that’s so rare in our culture.” Despite tea’s astounding popularity globally, the United States has long lagged behind many other countries when it comes to tea consumption, and that conception of tea has mostly been limited to iced black tea. This, however, appears to be changing, with the U.S. importing far more tea — in the hundreds of millions of dollars — this decade than it did 30 years ago, with millennials in particular the most likely to be tea drinkers. Matcha is, obviously, everywhere; according to the New Consumer, it usurped chai as the leading specialty tea drink in cafes. A lot more tea, it seems, is about to follow, as new tea-focused businesses sprout up across the country and as tea sees increased applications as a flavor element in food, desserts, and cocktails in addition to its consumption as a standalone drink. Across the country, teahouses with a similar ethos to Enoki’s are catering to the desire for another kind of space: one that feels slower and more intentional than the average coffee shop, and which offers a different experience than yet another restaurant or high-end cocktail bar. In July, “tea salon” Han Cha opened in Chicago, serving a selection of nine teas from Chicago-based tea company Spirit in the format of British high tea. Over the course of the two-hour-long booking, guests might sip Taiwanese black tea with notes of quince and orange blossom alongside bites of English cheddar and Korean-style quick pickles, or Thai white tea with Japanese curry pimento cheese sandwiches. Heiji Black, who partnered with artist Theaster Gates (in whose Stony Island Arts Bank building the concept is located) on the venture, is compelled by the way tea “makes people slow down and savor the experience.” She cites the teahouses she grew up going to in Korea, which were “really about being social and meeting with people and connecting with them,” as inspiration for Han Cha. At Tea at Shiloh, Enoki also tries to emphasize being in the moment. While the cafe welcomes co-working, especially during the day, she says she wanted to design the experience at night such that people “don’t want to be on their laptop or their phone.” Rather than enforce a hard no-laptop policy, Tea at Shiloh offers other things for people to do with their hands, like games, clay, and watercolors. The dim lighting and communal seating also offer “subtle cues” that the space, at night, isn’t a place for being lost in a screen, she explains. Even teahouses that don’t serve matcha, like Tea at Shiloh, cite its importance in the current teahouse moment. In May, the artist Juno Shen opened Soft Hours, a teahouse in Manhattan’s Chinatown. (A laptop-free space, it draws inspiration from the Song dynasty, which Shen describes as a “culturally rich era” in which scholars “built rituals around slowing down and shifting your attention.”) “Matcha and boba have done something really important in making tea culture relevant to a younger generation, and I think we’re reaching a point where people are asking, What else is there?” Shen says. At Soft Hours, there is no matcha whisked in front of you, poised for a TikTok video. Likewise, “we don’t do boba; we don’t do cold foam. We moved away from all the performance that a trendy tea place would have.” Instead, Shen’s menu hews toward a selection of Chinese teas: streamlined but still showing range. There’s green tea fragrant with jasmine; two kinds of oolong, one oxidized in a way that gives it notes of plum and the other roasted over charcoal until it evokes toasted nuts; black tea with a honey-like body; and a deeply woodsy fermented pu’erh. Perhaps the main concession to trends is that every tea can be ordered as an iced latte as well, which Shen considers a way for people to “softly get introduced” to tea. “I’m not presenting something that’s extremely traditional, so I think I’m just the next step of [people] exploring a little bit more about tea,” Shen says. “I think the next stage of tea culture in America should move beyond individual ingredients becoming trendy [and into] the understanding of tea as this incredibly diverse seasonal category.” Tian Tea House opened in Kansas City, Missouri, in late 2025. Matcha drinks are far and away the most popular, according to co-owner Saranya Hubbard. “I really don’t have to advertise anything that much — it already sells itself,” she says. But similarly to Shen, Hubbard, who grew up in Thailand surrounded by the tea culture in Bangkok’s Chinatown, sees her teahouse as an opportunity to showcase the wider variety of Asian tea culture. Tian brews and offers classes on Chinese gongfu tea and serves lesser-known Thai tea, including one made with hibiscus and bael (a fruit that’s sometimes called golden apple or stone apple). To make the most of the space, the teahouse turns into Moon, a cocktail bar, at night. Tea bridges the gap between the two concepts: There are highballs infused with tea and whisky drinks made with matcha. Further proof of tea’s rising moment can be found in Heytea’s current expansion across the United States. The Chinese chain got global attention when it popularized cheese tea in the late 2010s, but it didn’t enter the U.S. market until 2023, when it opened its first store in NYC; now, it has more than 40 locations nationwide. With drinks like milk tea boba, fruit teas with inclusions, and black teas finished with fluffy toppings, the chain sits at the intersection of the growing cultural fixations on bubble tea, matcha, and highly customized specialty beverages of all kinds, including coffee and dirty soda. The chain describes itself as offering “new-style” tea, which senior PR manager Yinnan Shen explains to mean “experimenting a lot with what tea can become.” Some of its beverages, Shen says, take the approach of crafting a cocktail: What botanics can be added to the drink? What layers of texture and flavor? McDonald’s Sweet Tea this is not. In June, Heytea also opened the first U.S. location of its Teabar offshoot. The concept — which serves dine-in only pots of tea as well as tea ice cream and elaborate beverages like jasmine milk tea topped with a “matcha cloud” — rapidly drew massive crowds. Unlike Heytea shops, which offer a more grab-and-go feel, Teabar was, like some of those independent teahouses, intended to be more of a place to slow down. Together, the interest in Teabar in addition to the original Heytea concept, represent what Shen calls tea’s “continued evolution.” “What Heytea is trying to do is find the most accurate contemporary interpretation of people’s needs around tea,” she says. That seems especially pertinent in the context of the U.S., where the tea culture is nascent compared to China. Now, according to Nethra Rajendran, a beverage experience developer at Oatly, black tea, jasmine, and oolong are starting to “re-emerge in new formats,” particularly in mainstream chains. Instead of boba being the medium for these flavors, they’re increasingly popping up as part of the growing “refresher” category,” she explains. Of course, the interest in tea is no longer limited to the teahouse or tea bar alone. “We can see a very real application of tea beyond a [drink] base in the 2025 resurgence of Earl Grey,” wrote Rajendran, noting the popularity of Earl Grey syrups and creamtops for use in matcha and coffee drinks. Tea is no longer a standalone drink, but, increasingly, a freeform flavor element. When NYC’s ambitious new soft serve shop Unnecessary opened this summer, it launched with a “not-so-plain vanilla,” enriched with osmanthus oolong. Oolong also appears as the grounding basenote of its watermelon-mint flavor, which it developed to be more refreshing than what people might expect from typical milk tea. The argument has been made that we, as modern society, are on a hedonistic hunt for more flavors, our tastebuds “spoiled” by the glut of “maple-matcha-blackberry-thyme-yuzu-miso-caramel everything.” Every drink is involved in a way that only the early days of the Starbucks Frappuccino could have foretold; every dish is a referential mashup of a handful of other dishes or other cultural fascinations. Perhaps tea, with its global breadth barely tapped in the U.S., can provide further flavors to mine. Nearly every culture has a tea to explore, Rajendran adds: the osmanthus and oolong of East Asia, the masala chai and Assam teas of South Asia, the rooibos and kineliba of Africa, the hibiscus in the Caribbean and Latin America, the sweet tea of the American South. Tea has been around for thousands of years, but perhaps we’ve yet to see how far it can continue to go. As Heytea’s Shen says, “Tea is a living culture, and living culture changes.”

item.title: The case for eating blood (sausage)
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 4.93
The case for eating blood (sausage) Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Should we be cooking and consuming more food with blood? A number of chefs and food writers believe so for reasons to do with taste, sustainability and nutrition: blood is rich in protein, iron and other micronutrients. In her upcoming book Blood, Guts & Black Pudding, Kate Ryan makes the particular case for Irish blood sausage (black pudding), the traditional making of which has become a dying art. “There were strong communal aspects around its production: people came together to kill the animal, catch the blood and make the pudding,” explains Ryan of the dish, which dates back to the first century in Ireland. “Every woman in every household had her own recipe, a variety that is still reflected on Irish supermarket shelves. And the range of bloods used was unique: not just pig or cow, but sheep and goose, all tied to different parts of the year.” Certain varieties of blood sausage such as Achill belly (a cross between haggis and black pudding made using sheep’s belly found in County Mayo) are already endangered, while A O’Reilly & Sons in Cork is now the last remaining maker of drisheen, a pudding made from blood serum with a grey hue and blancmange-like texture. “An acquired taste,” says Ryan. The loss of black pudding made using fresh blood is also a concern. Stricter legislation around animal welfare and rising costs have led to the closure of many small- and medium-scale abattoirs. Most black-pudding producers in Ireland and the UK now import dried blood from Spain or the Netherlands. The puddings from some of these (including MacSween in Edinburgh, Stornoway from the Outer Hebrides and Doreen’s from Yorkshire) are great. “But there is a superiority of taste when you use fresh blood,” says Ryan. “A richer flavour and better texture as the grains soak up the fresh blood better.” In Ireland, a handful of fresh blood producers remain. In the UK, Fruit Pig in East Anglia is the only one working at scale. Its recipe for Scottish-style black pudding is strong on white pepper and uses only natural ingredients, including fresh rather than kibbled (dried) onions. “Why put thin wheels on a Ferrari?” says founder Matthew Cockin of the value of pairing fresh blood with the best ingredients. His puddings are on the menu at gastropubs such as The Pig & Waffle in Kettering and The Hand & Flowers in Marlow, and are available to purchase online. For Ryan, not using domestically sourced blood is also wasteful. “Ninety per cent of the food we produce in Ireland is exported,” she says. “A vast majority is beef and dairy from cows. But we’re not catching blood from those animals because we don’t have the systems in place. If we’re serious about a sustainable-food policy and want to continue eating meat, we have to find solutions for making use of as much of the animal as possible. That includes the blood. We’d all be much healthier if we ate more.” The problem, of course, is that most people find blood disgusting. “We can make a logical case for eating this important protein source and argue that it makes practical and economic sense,” writes Australian chef Jennifer McLagan. “[But] the prejudice against blood is strong. Even adventurous eaters, who enjoy blood sausage, rarely consider cooking with blood.” Restaurants such as Albers in Dalston do a great job of making black pudding enticing beyond a fry-up, with a starter of pork and black pudding sausage with peach, shallot and parsley. And morcilla, the Spanish version of blood sausage, continues to be popular at tapas-style venues such as Legado in Shoreditch, where it’s served with chickpeas and baby squid, and Ox and Finch in Glasgow, where it comes with cod cheeks, chorizo and tomato on sourdough. McLagan’s 2019 cookbook Blood also proposes a number of recipes designed to change the ingredient’s reputation. Among them: blood pancakes (based on a popular Finnish recipe), rosemary sanguinaccio (inspired by the Italian sweet custard of blood and chocolate), blood marshmallows and blood meringues. The latter rely on the fact that eggs can be swapped out for blood: one egg white is equivalent to 43g blood. “There is no metallic blood taste,” McLagan reports of her marshmallows. “The only hint of the main ingredient is their dark raspberry colour.” If not from your butcher, the most likely place to source fresh blood is the freezer section of your local Asian supermarket. Despite our squeamishness in the west, blood features widely in other cuisines. “In China, blood usually comes as a curd or blood tofu, almost always duck or pork blood, with a flavour similar to liver,” says British-Chinese writer Michael Zee. “The most famous Sichuan dish, mao xue wang, includes tripe, eel, spam, vegetables and duck blood tofu in a soup and is really good.” Among the tastiest is the signature version at Grand Majestic Sichuan in Hong Kong, which is made with Wagyu beef and chicken blood curd and requires ordering 48 hours in advance. In her Brazilian-inspired cookbook Fusão, Ixta Belfrage includes a recipe drawing on her mother’s favourite dish, frango ao molho pardo (chicken in brown sauce), made with caramelised onions and “fresh chicken blood” (in other words, from a newly slaughtered animal). “The blood adds a rich, velvety texture,” says Belfrage, who adapted the recipe for western readers by using beetroot instead. This delivers a similar colour and earthy undertone without the need to catch, kill or drain a chicken. According to her mother, it also tastes better – a boon for the fainthearted. Comments

item.title: Why pissaladière is the perfect taste of late summer
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 4.58
Why pissaladière is the perfect taste of late summer Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. A savoury tart of caramelised onions beneath a latticework of salted anchovies and black olives, pissaladière may be the perfect late-summer dish. “Have it with a glass of rosé and you’re instantly in the south of France,” says food writer Sudi Pigott. “You’ve got sweetness from the onions, saltiness from anchovies, acidity from olives and fat from pastry. The perfect harmony,” says chef Adam Byatt of Michelin-starred Trinity in Clapham, where the dish has been on the menu every summer for 20 years. “Once you’ve got the ingredients, all you’re doing is constructing and letting the oven do its work.” Though the dish originates from Genoa and is often called “French pizza”, pissaladière’s name derives from peis salat, the Old Provençal name for salted fish. This was mixed with olive oil, herbs and spices to produce a sauce called pissalat, which was spread over bread, before adding onions, then baked. A pastry base is now more common. In his forthcoming book Trinity: The Cookbook, Byatt suggests using rough puff pastry “as it doesn’t rise as much”. In the south of France you also find the dish made with fougasse (similar to Italian focaccia) or other yeasted doughs. “Lighter puff pastry works better if you’re having pissaladière as a snack,” says French Classics author and chef Matthew Ryle. “For lunch or dinner, I prefer a more substantial bread.” Pissalat may be the traditional topping, but good luck finding any. Or making it yourself. In Consider the Anchovy, Pigott recounts tracking down a jar in a Nice market, where a stallholder explained the laborious process of macerating, sieving and pounding it requires. When asked how she uses the condiment, she answered: “As you anglais might use ketchup. In everything.” Pissalat adds “oomph, though it can be a bit much”, says Pigott, who compensates for the lack of it in her recipe by cooking the onions with garlic, rosemary, thyme and bay leaves. She uses red onions with shallots. Byatt prefers Italian white onions for their sweetness, cooked “low and slow” until they turn dark and jammy. To finish, top the pastry with the onions, decorate with Niçoise black olives and Ortiz or Consorcio anchovies, then bake for 20 minutes. Serve it just above room temperature. “If not as an appetiser, offer a crisp green salad alongside for a supremely pleasing supper,” says Pigott. “It adds a Riviera riff to picnic food too – if it survives late-night fridge raids.” Comments

item.title: Chicago: the ultimate insider addresses
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 4.21
Chicago: the ultimate insider addresses Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. This article is part of FT Globetrotter’s guide to Chicago When I say Chicago isn’t a celebrity town, that cuts both ways. We have limited tolerance for Instagram culture, we roll our eyes at round-the-block queues and, for most of us, the very notion of $20 trend smoothies triggers an allergic reaction. On the other hand, we can be provincial. At a recent concert at the Jay Pritzker Pavilion in Millennium Park, the Jumbotron cycled through drone footage of American skylines. At the sight of Chicago’s, the crowd exploded. At all others, including a glimmering and handsome New York City? Crickets. Chicagoans have a funny relationship to fame. Seeing a celebrity out and about is not just another Tuesday for us: it’s day-derailing. We’ll ignore the cardinal rule imparted by our peers on the coast and bug the hell out of them, then spend the rest of the day calling our cousins’ cousins. We keep our local celebrities close but feel inordinately stung when they decamp for another city. To better understand this hot-and-cold city, we spoke to eight cultural insiders who know it better than most. Some were forged in Chicago. Others enthusiastically adopted it. And many of them still choose to live here, even when New York and LA beckon. Jump straight to . . . Sandra Cisneros, writer and author of ‘The House on Mango Street’ (born and raised in Chicago; based in San Miguel de Allende, Mexico) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The Aon Center. After going to a concert downtown in Grant Park, we would walk over to what was the Standard Oil Building, now the Aon Center, on East Randolph Street. In the plaza’s sunken garden is the most fabulous treasure: wind sculptures by Harry Bertoia. They look like reeds, and at the dedication ceremony in 1972, the artist climbed inside the installation and “played” them. Bertoia was a furniture designer, too. When his sculptures were displayed at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1975, it was the first and only time I’d seen a sign that said, “Please touch.” I like the idea that he thought about the poetics of these sculptures moving and making these wonderful sounds. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Hot dogs. If you haven’t had a Chicago hot dog, you haven’t had a hot dog. You have to have a bun with little poppy seeds on it, it has to be bundled in waxed paper and the french fries have to be good. Now, there are even vegan hot dogs. Recently, my family and I got some at Portillo’s late at night, and they were really good — I was surprised! One more thing I didn’t realise until two years ago that the flowers in Chicago’s public parks were so much a part of the city. To me, lilacs, peonies and lilies of the valley are the quintessential flowers of Chicago. Jeff Tweedy, musician and lead vocalist/guitarist of Wilco (based in Chicago) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The parks. If you want to soak up what the city and culture are really like, I’d pick any of the Chicago Park District parks, like Independence in Irving Park or Gompers in North Park. Have a picnic and see how Chicagoans really recreate. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand “Dibs”. The concept of saving your parking spot, especially in heavy snow. Technically not legal, but ultimately, pretty fair and moral. If you’re the one who broke your ass shovelling snow, you should get to keep that spot for at least a day or so. What Chicago teaches you When you grow up in a smaller town like I did, there’s a belief that it’s a kinder way to live and that you can’t get that in a city. It’s not true. When I moved to Chicago, I knew more people in my neighbourhood than I did growing up — it’s all about block parties and meeting up with neighbours. Chicago has problems like everywhere else, but it’s a city that facilitates community. Rick Bayless, chef and restaurateur (based in Chicago) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The National Museum of Mexican Art. Rather than establishing the museum downtown, the founders chose Pilsen — a predominantly Latino neighbourhood — and they chose to keep this world-class collection free to all. NMMA is not only one of our city’s best museums but an integral player in this vibrant community. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Storefront theatre. Yes, we have grand old theatres that host Broadway touring companies, and yes, we have the internationally acclaimed Steppenwolf, Goodman and Chicago Shakespeare companies. But Chicago is a city of neighbourhoods, and most of them are home to a host of storefront theatres. One of the best is TimeLine Theatre Company, which does historical pieces that have contemporary relevance. Hungry yet? Forty years ago, when we opened Frontera Grill, farmers’ markets hadn’t taken off in Chicago. Today, with local chefs championing local products, there are over 40 and growing. Now communities are hosting “alternative” farmers’ markets that start at 3pm or 4pm and sell until around 7pm on specific weekdays, rather than weekend mornings. Eve L Ewing, author, scholar and co-owner of Build Coffee & Books in Woodlawn (based in Chicago) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The South Shore Nature Sanctuary and Montrose Point Bird Sanctuary. Our city motto is urbs in horto — city in a garden. Away from all the noise and the hubbub, the marshlands and prairie are also part of our identity. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Community. The city is famously corrupt, but there’s a more generous way to understand the “you scratch my back and I’ll scratch yours” way we do things, which is that Chicagoans look out for each other and take care of one another. If you’re my neighbour’s cousin’s pick-up basketball buddy, you’re in the circle and I’ve got to take care of you. The hill she’ll die on Everyone likes to share their (mostly ill-informed) opinions on Chicago pizza, but through and through we’re a taco city. Our ratio of great tacos per capita is off the charts. I grew up going to El Cid, a Mexican restaurant in Logan Square, while El Milagro in Pilsen both sells tacos and manufactures the best tortillas and chips. Enrique Mazzola, conductor and music director of the Lyric Opera of Chicago (divides time between Chicago and Paris) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The Driehaus Museum. This small museum just off the Magnificent Mile focuses on the art, architecture and design of the American Gilded Age and the Art Nouveau period. Inside is a magnificent auditorium with interesting and diverse programming. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand The walks. One of my favourites goes from downtown along the Lakefront Trail to Lincoln Park. Only a true Chicagoan can understand how beautiful this itinerary is. In general, I love walking around the city — I even walk to work at the Lyric Opera of Chicago and enjoy following the Chicago River every day. Bonus recommendation Wander around the boutique shops and cafés in the North Side neighbourhood of Andersonville. You’re still in Chicago but removed from the tourist areas and high-rises of downtown. Isaiah Collier, saxophonist and composer (divides time between Chicago and New York) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago 63rd Street Beach. The city has its madness, but it also has its tranquillity, usually by the water. Cats will get together here for drum circles — they’ve been doing it for decades. It’s therapeutic and uniquely ethnic. The overview of the city that you see from down there is kind of mythical, very cinematic. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Concerts at Pritzker Pavilion. No matter where you’re from in the city, I think we can all agree there’s something special about being able to witness a proper concert at Pritzker Pavilion. Not amateur stuff, but a full production from start to finish. It’s one hell of a location. A brutal truth We’re the most segregated major city in America. That residual effect has made people feel there are not enough opportunities. It can be disheartening for creatives. Grant Achatz, chef/creative director and co-owner of Chicago’s Alinea restaurant Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago Primitive on Jefferson Street. It’s a massive showroom packed with rare antiquities from all over the world. I’m into medieval and Egyptian history, so for me it’s a rabbit hole I can lose an afternoon in. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand The grit. When I showed up in 2001 with this weird, modernist way of cooking, this city embraced the risk and let me build. People here get that ambition runs quiet, that the winters bond everybody together, that nobody’s impressed with you until you’ve put in the work. You can’t feel any of that from a postcard. You’ve got to live here a while. Tasha, singer-songwriter and poet (born and raised in Chicago, based in New York) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago Promontory Point. We just call it The Point. I don’t think people who aren’t from Chicago really know the secret, stunning beauty it has, especially on the South Side. There is nothing more romantic than jumping from the rocks at sunset on a sticky, hot summer day, the sky pink behind the city skyline, cicadas buzzing. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Being from the city proper. I love the way we bond over that. Not the suburbs. Not the surrounding counties. Definitely not Indiana. A love letter No matter where I end up in the world, Chicago will always be my home, the place I return to, the place that understands me, that holds my whole family and first gave me courage. Chicago forever. What do you love most about Chicago? Tell us in the comments below. item.title: Secrets of the C-suite smoothie
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 3.99
Secrets of the C-suite smoothie Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Julia Baldet was a “burned out” 27-year-old pulling 100-hour weeks when she spotted the opportunity for a new kind of drinks brand last year. “I was working in finance, I was sick from stress, I didn’t have time to eat properly. But I also didn’t want something off the shelf from the supermarket.” The result was Elevate, a café in the City’s Royal Exchange that serves nutritionally enhanced smoothies in packaging that wouldn’t look out of place in a Space NK boutique. Bestsellers include The Glow (£8.90), a strawberry-pink mix of berries, yoghurt and skin-improving collagen. Muscle-boosting creatine – featured in the high-protein Lean Berries – “has also been trending”, says Baldet. A suite of £1.30 add-ons includes MCT oil (quick energy), lion’s mane (focus) pitaya (anti-oxidant) and prebiotic fibre. The brand recently opened a second café in Selfridges and is on target to hit £1mn in sales by the end of 2026. Functional nutrition is now one of the fastest-growing sectors in a wellness market worth $1.8tn globally. The rise of GLP-1s combined with an “always-on” culture means that more of us are skipping meals, and the comfortingly slurpable, customisable smoothie looks primed to fill the gap. Smoothies are also a cornerstone of the regime at Exalt, an “on-the-go nutrition” brand co-founded by Dan Wilson-Vaughan after 15 years in the banking world. Just like athletes, he says, deal makers are now looking to nutrition to give them the competitive edge. “Athletes want recovery and performance,” says Wilson-Vaughan, whose clients range from Premier League football clubs to City types. “Corporates traditionally needed a meal that actually replaces the one they skipped. They now want both.” What a lot of time-poor workers need most is protein, he says: “20g+ [a day] is a must alongside fibre and the right fats. We are also pushing the use of ashwagandha as a way of alleviating stress.” At Earthbar in Silicon Valley, the go-to smoothie is The Protocol ($14.95), a green, protein-packed blend of fruit, spinach and yerba mate (a natural source of caffeine, supposedly without the crash), plus blue spirulina, creatine, collagen and whey protein. There is also a choice of almost 50 further “add-ons”, including B12, probiotics and bee pollen, as well as L-carnitine, a supplement which some believe can help burn fat. As for whether we actually need all these add-ons, the jury is out. “Smoothies can be useful to deliver large amounts of a particular ingredient,” says James Collins, managing director of the INTRA Performance Group, which provides nutrition advice to both athletes and Fortune 500 CEOs. “However, we don’t recommend ‘functional smoothies’ for general, unstructured use. Marketing leads people to believe that a supplement can be the silver bullet for better health and performance without addressing the wider principles of nutrition, exercise and recovery.” Perhaps, just sometimes, all one needs to do is close the laptop and go out for dinner with some friends. Comments

item.title: Want to eat like a real Chicagoan? Go to these three neighbourhoods
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 2.49
Want to eat like a real Chicagoan? Go to these three neighbourhoods Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. This article is part of FT Globetrotter’s guide to Chicago I’m sick of talking about Italian beef. I don’t even remember the last time I ate it — partly out of stubbornness. But Chicago is not only about dripping beef sandwiches or doorstopper deep-dish pizza. In the almost 20 years I’ve lived here, and 15 writing about the city’s food scene, I am more frequently on the hunt for a standout banh mi or jibarito. Pounding the pavement of my hometown, I’ve come to know the delicate shatter of a Cantonese chicken wing fried to perfection and the quivering wobble of just-set chawanmushi seasoned with wild local alliums. I’ve eaten the best Mexican food in Chicago, slurping goat birria stained red from chillies in a hole in the wall, or wolfing tender lengua tacos in the middle of a grocery store. I’ve wept over corn smut-filled ravioli that honours every iota of this lifeblood crop down to its hairy silk. Chicago is a city of immigrants, proud natives and hearty blow-ins. Almost a quarter of our residents are foreign-born, meaning you can feast aplenty on traditional Sonoran, Sichuan, Pakistani, Polish, Korean, Greek, Ethiopian, Laotian, Colombian dishes and more. You can also taste what it’s like for someone to have to straddle two identities and cultures. In order to experience Chicago’s best culinary thrills, you have to get out of shuffling distance of the beef sandwich and deep-dish chains, away from the tourist attractions dotted amid The Loop’s glistening monoliths. That’s the other thing you need to know about Chicago. It’s a city of neighbourhoods — 77 of them to be exact. Here’s how to eat across three of my favourites. Logan Square I’ve spent much of the past two decades living four-ish miles north-west of downtown in Logan Square, an intoxicating and maddening nexus of contrasts, home to wide, tree-lined boulevards and some of the city’s finest cooking. Low-slung stone structures housing indie cafés, dives, taquerias and a historic jewel box of a movie theatre butt up against ugly, sprawling apartment complexes with lower floors occupied by chains proffering $18 grain bowls. Gentrification has ebbed away some of the neighbourhood’s grittier bits and charm. But with reinvestment have come delights like the 606, a 2.7-mile, foliage-lined walking and cycling trail on a derelict former rail line. The Logan Square Blue Line station deposits you in the neighbourhood’s beating heart. A towering Doric marble column overlooks a circular plaza that has been refurbished to create more walkable space and redubbed La Placita in honour of the neighbourhood’s Latino heritage. On the other side of the plaza is Chicago’s original farm-to-table restaurant, Lula Cafe. Jason Hammel and Amalea Tshilds opened this indie icon in 1999, and now it spills across three storefronts, faithfully churning out inventive seasonal cooking and comfy standbys such as Pasta “Yia Yia”, aka feta-laced, cinnamon-scented bucatini. It’s thanks in part to Lula that the neighbourhood remains a magnet for dynamic, heartfelt seasonal cooking, and why I consider it prerequisite eating to understand what makes Logan Logan. We’ll (officially) start three-quarters of a mile north-east of Lula at Cellar Door Provisions. This decade-old slip of a restaurant has, at various times, been a café and bakery, tasting-menu restaurant and wine bar, all under the same name, and with the same corner perch on a leafy, residential street. It’s now a bistro, and it’s restless, scrappy and exciting. The hyper-seasonal à la carte dinner menu, from chef-owner Ethan Pikas and chef de cuisine Alex Cochran, changes constantly and occasionally startles. You may get red wine-braised lamb’s tongue with herbaceous salsa verde, a pert, luscious burger or grilled mackerel with preserved mussels in sauce Américaine. The wine leans light, bracing and a little weird. Some 350 feet away from Cellar Door is Superkhana International, an Indian-ish restaurant from chefs and co-owners Zeeshan Shah and Yoshi Yamada that blurs lines with joyful abandon. Is their tangy, creamy Palak paneer pizza (with creamed spinach, chilli oil and crispy shallots) pizza or naan? Is their Maggi noodles bolognese umami (that’ll be the Maggi liquid seasoning), warmly tangy (that’ll be the achar masala) — or both? Don’t overthink; just indulge. And always add shareable chaat, which cleverly rotates with our challenging Midwestern seasons. Like the hot-pink-painted Superkhana, Mi Tocaya Antojería, a 15-minute walk south-east, is a riot of colour and bustling energy, though the latter holds a bit faster to dogma in the name of preserving Mexico’s gastronomic heritage. To walk in — Spanish mingling with English, the sizzle of marinated carne and mole-soused tortillas chiming with the metallic maraca of shaking cocktails — is to enter a kind of multicultural Chicago utopia. At the heart of this place is the outspoken chef and proprietor Diana Dávila who recreates the regional Mexican cooking of her childhood, hair swept into a braided crown, laugh reverberating from the pass. A Chicago native born to Mexican immigrants, Dávila would be the first to tell you that her luscious mole negro, comprising some 30 ingredients (and lately enveloping braised pork shank and celery root), is “f****** dope”. Here costra (cheese-crusted) tacos taste like Mexico City and beets get roasted in coffee and heaped on garlicky Mayan pepita spread. Don’t be surprised if you spot beloved Chicago chef Margaret Pak stopping by for a post-shift steak burrito. The big-hearted co-owner of the excellent Keralan restaurant, Thattu, in neighbouring Avondale, swears by this comfy handheld meal, with good reason. Revel in its grilled skirt steak, local black beans, queso chihuahua and sour cream. I’ve been known to wax poetic on Giant’s crab tagliatelle to anyone who will listen. This tangle of al dente pasta slaps the taste buds with sweet, brackish crab, fiery chilli butter and acidity. For almost a decade, I’ve darkened the door of this narrow joint on West Armitage Avenue, bound for a bar stool in the back overlooking the tiny galley kitchen that radiates heat and sweat. Chef Jason Vincent’s boisterous little restaurant has a gift for exceptional, likeable food (think ruffly layered lasagne and pork schnitzel). For summer 2025, this restless crew of creatives upped the ante with a Test Kitchen menu. This is the brave, invigorating food they cook for themselves and that we get to eat: Laotian steamed fish, green garlic chawanmushi with bonito flakes and black sesame and pistachio-studded pâté en croûte with foie gras. Other excellent Logan Square restaurants - Omarcito’s Latin Cafe for tangy marinated steak sandwiches and crispy consommé-drowned chicken tacos, doled out from a bright yellow shipping container. - Bungalow by Middle Brow for thick rafts of sourdough bread and cleverly topped char-speckled pizzas, washed down with house-brewed beer and house-made natural wine — all made from ingredients grown in and around Illinois. - Osteria Langhe for unfettered northern Italian cooking. - The Radicle for late-night pizza and tinned fish snacks, washed down with aperitif-heavy cocktails. - Longman & Eagle for a stiff whiskey cocktail and superb smashburger. Uptown There’s a nostalgic grandeur to Uptown that you can almost conjure into a grainy old film in your mind’s eye as you gaze up at the soaring, Prohibition-era Art Deco buildings. “Of course, Al Capone drank here,” you think, scooching into a beat-up, half-moon booth at the longstanding Green Mill Cocktail Lounge, as you await Chris Foreman’s Friday evening jazz piano set over an eye-poppingly stiff Old Fashioned. A century ago, this booming nightlife and entertainment district even housed the studio that produced a Charlie Chaplin film, but it struggled subsequently for decades after discriminatory housing practices sent property values plummeting. Yet the institutional malfeasance and low rents produced a richly diverse demographic with a penchant for social justice. JOIN (Jobs Or Income Now), an activism group that challenged racist welfare practices, was born here. Vacant storefronts remain, but Uptown is rising (read: gentrifying), as evidenced by the arrival of a Target where a burnt-out rail and bus yard once stood, but also by the bold cooking making a home here. The wind blows a bit harder and chillier up here. All the more reason to pop in for pho in one of the outstanding Vietnamese restaurants concentrated on West Argyle Street. (For a handheld delight, consider the ham and head cheese banh mi on a shattering baguette at Nhu Lan Bakery.) But the stalwart Hai Yen, its stark greyscale facade hiding amid shinier Little Saigon storefronts, is the one Chicago chefs will send you to for bò lá lốt (lemongrass-scented beef and pork sausage grilled in betel leaf) and phở đặc biệt with beef in half a dozen guises bobbing amid slippery rice noodles. I like prefacing said beef injection with a few springy tapioca shrimp dumplings. I’m admittedly not the biggest fan of a tasting menu, but one of the few exceptions is Cariño, whose executive chef and owner, Norman Fenton, nabbed a nomination for Best Chef: Great Lakes at the 2026 James Beard Foundation Awards. This Detroit-born chef, who previously cooked at WILD Tulum in Mexico and then at Grant Achatz’s world-renowned cocktail lounge The Aviary and the inventive, Michelin-starred Schwa in Chicago, has a gift for zhuzhing the stuff of everyday nourishment with imagination and humour. The familiar flavours of tacos al pastor jolt the senses when reimagined as a marinated lamb tartare tostada. Cariño’s dozen-plus-course tasting menu ($200 per person) moved me and made me think, laugh and, yes, cry, just once. (See the aforementioned tear-inducing corn smut ravioli, filled with the truffle-like corn fungus huitlacoche, a Mexican delicacy.) If you don’t mind a 10pm dinner, Cariño performs a more affordable second act in the form of an eight-course taco omakase ($125 per person, including drinks), a masa-centric romp through tetelas, tacos and quesadillas set to a thumping, upbeat soundtrack. The crackly-edged, suadero carnitas taco will change you. Chicagoans can’t go too many days without an outstanding sandwich. Fortunately, Ragadan, a deliciously uncommon mash-up of Jordanian street food joint and Midwestern diner, has several cures for that. Owner Danny Sweis’s parents hail from Amman, Jordan. He was born and raised in his family’s diner in Oklahoma City, hence the menu’s OKC burger, with shaved onion caramelised right into the minced beef. Anything between bread is superb here, but the sandwich that keeps me biking five miles to get there is the falafel ka’ak. Craggy outside, achingly soft inside, the falafel pucks exhale warming spices, layered amid bright, crunchy veg, sharp pickles and silky hummus. And oh, that Levantine bread: wispy, airy, caked in sesame seeds, and sourced from the Latin American and European bakery Markellos. Ask for a za’atar mayo side for dipping. If you don’t, Sweis may deposit a little cup alongside your sandwich anyway. Other excellent Uptown restaurants - Kie Gol Lanee for soul-soothing Oaxacan cooking (get the chapulines if they’re not sold out). - Demera for expert traditional Ethiopian cuisine and aromatic house honey wine. - Sun Wah BBQ for the off-menu Beijing (Peking) duck, starting with the whole crispy-skinned bird and ending with duck-fried rice. - YooYee for lip-tingling braised beef soup with fat hand-pulled noodle ribbons. Chinatown At the corner of Cermak and Wentworth, a landmark red gate denotes the technical start of Chicago’s Chinatown. But you can smell and feel that you’re here the moment you emerge from the Cermak-Chinatown Red Line station. Chinatown breathes and bustles impatiently, its residents endlessly streaming by laden with plastic Thank You bags. It smells, surprisingly perhaps, like Portuguese tarts baking and five-spice and fish. This 30,000-strong community is spilling into proximate districts and evolving as younger generations make their mark. In 2022, Lily Wang and Joe Briglio decided to fix a problem in Chinatown: there wasn’t, and had never been, a dedicated cocktail bar here. The couple took the reins at the classic Chinese restaurant Moon Palace, a 50-plus-year neighbourhood fixture owned by Wang’s parents. They shifted the restaurant into a permanent takeaway operation and built a sultry bar, Nine Bar, where the dining room used to be. You walk into what resembles any other brightly lit, tile-and-wood carry-out, save for a formidable metal door. You’re then deposited into a dim, neon-lit lounge that feels both lively and intimate, bar staff deftly mixing cocktails that mingle Japanese, Chinese and tropical influences, from the MSG-laced martini to a Sichuan peppercorn-spiked margarita called the Paper Dragon. A few doors down, Yao Yao provides a decidedly bright and turquoise-hued contrast to Nine Bar. Tuck yourself into a booth and prepare for the day’s simplest order: pickled fish, a soup of sharp pickled greens and mild, tender bass bobbing in a deliciously tacky broth. Order it mild if you want to feel the Sichuan tingle without missing all the beautiful nuance. Even the smallest size is too large for two, so prepare for leftovers. I like adding toothy thin glass noodles for heft. They come in little knotted bundles. Because we must end on a sweet note, follow your nose to the oldest bakery in town. The family-run, cash-only Chiu Quon Bakery has been open since 1986. It was founded by Pui Yip and Cora Chiu with recipes that Yip brought from Hong Kong, and the second generation owns it now. I’ve never been here when there wasn’t a queue, though I’m grateful for time to ponder my order from the packed wraparound case. For starters, I’ll take an always fluffy, sweet-savoury BBQ pork bun, custardy Portuguese egg tart and a bouncy mochi ball. Uncomfortably full? Me too. I’d suggest a ramble through Ping Tom Memorial Park, a former rail yard turned native prairie park that hugs the Chicago River. Paved paths and raised boardwalks carry you through rewilded grasses and past colourful murals. Glance north at every available opportunity, then gasp. Is that not the most gorgeous view of the skyline? Other excellent Chinatown restaurants - Dolo Restaurant and Bar for traditional and modern dim sum. - MCCB for charcoal-grilled whole fish and twice-cooked pork with leeks. - 3 Sauces Hainam Chicken Rice at the Richland Center food court for, you guessed it, Hainam chicken rice: soft, toothsome poached thigh meat served chilled over chicken fat-flavoured rice. - Yummy Yummy Noodles to slurp shrimp wonton noodle soup. Which is your favourite neighbourhood restaurant in Chicago? Tell us in the comments below. And read more of our Chicago guide here Follow us on Instagram at @FTGlobetrotter Cities with the FT FT Globetrotter, our insider guides to some of the world’s greatest cities, offers expert advice on eating and drinking, exercise, art and culture — and much more Find us in Chicago, London, Washington DC, Los Angeles, Tokyo, New York, Paris, Lagos, Rome, Frankfurt, Singapore, Hong Kong, Miami, Toronto, Madrid, Melbourne, Copenhagen, Zürich, Milan, Vancouver, Edinburgh, Venice and Istanbul Comments

item.title: Balvenie’s 88-year-old whisky is the oldest. Is it any good?
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 2.27
Balvenie’s 88-year-old whisky is the oldest. Is it any good? Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Next week, The Balvenie will set a new record for the oldest single malt Scotch whisky ever released. Its 88-year-old bottling breaks the previous record (an 85-year-old Glenlivet bottled by Gordon & MacPhail) by three years. This superannuated dram was distilled at The Balvenie in Speyside in 1931 from barley grown on the distillery’s estate. It was malted at Balvenie’s own home floor maltings facility, which, unusually, continues to operate to this day. The whisky was then placed in a single sherry butt that lay undisturbed in Dufftown until 2019, when the contents was decanted into glass. It is field-to-bottle in a way that modern grande marque malts rarely are. (There are whiskies in circulation that were distilled prior to 1931 – what makes this one record-breaking is the amount of time spent in the cask.) The whisky world loves a superlative – so I’m prone to be cynical. I’ve tasted a lot of antiquated spirits, and if it’s taught me anything it’s that older is not necessarily better. There are very mature whiskies with incredible flavour, but plenty more just taste as tannic, woody and lifeless as a creaky antique. Knowing how far you can push is a real skill. But simply seeking deliciousness is perhaps missing the point. Part of the thrill of tasting old whisky is that each sip is a step back in time. And the lineage of this particular whisky is unusually distinct: just before I tasted it, I was shown a black-and-white photo of the distillery team, which includes the malt men (and one distillery dog) who malted the barley for the liquid I was about to sip. Four record-breaking bottles The deep amber spirit is lively and concentrated on the nose, with some of the tropical aromas – passionfruit, mango – that often characterise malts of a great age. There are also maturer, umami-ish notes of Worcester sauce, coffee, tea and tobacco. The palate skews more savoury with a tannin that’s quite brittle at first before softening into a long finish with notes of juniper, bitter orange, dried apricot and fig leaf. It splices charm with gravitas. Each of the 17 bottles is housed in a patinated bronze-and-wood case designed by Daniel Arsham, an American artist known for works that explore the passage of time. He’ll also direct a live piece inspired by his visits to The Balvenie distillery when the bottles are unveiled at Frieze Seoul. The whisky is only available via private sale, and Balvenie won’t disclose the price. (For context, the RRP for the Gordon & MacPhail Glenlivet 85-year-old, released in 2025, was £125,000.) The estimates I sought from rare whisky specialists were mostly around £200,000-£250,000, though one well-placed source considered even £200,000 “aggressive”. Alongside the 88-year-old will also be a pair of more affordable 12-year-old (£80) and 15-year-old (£150) single malts that have been made using similar heirloom techniques. It’s only really in the past 20 years that ultra-aged whiskies (with correspondingly “ultra” packaging) have become a phenomenon – a movement spurred by a surge in whisky collecting and investment. Now barely a year goes by without a record being broken. “There is a status intrinsic to a whisky aged 50 years old or more,” says Sotheby’s head of whisky, Jonny Fowle, who sees the trend echoed in the secondary market. “It’s impressive. It’s expensive. The time taken to produce these whiskies is awe-inspiring. Whether or not old whiskies are your thing.” Everyone is now waiting for the world’s first 100-year-old malt. But how much older can whisky get? One important limiting factor is a whisky’s abv, which falls over time, in cask, due to evaporation (what’s known as the “angel’s share”). In Scotland, freshly distilled spirit (or new make) goes into the cask at around 63.5 per cent abv, and then declines in strength by an average of 0.5 per cent a year. It must be bottled before the strength dips below 40 per cent abv or it can no longer be legally called Scotch malt whisky. (It’s striking how many deluxe whiskies are about to cross this threshold when it is decided they have reached their peak.) Thanks to variations in warehouse microclimates and wood types, some whiskies survive in cask longer than this. And distillers are constantly exploring ways to artificially recreate these conditions – adjusting the temperature or humidity of the maturation warehouse, for example, or even wrapping casks in plastic to reduce evaporation. These may be innovative but they often come with risks: most methods are scalable, they might interfere with other important stages in flavour formation, or even contravening Scotch Whisky Association (SWA) rules. A 100-year-old malt, then, might be a little way off. And there are plenty of whisky aficionados who prefer bottles even a fraction of that age. Says Fowle: “I would choose a Springbank Samaroli 12-year-old over any 50-year-old whisky.” Perhaps, in this case, it’s a question of beauty before age. Comments

item.title: When Renting a Car in San Diego Makes Sense
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.37
San Diego is often described as easygoing, but the geography tells a practical story. The city is spread out, beaches are miles from business districts, and many useful stops are not connected by a single transit line. That is why mobility matters here. For visitors planning a short break, family holiday, or work trip with meetings across town, reliable transport can make the difference between a smooth day and a frustrating one. That is also where car hire for your stay in San Diego becomes relevant in a very practical sense. A rented vehicle is not only about convenience; it's often the most straightforward way to travel between hotels, the airport, coastal neighborhoods, and inland districts without having to build the itinerary around timetables. When a downtown lunch meeting is followed by a client visit in La Jolla, having flexible transportation can make the day much easier. However, a rental car is not necessary for every itinerary. Visitors staying downtown, in Little Italy, or near a trolley route may find public transit and occasional rideshares easier and less expensive once parking costs are considered. A car makes the strongest case when the itinerary includes several widely separated neighborhoods, substantial luggage, or destinations outside the best-connected areas. San Diego's rhythm rewards people who adapt. Morning fog may give way to warm afternoons. Traffic can change quickly near the waterfront, and weekend crowds shift flow around popular destinations. A transport choice that allows for these changes usually saves time and lessens stress, which matters when a trip has a tight schedule. What Travelers Actually Need on the Road Most trips do not fail because of the destination but because of small gaps in planning. Is there enough time between check-in and the first appointment? Will a late dinner in another neighborhood cause a long wait for a ride? These questions seem minor until they arise at the wrong moment. A vehicle lets travelers control the day rather than react to it. For leisure travelers, that control often means more than one beach stop. A morning near Mission Beach can turn into an afternoon in Balboa Park, and end with dinner in Little Italy, without worrying about carrying bags from one mode of transport to another. For business travelers, it means less time spent coordinating pickups and more time spent preparing for a presentation, which is often the real priority. San Diego also works well for people who mix city time with short escapes. A rental car makes it easier to move beyond central districts and explore places that are otherwise harder to reach efficiently.
