item.title: The Flatiron Steak Is Affordable and Versatile
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 4.21
Advertisement Say flatiron to a New Yorker and a triangular building on lower Fifth Avenue comes to mind. But to a butcher? It’s a prized but underappreciated cut of steak that’s finally having its moment. The flatiron delivers delectably rich beefy flavor and nice marbling to yield a tender bite, less grainy than flank steak, more succulent than hanger. It’s extremely versatile, excellent to sear or grill but also superb slivered and marinated for a Chinese stir-fry or sliced into a taco. It’s rarely recommended for stroganoff, which is a big mistake. And it can also be braised. The really good news, though, is that it’s often half the price, or less, than the marquee filet mignon, rib-eye or strip loin steaks. As for tenderness, it’s generally considered to be second only to the tenderloin, against which it’s also juicier, with more beefy flavor. “With cuts like flatiron you can give people a great meal without it costing a ton of money,” said Joe Carroll, an owner of the St. Anselm steakhouses in Brooklyn and in Washington, D.C. David Lowenberg has been serving it for years for steak frites: “Hanger and skirt have gotten more expensive,” said Mr. Lowenberg, who owns the Beacon and Bell & Anchor in Sag Harbor, N.Y. “Flatiron is delicious and costs less.” Home cooks can expect to pay about $20 to $30 a pound for the cut depending on the market. Costco’s price is a rock-bottom $10 to $12 a pound. Even at Eli’s Market on the Upper East Side, it’s $30 a pound, less than half the price of strip loin. But it comes with quality more typical of costlier choices. It’s so budget friendly because it’s from the shoulder muscle, a part of the animal usually considered better for stewing than for a splurge. A flatiron steak is a boneless rectangle of well-marbled meat, a scant inch thick, sometimes called blade steak. The muscle itself is a hefty hunk, suggesting a chuck roast, and great for pot roast. I have been happily buying flatiron steaks from Hudson & Charles, a nose-to-tail butcher in my neighborhood on the Upper West Side, and also in the West Village, for years. But it was only after discussing the cut with Daniel Boulud, who also has flatiron steak on the lunch menu at Le Pavillon and plans to include it at his new Brasserie Boulud at New York’s Lincoln Center, that I realized I grew up eating braised flatiron, or what Mr. Boulud and the rest of France calls paleron. For stews and pot roast it’s what my mother, for whom the flavor and texture of the more typical brisket wasn’t appealing, called chicken steak. And so did Anthony Bourdain in recommending it for his beef bourguignon. Why chicken steak? No one seems to know. “I have never been able to find out,” said Jake Dickson, another flatiron fan, of Dickson’s Farmstand Meats in Chelsea Market in Manhattan. The singular drawback is that the muscle has a vein of gristle running up the center. Remove the meat on either side and you have two big flatiron steaks. When you slowly braise the whole muscle, or thick slabs of it sliced against the grain as my mother did, or cut it in pieces for stew à la Bourdain, the gristle is less significant. At his new Brasserie, Mr. Boulud’s flatiron steak will come sliced with either a shallot and red wine pan sauce or prepared “au poivre,” a preparation favored at other restaurants, including Vaux Social and Lori Jayne, both in Brooklyn. Marinating first is in order at some. “It takes a marinade very well,” Mr. Lowenberg said. At the new Jack’s All Day on Restaurant Row in Manhattan, it’s treated with herbs, Worcestershire sauce, mustard, olive oil and tamari overnight before grilling. Elsewhere, a swipe of chimichurri or salsa verde is another typical flourish before serving. It’s the signature steak, rubbed with coffee and cocoa and finished with smoked chile butter, at Lazy Dog restaurants, a national chain. At the some places, including St. Anselm and the STK restaurants, salt and pepper is all the steak needs before it hits the grill. Robert Liberato, STK’s executive chef, called it a “rewarding cut” that easily holds its own. Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. item.title: The 100 Best Easy Dinner Ideas for Right Now
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 3.14
The Weeknight 100 is back, with so many fast, delicious dinner ideas for busy times. It’s here: September, and with it arrives the Weeknight 100, New York Times Cooking’s annual list of the dinner recipes you should make in the year ahead. Why publish it in September and not January? It’s back-to-school season, of course, the turning of the dial. It’s that transition from the languid late days of summer, when routine has long ago dissolved into the pool’s chlorine, to the first bell and a newly crammed calendar. Get even more recipes: Sign up for Emily Weinstein’s Five Weeknight Dishes newsletter I’m a summer person, and yet I appreciate the energy and optimism of September. It’s a moment to reset, to block out a new schedule and lay in new habits, to buy clothes, swear that we’ll get to the gym, get a full night of precious sleep or map out a week’s worth of dinners and stick to them. I can’t help you with the gym. But I can help you with dinner. Advertisement I’ve selected the 100 dinner recipes below for you to try. The emphasis is on efficient yet excellent cooking, recipes that are truly delicious and don’t take too much of your time. Everything on this list takes under an hour to make, and a vast majority are much faster than that. I kept kids — those picky, petulant, wonderful beings — in mind when I made this list, and there are many recipes that could work for them, either exactly as written or with simple modifications. But there are also recipes that are more likely to please the adults. Hopefully, whatever your needs are, there’s something here for you. Chicken Chicken and Pesto Rice With Peas A worthy use of a tub of pesto. Sheet-Pan Chicken With Black Beans and Squash Not all sheet-pan recipes are created equal, and this is an especially good one. Tomato Basil Chicken Breasts Take a cue from the blissed-out commenters and make it with the freshest tomatoes you can find (though plump supermarket cherry tomatoes work in a pinch). Keema Palak (Ground Chicken and Spinach Curry) A full pound of baby spinach is wilted into this dish, a quick, very green version of classic keema curries. Honey Ginger Chicken and Carrots The simple honey-ginger-soy marinade is the undisputed star of this stir-fry. Chile Chicken and Bean Guisado Cinnamon-tinged and chile-spiced, this quick stew starts with ground chicken, not rotisserie, for a truer chicken flavor. Creamy Tuscan Chicken A slab of cream cheese melts into this sauce to make it extra bodacious. Rosemary-Garlic Roasted Chicken and Gnocchi Pantry gnocchi subs in for potatoes in this clever sheet-pan recipe. Chicken and Kale Hatch Chile Bowl A can of mild diced green chiles is the key that unlocks this great, simple dinner. Miso-Maple Sheet-Pan Chicken With Brussels Sprouts Sensationally easy, this is the kind of high-reward meal that home cooks rave about. Za’atar Turkey Meatballs With Tahini Yogurt Just imagine these atop a rice bowl instead of falafel, heaped with chopped cucumbers and tomatoes. Greek Chicken With Cucumber-Feta Salad One herbed yogurt sauce, two distinct uses: Half serves as marinade for the chicken, while the other half dresses a briny, crunchy Greek salad. Chicken, Eggplant and Basil Stir-Fry The easy steam-frying technique here gives you eggplant that’s silky, golden and not at all oily. Lemon-Garlic Grilled Chicken Breasts This is it: the only method you need for grilling boneless chicken breasts to juicy perfection. Crispy Cheddar Chicken Tacos These Cheddar-lined tacos are more fun than any quick dinner has a right to be. Quick Harissa Apricot Chicken Intense, beguiling harissa paste is the key ingredient in this speedy recipe; apricot jam brings sweetness to offset any heat. One-Pan Kuku Paka (Chicken in Coconut Curry) Use skin-on chicken thighs in this creamy, richly spiced curry. Chicken With Peas and Mint Sweet peas and fresh mint make an even more pleasing pair when they’re served in a skillet with crisp-skinned chicken thighs. Spicy Paprika Chicken and Potato Stew Like chicken paprikash but in stew form, this recipe swaps out sweet paprika for its spicy cousin. Blackened Chicken Breasts A basic recipe that tastes like anything but, and the leftovers make amazing chicken salad. Stir-Fried Cumin Green Beans and Chicken Even quicker than the typical stir-fry, because you hardly need to do any chopping to prep. Chicken and White Bean Stew This flexible dish is made quickly with boneless breasts poached in broth and made creamy from smashed beans. Pasta, Noodles, Grains Coconut Curry Noodles With Shrimp A weeknight noodle bowl, but make it a luxuriously creamy slurp. Stir-Fried Salt and Pepper Dumplings This recipe convincingly makes the case for stir-frying your freezer dumplings. Ravioli With Roasted Red Pepper Sauce A brilliant and brilliantly simple sauce. Quick Pasta e Fagioli This is a speed-demon version of the classic and is remarkably satisfying for it. Farro With Blistered Tomatoes, Pesto and Spinach The combination of pesto and tomatoes can summon August any time of year. Cream Cheese Ramen In the words of its writer, this nine-minute recipe is a “break glass in case of noodle emergency” dinner, perfect for kids and hospitable to additions like peas. Smoky Chicken and Peppers Penne If fajitas were a pasta dish, it’d be this: sweet, smoky and fun to spear with a fork. Angel Hair Pasta A simple throwback that’s easy to love. Spicy Pork Noodle Soup Ramen is entangled with browned ground pork and thinly sliced veggies in this easy-to-throw-together soup. Salsa Macha Pasta With Shrimp This unique and delicious recipe brings the elements of salsa macha — nuts, seeds, garlic and chiles — into a skillet, where they are tossed with shrimp and spaghetti. Creamy Lemon Asparagus Gnocchi Pasta al limone inspired this pillowy one-pan dinner. Cold Noodles With Steak and Tomatoes This dish is both brawny (from sliced steak) and bright (from fish sauce, lime and juicy tomatoes). Peanut Noodles With Spicy Tofu Chewy, nubby tofu crumbles take this dish to the next level. Cheesy Baked Pasta With Sausage and Ricotta If love were a baked pasta dinner, it would be this one. Soy Sauce and Brown Butter Brussels Sprouts Pasta A surprisingly rich dish, with a soy-butter sauce and tender sliced brussels. Cumin Chicken Fried Rice You can prep all the ingredients ahead for this recipe, including the three-ingredient sauce that knits together all the elements. Tortellini Soup This is screaming, “Make me for dinner!” Creamy Cottage Cheese Basil Pasta We live in the golden age of cottage cheese; in this recipe, it’s blended with spinach and basil to make a silky pasta sauce. One-Pot Orzo and Meatballs This dish may sound Italian Americanish, but it actually has a Spanish streak, with pimentón and fresh chorizo featured in the pot. Kimchi Ramen Silken tofu softens the heat in this customizable soup. One-Pan Dumplings With Greens Just cook that kale right in the pan with your dumplings, drizzle with soy sauce and rice vinegar, and garnish to your heart’s content. Kale Caesar Pasta Salad A hefty, make-ahead pasta for Caesar lovers. Pasta With Tomato-Poached Eggs This is a pantry dish that, against all odds, feels like a luxury. Chilled Sesame Soba and Tofu A light dinner in minutes, substantiated with hunks of firm tofu. Lemony Pasta With Chickpeas and Parsley Use chickpeas to bulk up a simple bowl of pasta. Beef and Pork Beef, Asparagus and Tofu Stir-Fry This clever recipe uses less beef than a typical similar stir-fry without skimping on the protein; it’s better for the planet and more cost-effective, too. Smashed Beef Kebab With Cucumber Yogurt This was our most popular recipe of 2025, and if you make it you’ll see why. Roasted Sausages With Chickpeas and Spinach Keep sausages in your freezer so you can always throw together a dinner like this. Cheeseburger Soup This is the best cheeseburger soup recipe in the land, and yes, kids love it. Kielbasa Coins and Cabbage My favorite touch in this recipe is the apple cider vinegar and Dijon mustard that are stirred into the pan before serving. Sausage, Beans and Greens Soup Sausage is an ingenious base for this satisfying soup, generous with its fat and flavor. Sheet-Pan Charred Meat Pitas Definitely top these delicious pitas with abandon. Sausages With Tangy, Gingery Pineapple Don’t believe the haters: Pork and pineapple belong together. Chile-Garlic Steak and Zucchini A red wine vinegar dressing ties the seared steak and zucchini together. Shake and Bake Pork Chops Definitely serve with applesauce on the side. Sheet-Pan Steak and Pepper Tacos Steak is very satisfying here, but you could use any protein you want (including tofu or tempeh). Skillet Pork Chops With Buttered Corn This is at its best made with peak-season sweet corn, but frozen corn works well, too. Panko-Crusted Pork Tenderloin With Tahini Slaw This method produces utterly juicy pork that is difficult to stop eating. Glazed Chile-Garlic Meatballs Made with soy sauce and maple syrup, this glaze is salty-sweet in just the right way. Charros Corridos (Quick Spicy Bean Soup) Frijoles charros — cowboy beans, studded with sliced hot dogs — are from Northern Mexico, and this recipe lets you have that for dinner in a hurry. Smashed Bean and Sausage Toasts Normalize toasts for dinner, especially when they’re as garlicky and meaty as these; I’d make a green salad to go on the side. Perfect Soy-Grilled Steak Exactly as advertised and very easy to make. Vegetarian Halloumi and Sweet Potato Tacos An unexpected combination that works shockingly well, and a good dinner for kids who don’t eat meat. Skillet Chickpea Parmesan All the saucy, bubbling, dig-in joy of a baked Parmesan dish, but with the pantry-friendly convenience of a few cans of chickpeas. Creamy Butternut Squash and Coconut Noodle Soup An excellent showcase for sweetly familiar butternut squash, inspired by the Thai dish khao soi. Tofu Schnitzel With Buttermilk Slaw Use prepackaged slaw mix as a shortcut here; anything would be great tossed with that creamy, tangy buttermilk dressing. White Bean Shakshuka Heartier than more traditional shakshuka, thanks to those white beans, but no more taxing to make. Chickpea Tomato-Rice Soup The starch from the rice makes this soup creamier than you might imagine. Anda Bhurji (Tomato-Chile Scrambled Eggs) A spicy scramble for nights when it’s eggs for dinner. Buttery Gochujang Tofu and Broccoli You have to stir together only a few ingredients to make the incredible glaze. Charred Broccoli and White Bean Stew Searing the broccoli until it’s golden brown helps build flavor in this pleasingly simple soup. Chile Tofu A vegan take on chile paneer, this recipe soars on the strength of its spicy-sweet sauce. Crispy Tofu and Cheesy Bean Burritos The spiced-and-seared tofu crumbles in this recipe make a killer addition to beany burritos. Ras el Hanout Chickpea and Spinach Stew This is a pretty fabulous way to have chickpeas for dinner. Green Curry Beans and Greens Beans and greens get a bright, hot boost. Hearty Vegetable Tofu Soup Thick with cabbage, carrots and scoops of silken tofu, this gingery soup is a satisfying dinner. Old Bay Tofu Nuggets A gleefully fun vegetarian dinner, especially if you serve it with dipping sauce. Tofu and Sweet Potato Peanut Butter Curry Peanut butter is the heroine of this creamy, sweet-and-salty dish. Soy-Glazed Mushroom Rice Bowl Silky caramelized cabbage adds another layer of flavor; add sardines for protein if you’d like. Seafood Ginger Salmon Lettuce Wraps This great get-your-hands-messy dinner is brought to life by nước chấm, the punchy Vietnamese sauce. Harissa Shrimp With Greens and Feta A genius sheet-pan dinner; the shrimp and greens cook together quickly before they’re topped with feta, avocado and red onion. Spicy Tuna Salad With Crispy Rice A sushi restaurant staple is cleverly remade for home cooks. Salmon and Cherry Tomato Curry You can never go wrong with a coconut-milk curry; this one is flavored with ginger, garlic and the juices of those burst tomatoes. Broiled Wild Salmon and Peppers Running fish and quick-cooking vegetables under the broiler is a weeknight move that reliably delivers. One-Pot Salmon and Dill Rice With Peas The rice, salmon and peas all cook together in this convenient dinner, lightened with yogurt sauce and dill. Crispy Coconut Salmon Bring the tropical, shredded-sweet crunch of fried coconut shrimp to weeknight baked salmon fillets. Shrimp and Bacon Burritas “These were dope,” a commenter wrote. Cod With Caper-Orange Sauce This sauce has the power to make simple cod sing. Baked Salmon Meatballs An excellent use of canned salmon, and a gift from the meal-prep gods. Puttanesca Poached Fish Puttanesca sauce, as bold as can be, is a delicious medium for gently poaching fish. Roasted Cumin Salmon With Carrots A simple recipe that puts earthy cumin front and center (it’s especially nice contrasted with the carrots). Corn and Cod Green Curry This is a heavenly ingredient trio: fish, corn and coconut milk. Crispy Salmon With Lentil Salsa Verde Salsa verde with lentils is more than a sauce; it’s a side dish to this crisp-skinned salmon. Sautéed Shrimp With Lemon-Caper Dressing This is so fancy for how easy it is; serve it with toast, tossed with pasta, over rice or in a salad. Greek Salad With Sardines and Beans A main-course salad that could be made with just about any tinned fish. Sheet-Pan Citrus Salmon With White Beans This recipe is excellent all year round, but save it for the darkest part of winter, when citrus provides some sunshine. Spicy Shrimp Masala Shockingly complex for the speedy cook time, and truly alive with flavor. Tuna Melt This solid rendition of the classic is among the fastest recipes on this list. Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. Get regular updates from New York Times Cooking, with recipe suggestions, cooking tips and shopping advice.

With only a few hours to spare before sunset, the rescue had to wait until the next morning to head in (Photo: Courtesy of Tip Top Search and Rescue) Two stranded climbers had to spend the night on Pingora Peak, a nearly 12,000-foot granite mountain in the Wind River Range of Wyoming, before being rescued by lifesaving crews. On August 20, the duo tried to bail on a climbing route when their rope got stuck while rappelling, leaving them unable to descend. It was around 5 P.M. when they hit their SOS button from a ledge, according to responding agency Tip Top Search and Rescue. With only a few hours to spare before sunset, the rescue had to wait until the next morning. Around 7 A.M., a search-and-rescue group set in to rescue the two climbers. Two Lander Search and Rescue (LSAR) high-angle rescue teams, a specialized emergency response unit trained to reach and recover people from steep faces, also took part. “Multiple attempts were made to deliver long-line supplies to the two stranded climbers, but due to the wind and the clearance of the rotor blades, it was aborted,” Tip Top SAR said in a statement. “The two LSAR climbers were deployed. Once LSAR reached the two climbers, they lowered both to the base of Pingora.” One of the climbers was wearing a bright orange jacket, which helped the team spot the duo on their first pass into the Cirque, Tip Top wrote. “Despite spending a chilly night on the side of Pingora, the rescued climbers reported that they were okay, just thirsty and tired,” responders wrote. “Both were uninjured and declined transport. The rescued climbers continued their trip and hiked out.” Pingora Peak is a famed summit that forms the Cirque of the Towers, a granite amphitheater of jagged peaks in the southern part of the Winds. It’s unclear what route the two were on, but Pingora Peak is considered to be a “low-hanging fruit of accessible alpine climbing in the Wind River Range,” Colorado climber Adam McClatchie told Outside. Pingora Peak is included in the 50 Classic Climbs of North America, a list of coveted climbs made famous in the 1979 climbing guidebook by Yosemite climbing pioneers Steve Roper and Allen Steck. Although McClatchie considers Pingora Peak a bucket-list climb and a beginner route, its remote location makes it deceptively difficult. For starters, would-be climbers need to hike about ten miles to reach its base, which requires a certain level of alpine fitness. The routes can also be hard to spot, so climbers need a trained eye, and its steep terrain requires technical skills and proper rope management. McClatchie, 34, has been climbing for over a decade and has climbed routes on Pingora Peak on three occasions between 2020 and 2022. He says that it’s not uncommon for people to get in sticky situations and need rescue. “I have witnessed parties on Pingora very late at night that were very clearly struggling to get down,” McClatchie said. “I don’t think I witnessed a rescue per se, but I’ve seen headlamps on the wall in the wee hours of the night in rainstorms.” “That’s the nature of alpine climbing,” McClatchie added. “Things can turn really quickly.”

item.title: No, You’re Not Imagining It. Bear Encounters Really Are on the Rise.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.46
Between 1990 and 2019, North American black and grizzly bears have killed 150 people (Photo: Scott Suriano/Getty Images) On the evening of August 31, a bear attacked a woman walking with her dog in Columbia Falls, Montana, a small town just outside of Glacier National Park. According to Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks (FWP), the woman sustained significant injuries and was transferred to a medical facility for treatment. The attack marks the latest in a long list of bear run-ins across North America this summer. Experts say that human-bear encounters have been higher in 2026 than in recent years. “Especially with black bears, we’ve definitely seen an uptick in their activity and subsequent conflict activity across the state,” Dan Thompson, large carnivore biologist with the Wyoming Game and Fish Department, told Outside. Bears have already killed two people this year. Anthony Pollio, 33, died while hiking in Glacier National Park in May. A black bear attacked and killed a New Mexico man in August, marking the state’s second bear attack on record. A grizzly attacked two Yellowstone hikers, a Wyoming woman was bitten in the butt by a black bear, an Alaska woman fended off a grizzly using jiu-jitsu, and a black bear charged a group of students in Washington State. It seems the bears are everywhere. Thompson attributes the heightened bear activity to a one-two punch of weather extremes: an unusually low snowpack across the West last winter, followed by scorching summer temperatures. Together, those conditions have diminished the natural food sources bears rely on, including the berries, fruits, nuts, and grasses that make up the bulk of their diet. With less food available in the wild, more bears are venturing beyond their usual habitat and into neighborhoods in search of an easier meal. “Human-bear conflicts in general tend to increase when there are shortages of natural bear foods,” Frank van Manen, a bear expert and emeritus ecologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, told Outside. “It is possible that conflicts suddenly drop off if high-calorie foods that bears pursue in the fall are abundant. In areas where such foods are in low supply, human-bear conflicts may intensify.” Montana, home to nearly two-thirds of grizzly bears in the Lower 48, has reported 194 grizzly conflicts so far in 2026, and another 250 black bear-related incidents, according to Montana FWP data. “This year is panning out to be one of the worst natural food failure years on record,” Jamie Jonkel, Montana FWP bear conflict specialist, said in a statement. “Our regional bear team is working around the clock, and we are asking the public to be patient and to please be diligent with containing all attractants.” In Colorado, the state confirmed five black bear attacks amid an all-time high of more than 8,600 sightings, more than double the number of sightings in 2025. Connecticut wildlife officials reported that over 50 bears have entered homes. There have been at least 168 black bear incidents this year in Utah—also twice the amount from the previous year—and another 187 in New Mexico. Bear populations in some areas are also rebounding, moving beyond their recovery zones, and this year’s low food supply has only compounded those pressures. “There’s no silver bullet, no divine answer for why exactly,” Thompson said. “It’s a combination of factors: the lack of winter in other areas, moisture turning into a lot of heat, early blooms that froze and reduced the berry crop, and increased human use of these areas.” Vocabulary matters when you’re talking about bear data. Here’s how the experts distinguish between different events. Data suggests that brown bear attacks are rising around the world. According to a 2019 study, between 2000 and 2015 there were 183 attacks in North America, averaging 11 every year. Most of these victims were lone males recreating outside. Research on U.S. bear attacks is consistent with these numbers. Between 1990 and 2019, North American black and grizzly bears have killed at least 150 people, and more people have died in recent decades than a century ago. Scientists involved in the studies concluded that’s partly because far more people may be encountering bears. As remote bear territory diminishes, these encounters are even more likely to rise. Cody Miller, a wildlife scientist at Brigham Young University in Utah, wrote in his 2024 study that human–bear conflicts are still rare, but increasing at a steady rate because more people are hiking, camping, and hunting than ever before. Van Manen adds that more people in the landscape also increases the likelihood that bears encounter and pursue human foods, like garbage left behind at camp. Grizzlies account for more conflicts than black bears and are more likely to injure people, Miller concluded. Interestingly, though, black bear conflicts are more likely to be fatal. Most of these incidents began as surprise encounters, as with Pollio in Glacier. Van Manen cautions that although 2026 appears to be an unusually active year for encounters, it doesn’t necessarily mean that fatal bear attacks are on the rise—such a trend takes years of data to establish. “Because of the rarity of these events, comparisons of a single year with a ten-year average are not meaningful,” van Manen said. “Decadal comparisons for North America do not suggest distinct trends.” According to van Manen, grizzly bears killed 17 people in the United States during the 2010s, and 14 in the 2020s so far. American black bears, by comparison, killed ten people in the 2010s and 13 so far in the 2020s. Since 1892, researchers have documented 20 fatal attacks in the Greater Yellowstone area; some years have more, others less. “This is an example of how unpredictable these events are: there was a fatality in 1986 followed by a 25-year period with no fatal incidents and then several years with multiple incidents,” van Manen said. Nationwide tracking doesn’t exist—states hold the data—and establishing a full, nationwide picture of bear deaths is challenging. Chris Servheen, the former national grizzly bear recovery coordinator for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, told Outside that statistically speaking, a grizzly kills less than one person annually, on average. Even one death is a tragedy, and most fatal attacks are purely coincidental, van Manen adds. “These are chance events that are driven by human and bear numbers: in areas with increasing and expanding bear populations,” he said. “Combined with increases in recreational visits, the chance of a bear encounter that may end in a physical attack increases as well, however small that may be.” But all that could change as we head into the fall months. As more people move into bear country, and more bears come into towns looking for food, conflicts are sure to increase. Late summer and early autumn bring hyperphagia, a period during which bears spend almost all their time consuming calories to build fat reserves for winter. As more bears spend more time looking for food, the chances of people coming across them during fall hikes or bike rides increase. Nathaniel Bowersock is a biologist who spent nearly a decade working with bears in Yellowstone National Park. He is now a black bear specialist in Missouri and works with Bearwise, an interstate organization dedicated to mitigating human-bear conflict. He says the most important thing hikers can do is bring bear spray. “Bear spray continues to be shown to be an effective tool at deterring or lessening an encounter with a bear, both black bears and grizzly bears, and bear spray will work under many conditions, even on a windy day,” Bowersock told Outside. “In addition, bear spray has been found to be more effective than a firearm at deterring a bear encounter, and bear spray is easier to use than a firearm. Therefore, any time someone is looking to recreate in grizzly country, I strongly suggest they carry bear spray.” And if you see something, say something. “We have a lot of bears that don’t get reported until it’s too late, or until their behavior is at a level that we can’t tolerate from a human safety standpoint,” Thompson said. “Don’t let garbage be available. Don’t let food be available. Bring in pet food. When you’re camping, make sure you’re keeping a clean camp.”

item.title: Marmots Are Having a Moment and I’m Here for It
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.06
Marmots are having a moment (Photo: Getty Images) What’s chubby, hairy, and likes to lick rocks? No—it’s not a typical Pacific Crest Trail thru-hiker. I’m of course referring to a marmot, the cute and cuddly high-alpine critter that’s currently taking the internet by storm. Marmots are having a moment, and I couldn’t be happier. If you’re like me, then your social media algorithm this month has overflowed with adorable marmot content. My personal marmot deep dive began in mid-August when an outdoor influencer named Jared Shult posted this video of a particularly charismatic marmot at Mount Rainier National Park hugging his leg. Shult recorded himself petting and stroking the marmot, and was subsequently fined $230 for doing so. National Park Service rules specifically prohibit visitors from touching wild animals—even the cute ones. Oops! Shult’s video had auspicious timing, as it hit social media just before Colorado’s inaugural Fat Marmot Week, a highly entertaining online contest operated by the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory’s (RMBL) Marmot Project. Much like Fat Bear Week, the RMBL, which studies marmots outside of Crested Butte, Colorado, asked fans to vote between eight yellow-bellied marmots who were trying to gain the most weight before winter. The winner, a particularly chonky marmot named Dawn, gained 4.5 pounds (about half his body weight) over the summer. Between Shult’s video and Fat Marmot Week, I’ve now consumed a vast array of marmot content. Marmots licking GoPro cameras. Marmots hugging. Marmots munching on rocks? I have awww‘d and ohhhh’d my way through all of the video clips showing these sentient stuffed animals doing cute little human things with their paws. I also learned that, like all critters, marmots are undomesticated wild animals driven by instincts and hunger, and, if given the chance, they may ruin your afternoon. The Wall Street Journal published a story accusing marmots of “terrorizing” guests in California’s Sequoia National Park by licking hikers, stealing their shoes, and occasionally breaking into their vehicles. The WSJ reporters also point out that marmots will sometimes crawl into the engine compartments of a parked car and devour cables, wires and hoses. My newfound marmot interest left me with more questions than answers. So, I recently sought some info from the global expert on the critters: Professor Daniel Blumstein of the Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at the University of California, Los Angeles. Blumstein also oversees the Marmot Project at the RMBL, and spends his summers studying the cuddly critters near Gothic, Colorado. Here are some takeaways I got from our correspondence. OK, so that marmot didn’t crawl into the engine compartment of your Dodge Stratus looking to strand you at the trailhead parking lot. The critter was just really inquisitive—one of the familiar traits of the species, Blumstein told me. It’s the same reason why that marmot went up to Shult in Mount Rainier National Park. It wanted food. It wasn’t afraid. And, by nature, it wanted to investigate the situation. Alas, this curiosity can sometimes get marmots in trouble. Blumstein has seen marmots crawl into cars in Colorado and then go for an unplanned adventure. “One made it to the Phoenix area a few years ago and had to be flown back,” he said. “Once in a car, havoc sometimes results.” Those videos of marmots licking boulders and chewing pebbles are pretty weird, right? Well, it turns out the critters are on a lifelong quest to consume salt. A marmot’s normal diet of grasses and meadows that grow in alpine tundra leaves them salt-deficient, so they seek the stuff out wherever they can. Sometimes that means licking mineralized salt out of rocks. Blumstein believes that may also explain why some marmots venture into cars. “I’m told that radiator fluid tastes salty to animals,” he said. “It’s also possible that radiator hoses taste good to them!” This year the RMBL experienced a tragic die-off of marmots—the biggest since scientists started studying them outside of Crested Butte. Of the 160 marmots the group was studying, 100 died during the winter of 2025-26. This die-off corresponded with Colorado’s thinnest snowpack in more than 40 years. Blumstein and his team know that the die-off and dismal snow levels are related. Like many mountain mammals, marmots hibernate over the winter. And sometimes, many of the marmots that go to sleep in the fall never wake up in the spring. “Snow is insulation, so the snowpack acts as a blanket to keep the marmots warm over the winter,” he said. “It’s possible that those who were more likely to die were colder this year because they had less of a snowpack covering them.” Alas, the life of a marmot is full of dangers and pitfalls. Too deep of a snowpack can also spell certain doom for a marmot. They may starve to death while waiting for the melting snow to unearth the grass and flowers. Or, predators can pick them off while digging out of their burrows. “We’ve seen both happen in heavy snow years,” Blumstein added. Perhaps my favorite marmot fact involves the long sleep that the critters take during the winter. Like bears, marmots must fatten up in the late summer and fall to build up fat storage for the winter. But a marmot’s body is a miracle of efficiency once it is inactive. Yellow-bellied marmots will burn just a paperclip’s weight of fat a day when they’re hibernating. And during this time, Blumstein said, the marmot is not physiologically aging. “Hibernation is a secret to longevity,” Blumstein said. “Except that to live longer you have to miss ski season.” Blumstein’s favorite marmot trait is that the same individual critters generally return to the same trailheads, mountain meadows, and rocky slopes year after year. So, should the marmot that hugged Shult survive the cruel winter, he will probably be back at Mount Rainier to hug guests in 2027 and beyond. Just reminding everyone—don’t hug him back. For those of us who are drawn in by their cuddly ways, just know that even researchers feel the same way. “Plus, they look like little buddhas,” Blumstein added.

item.title: The Fastest Trail Shoes at the 2026 UTMB
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.21
On the left, Blandine L'Hirondel of France wears Kiprun Kipsummit Race and on the right Ben Dhiman of the United States wears Asics Metafuji Trail 2. (Photo: Jacob Zocherman) The 2026 Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) started ominously, with evening thunderstorms calling for a two-hour delay and a slight course reroute. But by the time 2,406 runners got rolling out of Chamonix the skies had basically cleared. And in the end, near-perfect concisions and a particularly fast course were simply a perfect storm for a super fast race. America’s Ben Dhiman (and last year’s runner-up) ran away from the field on the first major test piece up Col du Bonhomme before the 40K mark. He ultimately finished in 18:16:29, earning the first sub-19-hour time in the race’s history. French national treasure Blandine L’Hirondel matched it on the women’s side, becoming the first woman to break 22 hours with a 21:54:49 finish. She’s just the second woman (and third person) to win all three UTMB World Series Finals races, OCC, CCC, and UTMB. The editors of Trail Runner were on location in Chamonix, France, checking out the new gear, watching the race unfold, while putting together a list of the fastest shoes at UTMB 2026. I’ve personally used many of these shoes, so I include my own testing notes below, just in case you’re interested in emulating the elites (at least in what you’re wearing, anyway). On the shoe side, this was one of the more interesting UTMB races I’ve covered. The diversity of brands worn by the top-10 men and women was fascinating. Among the top 10 men and women, 15 brands were represented. And there were more niche shoe companies represented in the field than I’ve ever seen, brands such as Kiprun, the shoe brand from Decathlon; Kailas Fuga from China; Canada’s premium running shoe brand Norda; and Dynafit, best known for their ski mountaineering equipment. As someone who tests pretty much every trail shoe, I can tell you these brands all make solid shoes but often don’t get the attention they deserve. The 2026 UTMB changed that. Here’s what the top 10 men and women wore, and my take on each. | Place | Athlete | Country | Time | Footwear | | 1 | Ben Dhiman | U.S. | 18:16:29 | Asics Metafuji Trail 2 | | 2 | Baptiste Chassagne | France | 18:47:38 | On Cloudultra Pro | | 3 | Caleb Olson | U.S. | 18:48:24 | Nike ACG Ultrafly | | 4 | Virgile Moriset | France | 19:00:23 | Asics Metafuji Trail 2 | | 5 | Joaquin Lopez | Ecuador | 19:06:48 | Kailas Fuga EX 330 | | 6 | Hannes Namberger | Germany | 19:13:51 | Dynafit SS27 Ultra DNA 2 | | 7 | Gautier Bonnecarrere | France | 19:23:16 | La Sportiva Prodigio Pro 2 | | 8 | Antoine Charvolin | France | 19:40:33 | On Cloudultra Pro | | 9 | Yannick Noël | France | 19:51:42 | Inov8 Trailfly Pro | | 10 | Jean-Philippe Tschumi | Switzerland | 19:58:24 | Kailas Fuga EX 330 | | Place | Athlete | Country | Time | Footwear | | 1 | Blandine L’Hirondel | France | 21:54:49 | Kiprun Kipsummit Race | | 2 | Rachel Entrekin | U.S. | 22:15:54 | Norda 055 | | 3 | Emily Schmitz | U.S. | 22:17:28 | Hoka Prototype | | 4 | Careth Arnold | U.S. | 23:05:20 | Altra Prototype + Altra Mont Blanc Carbon | | 5 | Jazmine Lowther | Canada | 23:21:55 | Arc'teryx Sylan 2 | | 6 | Katarzyna Dombrowska | Poland | 23:27:34 | On Cloudultra Pro | | 7 | Lucy Bartholomew | Australia | 23:44:29 | Salomon Prototype | | 8 | Antonina Iushina | Unattached | 23:49:58 | | | 9 | Anne Cécile Thévenot | France | 24:02:00 | Mac Sport | | 10 | Anne-Sofie Pollestad | Norway | 24:04:56 | | This marks the second year in a row that an Asics shoe has crossed the finish line first. Ben Dhiman went with what worked for his second-place finish last year and ran the Asics Metafuji Trail 2 again. I just reviewed the Metafuji Trail 2 and was impressed with its speedy, agile ride. Asics clearly has its eyes on trail running at the highest level. The Metafuji Trail 2 features A-TPU, Asics’ highest-performing midsole foam, surrounded by firmer EVA to control and stabilize the soft foam. Embedded in the foam is a newly designed X-shaped carbon plate. The shoe is fast. I can see why Dhiman wore it again this year. Baptiste Chassagne wore the On Cloudultra Pro, which, in my opinion, is a hugely underrated shoe. I can’t tell if it was the first version or the second, but I’ve seen the second version, and it’s very similar to the original, which is good news. The original uses two layers of a PEBA foam (softer over firmer) with 38 millimeters of stack under the heel, but it runs like a lower-stack shoe. It’s one of the very few high-stack shoes, if not the only one, I feel comfortable wearing in Santa Barbara, California, where the trails are very rocky and technical. Coming in strong at the end, Caleb Olson went from eighth at the Courmayeur halfway point to third at the line. He wore the Nike ACG Ultrafly, Nike’s second-generation trail supershoe. It features Nike’s ZoomX, the original super foam found in the Vaporfly, here contained by a textile wrap in the forefoot to reduce side-to-side squish. The ACG Ultrafly is one of the heavier racing-focused shoes at 10.1 oz for men’s size 10 and women’s size 11.5, but makes up for it with responsiveness. I’ve found it to be one of the more stable carbon-plated super trail shoes thanks to a wide base. In front of a home-country crowd, Blandine L’Hirondel became the second woman to win OCC, CCC, and UTMB. She wore the Kiprun Kipsummit Race, Kiprun’s highest-performance trail shoe. The French brand was founded in 2008 under Decathlon, the world’s largest sporting goods retailer, and launched in the US in April 2026. While I haven’t tested the Kipsummit Race on the trails, I have tried it on and was impressed with its bouncy, airy feel. It uses an A-TPU midsole with an embedded carbon fiber plate. At 9.0 ounces for men and 7.8 ounces for women, it’s incredibly light for a shoe with a 37.5/31.5mm stack height. Three-time Cocodona 250 winner Rachel Entrekin, who signed with Norda in December 2025, wore the brand’s latest shoe, the 055. Norda has steadily gained a loyal following, and Entrekin’s second-place UTMB finish has put the brand in the spotlight. I’ve been testing it, and it’s my favorite Norda shoe by far. At first, it feels a little chunky because it sits so high on the ankle, but it’s surprisingly fun and fast. As always, Norda nails the intersection of aesthetics and function. I can’t tell you how many people stop and ask what shoe it is. The TPEE midsole is soft but very responsive. The upper uses tough-skinned, bio-circular Dyneema that really secures the foot. The $325 price tag is steep, but as carbon fiber and superfoams make their way into trail footwear, it’s not a lot more than comparable models. Hoka used UTMB week to debut its new Tecton X 4, a $247 trail super shoe with parallel carbon plates and dual-layer PEBA foam with PROFLY X construction. But in not unusual for Hoka’s top athletes, Schmitz elected for a shoe not on the market. When we asked Schmitz about her podium-landing shoe, she said simply that she wore “the prototype.” Well, two pairs of the prototype (she changed shoes midrace), but she told Trail Runner they were the same. From the outside, this undisclosed proto looks relatively similar to another Hoka trail super shoe, the Rocket X Trail. Inspired but the road variant, the Rocket X, the Rocket X Trail is Hoka’s trail racer designed for less technical terrain. The Rocket X Trail is made with an H-shaped parallel carbon fiber plate and ATPU midsole and has a more aggressive rocker than the Tecton X 4, and features slightly smaller (3 mm) lugs. Schmitz is a monster descender, so it’s possible she’s willing to trade a little stability for speed as she negotiates the more technical parts of the course. But it also looks like this shoe, if it is indeed a proto of the Rocket X Trail 2, has gotten a major update with a radical midsole geometry which may help give it some more stability.

item.title: The High-Altitude Journey of the World’s Most Famous Adventure Cat
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.75
Simon the adventure cat (Photo: Courtesy of JJ Yosh) Had JJ Yosh, an adventure content creator based in Boulder, Colorado, simply taken his cat, Simon, on a handful of hikes and posted the videos online, I would have dismissed it as a pet-thetic social media stunt. But a decade after adopting the black Bombay cat, the duo—better known to millions as Backpacking Kitty on Instagram and TikTok—has built something far more remarkable. Together they’ve hiked the Austrian Alps, whitewater rafted California’s Sacramento River, climbed a volcano in Guatemala, and traveled to more than 15 countries and four continents. They’ve flown on over 100 flights, including on a seaplane, and kayaked some of the most remote waterways in the world, taking an audience of 11 million followers along with them, and making Simon less of a novelty and more like a bona fide field companion. Now Yosh has something even more ambitious in mind. He’s preparing to take Simon on a multi-year Seven Summits spree. “I’m positive he’s the only cat who has summited a dozen of Colorado’s 14ers,” Yosh says of Simon who he rescued from euthanasia in 2016. Yet even those accomplishments, and, arguably, the title of one of the most famous cats in the world, pale beside this latest odyssey. Over the next three years, they plan to tackle the tallest mountain on every continent: Denali, Mount Kilimanjaro, Aconcagua, Mount Elbrus, Vinson Massif, Puncak Jaya, and the world’s highest peak, Mount Everest. Before you picture a cat being hauled into Everest’s notorious Death Zone—a place so hostile to life it contains only about a third of the oxygen available at sea level—rest easy. “I’m definitely not taking Simon to the summit. I’m not risking his life,” Yosh says. While Yosh makes his push for the top, Simon will be living the considerably cushier life at Everest Base Camp with a dedicated pet sitter, people he already knows and trusts. Yosh is emphatic that Simon’s health and safety come first. “How high he goes depends entirely on the mountain,” Yosh says. That means, for Everest, Base Camp is his ceiling. “Nothing above it, no exceptions.” For Kilimanjaro and Aconcagua? Those are non-technical walk-ups, so there is more room. “He could go higher than base camp on those, and how much higher gets decided on the ground rather than promised in advance.” As for everywhere else, Yosh will assess each peak one at a time, and veterinary opinions will inform each decision. Yosh says, “ If the answer is that it is too high for a cat, that is the end of it. He does not go.” It’s all part of the careful balance Yosh has spent the past decade striking with his feline partner. Simon may be born for adventure—while he does trek via leash, he’s happiest riding Yosh’s shoulders through forests and across alpine trails, even snowboarding—he’s still a cat, with very real limitations. For example, while Yosh was on a Mount Baker crevasse rescue training ahead of his Seven Summits bid recently, Simon wasn’t practicing self-arrests. Which begs the question: How do you prepare a house cat for extreme altitude? After all, Everest Base Camp sits at a breath-stealing 17,598 feet. The answer starts at home. In Boulder, where the pair live at roughly 6,000 feet above sea level, acclimatization is woven into everyday life. Yosh’s home—playfully known as “the house his cat built”—is tucked into a rocky cliff and outfitted with an indoor climbing wall scaled by both owner and pet. Outside, Colorado’s high country is Simon’s natural conditioning ground, where regular mountaineering outings have gradually exposed him to thinner air—one might say the purrfect conditions—long before the Himalayas come into view. Yosh has even taken Simon on technical rope climbs, securing him a small-dog harness. And when it comes to gear, Simon is just as outfitted as his owner: Yosh has assembled a wardrobe for Simon to rival any serious adventurer’s, with specialized gear for seemingly every climate, condition, and expedition. Add to that the deep relationship these two have built. Even talking about the possibility of something happening to Simon makes Yosh visibly shaken. The depth of that bond was forged early. Not long after Yosh adopted Simon, he left the cat with a friend while filming a commercial in Bolivia. What Yosh didn’t learn until later was that Simon had gone missing for three days. “Thankfully, they didn’t tell me at the time,” Yosh says. “They’d put up missing posters everywhere, but I had no idea.” Even now, the memory rattles him. “If that happened today and I found out while I was on a mountain, I’d turn around. I wouldn’t be able to finish the climb,” he says. “You have to be in a good mental place to climb a mountain, and I wouldn’t be.” “This work can be so taxing and draining. You question why you’re doing it over and over again,” Yosh says. “That’s where having Simon is such a huge emotional pillow. The hardest moments usually aren’t the scary, high-adrenaline ones. They’re when the weight of the whole expedition catches up with you.” Whether he’s just finished an ultrarun or a grueling climb, Yosh knows there’s one constant: Simon, curled up in the tent ready for a cuddle at the end of the day. In a life all about relentless forward motion, that ritual has become the reset that keeps him going. It will be tested during their next challenge. But first, there are the logistics to work through. Namely, the travel concerns of hop-scotching the planet with a cat. Fortunately, this isn’t Simon’s first rodeo. He has a U.S. ID card and an E.U. pet passport that allows him to easily cross borders, and he doesn’t fly cargo. “But of course he has to get all of these health certificates for each country,” Yosh says. Then there’s the tricky reality of lengthy flights and layovers. Naturally, I had to ask, does Simon get jet lag? “Simon gets so excited every time we reach a new hotel or destination,” Yosh says. “He’s like ready to go.” Apparently, when you’re an international adventuring cat of mystery, the only thing tougher than Everest is waiting for room service. That, and then clawing your way into mountaineering history.

item.title: Review: REI Co-op Traverse Modular Bear Canister
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 2.85
The REI Co-op Traverse Modular Bear Canister is a thoughtful alternative to conventional, fixed-size bear canisters. A traditional bear canister can be frustrating when its capacity does not match the length of an outing. A large model may be excessive for a weekend trip, while a small model may not hold enough food for a longer expedition. The Traverse addresses this problem with removable sections. You can carry the small configuration version for shorter trips and add the extra section to create the large configuration. That flexibility can appeal to backpackers whose food-storage needs change from trip to trip. - Large configuration (minus carry bag) weight: 3 lbs 9.1 oz - Large configuration capacity: 686 cubic inches (11.25L) - Large configuration dimensions: 9.1 x 13 inches - Small configuration (minus carry bag) weight: 2 lbs 8 oz - Small configuration capacity: 412 cubic inches (6.75L) - Small configuration dimensions: 9.1 x 8 inches - OGBC-Approval: Yes - Materials: polycarbonate - Nylon carry bag weight: 3.1 oz Design and Construction The Traverse uses a hard polycarbonate body, a material known for its impact resistance and durability. The canister is designed to withstand attempts by bears and other animals to access food, toiletries, and scented waste. Its rigid construction also protects food from being crushed in a backpack, a problem for soft bear-resistant containers like Ursacks. The modular body is made of separate sections that screw together. In its smaller configuration, the canister measures 9.1 inches in diameter and 8 inches high. With the additional section installed, it measures 9.1 inches in diameter and 13 inches high. While it is not 100% waterproof, the Traverse will keep its contents dry in the rain if it's positioned upright. The bottom section is tall enough that water or moisture will not seep into the container if a puddle forms around it or if it sits in water sloshing in the hull of a canoe or kayak. The canister can also serve as an improvised seat at camp. Its sturdy shape and 9.1-inch diameter make it useful when no convenient rocks or logs are available. The orange color of the Traverse also makes it much easier to find in the morning, since it stands out well in a forest. Blue or black bear canisters can be much more difficult to locate. Except in autumn, when they all become invisible. Capacity and Organization The smaller configuration provides 412 cubic inches of storage (6.75 liters). This is a reasonable size for an overnight trip or weekend trip with 4 person-days of food capacity. The larger configuration provides 686 cubic inches (11.25 liters), or about 7 person-days of food. For planning, it requires about 100 cubic inches per person-day of food, though you can often carry more if you remove excess packaging. Weight The smaller configuration weighs 2 pounds, 8 ounces, and the larger configuration weighs about 3 pounds, 9.1 ounces, not including the carry bag. That is substantial for backpackers who closely monitor every ounce. For hikers prioritizing minimum weight, a smaller fixed-size canister may be more attractive. For hikers who would otherwise purchase two different containers, the Traverse’s flexibility may justify its weight. Opening the Canister The Traverse is designed to open with your thumbs, something bears and other critters don't have. While this should be easy, the two buttons are highly tensioned and very difficult to press down. It's worse if they're wet. I've found it gets a little easier with practice, but the process can be hit or miss - Press one button and turn the lid so that the plastic just covers that button. - Next, press the other button and quickly twist the lid (or lower section if removing it) so it comes off The twisting direction is indicated on the canister's exterior but can be difficult to see depending on the light. If you don't twist quickly, the threads can seize, even though the buttons have depressed and unlocked. This happens way too often, and you'll be screwed if it happens in the field and you can't open it. The only cure I've found is to run the threaded section under hot water until the plastic expands and you can unthread the sections. I've also seen mention of using a silicone lubricant on the threads, such as Uberlube, but that didn't work for me. It does make the canister hilariously slippery though! My advice: don't put anything in this canister that you might need in a hurry, like your Nitroglycerin pills, other vital meds, Quickclot, driving glasses, or car keys. I recommend buying a different bear canister. You don't want this kind of grief in the backcountry. Carrying Comfort The Traverse’s cylindrical shape is typical of many bear canisters, but it can be awkward in some backpacks. It is generally easiest to carry the canister vertically and close to the center of the pack. Placing it high or far from the back can make the load feel unbalanced. If you've decided to strap the canister to the top of your pack, the included carry bag has daisy chains sewn on the exterior, which can make lashing it down easier, although scrunching it down under a floating lid is your best option if your pack has one. One trick to make a top-heavy canister manageable is to take all the food out and pack it in a stuff sack in your pack, so you can strap the empty canister on top. This keeps the center of gravity low, the canister is less likely to throw you off balance, and keeps the weight exactly the same as before. Competitive Products If you're trying to reduce the weight you carry, I'd recommend the BearVault BVOne and BV500 bear canisters instead of the REI Traverse. They're also much easier to use. Like the Traverse, the BVOne is modular and can be reconfigured on the fly for different volumes (see the comparison below.) Its lock mechanism is much easier to use, and it is significantly lighter. For larger volume needs, the BV500 is also much lighter. | Make / Model | Weight in oz. | Cubic In | Days Food | Price (USD) | |---|---|---|---|---| | BearVault BV500 | 41 oz | 700 | 7 | $100 | | Bearvault BVOne - Collapsed | 31.6 oz | 282 | 3 | $120 | | Bearvault BVOne- Expanded | 31.6 oz | 505 | 5 | $120 | | REI Traverse 6.75L (small configuration) | 39.6 oz | 412 | 4 | $90 | | REI Traverse 11.25L (large configuration) | 57.1 oz | 686 | 7 | $90 | Final Verdict While the modular REI Co-op Traverse Modular Bear Canister was a good idea on paper, it's quite difficult to use and frequently seizes up when you try to open it. For these reasons, we recommend getting a different bear canister that opens reliably, even if it means buying two canisters for short and long trips. item.title: A city break in Łódź, Poland’s capital of cinema and factories
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 4.66
Sometimes travel delivers a real shock. I’m moving along the boulevards in the Polish city of Łódź, enjoying the excellent cafes and warm sunshine, when I spot the vans. They are parked up on the verge, with racks of clothing and heavily laden tables behind. I can’t resist a Sunday morning market and walk towards a group of men huddled around a car that is covered in blankets. And then it happens. They turn – and I see they are weighing pistols in their hands. I recognise the lean profile of a German Luger, and then the bulkier Colt 45. There is a second of doubt. I hesitate. They replace the weapons on the display and walk away laughing. I approach. On the car roof is a row of dusty soldiers’ helmets. “We were repairing a pavement in the centre of town,” says the seller cheerfully, handing me a badge to inspect. “Imagine! For 80 years, all this stuff was just under our feet.” It’s a Wehrmacht shoulder badge from Kuban 1943, a last-ditch post-Stalingrad action on the Crimean peninsula. Who wore this, I wonder? A veteran of the Russian front who almost made it home? Nothing is clear, except that in Łódź, the past is never far away. I arrive the previous night, a little disoriented, whizzing past unlit buildings, huge brick structures like Victorian factories. “Are we in the city yet?” I ask. The taxi driver gives me a quizzical look. “Yes, this is Łódź.” I note the pronunciation, like “wudge”. I glimpse five-storey blocks, tree-lined streets, a tramline. “I could never live anywhere else,” he adds. A huge blue graffito is caught in the headlights, like a monstrous alien creature. “Why?” I ask, but we are already pulling up outside an immense red-brick building, my hotel, and he never answers my question. The reception area is huge, with a strange scalloped ceiling in red brick that hints at a previous incarnation as a factory. This is my first visit to Łódź, a city about 75 miles (120km) south-west of Warsaw. My interest has been piqued by a list of notable people associated with the place. It features an astonishing number of Oscar-winning or nominated film directors connected to the city: Andrzej Wajda (The Promised Land), Roman Polanski (The Pianist), Paweł Pawlikowski (Ida), Agnieszka Holland (Europa Europa), Krzysztof Kieślowski (Three Colours trilogy) and Zbigniew Rybczyński (Tango). But under the bonnet there is a vast array of talent in acting, production and technical excellence. The city’s film school is responsible, of course, but Łódź itself features as a setting, too, notably in David Lynch’s Inland Empire and Wajda’s masterpiece The Promised Land. Łódź, I had decided, must be fascinating. Any visit starts with Piotrkowska Street, the longest shopping street in Europe at about 2½ miles. My guide, Anna, takes me through Plac Wolności (Freedom Square), where a dance festival is in progress, with hooded hip‑hoppers rubbing shoulders with troupes of line dancers and girls in colourfully embroidered traditional dress. This is a city where music and dance are never far away. We dodge down a side alley and emerge in a striking art installation – an entire street, Pasaż Róży (Rosa’s Passage), covered in mirrors by the artist Joanna Rajkowska. Back on the main pedestrianised route, the mix of ancient and modern continues: 19th‑century porticoed palaces adorned with colourful graffiti. I ask Anna how Łódź fared in the second world war. “It was not too badly damaged,” she says. “Both the Germans and the Russians wanted the industry intact.” There is no medieval heart, no ornate houses like in Wrocław or Kraków. What Łódź possesses is an impressive array of 19th-century factories, mostly textiles, built to show off their owners’ power, wealth and architectural aspirations. Now, this heritage has become a stunning example of urban regeneration. We turn into OFF Piotrkowska, a complex of beautiful old textile mills reborn as a hive of small businesses. There are lots of vibrant restaurants and bars, but Anna wants to show me a shop that she likes: Pan Tu Nie Stał. “It was a saying in communist times: ‘You’re not in the queue.’ We said it to people trying to push in,” Anna says. This is the spot to pick up a T-shirt featuring Soviet combine harvesters or some Czas Pokaże (Time Will Tell) socks. The shop says a lot about the Polish attitude to communist times: none of the maudlin ostalgie of East Germany; this nostalgia comes with healthy dashes of colour and humour. It did all start, however, with a disaster. The old mills had survived two world wars, but died in the economic collapse after communism ended in 1989. “Everything closed down,” says Anna. “We call that time the transformacja. It was very hard.” We stroll into the Manufaktura area, once the site of a vast textile business started by a local scrap metal dealer, Izrael Poznański, in 1872, and now another beautifully restored collection of red-brick buildings housing restaurants, bars, shops and the fascinating Museum of the Factory. Next door is the palace that Poznański built, a neo-baroque monstrosity of bulging wealth, now the city museum. After the Congress of Vienna in 1815, Łódź became part of the Russian empire, a melting pot of German, Jewish, Polish and Russian influences. In the 1870s, Poznański was one of a group of men who saw the potential of steam power. They imported looms from England and were soon amassing unimaginable wealth, constructing a city of handsome red-brick factories, the core of which still remains. The Museum of the Factory houses a collection of working looms that date back to the 1880s. Only four machines are ever turned on due to noise pollution laws – in the old days, one factory might have had hundreds. This was the city of the deaf, but the deafest of all were the bosses, oblivious to the terrible hardships of their workforce, from the founders through to their communist successors. When Wajda came to these mills in the early 1970s, planning The Promised Land, he needed to make only minor adjustments to start filming. The tired faces, the crashing looms, the heat and the dust – it was all very much like 1880. Is that your favourite film, I ask Anna? She shakes her head. “Cold War by Pawlikowski,” she says. “I love that film.” This 2018 masterpiece is the story of a tragic love affair conducted across the Iron Curtain in the years following the second world war. Based on the lives of Pawlikowski’s parents, it is dark and sensuous, full of great music and dance. Pawlikowski has used Łodż as a location. We move on to the Museum of Cinematography, a tour de force that warrants some preparation (watch films by Polish directors). They have everything from early working equipment to props from the most recent Oscar triumphs. By the time I get to the end, I have only a few minutes to rush to the Central Museum of Textiles. There I find a technician, Przemysław, about to start up a 1893 Greenwood loom. He’s a former policeman with a few tales to tell, but right now one question is bothering me. “Why did film-making succeed so brilliantly in this city of textiles?” I ask him. He taps the cast iron loom and chuckles. “I’ll show you.” With the flick of a switch, the loom begins to clank and turn. The noise is incredible. Przemysław is moving around, adjusting and calibrating, his face concentrated. I see the spools of thread begin to unwind, the shuttle dashing back and forth, the warp and weft rhythmically rising and falling. The different colours, each no more than a thin line, but magically coming together. And from the lip of the machine spills a beautiful multicoloured cloth. Przemysław looks at me and raises a questioning eyebrow. “Like weaving a story, right?” The trip was provided by the Polish Tourism Organisation, with Holiday Extras lending travel support in car parking, insurance, airport transfers and hotels

item.title: Whisky galore – and now plenty more besides: exploring the Scottish island of Islay
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.58
The Paps of Jura disappear into the mist as I pedal along the shores of Loch Indaal, and the rain cloud I’ve been racing finally catches up. I stash my hire bike at Port Charlotte youth hostel, quickly change and make it to Lochindaal Seafood Kitchen just before the downpour. I’m soon warmed, by the welcome then by a bowl of creamy fish chowder. “We’ve plenty of fresh seafood just in,” is all the temptation I need to order the seafood plate. It’s a bowl for one, but a hungry one, and soon I’m picking and cracking my way through piles of fat langoustines and crab claws, with hot whisky-butter scallops and plenty of bread and butter. The island of Islay, off the west coast of Scotland, is far better known for its drinks than its food. With 10, soon to be 11, working whisky distilleries, Islay is synonymous with rich, heavily peated single malts. But, over several days cycling around the island, I find that whisky does much more than fill warehouses and attract tourists. It is helping to support an island where agriculture, fishing and hospitality have long struggled to provide year-round employment. At Bruichladdich, one of Islay’s smallest distilleries but the largest private employer, that begins with the barley. When the distillery was bought by a pair of wine merchants after being mothballed several times in the 1990s, they questioned why the barley arriving at the distillery was being sourced from so many different places. Surely, they thought, like vineyards, where the grain was grown would influence the whisky’s terroir. They began encouraging farmers to grow barley on Islay, which hadn’t been done since before the second world war. Farmers were understandably wary of taking on an unfamiliar crop, particularly as the tens of thousands of migratory geese from Greenland are partial to a field of young barley. When Islay’s last creamery closed in 2000, the dairy industry collapsed, so growing barley offered farmers another way to use their land, and Bruichladdich guaranteed to buy the crop regardless of the yield. Today, 21 Islay farms grow barley for the distillery, producing half of its requirements, and early experiments with rye have been promising. Eva MacIntyre grew up on Islay, tried living on the mainland and came back. She now works for Bruichladdich as a brand ambassador and takes me up the hill to see the distillery’s water source. “Growing up on Islay, whisky was a way of life,” she tells me. “It’s not just a drink; it’s all about who you share it with.” Before her whisky presentations, she practises with her grandfather. Her story is not unusual. “Every family has at least one person working in whisky,” she tells me. I meet Kate Hannett, a full-time forager responsible for gathering the 22 botanicals used in the Botanist gin across peaty bogs and hillsides. Her brother, Adam, is Bruichladdich’s master blender, having started his career as a tour guide. Lisa Matthews, the assistant blender, is also an Ileach (a person from Islay) and the distillery’s first female blender. Her brother is a brand ambassador in the US. There are jobs in whisky, and reasons to stay on the island, that most rural communities could only dream of offering their young people. The distilleries are woven into Islay life. I hear frequent stories of distilleries helping each other out and lending equipment when machinery breaks down. “It’s really not competitive,” Eva says. As well as the employment opportunities, whisky benefits the infrastructure. There’s a full-time fire service, unusual across rural Scotland. Even the swimming pool is heated by waste energy from Bowmore distillery. At Islay Ales, another island-made drink begins with barley and soft west coast water. The brewery, founded in 2004, opened a new brewhouse last year. Its spent grain, or draff, goes to local farms for feed and wastewater is treated through a reed bed. On an island where the growing season is short and the weather can change before you’ve finished your pint, making food and drink locally is not necessarily easy. “After the Agricultural Show, which is the third Thursday in August, it’s winter,” I’m told. Emma Goudie of Islay Cocoa began making chocolates as an easily transportable product that wouldn’t compete directly with other island food businesses. She uses local ingredients where they make sense, rather than simply because they are local. “It’s quality first, but I’m lucky that the produce we have here is excellent.” Her current range includes Orsay sea salt, Argyll coffee, and sourdough from neighbouring Jura. She also works with the whisky industry, creating chocolates designed to pair with Ardbeg and for Caol Ila tours. “It grew quite organically and in the best way,” she says. Iain and Alexander MacLellan are the fourth and fifth generations of a family whose hospitality business stretches back to the late 19th century. At Lochindaal Seafood Kitchen, Iain tells me he grew up with the fishers who supply the restaurant and remembers cooking mackerel and scallops on their boats. “I’ve been 52 years behind the bar,” he tells me. The restaurant grew out of the family pub at Lochindall hotel, partly because, as Iain puts it, “we ran out of space to serve our seafood platters”. Chef Ajish Johny came to Port Charlotte hotel after working in India and Dubai, on cruise ships and in Wales, and has now been here for four years. His menus feature a curry of the day alongside Loch Gruinart oysters, locally caught fish and burgers made with beef from nearby Octomore Farm. “We never compromise on quality,” he says. “People on Islay are well travelled. They know what good food is.” And then there is Ardbeg House in Port Ellen, a once tired traditional hotel that has been transformed into a maximalist extension of the Ardbeg brand. There are 12 quirkily themed bedrooms, a fishing boat suspended over the bar and a theatrical restaurant with a beaten-metal ceiling, bold lighting and tables made from marble bathroom offcuts. It’s an exuberant place, but the food is excellent and well priced. I eat bread made with eight-year-old Ardbeg and thyme; langoustine bisque with pickled fennel and tarragon, then the catch of the day, sea bass, with cabbage, kale, roast potatoes and split beurre blanc. My taxi driver insisted that I try the sticky toffee pudding. My server does the same, so I take the hint and am rewarded with a treacly wedge of cake with whisky ice-cream. Outside, it’s raining again. Before the Clearances, about 15,000 people lived on Islay. Today, there are just over 3,000. Islay may have been built, in part, on whisky. But increasingly, the whisky is helping build something back: farms, breweries, restaurants, food businesses and reasons to stay. Ailsa Sheldon was a guest of Hostelling Scotland and Bruichladdich Distillery. Port Charlotte youth hostel has dorm beds from £28 and private rooms from £78 (open late March to early October). Travel to Islay from the Scottish mainland by Caledonian MacBrayne (CalMac) ferry from Kennacraig or by flying with Loganair from Glasgow. Hire bikes from Islay E-Wheels in Port Ellen from £25 a day for non-electric, £35 for electric, delivery available across the island Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: TSA liquids rule: What to know about 3-1-1 before you head to the airport
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.97
TSA liquids rule: What to know about 3-1-1 before you head to the airport Editor's Note It's the rule every passenger has to consider when packing for a flight. For 20 years now, the Transportation Security Administration has enforced rules on the liquids passengers can bring in carry-on bags. This policy is the reason you can't bring a full-size bottle of shampoo or sunscreen through a TSA checkpoint. It's one of the biggest reasons bags get pulled for secondary screening. Last year, the TSA stopped requiring flyers to take off their shoes, but the liquids rule remains one of the biggest hurdles travelers still face when passing through security. But what exactly are the TSA liquid rules, and why do they exist? And, most importantly, what does this mean for packing ahead of your next trip? Here's a quick rundown. TSA liquids rules: Why do they exist? The TSA's restrictions on liquids date back to 2006. In the wake of a thwarted terrorism plot overseas, the agency started restricting the liquids, gels and aerosols passengers could bring in their carry-on baggage. Scores of other countries around the world put similar policies in place in the name of aviation security. What is the TSA's 3-1-1 rule? The TSA's ban on liquids — or at least large quantities of them — is governed by what's known as the "3-1-1 rule." The decades-old policy states that: - Liquids must be in containers no larger than 3.4 ounces, or roughly 100 milliliters (that's the "3"). - All containers must be placed in one clear, quart-size plastic bag ("1"). - Each passenger is only allowed one such plastic bag ("1"). These rules govern liquids, gels and aerosol products ranging from toothpaste to shampoo, conditioner, mouthwash and sunscreen — among other products. Liquid products larger than 3.4 ounces must be placed in a checked bag. That applies even to those large shampoo containers with just a tiny bit of shampoo left, per TSA policy. Exceptions to the TSA's 3-1-1 policy There are a few exceptions, though. The TSA will allow you to bring "medically necessary" liquids, gels and aerosols in reasonable quantities for your flight. However, you must declare those items to security officers at the checkpoint for inspection. The agency asks travelers with larger amounts of medically necessary liquids to remove them from the carry-on bag and place them in a bin or bowl. The TSA has a variety of alternative screening methods it can use. What can you bring through a TSA checkpoint? You can bring creamy cheeses, liquid chocolate, liquid coffee, creamy dips and spreads, gravy, honey, hummus, ice cream, jam, jelly, juice, syrup, peanut butter, salad dressing, sauce, salsa, soda, soup and yogurt as long as they are in a container of less than 3.4 ounces, according to the TSA. You can bring your water bottle with you — as long as it's empty. This can also be a great way to save money at the airport, since many now have postsecurity filling stations for reusable water bottles. When in doubt, consult the TSA's list of what you can carry through the airport and check with your airline. Or, better yet, download the MyTSA app. It contains a "Can I Bring?" section, allowing you to look up items and find out whether they're allowed outright, restricted to 3.4 ounces, permitted only in a checked bag, permitted only in a carry-on bag or prohibited altogether. Could 3-1-1 finally go away? While the TSA's 3-1-1 liquids rules remain in place, there's reason to wonder how long they'll be around. The U.K. has begun a long-planned rollback of its liquids rules. And after the TSA ended its long-standing "shoes-off" policy in 2025, the Trump administration signaled that the liquids restrictions could be next ... someday. "We're exploring technologies that might allow us to bring water bottles again through checkpoints," newly appointed TSA administrator David Cummins told Congress during his summer 2026 confirmation hearing. So, abide by the rules for now. But stay tuned.
