Reviews Citi / AAdvantage Executive review: Admirals Club access and premium travel perks Stephanie Stevens is an associate writer with TPG's credit cards team. She focuses on creating timely credit cards content for TPG readers. September 4, 2026 • 12 min read The cards we feature here are from partners who compensate us when you are approved through our site, and this may impact how or where these products appear. We don't cover all available credit cards, but our analysis, reviews, and opinions are entirely from our editorial team. Terms apply to the offers listed on this page. Please view our advertising policy and product review methodology for more information. Editorial note: This is a recurring post, regularly updated with new information and offers. Citi is a TPG advertising partner. Editorial disclaimer: Opinions expressed here are the author's alone, not those of any bank, credit card issuer, airline or hotel chain, and have not been reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any of these entities. Related stories Quick summary A premium airline card offers complimentary lounge membership, travel credits and elite-status perks for frequent flyers of a major U.S. carrier. The card is best suited for those who regularly use airport lounges and value airline-specific benefits, including credits for vacation packages and inflight purchases. Authorized users can access lounges for an additional fee, and the card provides hotel and car rental elite status with select partners. Compared to alternatives, this card is ideal for travelers seeking unlimited lounge access, while lower-fee options may suit occasional flyers. What to consider The card carries a high annual fee, making it most worthwhile for those maximizing lounge and airline benefits. Some credits require booking specific vacation packages or meeting ride thresholds, and not all perks are automatic—enrollment may be required. A 48-month application rule restricts bonus eligibility for those who have recently received a bonus on this product. What you'll miss from the article A detailed comparison of lounge access, credits, and elite-status perks to help determine which travel card best matches your flying habits. Generated by AI with support from our editorial team. Earn 4x AAdvantage® miles for every $1 spent on eligible American Airlines purchases. 1X 1 AAdvantage® miles for every $1 spent on other purchases Intro offer For a limited time, earn 125,000 American Airlines AAdvantage® bonus miles Annual fee $695 Regular APR 19.49% - 29.49% (Variable) Recommended credit 670-850 Excellent, Good The (see rates and fees) stands out for its complimentary Admirals Club membership and credits for frequent American Airlines flyers. However, the $695 annual fee makes it worthwhile only if you'll use Admirals Club access and its other benefits. Card Rating*: ⭐⭐⭐½ *Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer. Citi / AAdvantage Executive: The basics The is Citi's premium American Airlines card, standing out for its complimentary Admirals Club membership. It also offers travel credits, elite-status benefits and Loyalty Point bonuses. Unlike flexible travel rewards cards, the Citi / AA Executive earns AAdvantage miles rather than transferable points, so it's best suited to travelers who regularly fly American Airlines or Oneworld partners and value AAdvantage miles. Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Elite pros and cons Pros Cons Complimentary Admirals Club membership Authorized user Admirals Club access ($175 for three) American Airlines Vacations, inflight and Admirals Club credits Complimentary hotel and car rental status High annual fee Several credits require effort AAdvantage miles aren't as flexible as transferable points Citi / AAdvantage Executive benefits The comes with benefits designed primarily for frequent American Airlines travelers. Admirals Club membership The marquee benefit of the Citi / AA Executive is a complimentary Admirals Club membership for the primary cardholder. The primary cardholder receives a full Admirals Club membership, which allows them and their immediate family or up to two guests access to the club when they have a same-day boarding pass for American Airlines or an eligible partner airline. The membership provides access to nearly 50 Admirals Club locations and more than 60 partner lounges worldwide when flying American Airlines or an eligible partner. This benefit has become even more valuable since American increased the price of Admirals Club memberships in August. At $695 per year, the card is a compelling alternative to purchasing lounge access separately, especially when factoring in its other American Airlines benefits. For TPG editor-in-chief Nick Ewen, lounge access is the primary reason he keeps the card. He'll use it on upcoming American trips with his wife and daughter, and appreciates being able to add authorized users with their own Admirals Club access. You can add up to three authorized users for $175 each. They receive Admirals Club access when flying American or an eligible partner and can bring up to two guests, though they don't access partner lounges. Since Admirals Club day passes cost $79, this can be a valuable perk for frequent American flyers. The Citi / AA Executive offers valuable airport and inflight benefits: Enhanced airport experience: You and up to eight travelers on the same reservation get priority check-in, airport screening (where available) and priority boarding. First checked bag free: On eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries, the first checked bag for you and up to eight companions is free when traveling on the same reservation. Since American typically charges at least $45 per bag each way, this provides meaningful savings even for occasional check-bag users. Inflight and Admirals Club credit: Receive up to $100 back annually on eligible purchases. Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit: Up to $120 statement credit when you pay an eligible fee with the card (once every four years). I recommend Global Entry, which includes TSA PreCheck. To receive the credit, book an eligible American Airlines Vacations travel package or experience through AAVacations.com using your card. Eligible packages must include at least two components — a flight and hotel, a flight and a rental car, or a hotel and a rental car. This isn't as flexible as a general travel credit, so don't book a package solely for the benefit. But if you already book vacation packages or bundle flights with hotels or rental cars, the credit provides significant value. TPG principal spokesperson Clint Henderson is particularly interested in this benefit because he already uses American Airlines Vacations: "I've been a huge advocate for AAVacations over the years and I will definitely take advantage of this new perk." Automatic hotel and rental car elite status The Citi / AA Executive also offers complimentary Omni Hotels & Resorts Champion Status (enrollment required), which includes an annual free night reward after a qualifying stay,* and Avis President's Club status (enrollment available through Aug. 31, 2028). *A qualifying stay consists of two or more consecutive nights booked directly through Omni Hotels & Resorts at omnihotels.com. Benefits of Omni Champion Status can include complimentary one-level room upgrades and early check-in and late checkout (when available), while benefits of Avis President's Club include car upgrades, expedited service and complimentary additional drivers. I wouldn't recommend adding the card to your wallet just for these perks, but they're valuable additions if you already stay at Omni or rent with Avis. You'll earn 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points at each milestone: 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points (up to 40,000 bonus points per qualification year). This benefit is most valuable for frequent American Airlines flyers who already earn enough Loyalty Points to reach these thresholds. Cardholders can receive up to $15 in Lyft credits per month, or $180 annually, after taking three eligible rides that month. I consider this one of the weaker benefits of the card because the three-ride requirement means you can't simply take one Lyft trip and receive the monthly credit. How to earn and use your rewards The is most rewarding when you use it strategically rather than putting all your everyday spending on it. Earning miles on the Citi / AAdvantage Executive With the Citi / AA Executive, you'll earn: 12 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings 4 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases 1 mile per dollar on all other eligible purchases Spend $150,000 in a calendar year and you'll earn 5 miles per dollar on American Airlines purchases for the remainder of that year. You'll also earn 1 Loyalty Point for every eligible AAdvantage mile earned from purchases. The boosted earning rate on American's hotel and car rental portals is attractive if you regularly use those services, particularly since these purchases also earn Loyalty Points. Clint uses AAdvantage Hotels and likes the elevated earning rate: "I end up booking a lot of AAdvantage Hotels because of the generous Loyalty Point earning rates, so this is an added benefit, too." However, don't use the Citi / AAdvantage Executive for most everyday purchases — the base earning rate is weak compared with many other cards. If you're trying to maximize flexible rewards, you're generally better off using a card that earns transferable points on everyday spending and reserving the Executive for purchases where it offers a meaningful bonus or benefit. Redeeming AAdvantage miles AAdvantage miles can be redeemed for flights on American Airlines and its Oneworld and other airline partners. Award flights operated by American and Fiji Airways are dynamically priced, so the miles required vary by flight and date. All other partner awards follow AAdvantage's fixed, region-based award charts. For example, you can book a one-way business-class award on Qatar Airways from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) to Hamad International Airport (DOH) in Doha for 70,000 AAdvantage miles (and just $35 in taxes and fees). Where the Citi / AAdvantage Executive falls short The 's biggest drawback is its $695 annual fee. It's easiest to justify if you regularly use Admirals Clubs; otherwise, you may struggle to offset the cost. The card also isn't ideal for everyday spending. Most purchases earn just 1 AAdvantage mile per dollar, and AAdvantage miles aren't as flexible as Amex or Chase points, which transfer to multiple airline and hotel programs. Skip this card if lounge access isn't a priority, or if you want flexible rewards across broader categories. Citi / AA Executive vs. Citi / AA Globe If you want American Airlines benefits without unlimited Admirals Club access, the (see rates and fees) is the clear alternative. For a lower $350 annual fee, the Globe includes four Admirals Club passes yearly. One pass covers one adult and up to three children under 18; passes work at multiple lounges within 24 hours on American or Oneworld flights. The Globe also offers preferred boarding, a free first checked bag on eligible domestic American itineraries, and an annual companion certificate (starting year two) with substantial strategic value. Choose the Globe if you're an occasional American traveler who wants lounge access a few times a year. Choose the Executive if you regularly visit Admirals Clubs — unlimited access easily justifies the higher fee. For a limited time, new cardholders can earn 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening. According to TPG's September 2026 valuations, that welcome offer is worth roughly $1,813. This is the highest offer we have seen in the card’s history, making now a great time to apply if you can comfortably meet the spending required to earn the welcome offer. Citi's 48-month rule prevents you from earning a welcome bonus if you've received one on this card within the past four years. The clock starts from when you receive the bonus, not when approved or activated. Citi also applies this 48-month restriction to certain conversions from other Citi accounts. Other cards to consider if you don't want the Citi / AAdvantage Executive The is a strong choice for frequent American Airlines travelers, but it isn't the right fit for everyone. Here are a few alternatives: If you want a lower annual fee: The Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® offers a straightforward way to earn AAdvantage miles while receiving core American Airlines benefits such as a free checked bag and preferred boarding. To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select. If you want Oneworld perks without being tied to American: The is a strong option for travelers who want to earn Oneworld elite status while taking advantage of benefits with Alaska Airlines and its partners. To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Rewards Summit. If you want transferable points and lounge access: The (see rates and fees) earns transferable Citi ThankYou points and offers premium travel perks, including lounge access. It can be a better fit for American loyalists who want more flexibility from their rewards. To learn more, read our full review of the Citi Strata Elite. The information for the Citi Platinum Select has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Bottom line The is fundamentally an Admirals Club card, with additional perks that can help frequent American Airlines travelers offset its $695 annual fee. The card makes the most sense if you'll regularly use Admirals Club access and can take advantage of benefits like Loyalty Point bonuses and authorized user lounge access. But for travelers who rarely fly American, don't use airport lounges or prefer the flexibility of transferable points, there are better premium travel cards for your wallet.

item.title: Is the Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Legend Mastercard worth it?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.59
Is the Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Legend Mastercard worth it? Editor's Note If you fly American Airlines frequently, you may want to consider getting one of its cobranded Citi cards. At the top of the hierarchy is the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® (see rates and fees), which offers the most AA-specific perks of any credit card. The card recently underwent a significant refresh in August, which raised the annual fee to $695 but also added substantial new benefits. Doing the math on this card is now more important than ever — but there's also more value to potentially unlock if you maximize each of the new perks. So, is it worth the annual fee — both in year one and beyond? Let's do the math. Welcome bonus New Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Legend Mastercard cardholders can currently earn a limited time offer of 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening. This bonus is worth about $1,813, based on TPG's September 2026 valuations, and is the highest we've seen on the card, so now is the best time to apply. This bonus accounts for a significant portion of the card's overall value, so earning it and redeeming the miles wisely are crucial to offsetting the card's high annual fee. Related: The Citi / AAdvantage Executive's new benefits are live: 6 things to do now Lounge access Arguably, the most valuable ongoing benefit of this card is the complimentary Admirals Club membership you'll receive every year that you hold it. When you have the Citi / AA Executive, all you have to do is walk to the lounge and present a same-day boarding pass for an eligible flight. An annual membership costs $750 to $1,400, depending on your status level and whether you want access only to AA-branded lounges or to partner lounges as well. Given that this card carries a $695 annual fee, it doesn't make sense to buy an Admirals Club membership on its own, unless you aren't eligible for the card. With this card, you'll be able to access almost 50 Admirals Clubs and more than 60 partner lounges worldwide when flying American or one of its Oneworld partners. Notably, this includes Alaska Lounges in hubs like Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Portland International Airport (PDX), San Francisco International Airport (SFO) and Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA). You can bring in either your immediate family members (spouse or domestic partner and children under 18 years of age) or up to two guests. And they don't need to be on the same flight as you — just any American or Oneworld flight with a same-day boarding pass. Related: The best lounge access credit cards to add to your wallet Travel benefits The Citi / AA Executive offers valuable perks when flying American, including priority check-in at business-class counters (where available) and priority boarding privileges (where available) for you and up to eight travelers on the same reservation. You also get your first checked bag free on domestic itineraries with American Airlines, saving you at least $45 each time. (Note that this is only for domestic flights; I had to pay out of pocket when I traveled to Mexico, forgetting the restrictions of this perk.) Additionally, you'll receive a statement credit of up to $120 for Global Entry/TSA PreCheck. (I suggest maximizing your credit by applying for Global Entry, as it includes PreCheck anyway.) You'll also receive elite status with two partner programs: - Omni Champion, which includes room upgrades, early check-in and late checkout privileges (subject to availability), and an annual free night reward after qualifying stays at participating Omni Hotels properties. - Avis President's Club (through Aug. 31, 2028), providing car rental upgrades (subject to availability), the ability to skip the rental counter at major airports and complimentary additional drivers. Furthermore, the card includes travel protections, such as trip cancellation, trip interruption, trip delay, lost baggage protection and car rental insurance coverage. And there are no foreign transaction fees, making this card a good option for international purchases. Related: Which airline is now best if you don't want to pay bag fees? Elite status If chasing AAdvantage elite status is important to you, the Citi / AA Executive will help you achieve it. You'll earn 1 Loyalty Point for every mile you earn from purchases. Cardholders also earn 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points after reaching each of the following milestones in the same status qualification year: - 50,000 Loyalty Points - 90,000 Loyalty Points - 165,000 Loyalty Points - 240,000 Loyalty Points Related: 8 methods that earned American AAdvantage Executive Platinum Statement credits The statement credits on the Citi / AA Executive include: - Up to $500 in annual American Airlines Vacations statement credits (up to $250 every six months) - Up to $180 in annual Lyft credits ($15 monthly) — but you have to take three eligible rides each month first to receive this credit - Up to $120 back in statement credits on eligible prepaid rentals booked directly on Avis.com or Budget.com every calendar year - Up to $100 annual statement credit for eligible American Airlines inflight and Admirals Club purchases The American Airlines Vacations credits are only valuable if you'd book these packages anyway. Note that the credit splits into two $250 six-month periods — you must use one in the first half of the year and one in the second; unused credits don't roll over. Qualifying packages typically require at least two travel components (flight plus hotel, flight plus rental car, etc.), though you can often minimize costs by adding a cheap rental car to a flight or hotel booking. I've had issues with the car rental credit, so I wouldn't rely on it for value. Previously, a Budget rental in Cabo was not coded correctly, and Citi wouldn't manually apply the credit. Later, I completed another Budget rental in Ireland and waited the obligatory 10 weeks. Again, it didn't post, and again, Citi refused to apply a manual credit. I don't value the Lyft perk because you don't get the $15 credit until after you've taken three (non-discounted) rides in a month. Instead, I use my Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) to earn 5 points per dollar spent, plus a $10 monthly in-app credit on Lyft purchases (through Sept. 30, 2027). The inflight (and Admirals Club) credit is useful if you regularly buy onboard refreshments or snacks. Related: Frequent Uber or Lyft user? These are the best credit cards for you Earning and redeeming miles If you're looking to supercharge your points earning across several programs, I'd suggest putting your spending on a card that earns transferable points. However, if you want to maximize your AAdvantage mile balance specifically, the Citi / AA Executive will earn you: - 12 miles per dollar spent on eligible car rentals and hotels booked through American's car rental and hotel booking sites, respectively - 4 miles per dollar spent on eligible American Airlines purchases (jumps to 5 miles per dollar spent for the remainder of the calendar year once you've spent $150,000 on purchases in a calendar year) - 1 mile per dollar spent on all other eligible purchases AAdvantage miles are more valuable (at 1.45 cents each) than United MileagePlus miles (1.2 cents) and Delta SkyMiles (1.2 cents), according to our valuations. I redeemed part of the welcome bonus I received on this card for a luxurious flight. I used 70,000 miles plus $174 for a one-way business-class flight in Qatar Airways' fantastic Qsuite from Doha to Houston. Given that this flight retails for $3,910 one-way, I got a very high 5.6 cents per mile from this redemption, quadruple TPG's valuation of AAdvantage miles. Related: The best uses of American Airlines AAdvantage miles Authorized users Finally, the Citi / AA Executive is a great option if you want to extend Admirals Club access to friends and family affordably. You can add up to three authorized users for $175 total (about $58 each), and $175 each after that. Each authorized user receives Admirals Club access (with a same-day boarding pass for an eligible flight) for themselves and up to two traveling companions. However, authorized users only get Admirals Club access, not a full Admirals Club membership. Related: Everything you need to know about authorized credit card users Bottom line Ultimately, if you value Admirals Club access, priority perks on American flights and a large welcome bonus, this card can easily justify its fee. You'll get even more value if you take advantage of its statement credits and authorized user perks. But if lounge access isn't important to you, consider one of Citi's lower-fee AAdvantage cards instead. To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AA Executive World Legend Mastercard. item.title: Flighty app gets some upgrades: Why this flight-tracking app is a go-to travel companion
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.22
Flighty app gets some upgrades: Why this flight-tracking app is a go-to travel companion Editor's Note I know it's superstitious, but I always text myself my flight information ahead of a trip so I can track my route on JetLovers.com. Somehow, I'm convinced it wards off a canceled flight. I've also previously used Google Flights or another of my favorite apps, Flightradar24. But a new player in the flight-tracking space has made me a convert. Flighty is an app that helps me track my flights day-to-day and keeps an ongoing record of my travels worldwide. The paid version even provides a year-end summary that's fun to look back on. And Flighty just got some other new upgrades: In July, it unveiled a new gate prediction service. Often, Flighty will know your gate before you do. It has also launched Connection Assistant, which provides step-by-step guidance to help you manage your airport transfers. And last year, the app introduced a feature that, in many cases, lets users see why their flights are delayed. Flighty tracks late aircraft issues and airspace congestion to help predict delays hours in advance — helping you get a jump on potentially switching flights or even skipping the trip altogether. Here's everything you need to know about the Flighty app and its latest updates. What is Flighty? Flighty is an Apple iOS app that launched in 2019. It shares real-time updates on your flights, including delays and cancellations. Oftentimes, it knows when a flight is having issues before your airline app does. "I love Flighty because it organizes all my flights and lets me know about changes many times before the updates show on the board at the airport or at the gate," said Mike Panzarella, formerly the chief operating officer at Rocket Dollar. He said he started using Flighty in January 2023 and swears by it. "It helps you feel calm and helps you understand issues before the throngs of others do ahead of you, which is fantastic," he said. "It simplifies travel. It's almost like having an assistant or travel agent for $49 a year." There are paid and free versions of Flighty. The free version gives you real-time updates on delays or cancellations and will alert you to gate changes, departure and arrival times, and when to check in. You'll also be able to track your flight, but you won't get push notifications or many of the other advanced functionalities. The paid version has many more bells and whistles. Here are just a few of Flighty's features: - It automatically pulls in future and past flights from your calendar. - Passenger flights are displayed on the screen when you open the app. - You can import flights via email or sync with TripIt. - It gives you a countdown to your trip. - It supports all airlines worldwide, up to 365 days in advance. - It displays your booking code and check-in information. - Cancellation and schedule change monitoring starts 365 days in advance, and live tracking starts 48 hours in advance. - It will alert you to airport delays, late plane arrivals and other issues. - It shows you taxi, takeoff and landing times. - A progress bar displays while you are in flight. - It predicts your gate, often before the airline posts the information. - The app gives you step-by-step directions for connections. - Upon landing, you'll be made aware of your arrival gate and baggage claim carousel. "Flighty was named an Editor's Choice app by Apple within days of launch, won an Apple Design Award in 2023, and was a runner-up for iPhone App of the Year," according to the company. Indeed, I've found it a useful tool and especially fun because it appeals to my AvGeek interests. Flighty 4.1 This summer, Flighty unveiled several cool new features. Among them is a new step-by-step process for your connections. Flighty has inside information on almost every airport on the planet and can tell you if you need to clear passport control, recheck bags, change terminals and even if you'll need to go through security a second time. It also gives you clear time requirements. No more asking agents or fellow passengers where to go next. It could also help you get through transfers more quickly. "Making a connection is easily one of the most stressful moments of flying," Flighty CEO Ryan Jones said. "Knowing a connection is theoretically possible doesn't help anyone. What helps is knowing what it actually takes to reach your next gate. The new Connection Assistant shows you exactly that, so you can move through any airport like you've done it 100 times, even if it's your first." The company says the Connection Assistant feature, "combines Flighty's best-in-class flight tracking data with airport-specific procedures and statistical modeling of millions of prior flights, and then turns it all into guidance for your exact trip." Connection Assistant shows the typical connecting time and instructions based on your passport information. Flighty 4.0 In an August 2025 app update, Flighty added the ability to better predict delays and let you know why your plane is delayed. The app uses aviation authority data and machine learning to provide early warnings of delays and, in many cases, tell users the exact cause of the delay. Flighty analyzes late-arriving aircraft data and monitors airport airspace to predict delays or cancellations. The team says the new data collection means subscribers can learn how long a delay will actually be, rather than relying on airlines, which do not always provide the most accurate information about when a flight will actually take off. According to Flighty, late aircraft, air traffic control congestion and ground stops account for the majority of delays. "Flighty 4's monitoring predicts and deciphers those delays to give travelers what they've always wanted — a clear reason why their flight is delayed," Jones said. How much is Flighty? The upgraded version of Flighty is called Fighty Pro, and it costs $4.99 a week if you pay as you go. Jones says this option is perfect for less frequent flyers or those looking for information about individual trips. However, most users opt for the annual plan, which offers a hefty discount, bringing the annual total to $59.99. You can also buy a lifetime membership for $299. (I ended up buying a one-year membership because I wanted to give it a good test run, but wasn't ready to commit to a lifetime. Now I wish I had.) If you want a family plan, you can choose one for $15.99 per month, $119 per year, or $449 for lifetime access. Flighty lets you know when your flight is delayed Flighty will let you know if your flight is delayed in many cases. This can keep you from getting to the airport earlier than you need, thus saving you valuable time. According to the company, the No. 1 cause of delays is a late plane. The app automatically monitors flights for 25 hours prior to departure. Flighty will also alert you to airport delays and other issues with your flight. A good example of this is shown in the screenshots below. Flighty alerted me to a delay several hours before my flight to Cancun from San Francisco, and I was able to take my time getting to the airport. However, I have found that Flighty isn't perfect at tracking all delays. A long-haul flight between New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Honolulu's Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL) was held up for nearly three hours, with nary a notification from Flighty. Flighty did let me know when we pushed back from the gate, but failed to follow the flight after it was further delayed due to a mechanical issue, and returned to the gate. In fact, to this day, Flighty still shows the flight departed on time, even though we ended up leaving more than three hours late. The company said this can happen if a flight returns to the gate and the airline marks the following departure as a separate flight. Flighty is working to address this in a future update. Still, despite the imperfections, the app provides valuable information that most third-party tracking companies don't offer. For example, its "Where's My Plane?" feature tracks your plane starting 25 hours before your flight and is consistently reliable. With this feature, you can better anticipate a delay, giving you time to make other arrangements (if needed) before a formal announcement. Flighty notifies you while in the air Flighty lets you know which gate you are leaving from or arriving at, as well as any gate changes that occur on the day of travel. The app can also be used while you are on a flight. It will let you know if your flight is on time and how much time you have left. On a recent Atlanta flight, Flighty told me that my plane would arrive a bit early. The app can track delays while you're in the air, as shown by this notification for a flight from New Orleans to New York City. Flighty not only let me know that my flight was delayed but also how late the plane would arrive. Another example of an inflight delay notification came when I flew Hawaiian Airlines' brand-new Dreamliner from Honolulu to San Francisco. As you can see, the flight was slightly late. In addition to showing the new arrival time, Flighty displayed a nifty map of the San Francisco Bay Area and a view of San Francisco International Airport (SFO) that day. These features can be helpful or at least interesting when you are flying and may save you from opening another app. They can even update you when you aren't connected to the internet since the clock remains active in the app. For a traveler like me who gets anxious during travel, Flighty is super helpful. I feel like I'm always well-informed during my trips and a little ahead of the game compared to other passengers. Flighty can keep your friends and family in the loop You can also invite friends and family to share information with you on Flighty. Simply invite friends via a text message. Once they accept, you can set custom alerts and keep track of their flights, and vice versa. Flighty will update you if your friends and family have a flight change, cancellation or delay, or if any other issues arise, depending on how you've customized the settings. "No other service has ever successfully built 'friends for flying,'" Jones said in a press release. "They all try to make it social and public. But that's not what users want. They want to share with just a few friends and family, all privately, without signing up for a new service." Flighty will also give you data on your upcoming flights Flighty also provides useful data on your upcoming flights. You can see whether your flight is on time and the flight plan, among other options. Flighty can provide data on your past year of travel One of the app's best features is "Flighty Passport." This option lets users view and share their personal travel map, mileage and other fun stats from their past year of flights. It will even pull data for your lifetime of flying. As you can see, it shows flights from both my current travel year and prior years. According to Flighty, I've flown more than 870,000 miles on 33 different airlines. That's a pretty big undercount, but more on that below. The app also tells you how many hours you've lost to delays, both by the year and over your lifetime. In total, I've lost a whopping 87 hours to delays, according to Flighty. Flighty is an AvGeek's dream One of the best things about Flighty is all the information the app has about your flights. It's wildly appealing if you are any kind of AvGeek. The app tells you your most common aircraft type, the number of different jets you've flown, detailed information on each of your flights and lots of other interesting aircraft stats. These are only a few examples of what you'll find in the app. Flighty isn't perfect As I mentioned above, Flighty doesn't pick up all delayed flights, but there are a few other quirks that have frustrated me and some other users. Panzarella told me that Flighty lost a record of one of his travel segments after an Aeromexico flight he was on was diverted. "The final and original destination was never picked up from the diversion airport," he said. "It doesn't accurately reflect my flight totals for the year." He told me he even flagged it to Flighty, but it was never adjusted. "The recovery flight from a diversion is a separate flight," Jones said in an interview with TPG. "The app tells you this and presents a button to search for the recovery flight." Panzarella told me he'd had better luck by using a simple trick. "I integrated it with Tripit, and it's seamless," he said. "Tripit ingests my emails and then publishes them to Flighty automatically." I've found that the app hasn't found all of my historic flights either. Some of my flights aren't integrated with my work and personal calendars, and Flighty has had a hard time finding many of my flights, especially from years past. My lifetime totals are wildly inaccurate, and even last year's stats are missing a few flights. There is good news on that front: It looks like you can now add flight records manually. That's a welcome addition to the app. TPG reader Alex Setzler told me you can also email your itinerary to track@myflightyapp.com. Doing so "will automatically pull all the flight details/info into your Flighty account." As the year goes on, I can monitor my flight stats to ensure all my flights are recorded going forward. Plus, I can also go back in time now to add previous flights that might be missing from my lifetime totals — but that's going to be a project for another day.
